Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Dīghanikāyo

The Long Discourses

Mahāvaggapāḷi

The Great Division

1. Mahāpadānasuttaṃ

1. The Great Discourse on the Lineage

Pubbenivāsapaṭisaṃyuttakathā

The Account Connected with the Recollection of Past Lives

1. Evaṃ [M 2.0001][V 2.0001][P 2.0001][T 2.0001] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme karerikuṭikāyaṃ. Atha kho sambahulānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkantānaṃ karerimaṇḍalamāḷe sannisinnānaṃ sannipatitānaṃ pubbenivāsapaṭisaṃyuttā dhammī kathā udapādi – “itipi pubbenivāso, itipi pubbenivāso”ti.

1. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park, in the Kareri Hut. Then, for a number of monks who had returned from their alms-round after the meal, as they were sitting together, assembled in the Kareri Pavilion, a Dhamma talk connected with the recollection of past lives arose: 'Such is the recollection of past lives, such is the recollection of past lives.'

2. Assosi kho bhagavā dibbāya sotadhātuyā visuddhāya atikkantamānusikāya tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ [V 2.0002] imaṃ kathāsallāpaṃ. Atha kho bhagavā uṭṭhāyāsanā yena karerimaṇḍalamāḷo tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi, nisajja kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “kāyanuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā; kā ca pana vo antarākathā vippakatā”ti?

2. The Blessed One, with his divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human, heard that conversation of the monks. Then the Blessed One rose from his seat and approached the Kareri Pavilion. Having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the monks: 'For what talk, monks, are you now sitting together? And what was your discussion that was left unfinished?'

Evaṃ vutte te bhikkhū bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ – “idha, bhante, amhākaṃ pacchābhattaṃ [P 2.0002] piṇḍapātapaṭikkantānaṃ karerimaṇḍalamāḷe sannisinnānaṃ sannipatitānaṃ [T 2.0002] pubbenivāsapaṭisaṃyuttā dhammī kathā udapādi – ‘itipi pubbenivāso itipi pubbenivāso’ti. Ayaṃ kho no, bhante, antarākathā vippakatā. Atha bhagavā anuppatto”ti.

When this was said, those monks said to the Blessed One: 'Here, Venerable Sir, after our meal, on returning from our alms-round, as we were sitting together, assembled in the Kareri Pavilion, a Dhamma talk connected with the recollection of past lives arose among us: "Such is the recollection of past lives, such is the recollection of past lives." This, Venerable Sir, was our discussion that was left unfinished when the Blessed One arrived.'

3. “Iccheyyātha [M 2.0002] no tumhe, bhikkhave, pubbenivāsapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ dhammiṃ kathaṃ sotu”nti? “Etassa, bhagavā, kālo; etassa, sugata, kālo; yaṃ bhagavā pubbenivāsapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ dhammiṃ kathaṃ kareyya, bhagavato sutvā bhagavato vacanaṃ sutvā (syā.) bhikkhū dhāressantī”ti. “Tena hi, bhikkhave, suṇātha,sādhukaṃ manasi karotha, bhāsissāmī”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca –

3. 'Would you wish, monks, to hear a Dhamma talk connected with the recollection of past lives?' 'This is the time, Blessed One! This is the time, Well-farer! It is time for the Blessed One to give a Dhamma talk connected with the recollection of past lives. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will bear it in mind.' 'In that case, monks, listen and apply your minds well. I will speak.' 'Yes, Venerable Sir,' those monks replied in assent to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

4. “Ito so, bhikkhave, ekanavutikappe yaṃ ekanavuto kappo (syā. kaṃ. pī.) vipassī bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho loke udapādi. Ito so, bhikkhave, ekatiṃse kappe ekatiṃ sakappo (sī.) ekatiṃ so kappo (syā. kaṃ. pī.) yaṃ sikhī bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho loke udapādi. Tasmiññeva kho, bhikkhave, ekatiṃse kappe vessabhū bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho loke udapādi. Imasmiññeva imasmiṃ (katthacī) kho, bhikkhave, bhaddakappe kakusandho bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho loke udapādi. Imasmiññeva kho, bhikkhave, bhaddakappe koṇāgamano bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho loke udapādi. Imasmiññeva kho, bhikkhave, bhaddakappe kassapo bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho loke udapādi. Imasmiññeva kho, bhikkhave, bhaddakappe ahaṃ etarahi arahaṃ sammāsambuddho loke uppanno.

4. Monks, ninety-one eons ago from this one, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly and Completely Awakened One, arose in the world. Monks, thirty-one eons ago from this one, the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly and Completely Awakened One, arose in the world. In that very thirty-first eon, monks, the Blessed One Vessabhū, the Arahant, the Perfectly and Completely Awakened One, arose in the world. In this very auspicious eon, monks, the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly and Completely Awakened One, arose in the world. In this very auspicious eon, monks, the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, the Arahant, the Perfectly and Completely Awakened One, arose in the world. In this very auspicious eon, monks, the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly and Completely Awakened One, arose in the world. In this very auspicious eon, monks, I, at present, an Arahant, a Perfectly and Completely Awakened One, have arisen in the world.

5. “Vipassī, bhikkhave, bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho khattiyo jātiyā [T 2.0003] ahosi, khattiyakule udapādi. Sikhī, bhikkhave, bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho khattiyo jātiyā ahosi, khattiyakule udapādi. Vessabhū, bhikkhave, bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho [P 2.0003] khattiyo jātiyā ahosi, khattiyakule udapādi. Kakusandho, bhikkhave, bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho brāhmaṇo jātiyā ahosi, brāhmaṇakule udapādi. Koṇāgamano, bhikkhave, bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho [V 2.0003] brāhmaṇo jātiyā ahosi, brāhmaṇakule udapādi. Kassapo, bhikkhave, bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho brāhmaṇo jātiyā ahosi, brāhmaṇakule udapādi. Ahaṃ, bhikkhave, etarahi arahaṃ sammāsambuddho khattiyo jātiyā ahosiṃ, khattiyakule uppanno.

5. Monks, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly and Completely Awakened One, was a Khattiya by birth; he arose in a Khattiya family. Monks, the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly and Completely Awakened One, was a Khattiya by birth; he arose in a Khattiya family. Monks, the Blessed One Vessabhū, the Arahant, the Perfectly and Completely Awakened One, was a Khattiya by birth; he arose in a Khattiya family. Monks, the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly and Completely Awakened One, was a Brahmin by birth; he arose in a Brahmin family. Monks, the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, the Arahant, the Perfectly and Completely Awakened One, was a Brahmin by birth; he arose in a Brahmin family. Monks, the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly and Completely Awakened One, was a Brahmin by birth; he arose in a Brahmin family. I, monks, at present an Arahant, a Perfectly and Completely Awakened One, was a Khattiya by birth, born into a Khattiya family.

6. “Vipassī[M 2.0003], bhikkhave, bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho koṇḍañño gottena ahosi. Sikhī, bhikkhave, bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho koṇḍañño gottena ahosi. Vessabhū, bhikkhave, bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho koṇḍañño gottena ahosi. Kakusandho, bhikkhave, bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho kassapo gottena ahosi. Koṇāgamano, bhikkhave, bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho kassapo gottena ahosi. Kassapo, bhikkhave, bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho kassapo gottena ahosi. Ahaṃ, bhikkhave, etarahi arahaṃ sammāsambuddho gotamo gottena ahosiṃ.

6. Monks, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly and Completely Awakened One, was of the Koṇḍañña clan. Monks, the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly and Completely Awakened One, was of the Koṇḍañña clan. Monks, the Blessed One Vessabhū, the Arahant, the Perfectly and Completely Awakened One, was of the Koṇḍañña clan. Monks, the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly and Completely Awakened One, was of the Kassapa clan. Monks, the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, the Arahant, the Perfectly and Completely Awakened One, was of the Kassapa clan. Monks, the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly and Completely Awakened One, was of the Kassapa clan. I, monks, at present an Arahant, a Perfectly and Completely Awakened One, was of the Gotama clan.

7. “Vipassissa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa asītivassasahassāni [T 2.0004] āyuppamāṇaṃ ahosi. Sikhissa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa sattativassasahassāni āyuppamāṇaṃ ahosi. Vessabhussa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa saṭṭhivassasahassāni āyuppamāṇaṃ ahosi. Kakusandhassa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa cattālīsavassasahassāni āyuppamāṇaṃ ahosi. Koṇāgamanassa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa tiṃsavassasahassāni āyuppamāṇaṃ [P 2.0004] ahosi. Kassapassa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa vīsativassasahassāni āyuppamāṇaṃ ahosi. Mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, etarahi appakaṃ āyuppamāṇaṃ parittaṃ lahukaṃ; yo ciraṃ jīvati, so vassasataṃ appaṃ vā bhiyyo.

7. Monks, the measure of the lifespan of the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was eighty thousand years. Monks, the measure of the lifespan of the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was seventy thousand years. Monks, the measure of the lifespan of the Blessed One Vessabhū, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was sixty thousand years. Monks, the measure of the lifespan of the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was forty thousand years. Monks, the measure of the lifespan of the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was thirty thousand years. Monks, the measure of the lifespan of the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was twenty thousand years. Monks, at this present time, my measure of lifespan is little, limited, and fleeting. Whoever lives long lives for a hundred years, or a little less, or a little more.

8. “Vipassī, bhikkhave, bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho pāṭaliyā mūle abhisambuddho. Sikhī, bhikkhave, bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho puṇḍarīkassa mūle abhisambuddho. Vessabhū, bhikkhave, bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho sālassa mūle abhisambuddho. Kakusandho, bhikkhave, bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho sirīsassa mūle abhisambuddho. Koṇāgamano, bhikkhave, bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho udumbarassa mūle abhisambuddho. Kassapo, bhikkhave, bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho nigrodhassa mūle abhisambuddho. Ahaṃ, bhikkhave, etarahi arahaṃ sammāsambuddho assatthassa mūle abhisambuddho.

8. Monks, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, attained full enlightenment at the foot of a Pāṭali tree. Monks, the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, attained full enlightenment at the foot of a Puṇḍarīka tree. Monks, the Blessed One Vessabhū, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, attained full enlightenment at the foot of a Sāla tree. Monks, the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, attained full enlightenment at the foot of a Sirīsa tree. Monks, the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, attained full enlightenment at the foot of an Udumbara tree. Monks, the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, attained full enlightenment at the foot of a Nigrodha tree. I, monks, at this present time, being the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, have attained full enlightenment at the foot of an Assattha tree.

9. “Vipassissa[M 2.0004][V 2.0004], bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa khaṇḍatissaṃ [T 2.0005] nāma sāvakayugaṃ ahosi aggaṃ bhaddayugaṃ. Sikhissa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa abhibhūsambhavaṃ nāma sāvakayugaṃ ahosi aggaṃ bhaddayugaṃ. Vessabhussa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa soṇuttaraṃ nāma sāvakayugaṃ ahosi aggaṃ bhaddayugaṃ. Kakusandhassa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa vidhurasañjīvaṃ nāma sāvakayugaṃ ahosi aggaṃ bhaddayugaṃ. Koṇāgamanassa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa bhiyyosuttaraṃ nāma sāvakayugaṃ ahosi aggaṃ [P 2.0005] bhaddayugaṃ. Kassapassa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa tissabhāradvājaṃ nāma sāvakayugaṃ ahosi aggaṃ bhaddayugaṃ. Mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, etarahi sāriputtamoggallānaṃ nāma sāvakayugaṃ ahosi aggaṃ bhaddayugaṃ.

9. Monks, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had a pair of disciples named Khaṇḍa and Tissa, which was the chief and excellent pair. Monks, the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had a pair of disciples named Abhibhū and Sambhava, which was the chief and excellent pair. Monks, the Blessed One Vessabhū, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had a pair of disciples named Soṇa and Uttara, which was the chief and excellent pair. Monks, the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had a pair of disciples named Vidhura and Sañjīva, which was the chief and excellent pair. Monks, the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had a pair of disciples named Bhiyyosa and Uttara, which was the chief and excellent pair. Monks, the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had a pair of disciples named Tissa and Bhāradvāja, which was the chief and excellent pair. Monks, at this present time, my pair of disciples named Sāriputta and Moggallāna is the chief and excellent pair.

10. “Vipassissa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa tayo sāvakānaṃ sannipātā ahesuṃ. Eko sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi aṭṭhasaṭṭhibhikkhusatasahassaṃ, eko [T 2.0006] sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi bhikkhusatasahassaṃ, eko sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi asītibhikkhusahassāni. Vipassissa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa ime tayo sāvakānaṃ sannipātā ahesuṃ sabbesaṃyeva khīṇāsavānaṃ.

10. Monks, for the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, there were three assemblies of disciples. One assembly of disciples consisted of six million eight hundred thousand monks; one assembly of disciples consisted of one hundred thousand monks; and one assembly of disciples consisted of eighty thousand monks. Monks, for the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, these three assemblies of disciples consisted entirely of those who had destroyed the taints.

“Sikhissa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa tayo sāvakānaṃ sannipātā ahesuṃ. Eko sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi bhikkhusatasahassaṃ, eko sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi asītibhikkhusahassāni, eko sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi sattatibhikkhusahassāni. Sikhissa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa ime tayo sāvakānaṃ sannipātā ahesuṃ sabbesaṃyeva khīṇāsavānaṃ.

Monks, for the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, there were three assemblies of disciples. One assembly of disciples consisted of one hundred thousand monks; one assembly of disciples consisted of eighty thousand monks; and one assembly of disciples consisted of seventy thousand monks. Monks, for the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, these three assemblies of disciples consisted entirely of those who had destroyed the taints.

“Vessabhussa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa tayo sāvakānaṃ sannipātā ahesuṃ. Eko sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi asītibhikkhusahassāni, eko sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi sattatibhikkhusahassāni, eko sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi [M 2.0005] saṭṭhibhikkhusahassāni. Vessabhussa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa ime tayo sāvakānaṃ sannipātā ahesuṃ sabbesaṃyeva khīṇāsavānaṃ.

Monks, for the Blessed One Vessabhū, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, there were three assemblies of disciples. One assembly of disciples consisted of eighty thousand monks; one assembly of disciples consisted of seventy thousand monks; and one assembly of disciples consisted of sixty thousand monks. Monks, for the Blessed One Vessabhū, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, these three assemblies of disciples consisted entirely of those who had destroyed the taints.

“Kakusandhassa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa eko sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi [V 2.0005] cattālīsabhikkhusahassāni. Kakusandhassa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa ayaṃ eko sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi sabbesaṃyeva khīṇāsavānaṃ.

Monks, for the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, there was one assembly of disciples, which consisted of forty thousand monks. Monks, for the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, this one assembly of disciples consisted entirely of those who had destroyed the taints.

“Koṇāgamanassa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato [P 2.0006] sammāsambuddhassa eko sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi tiṃsabhikkhusahassāni. Koṇāgamanassa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa ayaṃ eko sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi sabbesaṃyeva khīṇāsavānaṃ.

Monks, for the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, there was one assembly of disciples, which consisted of thirty thousand monks. Monks, for the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, this one assembly of disciples consisted entirely of those who had destroyed the taints.

“Kassapassa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa eko sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi vīsatibhikkhusahassāni. Kassapassa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa ayaṃ eko sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi sabbesaṃyeva khīṇāsavānaṃ.

Monks, for the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, there was one assembly of disciples, which consisted of twenty thousand monks. Monks, for the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, this one assembly of disciples consisted entirely of those who had destroyed the taints.

“Mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, etarahi eko [T 2.0007] sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi aḍḍhateḷasāni bhikkhusatāni. Mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, ayaṃ eko sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi sabbesaṃyeva khīṇāsavānaṃ.

Monks, at present, there was one assembly of my disciples: one thousand two hundred and fifty monks. Monks, this one assembly of my disciples consisted entirely of those whose taints were destroyed.

11. “Vipassissa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa asoko nāma bhikkhu upaṭṭhāko ahosi aggupaṭṭhāko. Sikhissa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa khemaṅkaro nāma bhikkhu upaṭṭhāko ahosi aggupaṭṭhāko. Vessabhussa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa upasanto nāma bhikkhu upaṭṭhāko ahosi aggupaṭṭhāko. Kakusandhassa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa buddhijo nāma bhikkhu upaṭṭhāko ahosi aggupaṭṭhāko. Koṇāgamanassa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa sotthijo nāma bhikkhu upaṭṭhāko ahosi aggupaṭṭhāko. Kassapassa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa sabbamitto nāma [M 2.0006] bhikkhu upaṭṭhāko ahosi aggupaṭṭhāko. Mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, etarahi ānando nāma bhikkhu upaṭṭhāko ahosi aggupaṭṭhāko.

11. Monks, for the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the monk named Asoka was his attendant, his chief attendant. Monks, for the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the monk named Khemaṅkara was his attendant, his chief attendant. Monks, for the Blessed One Vessabhū, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the monk named Upasanta was his attendant, his chief attendant. Monks, for the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the monk named Buddhija was his attendant, his chief attendant. Monks, for the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the monk named Sotthija was his attendant, his chief attendant. Monks, for the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the monk named Sabbamitta was his attendant, his chief attendant. Monks, at present, for me, the monk named Ānanda is my attendant, my chief attendant.

12. “Vipassissa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa bandhumā nāma rājā pitā ahosi. [P 2.0007] Bandhumatī nāma devī mātā ahosi janetti janettī (syā.). Bandhumassa rañño bandhumatī nāma nagaraṃ rājadhānī ahosi.

12. Monks, for the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the king named Bandhumā was his father. The queen named Bandhumatī was his mother, his birth-giver. For King Bandhumā, the royal capital was the city named Bandhumatī.

“Sikhissa[V 2.0006], bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa aruṇo [T 2.0008] nāma rājā pitā ahosi. Pabhāvatī nāma devī mātā ahosi janetti. Aruṇassa rañño aruṇavatī nāma nagaraṃ rājadhānī ahosi.

Monks, for the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the king named Aruṇa was his father. The queen named Pabhāvatī was his mother, his birth-giver. For King Aruṇa, the royal capital was the city named Aruṇavatī.

“Vessabhussa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa suppatito nāma suppatīto nāma (syā.) rājā pitā ahosi. Vassavatī nāma yasavatī nāma (syā. pī.) devī mātā ahosi janetti. Suppatitassa rañño anomaṃ nāma nagaraṃ rājadhānī ahosi.

Monks, for the Blessed One Vessabhū, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the king named Suppatita was his father. The queen named Vassavatī was his mother, his birth-giver. For King Suppatita, the royal capital was the city named Anoma.

“Kakusandhassa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa aggidatto nāma brāhmaṇo pitā ahosi. Visākhā nāma brāhmaṇī mātā ahosi janetti. Tena kho pana, bhikkhave, samayena khemo nāma rājā ahosi. Khemassa rañño khemavatī nāma nagaraṃ rājadhānī ahosi.

Monks, for the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the brahmin named Aggidatta was his father. The brahmin woman named Visākhā was his mother, his birth-giver. Moreover, monks, at that time there was a king named Khema. For King Khema, the royal capital was the city named Khemavatī.

“Koṇāgamanassa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa yaññadatto nāma brāhmaṇo pitā ahosi. Uttarā nāma brāhmaṇī mātā ahosi janetti. Tena kho pana, bhikkhave, samayena sobho nāma rājā ahosi. Sobhassa rañño sobhavatī nāma nagaraṃ rājadhānī ahosi.

Monks, for the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the brahmin named Yaññadatta was his father. The brahmin woman named Uttarā was his mother, his birth-giver. Moreover, monks, at that time there was a king named Sobha. For King Sobha, the royal capital was the city named Sobhavatī.

“Kassapassa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa brahmadatto nāma brāhmaṇo pitā ahosi. Dhanavatī nāma brāhmaṇī mātā ahosi janetti. Tena kho pana, bhikkhave, samayena kikī [M 2.0007] nāma kiṃ kī nāma (syā.) rājā ahosi. Kikissa rañño bārāṇasī nāma nagaraṃ rājadhānī ahosi.

Monks, for the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the brahmin named Brahmadatta was his father. The brahmin woman named Dhanavatī was his mother, his birth-giver. Moreover, monks, at that time there was a king named Kikī. For King Kikī, the royal capital was the city named Bārāṇasī.

“Mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, etarahi suddhodano nāma rājā pitā ahosi. Māyā nāma devī mātā ahosi janetti. Kapilavatthu nāma nagaraṃ rājadhānī ahosī”ti. Idamavoca bhagavā, idaṃ vatvāna [T 2.0009] sugato uṭṭhāyāsanā vihāraṃ pāvisi.

Monks, at present, for me, the king named Suddhodana was my father. The queen named Māyā was my mother, my birth-giver. The royal capital was the city named Kapilavatthu.” Thus the Blessed One spoke. Having said this, the Well-Gone One rose from his seat and entered the dwelling.

13. Atha [P 2.0008] kho tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ acirapakkantassa bhagavato ayamantarākathā udapādi – “acchariyaṃ, āvuso, abbhutaṃ, āvuso, tathāgatassa mahiddhikatā mahānubhāvatā. Yatra hi nāma tathāgato atīte buddhe parinibbute chinnapapañce chinnavaṭume pariyādinnavaṭṭe sabbadukkhavītivatte [V 2.0007] jātitopi anussarissati, nāmatopi anussarissati, gottatopi anussarissati, āyuppamāṇatopi anussarissati, sāvakayugatopi anussarissati, sāvakasannipātatopi anussarissati – ‘evaṃjaccā te bhagavanto ahesuṃ itipi, evaṃnāmā evaṃgottā evaṃsīlā evaṃdhammā evaṃpaññā evaṃvihārī evaṃvimuttā te bhagavanto ahesuṃ itipī’”ti.

13. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, this conversation arose among those monks: “Friends, it is amazing! Friends, it is astounding, the great power and great might of the Tathāgata! For the Tathāgata recollects past Buddhas who have attained final Nibbāna, who have cut off proliferation, who have cut off the path, who have exhausted the cycle, who have transcended all suffering—recollecting them by birth, by name, by clan, by lifespan, by their pair of disciples, and by their assembly of disciples, thinking: ‘Those Blessed Ones were of such a birth,’ ‘Those Blessed Ones were of such a name, of such a clan, of such virtue, of such a nature, of such wisdom, of such an abiding, and of such a liberation.’”

“Kiṃ nu kho, āvuso, tathāgatasseva nu kho esā dhammadhātu suppaṭividdhā, yassā dhammadhātuyā suppaṭividdhattā tathāgato atīte buddhe parinibbute chinnapapañce chinnavaṭume pariyādinnavaṭṭe sabbadukkhavītivatte jātitopi anussarati, nāmatopi anussarati, gottatopi anussarati, āyuppamāṇatopi anussarati, sāvakayugatopi anussarati, sāvakasannipātatopi anussarati – ‘evaṃjaccā te bhagavanto ahesuṃ itipi, evaṃnāmā evaṃgottā evaṃsīlā evaṃdhammā evaṃpaññā evaṃvihārī evaṃvimuttā te [T 2.0010] bhagavanto ahesuṃ itipī’ti, udāhu devatā tathāgatassa etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ, yena tathāgato atīte buddhe parinibbute chinnapapañce chinnavaṭume [P 2.0009] pariyādinnavaṭṭe sabbadukkhavītivatte jātitopi anussarati, nāmatopi anussarati, gottatopi anussarati, āyuppamāṇatopi anussarati, sāvakayugatopi anussarati, sāvakasannipātatopi anussarati – ‘evaṃjaccā te bhagavanto ahesuṃ itipi, evaṃnāmā evaṃgottā evaṃsīlā evaṃdhammā evaṃpaññā evaṃvihārī evaṃvimuttā [M 2.0008] te bhagavanto ahesuṃ itipī’”ti. Ayañca hidaṃ tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ antarākathā vippakatā hoti.

“Friends, how can it be? Is it that this element of the Dhamma has been thoroughly penetrated by the Tathāgata himself, by the thorough penetration of which element of the Dhamma the Tathāgata recollects the Buddhas of the past who have attained final Nibbāna, who have cut off conceptual proliferation, cut off the round, exhausted the round, and transcended all suffering—recollecting them by birth, by name, by clan, by lifespan, by their pair of disciples, and by their assembly of disciples, thus: ‘Those Blessed Ones were of such a birth, of such a name, of such a clan, of such virtue, of such a nature, of such wisdom, abiding in such a way, and liberated in such a way’? Or is it that devas informed the Tathāgata of this matter, by which the Tathāgata recollects the Buddhas of the past who have attained final Nibbāna, who have cut off conceptual proliferation, cut off the round, exhausted the round, and transcended all suffering—recollecting them by birth, by name, by clan, by lifespan, by their pair of disciples, and by their assembly of disciples, thus: ‘Those Blessed Ones were of such a birth, of such a name, of such a clan, of such virtue, of such a nature, of such wisdom, abiding in such a way, and liberated in such a way’?” And this conversation in the interval among those monks was unfinished.

14. Atha kho bhagavā sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yena karerimaṇḍalamāḷo tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi. Nisajja kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “kāyanuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā; kā ca pana vo antarākathā vippakatā”ti?

14. Then, in the evening, the Blessed One, having risen from seclusion, approached the Kareri-tree circular hall; having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks, for what talk are you now assembled? And what was this unfinished conversation in the interval of yours?”

Evaṃ vutte te bhikkhū bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ – “idha, bhante, amhākaṃ acirapakkantassa bhagavato ayaṃ antarākathā udapādi – ‘acchariyaṃ, āvuso, abbhutaṃ, āvuso, tathāgatassa mahiddhikatā mahānubhāvatā, yatra hi nāma tathāgato atīte buddhe parinibbute chinnapapañce chinnavaṭume pariyādinnavaṭṭe sabbadukkhavītivatte jātitopi anussarissati, nāmatopi anussarissati, gottatopi anussarissati, āyuppamāṇatopi anussarissati, sāvakayugatopi anussarissati, sāvakasannipātatopi [T 2.0011] anussarissati – “evaṃjaccā [P 2.0010] te bhagavanto ahesuṃ itipi[V 2.0008], evaṃnāmā evaṃgottā evaṃsīlā evaṃdhammā evaṃpaññā evaṃvihārī evaṃvimuttā te bhagavanto ahesuṃ itipī”ti. Kiṃ nu kho, āvuso, tathāgatasseva nu kho esā dhammadhātu suppaṭividdhā, yassā dhammadhātuyā suppaṭividdhattā tathāgato atīte buddhe parinibbute chinnapapañce chinnavaṭume pariyādinnavaṭṭe sabbadukkhavītivatte jātitopi anussarati, nāmatopi anussarati, gottatopi anussarati, āyuppamāṇatopi anussarati, sāvakayugatopi anussarati, sāvakasannipātatopi anussarati – “evaṃjaccā te bhagavanto ahesuṃ itipi, evaṃnāmā evaṃgottā evaṃsīlā evaṃdhammā evaṃpaññā evaṃvihārī evaṃvimuttā te bhagavanto ahesuṃ itipī”ti. Udāhu devatā tathāgatassa etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ, yena tathāgato atīte buddhe parinibbute chinnapapañce chinnavaṭume pariyādinnavaṭṭe sabbadukkhavītivatte jātitopi anussarati, nāmatopi anussarati, gottatopi anussarati, āyuppamāṇatopi anussarati, sāvakayugatopi anussarati, sāvakasannipātatopi anussarati – ‘evaṃjaccā te bhagavanto ahesuṃ itipi, evaṃnāmā evaṃgottā evaṃsīlā evaṃdhammā evaṃpaññā evaṃvihārī evaṃvimuttā [M 2.0009] te bhagavanto ahesuṃ itipī’ti? Ayaṃ kho no, bhante, antarākathā vippakatā, atha bhagavā anuppatto”ti.

When this was said, those monks spoke thus to the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, here, not long after the Blessed One had departed, this conversation in the interval arose among us: ‘It is wonderful, friends, it is marvelous, friends, the great psychic power and great might of the Tathāgata, in that the Tathāgata can recollect the Buddhas of the past who have attained final Nibbāna, who have cut off conceptual proliferation, cut off the round, exhausted the round, and transcended all suffering—recollecting them by birth, by name, by clan, by lifespan, by their pair of disciples, and by their assembly of disciples, thus: “Those Blessed Ones were of such a birth, of such a name, of such a clan, of such virtue, of such a nature, of such wisdom, abiding in such a way, and liberated in such a way.” How can it be, friends? Is it that this element of the Dhamma has been thoroughly penetrated by the Tathāgata himself, by the thorough penetration of which element of the Dhamma the Tathāgata recollects the Buddhas of the past who have attained final Nibbāna, who have cut off conceptual proliferation, cut off the round, exhausted the round, and transcended all suffering—recollecting them by birth, by name, by clan, by lifespan, by their pair of disciples, and by their assembly of disciples, thus: “Those Blessed Ones were of such a birth, of such a name, of such a clan, of such virtue, of such a nature, of such wisdom, abiding in such a way, and liberated in such a way”? Or is it that devas informed the Tathāgata of this matter, by which the Tathāgata recollects the Buddhas of the past who have attained final Nibbāna, who have cut off conceptual proliferation, cut off the round, exhausted the round, and transcended all suffering—recollecting them by birth, by name, by clan, by lifespan, by their pair of disciples, and by their assembly of disciples, thus: “Those Blessed Ones were of such a birth, of such a name, of such a clan, of such virtue, of such a nature, of such wisdom, abiding in such a way, and liberated in such a way”?’ This, Venerable Sir, was our unfinished conversation in the interval; then the Blessed One arrived.”

15. “Tathāgatassevesā, bhikkhave, dhammadhātu suppaṭividdhā, yassā dhammadhātuyā suppaṭividdhattā tathāgato atīte buddhe parinibbute chinnapapañce chinnavaṭume pariyādinnavaṭṭe sabbadukkhavītivatte jātitopi anussarati, nāmatopi anussarati, gottatopi anussarati, āyuppamāṇatopi anussarati, sāvakayugatopi anussarati, sāvakasannipātatopi anussarati – ‘evaṃjaccā te bhagavanto ahesuṃ itipi, evaṃnāmā evaṃgottā evaṃsīlā evaṃdhammā evaṃpaññā evaṃvihārī evaṃvimuttā te bhagavanto ahesuṃ itipī’ti. Devatāpi tathāgatassa etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ, yena tathāgato atīte buddhe parinibbute chinnapapañce chinnavaṭume pariyādinnavaṭṭe sabbadukkhavītivatte jātitopi anussarati, nāmatopi anussarati, gottatopi anussarati, āyuppamāṇatopi anussarati, sāvakayugatopi [T 2.0012] anussarati, sāvakasannipātatopi anussarati – ‘evaṃjaccā te bhagavanto ahesuṃ itipi, evaṃnāmā evaṃgottā evaṃsīlā evaṃdhammā evaṃpaññā evaṃvihārī evaṃvimuttā te bhagavanto ahesuṃ itipī’ti.

15. “Monks, it is by the Tathāgata himself that this element of the Dhamma has been thoroughly penetrated, by the thorough penetration of which element of the Dhamma the Tathāgata recollects the Buddhas of the past who have attained final Nibbāna, who have cut off conceptual proliferation, cut off the round, exhausted the round, and transcended all suffering—recollecting them by birth, by name, by clan, by lifespan, by their pair of disciples, and by their assembly of disciples, thus: ‘Those Blessed Ones were of such a birth, of such a name, of such a clan, of such virtue, of such a nature, of such wisdom, abiding in such a way, and liberated in such a way.’ Devas, too, have informed the Tathāgata of this matter, by which the Tathāgata recollects the Buddhas of the past who have attained final Nibbāna, who have cut off conceptual proliferation, cut off the round, exhausted the round, and transcended all suffering—recollecting them by birth, by name, by clan, by lifespan, by their pair of disciples, and by their assembly of disciples, thus: ‘Those Blessed Ones were of such a birth, of such a name, of such a clan, of such virtue, of such a nature, of such wisdom, abiding in such a way, and liberated in such a way.’”

“Iccheyyātha no tumhe, bhikkhave, bhiyyosomattāya pubbenivāsapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ [P 2.0011] dhammiṃ kathaṃ sotu”nti? “Etassa, bhagavā, kālo; etassa, sugata, kālo; yaṃ bhagavā bhiyyosomattāya pubbenivāsapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ dhammiṃ kathaṃ kareyya, bhagavato sutvā bhikkhū dhāressantī”ti. “Tena hi, bhikkhave[V 2.0009], suṇātha, sādhukaṃ manasi karotha, bhāsissāmī”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca –

“Monks, would you wish to hear a Dhamma discourse connected with the recollection of past lives in greater detail?” “This is the time, Blessed One; this is the time, Sugata, for the Blessed One to give a Dhamma discourse connected with the recollection of past lives in greater detail. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will bear it in mind.” “In that case, monks, listen and attend carefully. I will speak.” “Even so, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

16. “Ito so, bhikkhave, ekanavutikappe yaṃ vipassī bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho loke udapādi. Vipassī, bhikkhave, bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho khattiyo jātiyā ahosi, khattiyakule udapādi. Vipassī, bhikkhave, bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho koṇḍañño gottena ahosi. Vipassissa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa asītivassasahassāni āyuppamāṇaṃ ahosi. Vipassī, bhikkhave, bhagavā arahaṃ [M 2.0010] sammāsambuddho pāṭaliyā mūle abhisambuddho. Vipassissa, bhikkhave[T 2.0013], bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa khaṇḍatissaṃ nāma sāvakayugaṃ ahosi aggaṃ bhaddayugaṃ. Vipassissa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa tayo sāvakānaṃ sannipātā ahesuṃ. Eko sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi aṭṭhasaṭṭhibhikkhusatasahassaṃ, eko sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi bhikkhusatasahassaṃ, eko sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi asītibhikkhusahassāni. Vipassissa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa ime tayo sāvakānaṃ sannipātā ahesuṃ sabbesaṃyeva khīṇāsavānaṃ. Vipassissa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa asoko nāma bhikkhu upaṭṭhāko ahosi aggupaṭṭhāko. Vipassissa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa bandhumā nāma rājā pitā ahosi. Bandhumatī nāma [P 2.0012] devī mātā ahosi janetti. Bandhumassa rañño bandhumatī nāma nagaraṃ rājadhānī ahosi.

16. “Monks, ninety-one aeons ago from this one, the Blessed One Vipassī, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, arose in the world. Monks, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was a Khattiya by birth and arose in a Khattiya family. Monks, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was of the Koṇḍañña clan by lineage. Monks, the lifespan of the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was eighty thousand years. Monks, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, became perfectly enlightened at the foot of a Pāṭali tree. Monks, for the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, there was a chief, excellent pair of disciples named Khaṇḍa and Tissa. Monks, for the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, there were three assemblies of disciples. One assembly of disciples consisted of six million, eight hundred thousand monks; one assembly of disciples consisted of one hundred thousand monks; and one assembly of disciples consisted of eighty thousand monks. Monks, for the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, these three assemblies of disciples were all composed entirely of those whose cankers were destroyed. Monks, for the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, a monk named Asoka was his attendant, his chief attendant. Monks, for the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the king named Bandhumā was his father. The queen named Bandhumatī was his mother, the one who gave him birth. The royal capital of King Bandhumā was the city named Bandhumatī.”

Bodhisattadhammatā

The Natural Course of a Bodhisatta

17. “Atha kho, bhikkhave, vipassī bodhisatto tusitā kāyā cavitvā sato sampajāno mātukucchiṃ okkami. Ayamettha dhammatā.

17. “Then, monks, the Bodhisatta Vipassī, having passed away from the Tusita host, mindful and clearly comprehending, descended into his mother’s womb. This, in this case, is the natural course.”

18. “Dhammatā, esā, bhikkhave, yadā bodhisatto tusitā kāyā cavitvā mātukucchiṃ okkamati. Atha sadevake loke samārake sabrahmake sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiyā pajāya sadevamanussāya appamāṇo uḷāro obhāso pātubhavati atikkammeva devānaṃ devānubhāvaṃ. Yāpi tā lokantarikā aghā asaṃvutā andhakārā andhakāratimisā[T 2.0014], yattha pime candimasūriyā evaṃmahiddhikā evaṃmahānubhāvā ābhāya nānubhonti, tatthapi appamāṇo uḷāro obhāso pātubhavati atikkammeva devānaṃ devānubhāvaṃ. Yepi tattha sattā upapannā, tepi tenobhāsena [V 2.0010] aññamaññaṃ sañjānanti – ‘aññepi kira, bho, santi sattā idhūpapannā’ti. Ayañca dasasahassī lokadhātu saṅkampati sampakampati sampavedhati. Appamāṇo ca uḷāro obhāso loke pātubhavati atikkammeva devānaṃ devānubhāvaṃ. Ayamettha dhammatā.

18. “Monks, this is the natural course: when a Bodhisatta passes away from the Tusita host and descends into his mother’s womb, an immeasurable, magnificent light appears in the world with its devas, its Māras, and its Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, with its devas and humans—surpassing even the divine majesty of the devas. And even in those world-interstices which are abysmal, unenclosed, utter darkness, the blackest of darknesses, where even this moon and sun, so mighty, so powerful, do not extend their light—even there an immeasurable, magnificent light appears, surpassing even the divine majesty of the devas. And those beings who have been reborn there, by that light they recognize one another: ‘Sirs, it seems other beings have also been reborn here!’ And this ten-thousandfold world system quakes, rocks, and trembles. And an immeasurable, magnificent light appears in the world, surpassing even the divine majesty of the devas. This, in this case, is the natural course.”

19. “Dhammatā [M 2.0011] esā, bhikkhave, yadā bodhisatto mātukucchiṃ okkanto hoti, cattāro naṃ devaputtā catuddisaṃ cātuddisaṃ (syā.) rakkhāya upagacchanti – ‘mā naṃ bodhisattaṃ vā bodhisattamātaraṃ vā manusso vā amanusso vā koci vā viheṭhesī’ti. Ayamettha dhammatā.

19. “Monks, this is the natural course: when a Bodhisatta has descended into his mother’s womb, four devaputtas approach from the four directions to guard him, thinking: ‘May no human or non-human or anyone at all harm the Bodhisatta or the Bodhisatta’s mother.’ This, in this case, is the natural course.”

20. “Dhammatā esā, bhikkhave, yadā bodhisatto mātukucchiṃ okkanto hoti, pakatiyā sīlavatī bodhisattamātā hoti, viratā pāṇātipātā, viratā adinnādānā, viratā kāmesumicchācārā[P 2.0013], viratā musāvādā, viratā surāmerayamajjappamādaṭṭhānā. Ayamettha dhammatā.

20. “Monks, this is the natural course: when a Bodhisatta has descended into his mother’s womb, the Bodhisatta’s mother is virtuous by nature: she abstains from the destruction of life, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, and abstains from distilled and fermented intoxicants which are the basis for heedlessness. This, in this case, is the natural course.”

21. “Dhammatā esā, bhikkhave, yadā bodhisatto mātukucchiṃ okkanto hoti, na bodhisattamātu purisesu mānasaṃ uppajjati kāmaguṇūpasaṃhitaṃ, anatikkamanīyā ca bodhisattamātā hoti kenaci purisena rattacittena. Ayamettha dhammatā.

21. “Monks, this is the natural course: when a Bodhisatta has descended into his mother’s womb, no mind connected with sensual pleasures arises in the Bodhisatta’s mother towards men, and the Bodhisatta's mother is inviolable by any man with a lustful mind. This, in this case, is the natural course.”

22. “Dhammatā esā, bhikkhave, yadā bodhisatto mātukucchiṃ okkanto [T 2.0015] hoti, lābhinī bodhisattamātā hoti pañcannaṃ kāmaguṇānaṃ. Sā pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappitā samaṅgībhūtā paricāreti. Ayamettha dhammatā.

22. “Monks, this is the natural course: when a Bodhisatta has descended into his mother’s womb, the Bodhisatta’s mother is a recipient of the five strands of sensual pleasure. She, being provided with and endowed with these five strands of sensual pleasure, enjoys them. This, in this case, is the natural course.”

23. “Dhammatā esā, bhikkhave, yadā bodhisatto mātukucchiṃ okkanto hoti, na bodhisattamātu kocideva ābādho uppajjati. Sukhinī bodhisattamātā hoti akilantakāyā, bodhisattañca bodhisattamātā tirokucchigataṃ passati sabbaṅgapaccaṅgiṃ ahīnindriyaṃ. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, maṇi veḷuriyo subho jātimā aṭṭhaṃso suparikammakato accho vippasanno anāvilo sabbākārasampanno. Tatrāssa tatrassa (syā.) suttaṃ āvutaṃ nīlaṃ vā pītaṃ vā lohitaṃ vā odātaṃ vā paṇḍusuttaṃ vā. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso hatthe karitvā paccavekkheyya – ‘ayaṃ kho maṇi veḷuriyo subho jātimā aṭṭhaṃso suparikammakato accho vippasanno anāvilo sabbākārasampanno. Tatridaṃ suttaṃ āvutaṃ nīlaṃ vā pītaṃ vā lohitaṃ vā odātaṃ vā paṇḍusuttaṃ vā’ti. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, yadā bodhisatto [M 2.0012] mātukucchiṃ okkanto hoti, na bodhisattamātu kocideva ābādho uppajjati, sukhinī bodhisattamātā hoti akilantakāyā[V 2.0011], bodhisattañca [P 2.0014] bodhisattamātā tirokucchigataṃ passati sabbaṅgapaccaṅgiṃ ahīnindriyaṃ. Ayamettha dhammatā.

23. This, monks, is the nature of things: when a Bodhisatta has entered his mother’s womb, no affliction whatsoever arises in the Bodhisatta’s mother. The Bodhisatta’s mother is happy, her body unwearied, and the Bodhisatta’s mother sees the Bodhisatta within her womb complete in all his major and minor limbs, with unimpaired faculties. Just as, monks, a beryl gem—beautiful, of fine quality, eight-faceted, well-fashioned, clear, exceptionally clear, unclouded, and perfect in every way—is strung on a blue, yellow, red, white, or pale thread, and a man with good eyesight, taking it in his hand, would examine it: ‘This beryl gem is beautiful, of fine quality, eight-faceted, well-fashioned, clear, exceptionally clear, unclouded, and perfect in every way, and on it is strung a blue, yellow, red, white, or pale thread’—so too, monks, when a Bodhisatta has entered his mother’s womb, no affliction whatsoever arises in the Bodhisatta’s mother. The Bodhisatta’s mother is happy, her body unwearied, and the Bodhisatta’s mother sees the Bodhisatta within her womb complete in all his major and minor limbs, with unimpaired faculties. This is the nature of things here.

24. “Dhammatā esā, bhikkhave, sattāhajāte bodhisatte bodhisattamātā kālaṅkaroti tusitaṃ kāyaṃ upapajjati. Ayamettha dhammatā.

24. This, monks, is the nature of things: seven days after the Bodhisatta is born, the Bodhisatta's mother passes away and is reborn in the Tusita realm. This is the nature of things here.

25. “Dhammatā [T 2.0016] esā, bhikkhave, yathā aññā itthikā nava vā dasa vā māse gabbhaṃ kucchinā pariharitvā vijāyanti, na hevaṃ bodhisattaṃ bodhisattamātā vijāyati. Daseva māsāni bodhisattaṃ bodhisattamātā kucchinā pariharitvā vijāyati. Ayamettha dhammatā.

25. This, monks, is the nature of things: whereas other women carry a fetus in the womb for nine or ten months before giving birth, the Bodhisatta's mother does not give birth to the Bodhisatta in that way. The Bodhisatta's mother carries the Bodhisatta in her womb for exactly ten months before giving birth. This is the nature of things here.

26. “Dhammatā esā, bhikkhave, yathā aññā itthikā nisinnā vā nipannā vā vijāyanti, na hevaṃ bodhisattaṃ bodhisattamātā vijāyati. Ṭhitāva bodhisattaṃ bodhisattamātā vijāyati. Ayamettha dhammatā.

26. This, monks, is the nature of things: whereas other women give birth while sitting or lying down, the Bodhisatta’s mother does not give birth to the Bodhisatta in that way. The Bodhisatta’s mother gives birth to the Bodhisatta only while standing. This is the nature of things here.

27. “Dhammatā esā, bhikkhave, yadā bodhisatto mātukucchimhā nikkhamati, devā paṭhamaṃ paṭiggaṇhanti, pacchā manussā. Ayamettha dhammatā.

27. This, monks, is the nature of things: when the Bodhisatta emerges from his mother’s womb, the devas receive him first, and humans afterward. This is the nature of things here.

28. “Dhammatā esā, bhikkhave, yadā bodhisatto mātukucchimhā nikkhamati, appattova bodhisatto pathaviṃ hoti, cattāro naṃ devaputtā paṭiggahetvā mātu purato ṭhapenti – ‘attamanā, devi, hohi; mahesakkho te putto uppanno’ti. Ayamettha dhammatā.

28. This, monks, is the nature of things: when the Bodhisatta emerges from his mother's womb, before the Bodhisatta has reached the earth, four divine youths receive him and place him before his mother, saying: 'Be of glad mind, O queen; a son of great power has been born to you.' This is the nature of things here.

29. “Dhammatā esā, bhikkhave, yadā bodhisatto mātukucchimhā nikkhamati, visadova nikkhamati amakkhito udena uddena (syā.), udarena (katthaci) amakkhito semhena amakkhito ruhirena amakkhito kenaci asucinā suddho visuddho (syā.) visado. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, maṇiratanaṃ kāsike vatthe nikkhittaṃ neva maṇiratanaṃ kāsikaṃ vatthaṃ makkheti, nāpi kāsikaṃ vatthaṃ maṇiratanaṃ makkheti. Taṃ kissa [T 2.0017] hetu? Ubhinnaṃ suddhattā. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, yadā bodhisatto mātukucchimhā nikkhamati, visadova nikkhamati amakkhito, udena amakkhito [M 2.0013] semhena [P 2.0015] amakkhito ruhirena amakkhito kenaci asucinā suddho visado. Ayamettha dhammatā.

29. This, monks, is the nature of things: when the Bodhisatta emerges from his mother's womb, he emerges unsullied, unstained by uterine fluid, unstained by phlegm, unstained by blood, unstained by any impurity—pure and spotless. Just as, monks, a precious gem placed on Kāsi cloth does not stain the Kāsi cloth, nor does the Kāsi cloth stain the precious gem. For what reason? Because of the purity of both. In the same way, monks, when the Bodhisatta emerges from his mother's womb, he emerges unsullied, unstained by uterine fluid, unstained by phlegm, unstained by blood, unstained by any impurity—pure and spotless. This is the nature of things here.

30. “Dhammatā esā, bhikkhave, yadā bodhisatto mātukucchimhā nikkhamati, dve udakassa [V 2.0012] dhārā antalikkhā pātubhavanti – ekā sītassa ekā uṇhassa yena bodhisattassa udakakiccaṃ karonti mātu ca. Ayamettha dhammatā.

30. This, monks, is the nature of things: when the Bodhisatta emerges from his mother’s womb, two streams of water appear from the sky—one cool and one warm—with which they perform the water rites for the Bodhisatta and his mother. This is the nature of things here.

31. “Dhammatā esā, bhikkhave, sampatijāto bodhisatto samehi pādehi patiṭṭhahitvā uttarābhimukho uttarenābhimukho (syā.) uttarenamukho (ka.) sattapadavītihārena gacchati setamhi chatte anudhāriyamāne, sabbā ca disā anuviloketi, āsabhiṃ vācaṃ bhāsati ‘aggohamasmi lokassa, jeṭṭhohamasmi lokassa, seṭṭhohamasmi lokassa, ayamantimā jāti, natthidāni punabbhavo’ti. Ayamettha dhammatā.

31. This, monks, is the nature of things: when the Bodhisatta is just born, he stands firmly with level feet, faces north, and takes seven strides while a white parasol is held over him. He surveys all directions and utters a bold utterance: ‘I am the chief of the world, I am the eldest of the world, I am the foremost of the world. This is my last birth; now there is no more renewed existence.’ This is the nature of things here.

32. “Dhammatā esā, bhikkhave, yadā bodhisatto mātukucchimhā nikkhamati, atha sadevake loke samārake sabrahmake sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiyā pajāya sadevamanussāya appamāṇo uḷāro obhāso [T 2.0018] pātubhavati, atikkammeva devānaṃ devānubhāvaṃ. Yāpi tā lokantarikā aghā asaṃvutā andhakārā andhakāratimisā, yattha pime candimasūriyā evaṃmahiddhikā evaṃmahānubhāvā ābhāya nānubhonti, tatthapi appamāṇo uḷāro obhāso pātubhavati atikkammeva devānaṃ devānubhāvaṃ. Yepi tattha sattā upapannā, tepi tenobhāsena aññamaññaṃ sañjānanti – ‘aññepi kira, bho, santi sattā idhūpapannā’ti. Ayañca dasasahassī lokadhātu saṅkampati sampakampati sampavedhati appamāṇo ca uḷāro obhāso loke pātubhavati atikkammeva devānaṃ devānubhāvaṃ. Ayamettha dhammatā.

32. This, monks, is the nature of things: when the Bodhisatta emerges from his mother's womb, then in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, with its population of ascetics and brahmins, devas and humans, an immeasurable, sublime radiance appears, surpassing even the divine power of the devas. And in those inter-world spaces that are abysmal, unclosed, dark, and shrouded in darkness, where even the moon and sun, so mighty and powerful, cannot spread their light, there too an immeasurable, sublime radiance appears, surpassing even the divine power of the devas. And the beings reborn there recognize one another by that light, saying: 'Indeed, sirs, other beings are reborn here!' And this ten-thousandfold world system shakes, quakes, and trembles, and an immeasurable, sublime radiance appears in the world, surpassing even the divine power of the devas. This is the nature of things here.

Dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇā

The Thirty-Two Marks of a Great Man

33. “Jāte [P 2.0016] kho pana, bhikkhave, vipassimhi kumāre bandhumato rañño paṭivedesuṃ – ‘putto te, deva deva te (ka.), jāto, taṃ devo passatū’ti. Addasā kho, bhikkhave, bandhumā rājā vipassiṃ kumāraṃ, disvā nemitte brāhmaṇe [M 2.0014] āmantāpetvā etadavoca – ‘passantu bhonto nemittā brāhmaṇā kumāra’nti. Addasaṃsu kho, bhikkhave, nemittā brāhmaṇā vipassiṃ kumāraṃ, disvā bandhumantaṃ rājānaṃ etadavocuṃ – ‘attamano, deva, hohi, mahesakkho te putto uppanno, lābhā te, mahārāja, suladdhaṃ te, mahārāja, yassa te kule evarūpo putto uppanno. Ayañhi, deva, kumāro dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇehi samannāgato, yehi samannāgatassa mahāpurisassa dveva gatiyo bhavanti anaññā. Sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasati, rājā hoti cakkavattī dhammiko dhammarājā cāturanto vijitāvī janapadatthāvariyappatto sattaratanasamannāgato. Tassimāni sattaratanāni bhavanti. Seyyathidaṃ – cakkaratanaṃ hatthiratanaṃ assaratanaṃ maṇiratanaṃ itthiratanaṃ gahapatiratanaṃ pariṇāyakaratanameva [T 2.0019][V 2.0013] sattamaṃ. Parosahassaṃ kho panassa puttā bhavanti sūrā vīraṅgarūpā parasenappamaddanā. So imaṃ pathaviṃ sāgarapariyantaṃ adaṇḍena asatthena dhammena abhivijiya ajjhāvasati. Sace kho pana agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajati, arahaṃ hoti sammāsambuddho loke vivaṭacchado.

33. When Prince Vipassī was born, monks, they announced to King Bandhuma: ‘A son is born to you, Your Majesty. May Your Majesty see him.’ King Bandhuma saw Prince Vipassī, monks, and having seen him, he had the brahmin sign-readers summoned and said: ‘May the honorable brahmin sign-readers examine the prince.’ The brahmin sign-readers saw Prince Vipassī, monks, and having seen him, they said to King Bandhuma: ‘Be of joyful mind, Your Majesty! A son of great power has been born to you. It is a gain for you, great king, it is well-gained by you, great king, that such a son has been born in your family. For this prince, Your Majesty, is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, and for a Great Man endowed with these, there are only two destinies, and no other. If he dwells ruling a household, he becomes a king, a wheel-turning monarch, a righteous king, a king of righteousness, a conqueror of the four quarters, one who has attained stability in the country, endowed with the seven treasures. These are his seven treasures: the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the adviser-treasure as the seventh. He will have over a thousand sons who are brave, of heroic form, and crushers of others' armies. Having conquered this earth to its ocean bounds, he rules without punishment and without weapons, by righteousness. But if he goes forth from the household life into homelessness, he becomes an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One in the world, one who has removed the covering.

34. ‘Katamehi cāyaṃ, deva, kumāro dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇehi samannāgato, yehi samannāgatassa mahāpurisassa dveva gatiyo bhavanti anaññā. Sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasati, rājā hoti cakkavattī dhammiko dhammarājā cāturanto vijitāpī janapadatthāvariyappatto sattaratanasamannāgato. Tassimāni sattaratanāni bhavanti[P 2.0017]. Seyyathidaṃ – cakkaratanaṃ hatthiratanaṃ assaratanaṃ maṇiratanaṃ itthiratanaṃ gahapatiratanaṃ pariṇāyakaratanameva sattamaṃ. Parosahassaṃ kho panassa puttā bhavanti sūrā vīraṅgarūpā parasenappamaddanā. So imaṃ pathaviṃ sāgarapariyantaṃ adaṇḍena asatthena dhammena abhivijiya ajjhāvasati. Sace kho pana agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajati, arahaṃ hoti sammāsambuddho loke vivaṭacchado.

34. And with which thirty-two marks of a Great Man, Your Majesty, is this prince endowed, for one endowed with which there are only two destinies, and no other? If he dwells ruling a household, he becomes a king, a wheel-turning monarch, a righteous king, a king of righteousness, a conqueror of the four quarters, one who has attained stability in the country, endowed with the seven treasures. These are his seven treasures: the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the adviser-treasure as the seventh. He will have over a thousand sons who are brave, of heroic form, and crushers of others' armies. Having conquered this earth to its ocean bounds, he rules without punishment and without weapons, by righteousness. But if he goes forth from the household life into homelessness, he becomes an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One in the world, one who has removed the covering.

35. ‘Ayañhi, deva, kumāro suppatiṭṭhitapādo. Yaṃ pāyaṃ, deva, kumāro suppatiṭṭhitapādo. Idampissa mahāpurisassa mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ bhavati.

35. This prince, O king, has well-planted feet. That this prince has well-planted feet, O king, this too is a mark of a Great Man.

‘Imassa, deva imassa hi deva (?), kumārassa heṭṭhā pādatalesu cakkāni jātāni sahassārāni sanemikāni sanābhikāni sabbākāraparipūrāni. Yampi, imassa [M 2.0015] deva, kumārassa heṭṭhā pādatalesu cakkāni jātāni sahassārāni sanemikāni sanābhikāni sabbākāraparipūrāni, idampissa mahāpurisassa mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ bhavati.

On the soles of this prince’s feet, O king, wheels have arisen with a thousand spokes, with rims and hubs, complete in all aspects. That on the soles of this prince’s feet, O king, wheels have arisen with a thousand spokes, with rims and hubs, complete in all aspects, this too is a mark of a Great Man.

‘Ayañhi [T 2.0020] deva, kumāro āyatapaṇhī…pe…

This prince, O king, has long heels...

‘Ayañhi, deva, kumāro dīghaṅgulī…

This prince, O king, has long fingers and toes...

‘Ayañhi, deva, kumāro mudutalunahatthapādo…

This prince, O king, has soft and tender hands and feet...

‘Ayañhi, deva kumāro jālahatthapādo…

This prince, O king, has net-like hands and feet...

‘Ayañhi, deva, kumāro ussaṅkhapādo…

This prince, O king, has feet with high insteps...

‘Ayañhi, deva, kumāro eṇijaṅgho…

This prince, O king, has shanks like an antelope...

‘Ayañhi, deva, kumāro ṭhitakova anonamanto ubhohi pāṇitalehi jaṇṇukāni parimasati parāmasati (ka.) parimajjati…

This prince, O king, while standing and without bending, can touch and rub his knees with both palms...

‘Ayañhi[V 2.0014], deva, kumāro kosohitavatthaguyho…

This prince, O king, has his male organ concealed in a sheath...

‘Ayañhi, deva, kumāro suvaṇṇavaṇṇo kañcanasannibhattaco…

This prince, O king, has a golden complexion, his skin like pure gold...

‘Ayañhi, deva, kumāro sukhumacchavī; sukhumattā [P 2.0018] chaviyā rajojallaṃ kāye na upalimpati upalippati (syā.) …

This prince, O king, has delicate skin; because of the delicacy of his skin, dust and dirt do not adhere to his body...

‘Ayañhi, deva, kumāro ekekalomo; ekekāni lomāni lomakūpesu jātāni…

This prince, O king, has one hair per pore; single hairs grow in each hair-pore...

‘Ayañhi, deva, kumāro uddhaggalomo; uddhaggāni lomāni jātāni nīlāni añjanavaṇṇāni kuṇḍalāvaṭṭāni dakkhiṇāvaṭṭakajātāni…

This prince, O king, has hairs with tips that point upward; the hairs that have grown have tips that point upward, are blue-black like collyrium, curled like rings, and coiled to the right...

‘Ayañhi, deva, kumāro brahmujugatto…

This prince, O king, has a body as straight as Brahma's...

‘Ayañhi, deva, kumāro sattussado…

This prince, O king, has firm flesh in seven places...

‘Ayañhi[T 2.0021], deva, kumāro sīhapubbaddhakāyo…

This prince, O king, has a torso like a lion's...

‘Ayañhi, deva, kumāro citantaraṃso pitantaraṃso (syā.) …

This prince, O king, is well-fleshed between the shoulders...

‘Ayañhi, deva, kumāro nigrodhaparimaṇḍalo yāvatakvassa kāyo tāvatakvassa byāmo, yāvatakvassa byāmo, tāvatakvassa kāyo…

This prince, O king, has the proportions of a banyan tree: the height of his body is the same as his arm-span, and his arm-span is the same as the height of his body...

‘Ayañhi[M 2.0016], deva, kumāro samavaṭṭakkhandho…

This prince, O king, has an evenly rounded neck...

‘Ayañhi, deva, kumāro rasaggasaggī…

This prince, O king, has a supreme faculty for taste...

‘Ayañhi, deva, kumāro sīhahanu…

This prince, O king, has a jaw like a lion's...

‘Ayañhi, deva, kumāro cattālīsadanto…

This prince, O king, has forty teeth...

‘Ayañhi, deva, kumāro samadanto…

This prince, O king, has even teeth...

‘Ayañhi, deva, kumāro aviraḷadanto…

This prince, O king, has teeth without gaps...

‘Ayañhi, deva, kumāro susukkadāṭho…

This prince, O king, has exceedingly white canine teeth...

‘Ayañhi, deva, kumāro pahūtajivho…

This prince, O king, has a long and broad tongue...

‘Ayañhi, deva, kumāro brahmassaro karavīkabhāṇī…

This prince, O king, has a voice like Brahmā and speaks with the voice of the karavīka bird…

‘Ayañhi, deva, kumāro abhinīlanetto…

This prince, O king, has deep blue-black eyes…

‘Ayañhi, deva, kumāro gopakhumo…

This prince, O king, has eyelashes like a newborn calf…

Imassa, deva, kumārassa uṇṇā bhamukantare jātā odātā mudutūlasannibhā. Yampi imassa deva kumārassa uṇṇā bhamukantare jātā odātā mudutūlasannibhā, idampimassa [P 2.0019] mahāpurisassa mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ bhavati.

Sire, between the eyebrows of this prince a tuft of hair has grown, white and soft like cotton down. That this tuft of hair has grown between the prince's eyebrows, sire, white and soft like cotton down, this too is a mark of a Great Man.

‘Ayañhi[T 2.0022][V 2.0015], deva, kumāro uṇhīsasīso. Yaṃ pāyaṃ, deva, kumāro uṇhīsasīso, idampissa mahāpurisassa mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ bhavati.

This prince, O king, has a turban-shaped head. That this prince has a turban-shaped head, O king, this too is a mark of a Great Man.

36. ‘Imehi kho ayaṃ, deva, kumāro dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇehi samannāgato, yehi samannāgatassa mahāpurisassa dveva gatiyo bhavanti anaññā. Sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasati, rājā hoti cakkavattī dhammiko dhammarājā cāturanto vijitāvī janapadatthāvariyappatto sattaratanasamannāgato. Tassimāni sattaratanāni bhavanti. Seyyathidaṃ – cakkaratanaṃ hatthiratanaṃ assaratanaṃ maṇiratanaṃ itthiratanaṃ gahapatiratanaṃ pariṇāyakaratanameva sattamaṃ. Parosahassaṃ kho panassa puttā bhavanti sūrā vīraṅgarūpā parasenappamaddanā. So imaṃ pathaviṃ sāgarapariyantaṃ adaṇḍena asatthena dhammena dhammena samena (syā.) abhivijiya ajjhāvasati. Sace kho pana [M 2.0017] agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajati, arahaṃ hoti sammāsambuddho loke vivaṭacchado’ti.

36. Indeed, sire, this prince is endowed with these thirty-two marks of a great man, and for a great man endowed with these, only two destinies are possible, no other. If he lives the household life, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch—a righteous king, a king of righteousness, ruler of the four quarters, victorious, having attained stability in his country, and possessed of the seven treasures. These are his seven treasures: the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh. He has over a thousand sons who are brave, of heroic form, and crushers of enemy armies. He rules this earth, bounded by the ocean, without rod or sword, by righteousness alone. But if he goes forth from the household life into homelessness, he becomes an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One in the world, who has removed the veil.

Vipassīsamaññā

The Designation of Vipassī

37. “Atha kho, bhikkhave, bandhumā rājā nemitte brāhmaṇe ahatehi vatthehi acchādāpetvā acchādetvā (syā.) sabbakāmehi santappesi. Atha kho, bhikkhave, bandhumā rājā vipassissa kumārassa dhātiyo upaṭṭhāpesi. Aññā khīraṃ pāyenti, aññā nhāpenti, aññā dhārenti, aññā aṅkena pariharanti. Jātassa kho pana, bhikkhave, vipassissa kumārassa setacchattaṃ dhārayittha divā ceva rattiñca – ‘mā naṃ sītaṃ vā [T 2.0023] uṇhaṃ vā tiṇaṃ vā rajo vā ussāvo vā bādhayitthā’ti. Jāto kho pana, bhikkhave, vipassī kumāro bahuno janassa piyo ahosi manāpo. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, uppalaṃ vā [P 2.0020] padumaṃ vā puṇḍarīkaṃ vā bahuno janassa piyaṃ manāpaṃ; evameva kho, bhikkhave, vipassī kumāro bahuno janassa piyo ahosi manāpo. Svāssudaṃ aṅkeneva aṅkaṃ parihariyati.

37. Then, monks, King Bandhumā had the soothsaying brahmins clothed in new garments and satisfied them with all kinds of sensual pleasures. Then, monks, King Bandhumā appointed nurses for Prince Vipassī. Some gave him milk, some bathed him, some held him, and some carried him in their arms. For the newborn Prince Vipassī, monks, a white parasol was held over him day and night, with the thought: ‘May neither cold nor heat, grass nor dust, nor dew drops trouble him.’ And the newborn Prince Vipassī, monks, was dear and beloved to many people. Just as, monks, a blue lotus, a red lotus, or a white lotus is dear and beloved to many people, so too, monks, was Prince Vipassī dear and beloved to many people. He was passed from one person's arms to another's.

38. “Jāto kho pana, bhikkhave, vipassī kumāro mañjussaro ca kumāro brahmassaro mañjussaro ca (sī. ka.) ahosi vaggussaro ca madhurassaro ca pemaniyassaro ca. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, himavante pabbate karavīkā nāma sakuṇajāti mañjussarā ca vaggussarā ca madhurassarā ca pemaniyassarā ca; evameva kho, bhikkhave, vipassī kumāro mañjussaro ca ahosi vaggussaro ca madhurassaro ca pemaniyassaro ca.

38. Furthermore, monks, the newborn Prince Vipassī had a voice that was gentle, articulate, sweet, and endearing. Just as, monks, in the Himālaya mountains there is a species of bird called the karavīka, which has a gentle, articulate, sweet, and endearing voice; even so, monks, Prince Vipassī had a voice that was gentle, articulate, sweet, and endearing.

39. “Jātassa [V 2.0016] kho pana, bhikkhave, vipassissa kumārassa kammavipākajaṃ dibbacakkhu pāturahosi yena sudaṃ yena dūraṃ (syā.) samantā yojanaṃ passati divā ceva rattiñca.

39. Furthermore, monks, for the newborn Prince Vipassī, there arose the divine eye, born as a result of kamma, with which he could see for a yojana all around, by day and by night.

40. “Jāto kho pana, bhikkhave, vipassī kumāro animisanto pekkhati seyyathāpi devā tāvatiṃsā. ‘Animisanto kumāro pekkhatī’ti kho, bhikkhave animisanto pekkhati, jātassa kho pana bhikkhave (ka.), vipassissa kumārassa ‘vipassī vipassī’ tveva samaññā udapādi.

40. Furthermore, monks, the newborn Prince Vipassī would gaze without blinking, just like the gods of the Tāvatiṃsa realm. Because ‘the prince gazes without blinking,’ monks, the designation ‘Vipassī, Vipassī’ arose for Prince Vipassī.

41. “Atha [M 2.0018] kho, bhikkhave, bandhumā rājā atthakaraṇe aṭṭa karaṇe (syā.) nisinno vipassiṃ kumāraṃ aṅke nisīdāpetvā atthe anusāsati[P 2.0021]. Tatra sudaṃ, bhikkhave, vipassī kumāro pituaṅke nisinno viceyya [T 2.0024] viceyya atthe panāyati ñāyena aṭṭe panāyati ñāṇena (syā.). Viceyya viceyya kumāro atthe panāyati ñāyenāti kho, bhikkhave, vipassissa kumārassa bhiyyosomattāya ‘vipassī vipassī’ tveva samaññā udapādi.

41. Then, monks, King Bandhumā, while seated administering justice, would place Prince Vipassī on his lap and instruct on the cases. There, monks, Prince Vipassī, seated on his father's lap, would, with wisdom and reflection, justly discern the matters at hand. Because the prince, with wisdom and reflection, justly discerned the matters at hand, monks, the designation ‘Vipassī, Vipassī’ arose for him all the more.

42. “Atha kho, bhikkhave, bandhumā rājā vipassissa kumārassa tayo pāsāde kārāpesi, ekaṃ vassikaṃ ekaṃ hemantikaṃ ekaṃ gimhikaṃ; pañca kāmaguṇāni upaṭṭhāpesi. Tatra sudaṃ, bhikkhave, vipassī kumāro vassike pāsāde cattāro māse vassike pāsāde vassike nippurisehi tūriyehi paricārayamāno na heṭṭhāpāsādaṃ orohatī”ti.

42. Then, monks, King Bandhumā had three palaces built for Prince Vipassī: one for the rainy season, one for the winter season, and one for the summer season; and he provided him with the five kinds of sensual pleasures. There, monks, in the rainy-season palace, Prince Vipassī dwelt for the four months of the rains, being entertained by female musicians, and he did not descend from the palace.

Paṭhamabhāṇavāro.

The First Recitation Section.

Jiṇṇapuriso

The Old Man

43. “Atha kho, bhikkhave, vipassī kumāro bahūnaṃ vassānaṃ bahūnaṃ vassasatānaṃ bahūnaṃ vassasahassānaṃ accayena sārathiṃ āmantesi – ‘yojehi, samma sārathi, bhaddāni bhaddāni yānāni uyyānabhūmiṃ gacchāma subhūmidassanāyā’ti. ‘Evaṃ, devā’ti kho, bhikkhave, sārathi vipassissa kumārassa paṭissutvā bhaddāni bhaddāni yānāni yojetvā vipassissa kumārassa paṭivedesi – ‘yuttāni kho te, deva, bhaddāni bhaddāni yānāni, yassa dāni kālaṃ maññasī’ti[V 2.0017]. Atha kho, bhikkhave, vipassī kumāro bhaddaṃ bhaddaṃ yānaṃ bhadraṃ yānaṃ (syā.), bhaddaṃ yānaṃ (pī.) cattāro māse (sī. pī.) abhiruhitvā bhaddehi bhaddehi yānehi uyyānabhūmiṃ niyyāsi.

43. Then, monks, after the lapse of many years, many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, Prince Vipassī addressed his charioteer: ‘Harness, good charioteer, the fine carriages; let us go to the pleasure ground to see the beautiful terrain.’ ‘As you command, lord,’ the charioteer replied to Prince Vipassī, monks. Having harnessed the fine carriages, he informed Prince Vipassī: ‘The fine carriages are yoked for you, lord; it is now time as you deem fit.’ Then, monks, Prince Vipassī mounted a fine carriage and set out for the pleasure ground in fine carriages.

44. “Addasā kho, bhikkhave, vipassī kumāro uyyānabhūmiṃ [P 2.0022] niyyanto purisaṃ jiṇṇaṃ gopānasivaṅkaṃ bhoggaṃ bhaggaṃ (syā.) daṇḍaparāyanaṃ pavedhamānaṃ gacchantaṃ āturaṃ [M 2.0019] gatayobbanaṃ. Disvā sārathiṃ āmantesi – ‘ayaṃ pana, samma sārathi, puriso kiṃkato? Kesāpissa na yathā aññesaṃ, kāyopissa [T 2.0025] na yathā aññesa’nti. ‘Eso kho, deva, jiṇṇo nāmā’ti. ‘Kiṃ paneso, samma sārathi, jiṇṇo nāmā’ti? ‘Eso kho, deva, jiṇṇo nāma. Na dāni tena ciraṃ jīvitabbaṃ bhavissatī’ti. ‘Kiṃ pana, samma sārathi, ahampi jarādhammo, jaraṃ anatīto’ti? ‘Tvañca, deva, mayañcamha sabbe jarādhammā, jaraṃ anatītā’ti. ‘Tena hi, samma sārathi, alaṃ dānajja uyyānabhūmiyā. Itova antepuraṃ paccaniyyāhī’ti. ‘Evaṃ, devā’ti kho, bhikkhave, sārathi vipassissa kumārassa paṭissutvā tatova antepuraṃ paccaniyyāsi. Tatra sudaṃ, bhikkhave, vipassī kumāro antepuraṃ gato dukkhī dummano pajjhāyati – ‘dhiratthu kira, bho, jāti nāma, yatra hi nāma jātassa jarā paññāyissatī’ti!

44. “As Prince Vipassī was going out to the pleasure ground, monks, he saw an old man—bent like a roof beam, stooped, leaning on a staff, trembling as he walked, ailing and past his youth. Seeing him, he addressed the charioteer: ‘What has happened to this man, good charioteer? His hair is not like that of others, nor is his body like that of others.’ ‘That, lord, is what is called an old man.’ ‘But what, good charioteer, is this “old man”?’ ‘He is called an old man, lord, because he will not now live for long.’ ‘But, good charioteer, am I also subject to old age, not beyond old age?’ ‘You, lord, and we too, are all subject to old age, not beyond old age.’ ‘Then enough, good charioteer, with the pleasure ground for today. Return to the inner palace from here.’ ‘As you command, lord,’ the charioteer replied to Prince Vipassī, monks, and from that very place returned to the inner palace. There, monks, Prince Vipassī, having gone to the inner palace, was sorrowful and dejected, pondering: ‘Shame on this thing called birth! For where there is birth, for one who is born, old age will surely appear!’”

45. “Atha kho, bhikkhave, bandhumā rājā sārathiṃ āmantāpetvā etadavoca – ‘kacci, samma sārathi, kumāro uyyānabhūmiyā abhiramittha? Kacci, samma sārathi, kumāro uyyānabhūmiyā attamano ahosī’ti? ‘Na kho, deva, kumāro uyyānabhūmiyā abhiramittha, na kho, deva, kumāro uyyānabhūmiyā attamano ahosī’ti. ‘Kiṃ pana, samma sārathi, addasa kumāro uyyānabhūmiṃ niyyanto’ti? ‘Addasā [P 2.0023] kho, deva, kumāro uyyānabhūmiṃ niyyanto purisaṃ jiṇṇaṃ gopānasivaṅkaṃ bhoggaṃ daṇḍaparāyanaṃ pavedhamānaṃ gacchantaṃ āturaṃ gatayobbanaṃ. Disvā maṃ etadavoca – “ayaṃ pana, samma sārathi, puriso kiṃkato, kesāpissa na yathā aññesaṃ, kāyopissa [T 2.0026] na yathā aññesa”nti? “Eso kho, deva, jiṇṇo nāmā”ti. “Kiṃ paneso, samma sārathi, jiṇṇo nāmā”ti? “Eso kho, deva, jiṇṇo nāma na dāni tena ciraṃ jīvitabbaṃ bhavissatī”ti. “Kiṃ pana, samma sārathi, ahampi jarādhammo, jaraṃ anatīto”ti? “Tvañca, deva, mayañcamha sabbe jarādhammā, jaraṃ anatītā”ti.

45. “Then, monks, King Bandhumā summoned the charioteer and said this: ‘Did the prince enjoy himself at the pleasure ground, good charioteer? Was the prince pleased at the pleasure ground?’ ‘No, Your Majesty, the prince did not enjoy himself at the pleasure ground, nor was the prince pleased at the pleasure ground.’ ‘But what did the prince see when going to the pleasure ground, good charioteer?’ ‘When going to the pleasure ground, Your Majesty, the prince saw an old man—bent like a roof beam, stooped, leaning on a staff, trembling as he walked, ailing and past his youth. Seeing him, he said to me: “What has happened to this man, good charioteer? His hair is not like that of others, nor is his body like that of others.” “That, lord, is what is called an old man.” “But what, good charioteer, is this ‘old man’?” “He is called an old man, lord, because he will not now live for long.” “But, good charioteer, am I also subject to old age, not beyond old age?” “You, lord, and we too, are all subject to old age, not beyond old age.”’

“‘Tena hi, samma sārathi, alaṃ dānajja uyyānabhūmiyā, itova antepuraṃ paccaniyyāhī’”ti. “Evaṃ, devā”ti kho ahaṃ, deva, vipassissa kumārassa paṭissutvā tatova [V 2.0018] antepuraṃ paccaniyyāsiṃ. So kho, deva, kumāro antepuraṃ gato dukkhī dummano pajjhāyati – “dhiratthu kira bho jāti nāma, yatra hi nāma jātassa jarā paññāyissatī’”ti.

“‘Then enough, good charioteer, with the pleasure ground for today. Return to the inner palace from here.’ Replying to Prince Vipassī, ‘As you command, lord,’ Your Majesty, I returned to the inner palace from that very place. That prince, Your Majesty, having gone to the inner palace, is sorrowful and dejected, pondering: ‘Shame on this thing called birth! For where there is birth, for one who is born, old age will surely appear!’”

Byādhitapuriso

The Sick Man

46. “Atha [M 2.0020] kho, bhikkhave, bandhumassa rañño etadahosi –

46. “Then, monks, it occurred to King Bandhumā:

‘Mā heva kho vipassī kumāro na rajjaṃ kāresi, mā heva vipassī kumāro agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbaji, mā heva nemittānaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ saccaṃ assa vacana’nti. Atha kho, bhikkhave, bandhumā rājā vipassissa kumārassa bhiyyosomattāya pañca kāmaguṇāni upaṭṭhāpesi – ‘yathā vipassī kumāro rajjaṃ kareyya, yathā vipassī kumāro na agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajeyya, yathā nemittānaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ micchā assa vacana’nti.

‘May it not be that Prince Vipassī does not rule, may it not be that Prince Vipassī goes forth from the household life into homelessness, may it not be that the words of the soothsayer brahmins are true.’ Then, monks, King Bandhumā provided Prince Vipassī with even more of the five strands of sensual pleasure—so that Prince Vipassī would rule, so that Prince Vipassī would not go forth from the household life into homelessness, so that the words of the soothsayer brahmins would be false.”

“Tatra sudaṃ, bhikkhave, vipassī kumāro pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappito samaṅgībhūto paricāreti. Atha kho, bhikkhave, vipassī kumāro bahūnaṃ vassānaṃ…pe…

“There indeed, monks, Prince Vipassī enjoyed himself, endowed and furnished with the five strands of sensual pleasure. Then, monks, after many years had passed…”

47. “Addasā [P 2.0024] kho, bhikkhave, vipassī kumāro uyyānabhūmiṃ niyyanto purisaṃ ābādhikaṃ [T 2.0027] dukkhitaṃ bāḷhagilānaṃ sake muttakarīse palipannaṃ semānaṃ sayamānaṃ (syā. ka.) aññehi vuṭṭhāpiyamānaṃ aññehi saṃvesiyamānaṃ. Disvā sārathiṃ āmantesi – ‘ayaṃ pana, samma sārathi, puriso kiṃkato? Akkhīnipissa na yathā aññesaṃ, saropissa siropissa (syā.) na yathā aññesa’nti? ‘Eso kho, deva, byādhito nāmā’ti. ‘Kiṃ paneso, samma sārathi, byādhito nāmā’ti? ‘Eso kho, deva, byādhito nāma appeva nāma tamhā ābādhā vuṭṭhaheyyā’ti. ‘Kiṃ pana, samma sārathi, ahampi byādhidhammo, byādhiṃ anatīto’ti? ‘Tvañca, deva, mayañcamha sabbe byādhidhammā, byādhiṃ anatītā’ti. ‘Tena hi, samma sārathi, alaṃ dānajja uyyānabhūmiyā, itova antepuraṃ paccaniyyāhī’ti. ‘Evaṃ devā’ti kho, bhikkhave, sārathi vipassissa kumārassa paṭissutvā tatova antepuraṃ paccaniyyāsi. Tatra sudaṃ, bhikkhave, vipassī kumāro antepuraṃ gato dukkhī dummano pajjhāyati – ‘dhiratthu kira bho jāti nāma, yatra hi nāma jātassa jarā paññāyissati, byādhi paññāyissatī’ti.

47. “While going to the pleasure grounds, monks, Prince Vipassī saw a man who was sick—afflicted, suffering, gravely ill, lying sunken in his own urine and excrement, being lifted up by others and laid down by others. Seeing this, he addressed the charioteer: ‘Good charioteer, what is the matter with this man? His eyes are not like those of others, and his voice is not like that of others.’ ‘That, lord, is what is called a sick man.’ ‘What, good charioteer, is a sick man?’ ‘That, lord, is what is called a sick man; it is uncertain if he might recover from that illness.’ ‘But, good charioteer, am I also subject to illness, not beyond illness?’ ‘You, lord, and we are all subject to illness, not beyond illness.’ ‘In that case, good charioteer, enough of the pleasure grounds for today. Return to the inner palace from here.’ ‘As you say, lord,’ the charioteer, monks, replied to Prince Vipassī, and returned to the inner palace from there. There indeed, monks, Prince Vipassī, having gone to the inner palace, was distressed and sorrowful, reflecting: ‘Contemptible indeed is this thing called birth! For where there is birth, for one who is born, aging will become apparent, illness will become apparent!’”

48. “Atha [V 2.0019] kho, bhikkhave, bandhumā rājā sārathiṃ āmantāpetvā etadavoca – ‘kacci, samma sārathi, kumāro uyyānabhūmiyā abhiramittha, kacci, samma [M 2.0021] sārathi, kumāro uyyānabhūmiyā attamano ahosī’ti? ‘Na kho, deva, kumāro uyyānabhūmiyā abhiramittha, na kho, deva, kumāro uyyānabhūmiyā attamano ahosī’ti. ‘Kiṃ pana, samma sārathi, addasa kumāro [T 2.0028] uyyānabhūmiṃ niyyanto’ti? ‘Addasā kho, deva, kumāro uyyānabhūmiṃ niyyanto purisaṃ ābādhikaṃ dukkhitaṃ bāḷhagilānaṃ sake muttakarīse [P 2.0025] palipannaṃ semānaṃ aññehi vuṭṭhāpiyamānaṃ aññehi saṃvesiyamānaṃ. Disvā maṃ etadavoca – “ayaṃ pana, samma sārathi, puriso kiṃkato, akkhīnipissa na yathā aññesaṃ, saropissa na yathā aññesa”nti? “Eso kho, deva, byādhito nāmā”ti. “Kiṃ paneso, samma sārathi, byādhito nāmā”ti? “Eso kho, deva, byādhito nāma appeva nāma tamhā ābādhā vuṭṭhaheyyā”ti. “Kiṃ pana, samma sārathi, ahampi byādhidhammo, byādhiṃ anatīto”ti? “Tvañca, deva, mayañcamha sabbe byādhidhammā, byādhiṃ anatītā”ti. “Tena hi, samma sārathi, alaṃ dānajja uyyānabhūmiyā, itova antepuraṃ paccaniyyāhī”ti. “Evaṃ, devā”ti kho ahaṃ, deva, vipassissa kumārassa paṭissutvā tatova antepuraṃ paccaniyyāsiṃ. So kho, deva, kumāro antepuraṃ gato dukkhī dummano pajjhāyati – “‘dhiratthu kira bho jāti nāma, yatra hi nāma jātassa jarā paññāyissati, byādhi paññāyissatī’”ti.

48. Then, mendicants, King Bandhumā, having summoned the charioteer, said this: ‘Well, good charioteer, did the prince enjoy the pleasure garden? Was the prince, good charioteer, pleased with the pleasure garden?’ ‘No, Your Majesty, the prince did not enjoy the pleasure garden. No, Your Majesty, the prince was not pleased with the pleasure garden.’ ‘But what, good charioteer, did the prince see while going to the pleasure garden?’ ‘Your Majesty, while going to the pleasure garden, the prince saw a man who was sick—afflicted, suffering, gravely ill, lying sunken in his own urine and excrement, being lifted up by others and laid down by others. Seeing him, he said this to me: “Good charioteer, what has happened to this man? His eyes are not like those of others, and his voice is not like that of others.” I replied: “That, Your Highness, is what is called a sick man.” He asked: “What, good charioteer, is a sick man?” I replied: “Your Highness, that is what is called a sick man; it is uncertain if he might recover from that illness.” He asked: “But, good charioteer, am I also subject to illness, not beyond illness?” I replied: “You, Your Highness, and we are all subject to illness, not beyond illness.” He said: “In that case, good charioteer, enough of the pleasure garden for today. Return to the inner palace from here.” “As you say, Your Highness,” I, Your Majesty, replied to Prince Vipassī, and returned to the inner palace from there. That prince, Your Majesty, having gone to the inner palace, is distressed and sorrowful, reflecting: “Contemptible indeed is this thing called birth! For where there is birth, for one who is born, aging will become apparent, illness will become apparent!”’

Kālaṅkatapuriso

The Dead Man
