Api [P 2.0048] ca, bhante, mayaṃ tathā karissāma, yathā bhikkhū channaṃ channaṃ vassānaṃ accayena bandhumatiṃ rājadhāniṃ upasaṅkamissanti pātimokkhuddesāyā”ti. Idamavoca, bhikkhave, so mahābrahmā, idaṃ vatvā maṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā tattheva antaradhāyi’.

Then, monks, a certain Great Brahmā, having known with his mind the thought in my mind, just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm or bend his outstretched arm, so did he vanish from the Brahmā-world and appear before me. Then, monks, that Great Brahmā, arranging his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms towards me and said this: 'So it is, Blessed One, so it is, Well-farer. At present, venerable sir, a great community of monks resides in the royal capital of Bandhumatī—one hundred and sixty-eight thousand monks. Let the Blessed One, venerable sir, permit the monks: “Wander forth, monks, for the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans. Let not two go by the same path. Teach, monks, the Dhamma… There are beings with little dust in their eyes; from not hearing the Dhamma, they decline. There will be those who will understand the Dhamma.” Moreover, venerable sir, we will act in such a way that the monks will approach the royal capital of Bandhumatī after the passing of every six years for the purpose of reciting the Pātimokkha.' Monks, that Great Brahmā said this. Having said this, he paid homage to me, circumambulated me respectfully, and vanished right there.

“‘Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, caratha cārikaṃ bahujanahitāya bahujanasukhāya lokānukampāya atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ; mā ekena dve agamittha; desetha, bhikkhave, dhammaṃ ādikalyāṇaṃ majjhekalyāṇaṃ pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ parisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ pakāsetha. Santi sattā apparajakkhajātikā, assavanatā dhammassa parihāyanti, bhavissanti dhammassa aññātāro. Api ca, bhikkhave, channaṃ channaṃ vassānaṃ accayena bandhumatī rājadhānī upasaṅkamitabbā pātimokkhuddesāyā’ti. Atha kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhū yebhuyyena ekāheneva janapadacārikaṃ pakkamiṃsu.

I permit, monks: ‘Wander forth on tour for the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans. Let not two go by the same path. Teach, monks, the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, complete in its meaning and phrasing. Proclaim the holy life, utterly complete and pure. There are beings with little dust in their eyes; from not hearing the Dhamma, they decline. There will be those who will understand the Dhamma. Moreover, monks, after the passing of every six years, the royal capital of Bandhumatī is to be approached for the purpose of reciting the Pātimokkha.’ Then, monks, the monks for the most part departed on their tour of the country in a single day.

89. “Tena kho pana samayena jambudīpe caturāsīti āvāsasahassāni honti. Ekamhi hi vasse nikkhante devatā saddamanussāvesuṃ – ‘nikkhantaṃ kho, mārisā, ekaṃ vassaṃ; pañca dāni vassāni sesāni[P 2.0049]; pañcannaṃ vassānaṃ accayena bandhumatī rājadhānī upasaṅkamitabbā pātimokkhuddesāyā’ti. Dvīsu vassesu nikkhantesu… [T 2.0056] tīsu vassesu nikkhantesu… catūsu vassesu nikkhantesu… pañcasu vassesu nikkhantesu devatā saddamanussāvesuṃ – ‘nikkhantāni kho[V 2.0038], mārisā, pañcavassāni; ekaṃ dāni vassaṃ sesaṃ; ekassa vassassa accayena bandhumatī rājadhānī upasaṅkamitabbā pātimokkhuddesāyā’ti. Chasu vassesu nikkhantesu devatā saddamanussāvesuṃ – ‘nikkhantāni kho, mārisā, chabbassāni, samayo dāni bandhumatiṃ rājadhāniṃ upasaṅkamituṃ pātimokkhuddesāyā’ti. Atha kho te, bhikkhave, bhikkhū appekacce sakena iddhānubhāvena appekacce devatānaṃ iddhānubhāvena ekāheneva bandhumatiṃ rājadhāniṃ upasaṅkamiṃsu pātimokkhuddesāyāti pātimokkhuddesāya (?).

89. At that time, in Jambudīpa, there were eighty-four thousand monasteries. When one year had passed, the devas announced: 'Sirs, one year has passed; now five years remain; after the passing of five years, the royal capital of Bandhumatī is to be approached for the purpose of reciting the Pātimokkha.' When two years had passed… when three years had passed… when four years had passed… when five years had passed, the devas announced: 'Sirs, five years have passed; now one year remains; after the passing of one year, the royal capital of Bandhumatī is to be approached for the purpose of reciting the Pātimokkha.' When six years had passed, the devas announced: 'Sirs, six years have passed; now is the time to approach the royal capital of Bandhumatī for the purpose of reciting the Pātimokkha.' Then, monks, those monks—some by their own psychic power, some by the psychic power of the devas—approached the royal capital of Bandhumatī in a single day for the purpose of reciting the Pātimokkha.

90. “Tatra [M 2.0042] sudaṃ, bhikkhave, vipassī bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho bhikkhusaṅghe evaṃ pātimokkhaṃ uddisati –

90. There, monks, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, recited the Pātimokkha thus in the midst of the community of monks:

‘Khantī [T 2.0057] paramaṃ tapo titikkhā,

Nibbānaṃ paramaṃ vadanti buddhā;

Na hi pabbajito parūpaghātī,

Na samaṇo samaṇo (sī. syā. pī.) hoti paraṃ viheṭhayanto.

Forbearance, patience, is the supreme austerity. The Buddhas declare Nibbāna to be supreme. One who harms others is not a renunciate, nor is one who oppresses another an ascetic.

‘Sabbapāpassa akaraṇaṃ, kusalassa upasampadā;

Sacittapariyodapanaṃ, etaṃ buddhānasāsanaṃ.

The non-doing of all evil, the accomplishment of the wholesome, the purification of one's own mind—this is the teaching of the Buddhas.

‘Anūpavādo anūpaghāto anupavādo anupaghāto (pī. ka.), pātimokkhe ca saṃvaro;

Mattaññutā [P 2.0050] ca bhattasmiṃ, pantañca sayanāsanaṃ;

Adhicitte ca āyogo, etaṃ buddhānasāsana’nti.

Not reviling, not harming, restraint in the Pātimokkha, knowing the measure in food, a secluded lodging, and application to the higher mind—this is the teaching of the Buddhas.

Devatārocanaṃ

The Announcement by the Deities.

91. “Ekamidāhaṃ, bhikkhave, samayaṃ ukkaṭṭhāyaṃ viharāmi subhagavane sālarājamūle. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, rahogatassa paṭisallīnassa evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi – ‘na kho so sattāvāso sulabharūpo, yo mayā anāvutthapubbo anajjhāvuṭṭhapubbo (ka. sī. ka.) iminā dīghena addhunā aññatra suddhāvāsehi devehi. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ yena suddhāvāsā devā tenupasaṅkameyya’nti. Atha khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, seyyathāpi nāma balavā puriso samiñjitaṃ vā bāhaṃ pasāreyya, pasāritaṃ vā bāhaṃ samiñjeyya, evameva ukkaṭṭhāyaṃ subhagavane sālarājamūle antarahito avihesu devesu pāturahosiṃ[V 2.0039]. Tasmiṃ, bhikkhave, devanikāye anekāni devatāsahassāni anekāni devatāsatasahassāni anekāni devatāsatāni anekāni devatāsahassāni (syā.) yenāhaṃ tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā maṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhaṃsu. Ekamantaṃ [T 2.0058] ṭhitā kho, bhikkhave, tā devatā maṃ etadavocuṃ – ‘ito so, mārisā, ekanavutikappe yaṃ vipassī bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho loke udapādi. Vipassī, mārisā, bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho khattiyo jātiyā ahosi, khattiyakule udapādi. Vipassī, mārisā, bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho koṇḍañño gottena ahosi[M 2.0043]. Vipassissa, mārisā, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa asītivassasahassāni āyuppamāṇaṃ ahosi. Vipassī, mārisā, bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho pāṭaliyā mūle abhisambuddho. Vipassissa, mārisā, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa khaṇḍatissaṃ nāma sāvakayugaṃ ahosi aggaṃ bhaddayugaṃ. Vipassissa, mārisā, bhagavato [P 2.0051] arahato sammāsambuddhassa tayo sāvakānaṃ sannipātā ahesuṃ. Eko sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi aṭṭhasaṭṭhibhikkhusatasahassaṃ. Eko sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi bhikkhusatasahassaṃ. Eko sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi asītibhikkhusahassāni. Vipassissa, mārisā, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa ime tayo sāvakānaṃ sannipātā ahesuṃ sabbesaṃyeva khīṇāsavānaṃ. Vipassissa, mārisā, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa asoko nāma bhikkhu upaṭṭhāko ahosi aggupaṭṭhāko. Vipassissa, mārisa, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa bandhumā nāma rājā pitā ahosi. Bandhumatī nāma devī mātā ahosi janetti. Bandhumassa rañño bandhumatī nāma nagaraṃ rājadhānī ahosi. Vipassissa, mārisā[T 2.0059], bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa evaṃ abhinikkhamanaṃ ahosi evaṃ pabbajjā evaṃ padhānaṃ evaṃ abhisambodhi evaṃ dhammacakkappavattanaṃ. Te mayaṃ, mārisā, vipassimhi bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ caritvā kāmesu kāmacchandaṃ virājetvā idhūpapannā’ti …pe…

91. “Monks, on one occasion, I was dwelling in Ukkaṭṭhā, in the Subhaga Grove, at the foot of a great Sāla tree. To me, monks, who had gone to a secluded place and was dwelling in solitude, this thought arose in my mind: ‘Indeed, there is no abode of beings that is easy to find where I have not dwelt before during this long period of time, with the exception of the Suddhāvāsa devas. What if I were to approach the place where the Suddhāvāsa devas are?’ Then, monks, just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm, or bend his outstretched arm, even so, having disappeared from Ukkaṭṭhā, in the Subhaga Grove, at the foot of the great Sāla tree, I appeared among the Aviha devas. In that host of devas, monks, many thousands of devas, many hundreds of thousands of devas, approached me. Having approached, they paid homage to me and stood to one side. Standing to one side, monks, those devas said this to me: ‘Venerable Sir, ninety-one kappas ago from now, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, arose in the world. Venerable Sir, the Blessed One Vipassī was a Khattiya by birth and arose in a Khattiya family. Venerable Sir, the Blessed One Vipassī was of the Koṇḍañña clan by lineage. Venerable Sir, the lifespan of the Blessed One Vipassī was eighty thousand years. Venerable Sir, the Blessed One Vipassī became fully enlightened at the foot of a Pāṭali tree. Venerable Sir, the Blessed One Vipassī had a chief, excellent pair of disciples named Khaṇḍa and Tissa. Venerable Sir, the Blessed One Vipassī had three assemblies of disciples. One assembly consisted of one hundred and sixty-eight thousand bhikkhus, one assembly consisted of one hundred thousand bhikkhus, and one assembly consisted of eighty thousand bhikkhus. Venerable Sir, these three assemblies of disciples were all composed of arahants. Venerable Sir, the Blessed One Vipassī had a bhikkhu named Asoka as his attendant, his chief attendant. Venerable Sir, the father of the Blessed One Vipassī was the king named Bandhumā, and his mother who gave him birth was the queen named Bandhumatī. The capital city of King Bandhumā was the city named Bandhumatī. Venerable Sir, for the Blessed One Vipassī, thus was his renunciation, thus was his going forth, thus was his striving, thus was his full enlightenment, and thus was his setting in motion of the wheel of Dhamma. We, Venerable Sir, having lived the holy life under the Blessed One Vipassī and having become dispassionate towards sensual desires, have been reborn here.’ …and so on…

“Tasmiṃyeva kho, bhikkhave, devanikāye anekāni devatāsahassāni anekāni devatāsatasahassāni anekāni devatāsatāni anekāni devatāsahassāni (syā. evamuparipi) yenāhaṃ tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā maṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhaṃsu. Ekamantaṃ ṭhitā kho, bhikkhave, tā devatā maṃ etadavocuṃ – ‘imasmiṃyeva kho, mārisā, bhaddakappe bhagavā etarahi arahaṃ sammāsambuddho loke uppanno. Bhagavā, mārisā, khattiyo jātiyā khattiyakule uppanno. Bhagavā, mārisā, gotamo gottena. Bhagavato, mārisā, appakaṃ [P 2.0052] āyuppamāṇaṃ parittaṃ lahukaṃ [T 2.0060] yo ciraṃ jīvati, so vassasataṃ appaṃ vā bhiyyo. Bhagavā, mārisā, assatthassa mūle abhisambuddho. Bhagavato, mārisā, sāriputtamoggallānaṃ nāma sāvakayugaṃ ahosi aggaṃ bhaddayugaṃ[M 2.0044]. Bhagavato, mārisā, eko sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi aḍḍhateḷasāni bhikkhusatāni. Bhagavato, mārisā, ayaṃ eko sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi [V 2.0040] sabbesaṃyeva khīṇāsavānaṃ. Bhagavato, mārisā, ānando nāma bhikkhu upaṭṭhāko ahosi aggupaṭṭhāko. Bhagavato, mārisā, suddhodano nāma rājā pitā ahosi. Māyā nāma devī mātā ahosi janetti. Kapilavatthu nāma nagaraṃ rājadhānī ahosi. Bhagavato, mārisā, evaṃ abhinikkhamanaṃ ahosi evaṃ pabbajjā evaṃ padhānaṃ evaṃ abhisambodhi evaṃ dhammacakkappavattanaṃ. Te mayaṃ, mārisā, bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ caritvā kāmesu kāmacchandaṃ virājetvā idhūpapannā’ti.

“In that very host of devas, monks, many thousands of devas, many hundreds of thousands of devas, approached me. Having approached, they paid homage to me and stood to one side. Standing to one side, monks, those devas said this to me: ‘Venerable Sir, in this very Bhadda kappa, the Blessed One has now arisen in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One. Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is a Khattiya by birth, arisen in a Khattiya family. Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is a Gotama by lineage. Venerable Sir, the lifespan of the Blessed One is small, limited, and short; one who lives long lives for a hundred years, or a little less or more. Venerable Sir, the Blessed One became fully enlightened at the foot of an Assattha tree. Venerable Sir, the Blessed One has a chief, excellent pair of disciples named Sāriputta and Moggallāna. Venerable Sir, the Blessed One had one assembly of disciples, consisting of twelve hundred and fifty bhikkhus. Venerable Sir, this one assembly of disciples was composed entirely of arahants. Venerable Sir, the Blessed One has a bhikkhu named Ānanda as his attendant, his chief attendant. Venerable Sir, the father of the Blessed One was the king named Suddhodana. His mother who gave him birth was the queen named Māyā. The capital city was the city named Kapilavatthu. Venerable Sir, for the Blessed One, thus was his renunciation, thus was his going forth, thus was his striving, thus was his full enlightenment, and thus was his setting in motion of the wheel of Dhamma. We, Venerable Sir, having lived the holy life under the Blessed One and having become dispassionate towards sensual desires, have been reborn here.’”

92. “Atha khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, avihehi devehi saddhiṃ yena atappā devā tenupasaṅkamiṃ…pe… atha khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, avihehi ca devehi atappehi ca devehi saddhiṃ yena sudassā devā tenupasaṅkamiṃ. Atha khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, avihehi ca devehi atappehi ca devehi sudassehi ca devehi saddhiṃ yena sudassī devā tenupasaṅkamiṃ. Atha khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, avihehi ca devehi atappehi ca devehi sudassehi ca devehi sudassīhi ca devehi saddhiṃ yena akaniṭṭhā devā tenupasaṅkamiṃ. Tasmiṃ, bhikkhave, devanikāye anekāni devatāsahassāni anekāni devatāsatasahassāni yenāhaṃ tenupasaṅkamiṃsu, upasaṅkamitvā maṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhaṃsu[T 2.0061].

92. Then, monks, together with the Aviha devas, I approached where the Atappa devas were… Then, monks, together with the Aviha and Atappa devas, I approached where the Sudassa devas were. Then, monks, together with the Aviha, Atappa, and Sudassa devas, I approached where the Sudassi devas were. Then, monks, together with the Aviha, Atappa, Sudassa, and Sudassi devas, I approached where the Akaniṭṭha devas were. In that assembly of devas, monks, many thousands of devas, many hundreds of thousands of devas approached where I was. Having approached, they paid homage to me and stood to one side.

“Ekamantaṃ ṭhitā kho, bhikkhave, tā devatā maṃ etadavocuṃ – ‘ito so, mārisā, ekanavutikappe yaṃ vipassī bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho loke udapādi. Vipassī, mārisā, bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho khattiyo jātiyā ahosi. Khattiyakule udapādi. Vipassī, mārisā, bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho koṇḍañño gottena ahosi. Vipassissa, mārisā, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa asītivassasahassāni āyuppamāṇaṃ ahosi. Vipassī, mārisā, bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho pāṭaliyā mūle abhisambuddho. Vipassissa, mārisā, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa khaṇḍatissaṃ nāma sāvakayugaṃ ahosi aggaṃ bhaddayugaṃ. Vipassissa, mārisā, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa tayo sāvakānaṃ sannipātā ahesuṃ. Eko sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi aṭṭhasaṭṭhibhikkhusatasahassaṃ. Eko sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi [M 2.0045] bhikkhusatasahassaṃ. Eko sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi asītibhikkhusahassāni. Vipassissa, mārisā, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa ime tayo sāvakānaṃ sannipātā ahesuṃ sabbesaṃyeva khīṇāsavānaṃ. Vipassissa, mārisā, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa asoko nāma bhikkhu upaṭṭhāko ahosi aggupaṭṭhāko. Vipassissa, mārisā, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa bandhumā nāma rājā pitā ahosi bandhumatī nāma devī mātā ahosi [V 2.0041] janetti. Bandhumassa rañño bandhumatī nāma nagaraṃ rājadhānī ahosi. Vipassissa, mārisā, bhagavato arahato [T 2.0062] sammāsambuddhassa evaṃ abhinikkhamanaṃ ahosi evaṃ pabbajjā evaṃ padhānaṃ evaṃ abhisambodhi, evaṃ dhammacakkappavattanaṃ. Te mayaṃ, mārisā, vipassimhi bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ caritvā kāmesu kāmacchandaṃ virājetvā idhūpapannā’ti. Tasmiṃyeva kho, bhikkhave, devanikāye anekāni devatāsahassāni anekāni devatāsatasahassāni yenāhaṃ tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā maṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhaṃsu. Ekamantaṃ ṭhitā kho, bhikkhave, tā devatā maṃ etadavocuṃ – ‘ito so, mārisā, ekatiṃse kappe yaṃ sikhī bhagavā…pe… te mayaṃ, mārisā, sikhimhi bhagavati tasmiññeva kho mārisā, ekatiṃse kappe yaṃ vessabhū bhagavā…pe… te mayaṃ, mārisā, vessabhumhi bhagavati…pe… imasmiṃyeva kho, mārisā, bhaddakappe kakusandho koṇāgamano kassapo bhagavā…pe… te mayaṃ, mārisā, kakusandhamhi koṇāgamanamhi kassapamhi bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ caritvā kāmesu kāmacchandaṃ virājetvā idhūpapannā’ti.

Standing to one side, monks, those devas said this to me: ‘Ninety-one kappas ago from now, Venerable Sir, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, arose in the world. The Blessed One Vipassī, Venerable Sir, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was a khattiya by birth; he was born into a khattiya family. The Blessed One Vipassī, Venerable Sir, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was of the Koṇḍañña clan by lineage. The lifespan of the Blessed One Vipassī, Venerable Sir, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was eighty thousand years. The Blessed One Vipassī, Venerable Sir, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was fully enlightened at the foot of a Pāṭali tree. The Blessed One Vipassī, Venerable Sir, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had a foremost, excellent pair of disciples named Khaṇḍa and Tissa. The Blessed One Vipassī, Venerable Sir, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had three assemblies of disciples. One assembly of disciples consisted of one hundred and sixty-eight thousand monks. One assembly of disciples consisted of one hundred thousand monks. One assembly of disciples consisted of eighty thousand monks. The Blessed One Vipassī, Venerable Sir, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had these three assemblies of disciples, all of whom were indeed free from taints. The Blessed One Vipassī, Venerable Sir, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had a monk named Asoka as his attendant, his chief attendant. The Blessed One Vipassī, Venerable Sir, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had King Bandhumā as his father and Queen Bandhumatī as the mother who bore him. The royal capital of King Bandhumā was the city named Bandhumatī. For the Blessed One Vipassī, Venerable Sir, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, such was the going forth, such was the renunciation, such was the striving, such was the full enlightenment, and such was the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma. We, Venerable Sir, having lived the holy life under the Blessed One Vipassī and having become dispassionate towards sensual desires, have been reborn here.’ In that very assembly of devas, monks, many thousands of devas, many hundreds of thousands of devas approached me; having approached, they paid homage to me and stood to one side. Standing to one side, monks, those devas said this to me: ‘Thirty-one kappas ago from now, Venerable Sir, the Blessed One Sikhī… We, Venerable Sir, under the Blessed One Sikhī… In that very thirty-first kappa, Venerable Sir, the Blessed One Vessabhū… We, Venerable Sir, under the Blessed One Vessabhū… In this very Bhadda kappa, Venerable Sir, the Blessed Ones Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa… We, Venerable Sir, having lived the holy life under the Blessed Ones Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa, and having become dispassionate towards sensual desires, have been reborn here.’

93. “Tasmiṃyeva kho, bhikkhave, devanikāye anekāni devatāsahassāni anekāni devatāsatasahassāni yenāhaṃ tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā maṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhaṃsu. Ekamantaṃ [P 2.0053] ṭhitā kho, bhikkhave, tā devatā maṃ etadavocuṃ – ‘imasmiṃyeva kho, mārisā, bhaddakappe bhagavā etarahi arahaṃ sammāsambuddho loke uppanno. Bhagavā, mārisā, khattiyo jātiyā, khattiyakule uppanno. Bhagavā, mārisā, gotamo gottena. Bhagavato, mārisā, appakaṃ āyuppamāṇaṃ parittaṃ lahukaṃ yo ciraṃ jīvati, so vassasataṃ [T 2.0063] appaṃ vā bhiyyo. Bhagavā, mārisā, assatthassa mūle abhisambuddho. Bhagavato, mārisā, sāriputtamoggallānaṃ nāma sāvakayugaṃ ahosi aggaṃ bhaddayugaṃ. Bhagavato[M 2.0046], mārisā, eko sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi aḍḍhateḷasāni bhikkhusatāni. Bhagavato, mārisā, ayaṃ eko sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi sabbesaṃyeva khīṇāsavānaṃ. Bhagavato, mārisā, ānando nāma bhikkhu upaṭṭhāko aggupaṭṭhāko ahosi. Bhagavato, mārisā, suddhodano nāma rājā pitā ahosi. Māyā nāma devī mātā ahosi janetti. Kapilavatthu nāma nagaraṃ rājadhānī ahosi. Bhagavato, mārisā, evaṃ abhinikkhamanaṃ ahosi, evaṃ pabbajjā, evaṃ padhānaṃ, evaṃ abhisambodhi, evaṃ dhammacakkappavattanaṃ. Te mayaṃ, mārisā, bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ caritvā kāmesu kāmacchandaṃ virājetvā idhūpapannā’ti.

93. In that very same assembly of devas, monks, many thousands of devas, many hundreds of thousands of devas approached me. Having approached, they paid homage to me and stood to one side. Standing to one side, those devas said this to me: ‘In this very same Bhadda kappa, Venerable Sir, the Blessed One has now arisen in the world as an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One. The Blessed One, Venerable Sir, is a khattiya by birth, born into a khattiya family. The Blessed One, Venerable Sir, is of the Gotama clan by lineage. The Blessed One’s lifespan, Venerable Sir, is short, limited, and brief—one who lives long lives for a hundred years, or a little less, or more. The Blessed One, Venerable Sir, was fully enlightened at the foot of an Assattha tree. The Blessed One, Venerable Sir, had a foremost, excellent pair of disciples named Sāriputta and Moggallāna. The Blessed One, Venerable Sir, had one assembly of disciples consisting of twelve hundred and fifty monks. The Blessed One, Venerable Sir, had this one assembly of disciples, all of whom were indeed free from taints. The Blessed One, Venerable Sir, had a monk named Ānanda as his attendant, his chief attendant. The Blessed One, Venerable Sir, had King Suddhodana as his father and Queen Māyā as the mother who bore him. The royal capital was the city named Kapilavatthu. For the Blessed One, Venerable Sir, such was the going forth, such was the renunciation, such was the striving, such was the full enlightenment, and such was the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma. We, Venerable Sir, having lived the holy life under the Blessed One and having become dispassionate towards sensual desires, have been reborn here.’

94. “Iti kho, bhikkhave, tathāgatassevesā dhammadhātu suppaṭividdhā, yassā dhammadhātuyā suppaṭividdhattā [V 2.0042] tathāgato atīte buddhe parinibbute chinnapapañce chinnavaṭume pariyādinnavaṭṭe sabbadukkhavītivatte jātitopi anussarati, nāmatopi anussarati, gottatopi [P 2.0054] anussarati, āyuppamāṇatopi anussarati, sāvakayugatopi anussarati, sāvakasannipātatopi anussarati ‘evaṃjaccā te bhagavanto ahesuṃ’ itipi. ‘Evaṃnāmā evaṃgottā evaṃsīlā evaṃdhammā evaṃpaññā evaṃvihārī evaṃvimuttā te bhagavanto ahesuṃ’ itipīti.

94. Thus, monks, this element of the Dhamma is well penetrated by the Tathāgata himself. Because this element of the Dhamma is well penetrated, the Tathāgata recollects past Buddhas who have attained final Nibbāna—who have cut off proliferation, severed the round of kamma, exhausted the round of suffering, and gone beyond all suffering—recollecting them by birth, by name, by clan, by lifespan, by their pair of disciples, and by their assembly of disciples, thus: ‘Those Blessed Ones were of such a birth.’ And thus: ‘Those Blessed Ones were of such a name, of such a clan, of such virtue, of such a Dhamma, of such wisdom, of such an abiding, and of such liberation.’

“Devatāpi tathāgatassa etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ, yena tathāgato atīte buddhe [T 2.0064] parinibbute chinnapapañce chinnavaṭume pariyādinnavaṭṭe sabbadukkhavītivatte jātitopi anussarati, nāmatopi anussarati, gottatopi anussarati, āyuppamāṇatopi anussarati, sāvakayugatopi anussarati, sāvakasannipātatopi anussarati ‘evaṃjaccā te bhagavanto ahesuṃ’ itipi. ‘Evaṃnāmā evaṃgottā evaṃsīlā evaṃdhammā evaṃpaññā evaṃvihārī evaṃvimuttā te bhagavanto ahesuṃ’ itipī”ti.

The deities also informed the Tathāgata of this matter, whereby the Tathāgata recollects past Buddhas who have attained final Nibbāna—who have cut off proliferation, severed the round of kamma, exhausted the round of suffering, and gone beyond all suffering—recollecting them by birth, by name, by clan, by lifespan, by their pair of disciples, and by their assembly of disciples, thus: ‘Those Blessed Ones were of such a birth.’ And thus: ‘Those Blessed Ones were of such a name, of such a clan, of such virtue, of such a Dhamma, of such wisdom, of such an abiding, and of such liberation.’

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

The Blessed One said this. Delighted, those monks rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.

Mahāpadānasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

The Mahāpadāna Sutta, the first, is concluded.

2. Mahānidānasuttaṃ

2. The Great Discourse on Causation

Paṭiccasamuppādo

Dependent Origination

95. Evaṃ [T 2.0065][M 2.0047][P 2.0055][V 2.0043] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā kurūsu viharati kammāsadhammaṃ nāma kammāsadammaṃ nāma (syā.) kurūnaṃ nigamo. Atha kho āyasmā ānando yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami, upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā ānando bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “acchariyaṃ, bhante, abbhutaṃ, bhante! Yāva gambhīro cāyaṃ, bhante, paṭiccasamuppādo gambhīrāvabhāso ca, atha ca pana me uttānakuttānako viya khāyatī”ti. “Mā hevaṃ, ānanda, avaca, mā hevaṃ, ānanda, avaca. Gambhīro cāyaṃ, ānanda, paṭiccasamuppādo gambhīrāvabhāso ca. Etassa, ānanda, dhammassa ananubodhā appaṭivedhā evamayaṃ pajā tantākulakajātā kulagaṇṭhikajātā gulāguṇṭhikajātā (sī. pī.), guṇagaṇṭhikajātā (syā.) muñjapabbajabhūtā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ saṃsāraṃ nātivattati.

95. Thus have I heard. At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kurus at a market town of the Kurus named Kammāsadhamma. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: 'Wonderful, venerable sir! Amazing, venerable sir! How profound is this dependent origination, and how profound it appears! And yet to me, it seems as if it were shallow.' 'Do not say so, Ānanda! Do not say so, Ānanda! Profound, Ānanda, is this dependent origination, and profound it appears. It is through not understanding, through not penetrating this Dhamma, that this generation has become like a tangled skein of thread, like a knotted ball of thread, like matted muñja and babbaja grass, and does not transcend the state of loss, the bad destination, the downfall, this saṃsāra.'

96. “‘Atthi idappaccayā jarāmaraṇa’nti iti puṭṭhena satā, ānanda, atthītissa vacanīyaṃ. ‘Kiṃpaccayā jarāmaraṇa’nti iti ce vadeyya, ‘jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇa’nti iccassa vacanīyaṃ.

96. Ānanda, if one were asked, 'Is there aging and death with this as its condition?' it should be said, 'There is.' If one were to say, 'With what as its condition is there aging and death?' it should be said, 'With birth as its condition, there is aging and death.'

“‘Atthi idappaccayā jātī’ti iti puṭṭhena satā, ānanda, atthītissa [P 2.0056] vacanīyaṃ. ‘Kiṃpaccayā jātī’ti iti ce vadeyya, ‘bhavapaccayā jātī’ti iccassa vacanīyaṃ.

Ānanda, if one were asked, 'Is there birth with this as its condition?' it should be said, 'There is.' If one were to say, 'With what as its condition is there birth?' it should be said, 'With becoming as its condition, there is birth.'

“‘Atthi idappaccayā bhavo’ti iti puṭṭhena satā, ānanda, atthītissa vacanīyaṃ[T 2.0066]. ‘Kiṃpaccayā bhavo’ti iti ce vadeyya, ‘upādānapaccayā bhavo’ti iccassa vacanīyaṃ.

Ānanda, if one were asked, 'Is there becoming with this as its condition?' it should be said, 'There is.' If one were to say, 'With what as its condition is there becoming?' it should be said, 'With clinging as its condition, there is becoming.'

“‘Atthi [V 2.0044] idappaccayā upādāna’nti iti puṭṭhena satā, ānanda, atthītissa vacanīyaṃ. ‘Kiṃpaccayā upādāna’nti iti ce vadeyya, ‘taṇhāpaccayā upādāna’nti iccassa vacanīyaṃ.

Ānanda, if one were asked, 'Is there clinging with this as its condition?' it should be said, 'There is.' If one were to say, 'With what as its condition is there clinging?' it should be said, 'With craving as its condition, there is clinging.'

“‘Atthi [M 2.0048] idappaccayā taṇhā’ti iti puṭṭhena satā, ānanda, atthītissa vacanīyaṃ. ‘Kiṃpaccayā taṇhā’ti iti ce vadeyya, ‘vedanāpaccayā taṇhā’ti iccassa vacanīyaṃ.

Ānanda, if one were asked, 'Is there craving with this as its condition?' it should be said, 'There is.' If one were to say, 'With what as its condition is there craving?' it should be said, 'With feeling as its condition, there is craving.'

“‘Atthi idappaccayā vedanā’ti iti puṭṭhena satā, ānanda, atthītissa vacanīyaṃ. ‘Kiṃpaccayā vedanā’ti iti ce vadeyya, ‘phassapaccayā vedanā’ti iccassa vacanīyaṃ.

Ānanda, if one were asked, 'Is there feeling with this as its condition?' it should be said, 'There is.' If one were to say, 'With what as its condition is there feeling?' it should be said, 'With contact as its condition, there is feeling.'

“‘Atthi idappaccayā phasso’ti iti puṭṭhena satā, ānanda, atthītissa vacanīyaṃ. ‘Kiṃpaccayā phasso’ti iti ce vadeyya, ‘nāmarūpapaccayā phasso’ti iccassa vacanīyaṃ.

Ānanda, if one were asked, 'Is there contact with this as its condition?' it should be said, 'There is.' If one were to say, 'With what as its condition is there contact?' it should be said, 'With name-and-form as its condition, there is contact.'

“‘Atthi idappaccayā nāmarūpa’nti iti puṭṭhena satā, ānanda, atthītissa vacanīyaṃ. ‘Kiṃpaccayā nāmarūpa’nti iti ce vadeyya, ‘viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpa’nti iccassa vacanīyaṃ.

Ānanda, if one were asked, 'Is there name-and-form with this as its condition?' it should be said, 'There is.' If one were to say, 'With what as its condition is there name-and-form?' it should be said, 'With consciousness as its condition, there is name-and-form.'

“‘Atthi idappaccayā viññāṇa’nti iti puṭṭhena satā, ānanda, atthītissa vacanīyaṃ. ‘Kiṃpaccayā viññāṇa’nti iti ce vadeyya, ‘nāmarūpapaccayā viññāṇa’nti iccassa vacanīyaṃ.

Ānanda, if one were asked, 'Is there consciousness with this as its condition?' it should be said, 'There is.' If one were to say, 'With what as its condition is there consciousness?' it should be said, 'With name-and-form as its condition, there is consciousness.'

97. “Iti kho, ānanda, nāmarūpapaccayā viññāṇaṃ, viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpaṃ, nāmarūpapaccayā phasso, phassapaccayā vedanā, vedanāpaccayā taṇhā, taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ, upādānapaccayā bhavo, bhavapaccayā jāti[T 2.0067], jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā [P 2.0057] sambhavanti. Evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti.

97. Thus, Ānanda, with name-and-form as condition, consciousness comes to be; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form comes to be; with name-and-form as condition, contact comes to be; with contact as condition, feeling comes to be; with feeling as condition, craving comes to be; with craving as condition, clinging comes to be; with clinging as condition, becoming comes to be; with becoming as condition, birth comes to be; with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.

98. “‘Jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇa’nti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ. Jāti ca hi, ānanda, nābhavissa sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ kassaci kimhici, seyyathidaṃ – devānaṃ vā devattāya, gandhabbānaṃ vā gandhabbattāya, yakkhānaṃ vā yakkhattāya, bhūtānaṃ vā bhūtattāya, manussānaṃ vā manussattāya, catuppadānaṃ vā catuppadattāya, pakkhīnaṃ vā pakkhittāya, sarīsapānaṃ vā sarīsapattāya siriṃsapānaṃ siriṃsapattāya (sī. syā.), tesaṃ tesañca hi, ānanda, sattānaṃ tadattāya [M 2.0049] jāti nābhavissa. Sabbaso jātiyā asati jātinirodhā [V 2.0045] api nu kho jarāmaraṇaṃ paññāyethā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo jarāmaraṇassa, yadidaṃ jāti”.

98. “‘With birth as condition, aging and death’—this has been said. And Ānanda, this is to be understood in this way: how with birth as condition comes aging and death. For if, Ānanda, there were no birth at all, in every way, in every respect, for anyone whatsoever in any state of existence—that is, of devas for the state of being a deva, of gandhabbas for the state of being a gandhabba, of yakkhas for the state of being a yakkha, of beings for the state of being a being, of humans for the state of being human, of quadrupeds for the state of being a quadruped, of birds for the state of being a bird, of reptiles for the state of being a reptile—if, Ānanda, for those various beings there were no birth into their respective states. With birth being completely absent, from the cessation of birth, would aging and death be discerned?” “That is not so, venerable sir.” “Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this the source, this the origin, this the condition for aging and death, namely, birth.”

99. “‘Bhavapaccayā jātī’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā bhavapaccayā jāti. Bhavo ca hi, ānanda, nābhavissa sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ kassaci kimhici, seyyathidaṃ – kāmabhavo vā rūpabhavo vā arūpabhavo vā, sabbaso bhave asati bhavanirodhā api nu kho jāti paññāyethā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo jātiyā, yadidaṃ bhavo”.

99. “‘With becoming as condition, birth’—this has been said. And Ānanda, this is to be understood in this way: how with becoming as condition comes birth. For if, Ānanda, there were no becoming at all, in every way, in every respect, for anyone whatsoever in any state of existence—that is, sensual-sphere becoming, form-sphere becoming, or formless-sphere becoming—with becoming being completely absent, from the cessation of becoming, would birth be discerned?” “That is not so, venerable sir.” “Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this the source, this the origin, this the condition for birth, namely, becoming.”

100. “‘Upādānapaccayā bhavo’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā upādānapaccayā bhavo. Upādānañca hi, ānanda, nābhavissa sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ kassaci kimhici[P 2.0058], seyyathidaṃ – kāmupādānaṃ vā diṭṭhupādānaṃ vā sīlabbatupādānaṃ vā attavādupādānaṃ vā, sabbaso upādāne asati upādānanirodhā api nu kho bhavo paññāyethā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu [T 2.0068] etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo bhavassa, yadidaṃ upādānaṃ”.

100. “‘With clinging as condition, becoming’—this has been said. And Ānanda, this is to be understood in this way: how with clinging as condition comes becoming. For if, Ānanda, there were no clinging at all, in every way, in every respect, for anyone whatsoever in any state of existence—that is, clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to rites and rituals, or clinging to the doctrine of self—with clinging being completely absent, from the cessation of clinging, would becoming be discerned?” “That is not so, venerable sir.” “Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this the source, this the origin, this the condition for becoming, namely, clinging.”

101. “‘Taṇhāpaccayā upādāna’nti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ. Taṇhā ca hi, ānanda, nābhavissa sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ kassaci kimhici, seyyathidaṃ – rūpataṇhā saddataṇhā gandhataṇhā rasataṇhā phoṭṭhabbataṇhā dhammataṇhā, sabbaso taṇhāya asati taṇhānirodhā api nu kho upādānaṃ paññāyethā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo upādānassa, yadidaṃ taṇhā”.

101. “‘With craving as condition, clinging’—this has been said. And Ānanda, this is to be understood in this way: how with craving as condition comes clinging. For if, Ānanda, there were no craving at all, in every way, in every respect, for anyone whatsoever in any state of existence—that is, craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for odors, craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, craving for mental phenomena—with craving being completely absent, from the cessation of craving, would clinging be discerned?” “That is not so, venerable sir.” “Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this the source, this the origin, this the condition for clinging, namely, craving.”

102. “‘Vedanāpaccayā taṇhā’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā vedanāpaccayā taṇhā. Vedanā [M 2.0050] ca hi, ānanda, nābhavissa sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ kassaci [T 2.0069] kimhici, seyyathidaṃ – cakkhusamphassajā vedanā sotasamphassajā vedanā ghānasamphassajā vedanā jivhāsamphassajā vedanā kāyasamphassajā vedanā manosamphassajā vedanā, sabbaso vedanāya asati vedanānirodhā api nu kho taṇhā paññāyethā”ti[V 2.0046]? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo taṇhāya, yadidaṃ vedanā”.

102. “‘With feeling as condition, craving’—this has been said. And Ānanda, this is to be understood in this way: how with feeling as condition comes craving. For if, Ānanda, there were no feeling at all, in every way, in every respect, for anyone whatsoever in any state of existence—that is, feeling born of eye-contact, feeling born of ear-contact, feeling born of nose-contact, feeling born of tongue-contact, feeling born of body-contact, feeling born of mind-contact—with feeling being completely absent, from the cessation of feeling, would craving be discerned?” “That is not so, venerable sir.” “Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this the source, this the origin, this the condition for craving, namely, feeling.”

103. “Iti kho panetaṃ, ānanda, vedanaṃ paṭicca taṇhā, taṇhaṃ paṭicca pariyesanā, pariyesanaṃ paṭicca lābho, lābhaṃ paṭicca vinicchayo, vinicchayaṃ paṭicca chandarāgo, chandarāgaṃ paṭicca ajjhosānaṃ, ajjhosānaṃ paṭicca pariggaho, pariggahaṃ paṭicca macchariyaṃ, macchariyaṃ paṭicca [P 2.0059] ārakkho. Ārakkhādhikaraṇaṃ daṇḍādānasatthādānakalahaviggahavivādatuvaṃtuvaṃpesuññamusāvādā aneke pāpakā akusalā dhammā sambhavanti.

103. “Thus, Ānanda, dependent on feeling, there is craving; dependent on craving, there is seeking; dependent on seeking, there is gain; dependent on gain, there is decision; dependent on decision, there is desire and passion; dependent on desire and passion, there is attachment; dependent on attachment, there is possession; dependent on possession, there is stinginess; dependent on stinginess, there is guarding. Because of guarding, taking up rods, taking up weapons, quarrels, conflicts, disputes, speaking ‘you, you,’ slander, and false speech—numerous evil, unwholesome states come to be.”

104. “‘Ārakkhādhikaraṇaṃ ārakkhaṃ paṭicca ārakkhādhikaraṇaṃ (syā.) daṇḍādānasatthādānakalahaviggahavivādatuvaṃtuvaṃpesuññamusāvādā aneke pāpakā akusalā dhammā sambhavantī’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā ārakkhādhikaraṇaṃ daṇḍādānasatthādānakalahaviggahavivādatuvaṃtuvaṃpesuññamusāvādā aneke pāpakā akusalā dhammā sambhavanti. Ārakkho ca hi, ānanda, nābhavissa sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ kassaci kimhici, sabbaso ārakkhe asati ārakkhanirodhā api nu kho daṇḍādānasatthādānakalahaviggahavivādatuvaṃtuvaṃpesuññamusāvādā aneke pāpakā akusalā dhammā sambhaveyyu”nti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa [T 2.0070] samudayo esa paccayo daṇḍādānasatthādānakalahaviggahavivādatuvaṃtuvaṃpesuññamusāvādānaṃ anekesaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ sambhavāya yadidaṃ ārakkho.

104. “‘Because of guarding, taking up rods, taking up weapons, quarrels, conflicts, disputes, speaking “you, you,” slander, and false speech—numerous evil, unwholesome states come to be’—this has been said. And Ānanda, this is to be understood in this way: how, because of guarding, numerous evil, unwholesome states come to be. For if, Ānanda, there were no guarding at all, in every way, in every respect, for anyone whatsoever in any state of existence, then with guarding being completely absent, from the cessation of guarding, would taking up rods, taking up weapons, quarrels, conflicts, disputes, speaking ‘you, you,’ slander, and false speech—numerous evil, unwholesome states—come to be?” “That is not so, venerable sir.” “Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this the source, this the origin, this the condition for the arising of these numerous evil, unwholesome states—taking up rods, taking up weapons, quarrels, conflicts, disputes, speaking ‘you, you,’ slander, and false speech—namely, guarding.”

105. “‘Macchariyaṃ paṭicca ārakkho’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā macchariyaṃ paṭicca ārakkho. Macchariyañca hi, ānanda, nābhavissa sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ kassaci kimhici[M 2.0051], sabbaso macchariye asati macchariyanirodhā api nu kho ārakkho paññāyethā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo ārakkhassa, yadidaṃ macchariyaṃ”.

105. “‘With stinginess as condition, guarding arises’—this was said. And, Ānanda, it should be understood by this method how, with stinginess as condition, guarding arises. For if, Ānanda, there were no stinginess at all, in any way, in any respect, for anyone in regard to anything, with the complete absence of stinginess, from the cessation of stinginess, would guarding be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.” “Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for guarding, namely, stinginess.”

106. “‘Pariggahaṃ paṭicca macchariya’nti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā pariggahaṃ paṭicca macchariyaṃ. Pariggaho [P 2.0060] ca hi, ānanda, nābhavissa sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ kassaci kimhici, sabbaso pariggahe asati [V 2.0047] pariggahanirodhā api nu kho macchariyaṃ paññāyethā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo macchariyassa, yadidaṃ pariggaho”.

106. “‘With possessiveness as condition, stinginess arises’—this was said. And, Ānanda, it should be understood by this method how, with possessiveness as condition, stinginess arises. For if, Ānanda, there were no possessiveness at all, in any way, in any respect, for anyone in regard to anything, with the complete absence of possessiveness, from the cessation of possessiveness, would stinginess be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.” “Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for stinginess, namely, possessiveness.”

107. “‘Ajjhosānaṃ paṭicca pariggaho’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā ajjhosānaṃ paṭicca pariggaho. Ajjhosānañca hi, ānanda, nābhavissa sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ kassaci kimhici, sabbaso ajjhosāne asati ajjhosānanirodhā api nu kho pariggaho paññāyethā”ti[T 2.0071]? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo pariggahassa – yadidaṃ ajjhosānaṃ”.

107. “‘With clinging as condition, possessiveness arises’—this was said. And, Ānanda, it should be understood by this method how, with clinging as condition, possessiveness arises. For if, Ānanda, there were no clinging at all, in any way, in any respect, for anyone in regard to anything, with the complete absence of clinging, from the cessation of clinging, would possessiveness be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.” “Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for possessiveness, namely, clinging.”

108. “‘Chandarāgaṃ paṭicca ajjhosāna’nti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā chandarāgaṃ paṭicca ajjhosānaṃ. Chandarāgo ca hi, ānanda, nābhavissa sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ kassaci kimhici, sabbaso chandarāge asati chandarāganirodhā api nu kho ajjhosānaṃ paññāyethā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo ajjhosānassa, yadidaṃ chandarāgo”.

108. “‘With desire and lust as condition, clinging arises’—this was said. And, Ānanda, it should be understood by this method how, with desire and lust as condition, clinging arises. For if, Ānanda, there were no desire and lust at all, in any way, in any respect, for anyone in regard to anything, with the complete absence of desire and lust, from the cessation of desire and lust, would clinging be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.” “Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for clinging, namely, desire and lust.”

109. “‘Vinicchayaṃ paṭicca chandarāgo’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā vinicchayaṃ paṭicca chandarāgo. Vinicchayo ca hi, ānanda, nābhavissa sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ kassaci kimhici, sabbaso vinicchaye asati vinicchayanirodhā api nu kho chandarāgo paññāyethā”ti? “No hetaṃ[P 2.0061], bhante”. “Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo chandarāgassa, yadidaṃ vinicchayo”.

109. “‘With decision as condition, desire and lust arise’—this was said. And, Ānanda, it should be understood by this method how, with decision as condition, desire and lust arise. For if, Ānanda, there were no decision at all, in any way, in any respect, for anyone in regard to anything, with the complete absence of decision, from the cessation of decision, would desire and lust be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.” “Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for desire and lust, namely, decision.”

110. “‘Lābhaṃ [M 2.0052] paṭicca vinicchayo’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā lābhaṃ paṭicca vinicchayo. Lābho ca hi, ānanda, nābhavissa sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ kassaci kimhici, sabbaso lābhe asati lābhanirodhā api nu kho vinicchayo paññāyethā”ti? “No hetaṃ, [T 2.0072] bhante”. “Tasmātihānanda eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo vinicchayassa, yadidaṃ lābho”.

110. “‘With gain as condition, decision arises’—this was said. And, Ānanda, it should be understood by this method how, with gain as condition, decision arises. For if, Ānanda, there were no gain at all, in any way, in any respect, for anyone in regard to anything, with the complete absence of gain, from the cessation of gain, would decision be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.” “Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for decision, namely, gain.”

111. “‘Pariyesanaṃ [V 2.0048] paṭicca lābho’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā pariyesanaṃ paṭicca lābho. Pariyesanā ca hi, ānanda, nābhavissa sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ kassaci kimhici, sabbaso pariyesanāya asati pariyesanānirodhā api nu kho lābho paññāyethā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo lābhassa, yadidaṃ pariyesanā”.

111. “‘With seeking as condition, gain arises’—this was said. And, Ānanda, it should be understood by this method how, with seeking as condition, gain arises. For if, Ānanda, there were no seeking at all, in any way, in any respect, for anyone in regard to anything, with the complete absence of seeking, from the cessation of seeking, would gain be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.” “Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for gain, namely, seeking.”

112. “‘Taṇhaṃ paṭicca pariyesanā’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā taṇhaṃ paṭicca pariyesanā. Taṇhā ca hi, ānanda, nābhavissa sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ kassaci kimhici, seyyathidaṃ – kāmataṇhā bhavataṇhā vibhavataṇhā, sabbaso taṇhāya asati taṇhānirodhā api nu kho pariyesanā paññāyethā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo pariyesanāya, yadidaṃ taṇhā. Iti kho, ānanda, ime dve dhammā ime dhammā (ka.) dvayena vedanāya ekasamosaraṇā bhavanti”.

112. “‘With craving as condition, seeking arises’—this was said. And, Ānanda, it should be understood by this method how, with craving as condition, seeking arises. For if, Ānanda, there were no craving at all, in any way, in any respect, for anyone in regard to anything—that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence—with the complete absence of craving, from the cessation of craving, would seeking be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.” “Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for seeking, namely, craving. Thus, Ānanda, these two phenomena, in two ways, have a single convergence in feeling.”

113. “‘Phassapaccayā [P 2.0062] vedanā’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā ‘phassapaccayā vedanā. Phasso ca hi, ānanda, nābhavissa sabbena sabbaṃ [T 2.0073] sabbathā sabbaṃ kassaci kimhici, seyyathidaṃ – cakkhusamphasso sotasamphasso ghānasamphasso jivhāsamphasso kāyasamphasso manosamphasso, sabbaso phasse asati phassanirodhā api nu kho vedanā paññāyethā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Tasmātihānanda[M 2.0053], eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo vedanāya, yadidaṃ phasso”.

113. “‘With contact as condition, feeling arises’—this was said. And, Ānanda, it should be understood by this method how, with contact as condition, feeling arises. For if, Ānanda, there were no contact at all, in any way, in any respect, for anyone in regard to anything—namely, eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact—with the complete absence of contact, from the cessation of contact, would feeling be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.” “Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for feeling, namely, contact.”

114. “‘Nāmarūpapaccayā phasso’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā nāmarūpapaccayā phasso. Yehi, ānanda, ākārehi yehi liṅgehi yehi nimittehi yehi uddesehi nāmakāyassa paññatti hoti, tesu ākāresu tesu liṅgesu tesu nimittesu tesu uddesesu asati api nu kho rūpakāye adhivacanasamphasso paññāyethā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Yehi, ānanda, ākārehi yehi liṅgehi yehi nimittehi yehi uddesehi rūpakāyassa paññatti hoti, tesu ākāresu…pe… tesu uddesesu asati api nu kho nāmakāye paṭighasamphasso paññāyethā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Yehi, ānanda, ākārehi…pe… yehi uddesehi nāmakāyassa ca rūpakāyassa ca paññatti hoti[V 2.0049], tesu ākāresu…pe… tesu uddesesu asati api nu kho adhivacanasamphasso vā paṭighasamphasso vā paññāyethā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Yehi, ānanda, ākārehi…pe… yehi uddesehi nāmarūpassa paññatti hoti, tesu ākāresu [T 2.0074] …pe… tesu uddesesu asati api nu kho phasso paññāyethā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo phassassa, yadidaṃ nāmarūpaṃ”.

114. “‘With name-and-form as condition, contact comes to be’—so it has been said. And, Ānanda, it is in this way that it should be understood how with name-and-form as condition, contact comes to be. By whatever modes, marks, signs, or designations the designation of the mental aggregate occurs, if those modes, marks, signs, or designations were absent, would designation-contact be discerned in the physical aggregate?” “No, venerable sir.” “By whatever modes, marks, signs, or designations the designation of the physical aggregate occurs, if those modes, marks, signs, or designations were absent, would resistance-contact be discerned in the mental aggregate?” “No, venerable sir.” “By whatever modes, marks, signs, or designations the designation of both the mental aggregate and the physical aggregate occurs, if those modes, marks, signs, or designations were absent, would either designation-contact or resistance-contact be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.” “By whatever modes, marks, signs, or designations the designation of name-and-form occurs, if those modes, marks, signs, or designations were absent, would contact be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.” “Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for contact—namely, name-and-form.”

115. “‘Viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpa’nti iti kho panetaṃ [P 2.0063] vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpaṃ. Viññāṇañca hi, ānanda, mātukucchismiṃ na okkamissatha, api nu kho nāmarūpaṃ mātukucchismiṃ samuccissathā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Viññāṇañca hi, ānanda, mātukucchismiṃ okkamitvā vokkamissatha, api nu kho nāmarūpaṃ itthattāya abhinibbattissathā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Viññāṇañca hi, ānanda, daharasseva sato vocchijjissatha kumārakassa vā kumārikāya vā, api nu kho nāmarūpaṃ vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ āpajjissathā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo nāmarūpassa – yadidaṃ viññāṇaṃ”.

115. “‘With consciousness as condition, name-and-form comes to be’—so it has been said. And, Ānanda, it is in this way that it should be understood how with consciousness as condition, name-and-form comes to be. If, Ānanda, consciousness were not to descend into the mother’s womb, would name-and-form coalesce in the mother's womb?” “No, venerable sir.” “If, Ānanda, consciousness, having descended into the mother’s womb, were to depart, would name-and-form be produced for this state of being?” “No, venerable sir.” “If, Ānanda, the consciousness of a young boy or girl were to be cut off, would name-and-form attain growth, development, and fullness?” “No, venerable sir.” “Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for name-and-form—namely, consciousness.”

116. “‘Nāmarūpapaccayā [M 2.0054] viññāṇa’nti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā nāmarūpapaccayā viññāṇaṃ. Viññāṇañca hi, ānanda, nāmarūpe patiṭṭhaṃ na labhissatha, api nu kho āyatiṃ jātijarāmaraṇaṃ dukkhasamudayasambhavo jātijarāmaraṇadukkhasamudayasambhavo (sī. syā. pī.) paññāyethā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo viññāṇassa yadidaṃ nāmarūpaṃ. Ettāvatā kho, ānanda, [T 2.0075] jāyetha vā jīyetha jiyyetha (ka.) vā mīyetha miyyetha (ka.) vā cavetha vā upapajjetha vā. Ettāvatā adhivacanapatho, ettāvatā niruttipatho, ettāvatā paññattipatho, ettāvatā paññāvacaraṃ, ettāvatā vaṭṭaṃ vattati itthattaṃ [P 2.0064] paññāpanāya yadidaṃ nāmarūpaṃ saha viññāṇena aññamaññapaccayatā pavattati.

116. “‘With name-and-form as condition, consciousness comes to be’—so it has been said. And, Ānanda, it is in this way that it should be understood how with name-and-form as condition, consciousness comes to be. If, Ānanda, consciousness were not to gain a footing in name-and-form, would the future arising of a mass of suffering—of birth, aging, and death—be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.” “Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for consciousness—namely, name-and-form. To this extent, Ānanda, one might be born or age or die or pass away or be reborn. To this extent is the path of designation, to this extent the path of expression, to this extent the path of concepts, to this extent the range of wisdom; to this extent the round turns for the designation of this state of being, that is to say, name-and-form together with consciousness, which proceeds by way of mutual conditionality.”

Attapaññatti

Designation of Self

117. “Kittāvatā ca, ānanda, attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti? Rūpiṃ vā hi, ānanda, parittaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti – “rūpī me paritto attā”ti. Rūpiṃ vā hi[V 2.0050], ānanda, anantaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti – ‘rūpī me ananto attā’ti. Arūpiṃ vā hi, ānanda, parittaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti – ‘arūpī me paritto attā’ti. Arūpiṃ vā hi, ānanda, anantaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti – ‘arūpī me ananto attā’ti.

117. “And to what extent, Ānanda, does one who designates a self, designate it? One who designates a self with form as limited, Ānanda, designates it thus: ‘My self has form and is limited.’ Or one who designates a self with form as boundless, Ānanda, designates it thus: ‘My self has form and is boundless.’ Or one who designates a self that is formless as limited, Ānanda, designates it thus: ‘My self is formless and is limited.’ Or one who designates a self that is formless as boundless, Ānanda, designates it thus: ‘My self is formless and is boundless.’”

118. “Tatrānanda, yo so rūpiṃ parittaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti. Etarahi vā so rūpiṃ parittaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti, tattha bhāviṃ vā so rūpiṃ parittaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti, ‘atathaṃ vā pana santaṃ tathattāya upakappessāmī’ti iti vā panassa hoti. Evaṃ santaṃ kho, ānanda, rūpiṃ rūpī (ka.) parittattānudiṭṭhi anusetīti iccālaṃ vacanāya.

118. “Therein, Ānanda, as to that one who designates a self with form as limited: one may designate a self with form as limited in the present; or one may designate a self with form as limited that will be so in a future state; or one may think, ‘Though it is unreal, I will contrive it to become real.’ This being so, Ānanda, it is fit to say that the underlying view ‘the self has form and is limited’ is latent in that person.”

“Tatrānanda, yo so rūpiṃ anantaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti. Etarahi vā so rūpiṃ anantaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti, tattha bhāviṃ vā so rūpiṃ anantaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti, ‘atathaṃ [T 2.0076] vā pana [M 2.0055] santaṃ tathattāya upakappessāmī’ti iti vā panassa hoti. Evaṃ santaṃ kho, ānanda, rūpiṃ rūpī (ka.) anantattānudiṭṭhi anusetīti iccālaṃ vacanāya.

“Therein, Ānanda, as to that one who designates a self with form as boundless: one may designate a self with form as boundless in the present; or one may designate a self with form as boundless that will be so in a future state; or one may think, ‘Though it is unreal, I will contrive it to become real.’ This being so, Ānanda, it is fit to say that the underlying view ‘the self has form and is boundless’ is latent in that person.”

“Tatrānanda, yo so arūpiṃ parittaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti. Etarahi vā so arūpiṃ parittaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti, tattha bhāviṃ vā so arūpiṃ parittaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti, ‘atathaṃ vā pana santaṃ tathattāya upakappessāmī’ti iti vā panassa hoti. Evaṃ santaṃ kho, ānanda, arūpiṃ arūpī (ka.) parittattānudiṭṭhi anusetīti iccālaṃ vacanāya.

“Therein, Ānanda, as to that one who designates a formless self as limited: one may designate a formless self as limited in the present; or one may designate a formless self as limited that will be so in a future state; or one may think, ‘Though it is unreal, I will contrive it to become real.’ This being so, Ānanda, it is fit to say that the underlying view ‘the self is formless and is limited’ is latent in that person.”

“Tatrānanda, yo so arūpiṃ anantaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti. Etarahi vā so arūpiṃ anantaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti, tattha bhāviṃ vā so arūpiṃ anantaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti, ‘atathaṃ vā pana santaṃ tathattāya upakappessāmī’ti iti vā panassa hoti. Evaṃ santaṃ kho, ānanda, arūpiṃ arūpī (ka.) anantattānudiṭṭhi anusetīti iccālaṃ vacanāya. Ettāvatā kho, ānanda, attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti.

“Ānanda, among them, a certain person designates a self as formless and boundless. He designates a self as formless and boundless either in the present, or as becoming so in a future state; or it occurs to him thus: ‘Though it is unreal, I will contrive for it to become real.’ This being so, Ānanda, it is fit to say that the underlying view ‘the self is formless and boundless’ lies latent. To this extent, Ānanda, one who designates a self so designates it.

Naattapaññatti

Non-designation of Self

119. “Kittāvatā ca, ānanda, attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti? Rūpiṃ vā hi, ānanda, parittaṃ attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti – ‘rūpī me paritto attā’ti. Rūpiṃ [V 2.0051] vā hi, ānanda, anantaṃ attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti – ‘rūpī me ananto attā’ti. Arūpiṃ vā hi, ānanda, parittaṃ attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti – ‘arūpī me paritto attā’ti. Arūpiṃ vā hi, ānanda, anantaṃ [T 2.0077] attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti – ‘arūpī me ananto attā’ti.

119. “And to what extent, Ānanda, does one who does not designate a self not so designate it? Ānanda, one who does not designate a self does not designate it as having form and being limited, thinking: ‘My self has form and is limited.’ Nor does he designate a self as having form and being boundless, thinking: ‘My self has form and is boundless.’ Nor does he designate a self as being formless and limited, thinking: ‘My self is formless and is limited.’ Nor does he designate a self as being formless and boundless, thinking: ‘My self is formless and is boundless.’”

120. “Tatrānanda, yo so rūpiṃ parittaṃ attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti. Etarahi vā so rūpiṃ parittaṃ attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti, tattha bhāviṃ vā so rūpiṃ parittaṃ attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti, ‘atathaṃ vā pana santaṃ tathattāya upakappessāmī’ti iti vā panassa [P 2.0065] na hoti. Evaṃ santaṃ kho, ānanda, rūpiṃ parittattānudiṭṭhi nānusetīti iccālaṃ vacanāya.

120. “Ānanda, among them, a person who does not designate a self as having form and being limited, does not so designate it. He does not designate a self as having form and being limited either in the present, nor as becoming so in a future state; nor does it occur to him: ‘Though it is unreal, I will contrive for it to become real.’ This being so, Ānanda, it is fit to say that the underlying view ‘the self has form and is limited’ does not lie latent.

“Tatrānanda[M 2.0056], yo so rūpiṃ anantaṃ attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti. Etarahi vā so rūpiṃ anantaṃ attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti, tattha bhāviṃ vā so rūpiṃ anantaṃ attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti, ‘atathaṃ vā pana santaṃ tathattāya upakappessāmī’ti iti vā panassa na hoti. Evaṃ santaṃ kho, ānanda, rūpiṃ anantattānudiṭṭhi nānusetīti iccālaṃ vacanāya.

“Ānanda, among them, a person who does not designate a self as having form and being boundless, does not so designate it. He does not designate a self as having form and being boundless either in the present, nor as becoming so in a future state; nor does it occur to him: ‘Though it is unreal, I will contrive for it to become real.’ This being so, Ānanda, it is fit to say that the underlying view ‘the self has form and is boundless’ does not lie latent.

“Tatrānanda, yo so arūpiṃ parittaṃ attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti. Etarahi vā so arūpiṃ parittaṃ attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti, tattha bhāviṃ vā so arūpiṃ parittaṃ attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti, ‘atathaṃ vā pana santaṃ tathattāya upakappessāmī’ti iti vā panassa na hoti. Evaṃ santaṃ kho, ānanda, arūpiṃ parittattānudiṭṭhi nānusetīti iccālaṃ vacanāya.

“Ānanda, among them, a person who does not designate a self as being formless and limited, does not so designate it. He does not designate a self as being formless and limited either in the present, nor as becoming so in a future state; nor does it occur to him: ‘Though it is unreal, I will contrive for it to become real.’ This being so, Ānanda, it is fit to say that the underlying view ‘the self is formless and is limited’ does not lie latent.

“Tatrānanda, yo so arūpiṃ anantaṃ attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti. Etarahi vā so arūpiṃ anantaṃ attānaṃ na paññapento na [T 2.0078] paññapeti, tattha bhāviṃ vā so arūpiṃ anantaṃ attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti, ‘atathaṃ vā pana santaṃ tathattāya upakappessāmī’ti iti vā panassa na [P 2.0066] hoti. Evaṃ santaṃ kho, ānanda, arūpiṃ anantattānudiṭṭhi nānusetīti iccālaṃ vacanāya. Ettāvatā kho, ānanda, attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti.

“Ānanda, among them, a person who does not designate a self as being formless and boundless, does not so designate it. He does not designate a self as being formless and boundless either in the present, nor as becoming so in a future state; nor does it occur to him: ‘Though it is unreal, I will contrive for it to become real.’ This being so, Ānanda, it is fit to say that the underlying view ‘the self is formless and is boundless’ does not lie latent. To this extent, Ānanda, one who does not designate a self does not so designate it.

Attasamanupassanā

Regarding the Self

121. “Kittāvatā [V 2.0052] ca, ānanda, attānaṃ samanupassamāno samanupassati? Vedanaṃ vā hi, ānanda, attānaṃ samanupassamāno samanupassati – ‘vedanā me attā’ti. ‘Na heva kho me vedanā attā, appaṭisaṃvedano me attā’ti iti vā hi, ānanda, attānaṃ samanupassamāno samanupassati. ‘Na heva kho me vedanā attā, nopi appaṭisaṃvedano me attā, attā me vediyati, vedanādhammo hi me attā’ti iti vā hi, ānanda, attānaṃ samanupassamāno samanupassati.

121. “And in what way, Ānanda, does one who regards the self regard it? One, Ānanda, regarding the self, regards feeling as the self, thus: ‘Feeling is my self.’ Or else, Ānanda, regarding the self, one regards it thus: ‘Feeling is not my self; my self is insentient.’ Or else, Ānanda, regarding the self, one regards it thus: ‘Feeling is not my self, nor is my self insentient; my self feels, for my self has the nature of feeling.’”

122. “Tatrānanda, yo so evamāha – ‘vedanā me attā’ti, so evamassa vacanīyo – ‘tisso kho imā, āvuso, vedanā – sukhā vedanā dukkhā vedanā adukkhamasukhā vedanā. Imāsaṃ kho tvaṃ tissannaṃ [M 2.0057] vedanānaṃ katamaṃ attato samanupassasī’ti? Yasmiṃ, ānanda, samaye sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, neva tasmiṃ samaye dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, na adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti; sukhaṃyeva tasmiṃ samaye vedanaṃ vedeti. Yasmiṃ, ānanda, samaye dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, neva tasmiṃ samaye sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, na adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti; dukkhaṃyeva tasmiṃ samaye vedanaṃ vedeti. Yasmiṃ, ānanda, samaye adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ [T 2.0079] vedeti, neva tasmiṃ samaye sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, na dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti; adukkhamasukhaṃyeva tasmiṃ samaye vedanaṃ vedeti.

122. “Therein, Ānanda, one who says, ‘Feeling is my self,’ should be told thus: ‘Friend, there are these three feelings: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Which of these three feelings do you regard as self?’ When, Ānanda, one experiences a pleasant feeling, at that time one does not experience a painful feeling or a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; at that time one experiences only a pleasant feeling. When, Ānanda, one experiences a painful feeling, at that time one does not experience a pleasant feeling or a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; at that time one experiences only a painful feeling. When, Ānanda, one experiences a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, at that time one does not experience a pleasant feeling or a painful feeling; at that time one experiences only a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.”

123. “Sukhāpi kho, ānanda, vedanā aniccā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā khayadhammā vayadhammā virāgadhammā nirodhadhammā. Dukkhāpi kho, ānanda, vedanā aniccā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā khayadhammā [P 2.0067] vayadhammā virāgadhammā nirodhadhammā. Adukkhamasukhāpi kho, ānanda, vedanā aniccā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā khayadhammā vayadhammā virāgadhammā nirodhadhammā. Tassa sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vediyamānassa ‘eso me attā’ti hoti. Tassāyeva sukhāya vedanāya nirodhā ‘byagā byaggā (sī. ka.) me attā’ti hoti. Dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vediyamānassa ‘eso me attā’ti hoti. Tassāyeva dukkhāya vedanāya nirodhā ‘byagā me attā’ti hoti. Adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vediyamānassa ‘eso me attā’ti hoti. Tassāyeva adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya nirodhā ‘byagā me attā’ti hoti. Iti so diṭṭheva dhamme aniccasukhadukkhavokiṇṇaṃ uppādavayadhammaṃ attānaṃ samanupassamāno samanupassati, yo so evamāha – ‘vedanā me attā’ti. Tasmātihānanda, etena petaṃ nakkhamati – ‘vedanā me attā’ti samanupassituṃ.

123. “Pleasant feeling, Ānanda, is also impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, of a nature to be destroyed, of a nature to vanish, of a nature to fade away, and of a nature to cease. Painful feeling, Ānanda, is also impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, of a nature to be destroyed, of a nature to vanish, of a nature to fade away, and of a nature to cease. Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, Ānanda, is also impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, of a nature to be destroyed, of a nature to vanish, of a nature to fade away, and of a nature to cease. For one who is experiencing a pleasant feeling, the thought arises, ‘This is my self.’ With the cessation of that very pleasant feeling, the thought arises, ‘My self has perished.’ For one who is experiencing a painful feeling, the thought arises, ‘This is my self.’ With the cessation of that very painful feeling, the thought arises, ‘My self has perished.’ For one who is experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, the thought arises, ‘This is my self.’ With the cessation of that very neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, the thought arises, ‘My self has perished.’ Thus, one who says, ‘Feeling is my self,’ regards a self that in this very life is impermanent, mixed with pleasure and pain, and subject to arising and passing away. Therefore, Ānanda, for this reason it is not fitting to regard thus: ‘Feeling is my self.’”

124. “Tatrānanda[V 2.0053], yo so evamāha – ‘na heva kho me vedanā attā, appaṭisaṃvedano me attā’ti, so evamassa vacanīyo – ‘yattha panāvuso, sabbaso vedayitaṃ natthi api nu kho, tattha “ayamahamasmī”ti siyā’”ti[T 2.0080]? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Tasmātihānanda, etena petaṃ nakkhamati – ‘na heva kho me vedanā attā, appaṭisaṃvedano me attā’ti samanupassituṃ.

124. “Therein, Ānanda, one who says, ‘Feeling is not my self; my self is insentient,’ should be told thus: ‘Friend, where there is no feeling whatsoever, could there be the thought, “I am”?’ ‘No, venerable sir.’ ‘Therefore, Ānanda, for this reason it is not fitting to regard thus: “Feeling is not my self; my self is insentient.”’”

125. “Tatrānanda[M 2.0058], yo so evamāha – ‘na heva kho me vedanā attā, nopi appaṭisaṃvedano me attā, attā me vediyati, vedanādhammo hi me attā’ti. So evamassa vacanīyo – vedanā ca hi, āvuso, sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ aparisesā nirujjheyyuṃ. Sabbaso vedanāya asati vedanānirodhā api nu kho tattha ‘ayamahamasmī’ti siyā”ti? ‘No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Tasmātihānanda, etena petaṃ nakkhamati – “na heva kho [P 2.0068] me vedanā attā, nopi appaṭisaṃvedano me attā, attā me vediyati, vedanādhammo hi me attā’ti samanupassituṃ.

125. “Therein, Ānanda, one who says, ‘Feeling is not my self, nor is my self insentient; my self feels, for my self has the nature of feeling,’ should be told thus: ‘Friend, if feelings were to cease completely, in every way, in every respect, without remainder, with feeling being totally absent due to the cessation of feeling, could there be the thought, “I am”?’ ‘No, venerable sir.’ ‘Therefore, Ānanda, for this reason it is not fitting to regard thus: “Feeling is not my self, nor is my self insentient; my self feels, for my self has the nature of feeling.”’”

126. “Yato kho, ānanda, bhikkhu neva vedanaṃ attānaṃ samanupassati, nopi appaṭisaṃvedanaṃ attānaṃ samanupassati, nopi ‘attā me vediyati, vedanādhammo hi me attā’ti samanupassati. So evaṃ na samanupassanto na ca kiñci loke upādiyati, anupādiyaṃ na paritassati, aparitassaṃ aparitassanaṃ (ka.) paccattaññeva parinibbāyati, ‘khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānāti. Evaṃ vimuttacittaṃ kho, ānanda, bhikkhuṃ yo evaṃ vadeyya – ‘hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā itissa iti sā (aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pāṭhantaraṃ) diṭṭhī’ti, tadakallaṃ. ‘Na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā itissa [T 2.0081] diṭṭhī’ti, tadakallaṃ. ‘Hoti ca na ca hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā itissa diṭṭhī’ti, tadakallaṃ. ‘Neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā itissa diṭṭhī’ti, tadakallaṃ. Taṃ kissa hetu? Yāvatā, ānanda, adhivacanaṃ yāvatā adhivacanapatho, yāvatā nirutti yāvatā niruttipatho, yāvatā paññatti yāvatā paññattipatho, yāvatā paññā yāvatā paññāvacaraṃ, yāvatā vaṭṭaṃ yāvatā vaṭṭaṃ vaṭṭati (ka. sī.), yāvatā vaṭṭati yāvatā vaṭṭaṃ vaṭṭati (ka. sī.), tadabhiññāvimutto bhikkhu, tadabhiññāvimuttaṃ bhikkhuṃ ‘na jānāti na passati itissa diṭṭhī’ti, tadakallaṃ.

126. “When, Ānanda, a bhikkhu regards neither feeling as the self, nor the insentient as the self, nor does he regard thus: ‘My self feels, for my self has the nature of feeling,’ so not regarding, he does not cling to anything in the world. Not clinging, he is not agitated. Being unagitated, he personally attains Parinibbāna. He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of existence.’ Concerning a bhikkhu whose mind is thus liberated, Ānanda, if one were to say: ‘The Tathāgata exists after death—this is his view,’ that would be unfitting. ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death—this is his view,’ that would be unfitting. ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death—this is his view,’ that would be unfitting. ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death—this is his view,’ that would be unfitting. For what reason? As far, Ānanda, as there is designation and the path of designation, as far as there is expression and the path of expression, as far as there is concept and the path of concept, as far as there is wisdom and the sphere of wisdom, as far as the round of existence extends and as far as it revolves—a bhikkhu is liberated by directly knowing that. To say of a bhikkhu who is liberated by directly knowing that, ‘He does not know, he does not see—this is his view,’ that would be unfitting.”

Satta viññāṇaṭṭhiti

The Seven Stations of Consciousness

127. “Satta kho, ānanda satta kho imā ānanda (ka. sī. syā.), viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo, dve āyatanāni. Katamā satta? Santānanda, sattā nānattakāyā [P 2.0069] nānattasaññino, seyyathāpi manussā[M 2.0059], ekacce ca devā, ekacce ca [V 2.0054] vinipātikā. Ayaṃ paṭhamā viññāṇaṭṭhiti. Santānanda, sattā nānattakāyā ekattasaññino, seyyathāpi devā brahmakāyikā paṭhamābhinibbattā. Ayaṃ dutiyā viññāṇaṭṭhiti. Santānanda, sattā ekattakāyā nānattasaññino, seyyathāpi devā ābhassarā. Ayaṃ tatiyā viññāṇaṭṭhiti. Santānanda, sattā ekattakāyā ekattasaññino, seyyathāpi devā subhakiṇhā. Ayaṃ catutthī viññāṇaṭṭhiti. Santānanda, sattā sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā ‘ananto ākāso’ti ākāsānañcāyatanūpagā. Ayaṃ pañcamī viññāṇaṭṭhiti[T 2.0082]. Santānanda, sattā sabbaso ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘anantaṃ viññāṇa’nti viññāṇañcāyatanūpagā. Ayaṃ chaṭṭhī viññāṇaṭṭhiti. Santānanda, sattā sabbaso viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘natthi kiñcī’ti ākiñcaññāyatanūpagā. Ayaṃ sattamī viññāṇaṭṭhiti. Asaññasattāyatanaṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatanameva dutiyaṃ.

127. “Ānanda, there are seven stations of consciousness and two spheres. What are the seven? There are, Ānanda, beings with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, such as human beings, some devas, and some beings in states of woe. This is the first station of consciousness. There are, Ānanda, beings with diverse bodies and singular perception, such as the devas of Brahmā’s retinue, first reborn through the first jhāna. This is the second station of consciousness. There are, Ānanda, beings with singular bodies and diverse perceptions, such as the devas of Streaming Radiance. This is the third station of consciousness. There are, Ānanda, beings with singular bodies and singular perception, such as the devas of Refulgent Glory. This is the fourth station of consciousness. There are, Ānanda, beings who, by completely transcending perceptions of form, by the cessation of perceptions of resistance, by not attending to perceptions of diversity, perceiving ‘space is infinite,’ have reached the sphere of infinite space. This is the fifth station of consciousness. There are, Ānanda, beings who, by completely transcending the sphere of infinite space, perceiving ‘consciousness is infinite,’ have reached the sphere of infinite consciousness. This is the sixth station of consciousness. There are, Ānanda, beings who, by completely transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, perceiving ‘there is nothing,’ have reached the sphere of nothingness. This is the seventh station of consciousness. The sphere of non-percipient beings, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the second.”

128. “Tatrānanda, yāyaṃ paṭhamā viññāṇaṭṭhiti nānattakāyā nānattasaññino, seyyathāpi manussā, ekacce ca devā, ekacce ca vinipātikā. Yo nu kho, ānanda, tañca pajānāti, tassā ca samudayaṃ pajānāti, tassā ca atthaṅgamaṃ pajānāti, tassā ca assādaṃ pajānāti, tassā ca ādīnavaṃ pajānāti, tassā ca nissaraṇaṃ pajānāti, kallaṃ nu tena tadabhinanditu”nti? “No [P 2.0070] hetaṃ, bhante”…pe… “tatrānanda, yamidaṃ asaññasattāyatanaṃ. Yo nu kho, ānanda, tañca pajānāti, tassa ca samudayaṃ pajānāti, tassa ca atthaṅgamaṃ pajānāti, tassa ca assādaṃ pajānāti, tassa ca ādīnavaṃ pajānāti, tassa ca nissaraṇaṃ pajānāti, kallaṃ nu tena tadabhinanditu”nti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Tatrānanda, yamidaṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ. Yo nu kho, ānanda, tañca pajānāti, tassa ca samudayaṃ pajānāti, tassa ca atthaṅgamaṃ pajānāti, [T 2.0083] tassa ca assādaṃ pajānāti, tassa ca ādīnavaṃ pajānāti, tassa ca nissaraṇaṃ pajānāti, kallaṃ nu tena tadabhinanditu”nti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. Yato kho, ānanda, bhikkhu imāsañca sattannaṃ viññāṇaṭṭhitīnaṃ imesañca dvinnaṃ āyatanānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ viditvā anupādā vimutto hoti, ayaṃ vuccatānanda, bhikkhu paññāvimutto.

128. “Therein, Ānanda, as to this first station of consciousness—beings with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, such as human beings, some devas, and some beings in states of woe: if a bhikkhu knows it, knows its origin, knows its cessation, knows its gratification, knows its danger, and knows its escape, would it be proper for him to delight in it?” “Indeed not, venerable sir.” … “Therein, Ānanda, as to this sphere of non-percipient beings: if a bhikkhu knows it, knows its origin, knows its cessation, knows its gratification, knows its danger, and knows its escape, would it be proper for him to delight in it?” “Indeed not, venerable sir.” “Therein, Ānanda, as to this sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception: if a bhikkhu knows it, knows its origin, knows its cessation, knows its gratification, knows its danger, and knows its escape, would it be proper for him to delight in it?” “Indeed not, venerable sir.” When, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having known as they really are the origin, cessation, gratification, danger, and escape concerning these seven stations of consciousness and these two spheres, is liberated without clinging, this bhikkhu, Ānanda, is called one liberated by wisdom.”

Aṭṭha vimokkhā

The Eight Liberations
