When this was said, the Mallas of Kusinārā said this to those assemblies and groups: 'The Blessed One attained parinibbāna in our village territory. We will not give a share of the Blessed One's bodily relics.'

237. Evaṃ vutte doṇo brāhmaṇo te saṅghe gaṇe etadavoca –

237. When this was said, the brahmin Doṇa said this to those assemblies and groups:

“Suṇantu [M 2.0137] bhonto mama ekavācaṃ,

Amhāka chandānurakkhaṇatthaṃ niggahītalopo; Buddho ahu khantivādo;

Na [T 2.0193][V 2.0125] hi sādhu yaṃ uttamapuggalassa,

Sarīrabhāge siyā sampahāro.

‘Sirs, please listen to my one utterance. Our Buddha was one who taught forbearance. It is indeed not good that there should be conflict over the division of the bodily relics of the supreme person.’

Sabbeva bhonto sahitā samaggā,

Sammodamānā karomaṭṭhabhāge;

Vitthārikā hontu disāsu thūpā,

Bahū janā cakkhumato pasannā”ti.

‘Sirs, let us all, united, harmonious, and rejoicing, make eight shares. May stūpas be widespread in the directions, for many people have faith in the One with the Eye.’

238. “Tena hi, brāhmaṇa, tvaññeva bhagavato sarīrāni aṭṭhadhā samaṃ savibhattaṃ vibhajāhī”ti. “Evaṃ, bho”ti kho doṇo brāhmaṇo tesaṃ saṅghānaṃ gaṇānaṃ paṭissutvā bhagavato sarīrāni aṭṭhadhā samaṃ suvibhattaṃ vibhajitvā te saṅghe gaṇe etadavoca – “imaṃ me bhonto tumbaṃ dadantu ahampi tumbassa thūpañca mahañca karissāmī”ti. Adaṃsu kho te doṇassa brāhmaṇassa tumbaṃ.

238. “Then, Brahmin, you yourself divide the Blessed One’s relics into eight equal and well-divided shares.” “Very well, sirs,” replied the brahmin Doṇa. Having assented to those assemblies and groups, he divided the Blessed One’s relics into eight equal and well-divided shares. Then he addressed those assemblies and groups: “Sirs, give me this measuring urn. I too will build a stupa and hold a festival for the measuring urn.” They gave the measuring urn to the brahmin Doṇa.

Assosuṃ kho pippalivaniyā pipphalivaniyā (syā.) moriyā – “bhagavā kira kusinārāyaṃ parinibbuto”ti. Atha kho pippalivaniyā moriyā kosinārakānaṃ mallānaṃ dūtaṃ pāhesuṃ – “bhagavāpi khattiyo mayampi khattiyā, mayampi arahāma bhagavato sarīrānaṃ bhāgaṃ, mayampi bhagavato sarīrānaṃ thūpañca mahañca karissāmā”ti. “Natthi bhagavato sarīrānaṃ bhāgo, vibhattāni bhagavato sarīrāni. Ito aṅgāraṃ harathā”ti. Te tato aṅgāraṃ hariṃsu āhariṃsu (syā. ka.).

The Moriyas of Pippalivana heard: “The Blessed One, it is said, has attained parinibbāna at Kusinārā.” Then the Moriyas of Pippalivana sent a messenger to the Mallas of Kusinārā, saying: “The Blessed One was a Khattiya, and we too are Khattiyas. We too are worthy of a share of the Blessed One’s relics. We too will build a stupa and hold a festival for the Blessed One’s relics.” The Mallas replied: “There is no share of the Blessed One’s relics left. The Blessed One’s relics have been divided. Take the embers from here.” So they took the embers from there.

Dhātuthūpapūjā

The Veneration of the Relic Stupas

239. Atha kho rājā māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto rājagahe bhagavato sarīrānaṃ thūpañca mahañca akāsi. Vesālikāpi [P 2.0167] licchavī vesāliyaṃ [T 2.0194] bhagavato sarīrānaṃ thūpañca mahañca akaṃsu. Kapilavatthuvāsīpi sakyā kapilavatthusmiṃ bhagavato sarīrānaṃ thūpañca mahañca akaṃsu. Allakappakāpi bulayo allakappe bhagavato sarīrānaṃ thūpañca mahañca akaṃsu. Rāmagāmakāpi koḷiyā rāmagāme bhagavato sarīrānaṃ thūpañca mahañca akaṃsu. Veṭṭhadīpakopi brāhmaṇo veṭṭhadīpe bhagavato [M 2.0138] sarīrānaṃ thūpañca mahañca akāsi. Pāveyyakāpi mallā pāvāyaṃ bhagavato sarīrānaṃ thūpañca mahañca akaṃsu. Kosinārakāpi mallā kusinārāyaṃ bhagavato sarīrānaṃ thūpañca mahañca akaṃsu. Doṇopi brāhmaṇo tumbassa thūpañca mahañca akāsi. Pippalivaniyāpi moriyā pippalivane [V 2.0126] aṅgārānaṃ thūpañca mahañca akaṃsu. Iti aṭṭha sarīrathūpā navamo tumbathūpo dasamo aṅgārathūpo. Evametaṃ bhūtapubbanti.

239. Then the King of Magadha, Ajātasattu, son of the Videhī queen, built a stupa for the Blessed One’s relics and held a festival at Rājagaha. The Licchavis of Vesālī also built a stupa for the Blessed One’s relics and held a festival at Vesālī. The Sakyans of Kapilavatthu also built a stupa for the Blessed One’s relics and held a festival at Kapilavatthu. The Bulis of Allakappa also built a stupa for the Blessed One’s relics and held a festival at Allakappa. The Koliyas of Rāmagāma also built a stupa for the Blessed One’s relics and held a festival at Rāmagāma. The brahmin of Veṭṭhadīpa also built a stupa for the Blessed One’s relics and held a festival at Veṭṭhadīpa. The Mallas of Pāvā also built a stupa for the Blessed One’s relics and held a festival at Pāvā. The Mallas of Kusinārā also built a stupa for the Blessed One’s relics and held a festival at Kusinārā. The brahmin Doṇa also built a stupa for the measuring urn and held a festival. The Moriyas of Pippalivana also built a stupa for the embers and held a festival at Pippalivana. Thus, there were eight stupas for the bodily relics, the ninth was the stupa for the measuring urn, and the tenth was the stupa for the embers. Thus it was in the past.

240. Aṭṭhadoṇaṃ cakkhumato sarīraṃ, sattadoṇaṃ jambudīpe mahenti.

240. The relics of the One with Vision were eight measures; seven measures are venerated in Jambudīpa.

Ekañca doṇaṃ purisavaruttamassa, rāmagāme nāgarājā maheti.

And one measure of the foremost of men, the Nāga king venerates at Rāmagāma.

Ekāhi dāṭhā tidivehi pūjitā, ekā pana gandhārapure mahīyati;

Kāliṅgarañño vijite punekaṃ, ekaṃ pana nāgarājā maheti.

One tooth relic is worshipped by the gods of Tāvatiṃsa, another is venerated in the city of Gandhāra; yet another is in the realm of the Kāliṅga king, and one is venerated by the Nāga king.

Tasseva [T 2.0195] tejena ayaṃ vasundharā,

Āyāgaseṭṭhehi mahī alaṅkatā;

Evaṃ imaṃ cakkhumato sarīraṃ,

Susakkataṃ sakkatasakkatehi.

By his very power, this earth is adorned, the ground embellished with the foremost objects of veneration. Thus, these relics of the One with Vision are well-venerated by those who are to be venerated.

Devindanāgindanarindapūjito[P 2.0168],

Manussindaseṭṭhehi tatheva pūjito;

Taṃ vandatha taṃ taṃ vandatha (syā.) pañjalikā labhitvā,

Buddho have kappasatehi dullabhoti.

Worshipped by lords of devas, lords of nāgas, and lords of men, likewise worshipped by the foremost of human lords; having obtained this, venerate them with joined palms, for a Buddha is indeed hard to find even in hundreds of aeons.

Cattālīsa samā dantā, kesā lomā ca sabbaso;

Devā hariṃsu ekekaṃ, cakkavāḷaparamparāti.

The forty even teeth, and all the head-hairs and body-hairs, became relics; the devas carried them off one by one, through successive world-systems.

Mahāparinibbānasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The third recitation section of the Great Discourse on the Final Parinibbāna is concluded.

4. Mahāsudassanasuttaṃ

4. The Discourse on the Great King of Glory

241. Evaṃ [T 2.0196][M 2.0139][V 2.0127][P 2.0169] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā kusinārāyaṃ viharati upavattane mallānaṃ sālavane antarena yamakasālānaṃ parinibbānasamaye. Atha kho āyasmā ānando yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā ānando bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “mā, bhante, bhagavā imasmiṃ khuddakanagarake ujjaṅgalanagarake sākhānagarake parinibbāyi. Santi, bhante, aññāni mahānagarāni. Seyyathidaṃ – campā, rājagahaṃ, sāvatthi, sāketaṃ, kosambī, bārāṇasī; ettha bhagavā parinibbāyatu. Ettha bahū khattiyamahāsālā brāhmaṇamahāsālā gahapatimahāsālā tathāgate abhippasannā, te tathāgatassa sarīrapūjaṃ karissantī”ti.

241. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling in Kusinārā, at the Upavattana sal-grove of the Mallas, between the twin sal trees, at the time of his final attainment of Nibbāna. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One not attain final Nibbāna in this small town, this undeveloped town, this branch-town. Venerable Sir, there are other great cities, such as Campā, Rājagaha, Sāvatthī, Sāketa, Kosambī, and Bārāṇasī. Let the Blessed One attain final Nibbāna there. In those cities, there are many wealthy nobles, wealthy brahmins, and wealthy householders who are deeply devoted to the Tathāgata. They will perform the veneration of the Tathāgata’s bodily relics.”

242. “Mā hevaṃ, ānanda, avaca; mā hevaṃ, ānanda, avaca – khuddakanagarakaṃ ujjaṅgalanagarakaṃ sākhānagaraka”nti.

242. “Do not say so, Ānanda. Do not say, Ānanda, that this is a small town, an undeveloped town, a branch-town.”

Kusāvatīrājadhānī

The Royal Capital of Kusāvatī

“Bhūtapubbaṃ, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano nāma ahosi khattiyo muddhāvasitto khattiyo muddhābhisitto (ka.), cakkavattīdhammiko dhammarājā (mahāparinibbānasutta) cāturanto vijitāvī janapadatthāvariyappatto[P 2.0170]. Rañño, ānanda, mahāsudassanassa ayaṃ kusinārā kusāvatī nāma rājadhānī ahosi. Puratthimena ca pacchimena ca dvādasayojanāni āyāmena, uttarena ca dakkhiṇena ca sattayojanāni vitthārena. Kusāvatī, ānanda, rājadhānī iddhā ceva ahosi phītā ca bahujanā ca ākiṇṇamanussā ca subhikkhā ca. Seyyathāpi, ānanda[T 2.0197], devānaṃ āḷakamandā nāma rājadhānī iddhā ceva hoti phītā ca iddhā ceva ahosi phītā ca (syā.) bahujanā ca ākiṇṇayakkhā ca subhikkhā ca; evameva kho, ānanda, kusāvatī rājadhānī iddhā ceva ahosi phītā ca bahujanā ca ākiṇṇamanussā ca subhikkhā ca. Kusāvatī, ānanda[V 2.0128], rājadhānī dasahi saddehi avivittā ahosi divā ceva rattiñca, seyyathidaṃ – hatthisaddena assasaddena rathasaddena bherisaddena mudiṅgasaddena vīṇāsaddena gītasaddena saṅkhasaddena [M 2.0140] sammasaddena pāṇitāḷasaddena ‘asnātha pivatha khādathā’ti dasamena saddena.

“Formerly, Ānanda, there was a king named Mahāsudassana, a noble, an anointed king, ruler of the four quarters, victorious, who had achieved stability in his country. Ānanda, this Kusinārā was the royal capital of King Mahāsudassana, and it was named Kusāvatī. From east to west, it was twelve yojanas in length, and from north to south, it was seven yojanas in breadth. The royal capital of Kusāvatī, Ānanda, was prosperous and flourishing, populous, teeming with people, and had an abundance of food. Just as Āḷakamandā, the royal capital of the devas, is prosperous and flourishing, populous, teeming with yakkhas, and has an abundance of food, so too, Ānanda, was the royal capital of Kusāvatī. Ānanda, the royal capital of Kusāvatī was never free, day or night, from ten sounds: the sound of elephants, the sound of horses, the sound of chariots, the sound of drums, the sound of tabors, the sound of lutes, the sound of singing, the sound of conches, the sound of cymbals, and the tenth sound, ‘Eat, drink, and feast!’”

“Kusāvatī, ānanda, rājadhānī sattahi pākārehi parikkhittā ahosi. Eko pākāro sovaṇṇamayo, eko rūpiyamayo, eko veḷuriyamayo, eko phalikamayo, eko lohitaṅkamayo [T 2.0198] lohitaṅgamayo (ka.), lohitakamayo (byākaraṇesu), eko masāragallamayo, eko sabbaratanamayo. Kusāvatiyā, ānanda, rājadhāniyā catunnaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ dvārāni ahesuṃ. Ekaṃ dvāraṃ sovaṇṇamayaṃ, ekaṃ rūpiyamayaṃ, ekaṃ veḷuriyamayaṃ, ekaṃ phalikamayaṃ[P 2.0171]. Ekekasmiṃ dvāre satta satta esikā nikhātā ahesuṃ tiporisaṅgā tiporisanikhātā dvādasaporisā ubbedhena. Ekā esikā sovaṇṇamayā, ekā rūpiyamayā, ekā veḷuriyamayā, ekā phalikamayā, ekā lohitaṅkamayā, ekā masāragallamayā, ekā sabbaratanamayā. Kusāvatī, ānanda, rājadhānī sattahi tālapantīhi parikkhittā ahosi. Ekā tālapanti sovaṇṇamayā, ekā rūpiyamayā, ekā veḷuriyamayā, ekā phalikamayā, ekā lohitaṅkamayā, ekā masāragallamayā, ekā sabbaratanamayā. Sovaṇṇamayassa tālassa sovaṇṇamayo khandho ahosi, rūpiyamayāni pattāni ca phalāni ca. Rūpiyamayassa tālassa rūpiyamayo khandho ahosi, sovaṇṇamayāni pattāni ca phalāni ca. Veḷuriyamayassa tālassa veḷuriyamayo khandho ahosi, phalikamayāni pattāni ca phalāni ca. Phalikamayassa tālassa phalikamayo khandho ahosi, veḷuriyamayāni pattāni ca phalāni ca. Lohitaṅkamayassa tālassa lohitaṅkamayo khandho ahosi, masāragallamayāni pattāni ca phalāni ca. Masāragallamayassa tālassa masāragallamayo khandho ahosi, lohitaṅkamayāni pattāni ca phalāni ca. Sabbaratanamayassa tālassa sabbaratanamayo khandho ahosi, sabbaratanamayāni pattāni ca phalāni ca. Tāsaṃ kho panānanda, tālapantīnaṃ vāteritānaṃ saddo ahosi vaggu ca rajanīyo ca khamanīyo kamanīyo (sī. syā. pī.) ca madanīyo ca. Seyyathāpi, ānanda, pañcaṅgikassa tūriyassa suvinītassa suppaṭitāḷitassa sukusalehi samannāhatassa saddo hoti vaggu ca [M 2.0141] rajanīyo ca khamanīyo ca madanīyo ca[P 2.0172], evameva kho, ānanda, tāsaṃ tālapantīnaṃ vāteritānaṃ saddo ahosi vaggu ca rajanīyo ca khamanīyo ca madanīyo ca. Ye kho panānanda, tena samayena kusāvatiyā rājadhāniyā dhuttā ahesuṃ soṇḍā pipāsā, te tāsaṃ tālapantīnaṃ vāteritānaṃ saddena [T 2.0199] paricāresuṃ.

“Ānanda, the royal capital of Kusāvatī was surrounded by seven ramparts. One rampart was of gold, one of silver, one of beryl, one of crystal, one of ruby, one of agate, and one of all kinds of gems. In the royal capital of Kusāvatī, Ānanda, there were gates of four materials: one gate was of gold, one of silver, one of beryl, and one of crystal. At each gate, seven pillars were erected, each three men's heights in girth, buried three men's heights deep, and twelve men's heights in height. One pillar was of gold, one of silver, one of beryl, one of crystal, one of ruby, one of agate, and one of all kinds of gems. Ānanda, the royal capital of Kusāvatī was surrounded by seven rows of palm trees. One row was of gold, one of silver, one of beryl, one of crystal, one of ruby, one of agate, and one of all kinds of gems. For the golden palm tree, the trunk was of gold, and its leaves and fruits were of silver. For the silver palm tree, the trunk was of silver, and its leaves and fruits were of gold. For the beryl palm tree, the trunk was of beryl, and its leaves and fruits were of crystal. For the crystal palm tree, the trunk was of crystal, and its leaves and fruits were of beryl. For the ruby palm tree, the trunk was of ruby, and its leaves and fruits were of agate. For the agate palm tree, the trunk was of agate, and its leaves and fruits were of ruby. For the palm tree of all gems, the trunk was of all kinds of gems, and its leaves and fruits were of all kinds of gems. Ānanda, when these rows of palm trees were shaken by the wind, their sound was beautiful, enchanting, pleasing, and intoxicating. Just as, Ānanda, the sound of a five-piece orchestra, well-composed, well-played, and performed by skilled musicians, is beautiful, enchanting, pleasing, and intoxicating, so too, Ānanda, was the sound of these rows of palm trees when shaken by the wind. And those in the royal capital of Kusāvatī at that time who were gamblers and drunkards amused themselves with the sound of these rows of palm trees when shaken by the wind.”

Cakkaratanaṃ

The Wheel-Treasure

243. “Rājā[V 2.0129], ānanda, mahāsudassano sattahi ratanehi samannāgato ahosi catūhi ca iddhīhi. Katamehi sattahi? Idhānanda, rañño mahāsudassanassa tadahuposathe pannarase sīsaṃnhātassa uposathikassa uparipāsādavaragatassa dibbaṃ cakkaratanaṃ pāturahosi sahassāraṃ sanemikaṃ sanābhikaṃ sabbākāraparipūraṃ. Disvā rañño mahāsudassanassa etadahosi – ‘sutaṃ kho panetaṃ – “yassa rañño khattiyassa muddhāvasittassa tadahuposathe pannarase sīsaṃnhātassa uposathikassa uparipāsādavaragatassa dibbaṃ cakkaratanaṃ pātubhavati sahassāraṃ sanemikaṃ sanābhikaṃ sabbākāraparipūraṃ, so hoti rājā cakkavattī”ti. Assaṃ nu kho ahaṃ rājā cakkavattī’ti.

243. “Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana was endowed with seven treasures and four spiritual powers. What were the seven? Here, Ānanda, for King Mahāsudassana, on the fifteenth day, it being the Uposatha, having bathed his head and observing the Uposatha precepts, while abiding in the upper chamber of his excellent palace, a divine wheel-treasure appeared, with a thousand spokes, with a rim, with a hub, complete in every aspect. Seeing it, this thought occurred to King Mahāsudassana: ‘I have heard this: “For whichever anointed Khattiya king, on the fifteenth day, it being the Uposatha, having bathed his head and observing the Uposatha precepts, while abiding in the upper chamber of his excellent palace, a divine wheel-treasure appears, with a thousand spokes, with a rim, with a hub, complete in every aspect, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch.” Might I be a wheel-turning monarch?’”

244. “Atha kho, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano uṭṭhāyāsanā ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā vāmena hatthena suvaṇṇabhiṅkāraṃ gahetvā dakkhiṇena hatthena cakkaratanaṃ abbhukkiri – ‘pavattatu bhavaṃ cakkaratanaṃ, abhivijinātu bhavaṃ cakkaratana’nti. Atha kho taṃ, ānanda, cakkaratanaṃ puratthimaṃ disaṃ pavatti pavattati (syā. ka.), anvadeva anudeva (syā.) rājā mahāsudassano saddhiṃ caturaṅginiyā senāya, yasmiṃ kho panānanda, padese cakkaratanaṃ [P 2.0173] patiṭṭhāsi, tattha rājā mahāsudassano vāsaṃ upagacchi saddhiṃ caturaṅginiyā senāya. Ye kho panānanda, puratthimāya disāya paṭirājāno, te rājānaṃ mahāsudassanaṃ upasaṅkamitvā [T 2.0200] evamāhaṃsu – ‘ehi kho mahārāja, svāgataṃ te mahārāja, sakaṃ te mahārāja, anusāsa mahārājā’ti. Rājā mahāsudassano evamāha – ‘pāṇo na hantabbo, adinnaṃ na ādātabbaṃ, kāmesu micchā na caritabbā, musā na bhaṇitabbā, majjaṃ na pātabbaṃ, yathābhuttañca bhuñjathā’ti[M 2.0142]. Ye kho panānanda, puratthimāya disāya paṭirājāno, te rañño mahāsudassanassa anuyantā ahesuṃ. Atha kho taṃ, ānanda, cakkaratanaṃ puratthimaṃ samuddaṃ ajjhogāhetvā paccuttaritvā dakkhiṇaṃ disaṃ pavatti…pe… dakkhiṇaṃ samuddaṃ ajjhogāhetvā paccuttaritvā pacchimaṃ disaṃ pavatti…pe… pacchimaṃ samuddaṃ ajjhogāhetvā paccuttaritvā uttaraṃ disaṃ pavatti, anvadeva rājā mahāsudassano saddhiṃ caturaṅginiyā senāya. Yasmiṃ kho panānanda, padese cakkaratanaṃ patiṭṭhāsi, tattha rājā mahāsudassano vāsaṃ upagacchi saddhiṃ caturaṅginiyā senāya. Ye kho panānanda, uttarāya disāya paṭirājāno, te rājānaṃ mahāsudassanaṃ upasaṅkamitvā evamāhaṃsu – ‘ehi kho mahārāja, svāgataṃ te mahārāja, sakaṃ te mahārāja, anusāsa mahārājā’ti. Rājā mahāsudassano evamāha – ‘pāṇo na hantabbo, adinnaṃ na ādātabbaṃ, kāmesu micchā na caritabbā, musā [P 2.0174] na bhaṇitabbā, majjaṃ na pātabbaṃ[V 2.0130], yathābhuttañca bhuñjathā’ti. Ye kho panānanda, uttarāya disāya paṭirājāno[T 2.0201], te rañño mahāsudassanassa anuyantā ahesuṃ.

244. “Then, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, took a golden water pot in his left hand, and with his right hand sprinkled the Wheel-Treasure, saying: ‘Roll forth, venerable Wheel-Treasure! Conquer, venerable Wheel-Treasure!’ Then, Ānanda, that Wheel-Treasure rolled to the eastern direction, and King Mahāsudassana followed right after with his fourfold army. And wherever, Ānanda, the Wheel-Treasure came to a standstill, there King Mahāsudassana took up residence with his fourfold army. The opposing kings of the eastern region, Ānanda, approached King Mahāsudassana and said this: ‘Come, great king! Welcome, great king! This is yours, great king! Instruct us, great king!’ King Mahāsudassana said this: ‘A living being is not to be killed; what is not given is not to be taken; in regard to sensual pleasures, misconduct is not to be practiced; falsehood is not to be spoken; intoxicants are not to be drunk. And enjoy your revenues as was customary.’ And so, Ānanda, the opposing kings of the eastern region became followers of King Mahāsudassana. Then, Ānanda, that Wheel-Treasure, having plunged into the eastern ocean and re-emerged, rolled to the southern direction… having plunged into the southern ocean and re-emerged, rolled to the western direction… having plunged into the western ocean and re-emerged, rolled to the northern direction, and King Mahāsudassana followed right after with his fourfold army. And wherever, Ānanda, the Wheel-Treasure came to a standstill, there King Mahāsudassana took up residence with his fourfold army. The opposing kings of the northern region approached King Mahāsudassana and said this: ‘Come, great king! Welcome, great king! This is yours, great king! Instruct us, great king!’ King Mahāsudassana said this: ‘A living being is not to be killed; what is not given is not to be taken; in regard to sensual pleasures, misconduct is not to be practiced; falsehood is not to be spoken; intoxicants are not to be drunk. And enjoy your revenues as was customary.’ And so, Ānanda, the opposing kings of the northern region became followers of King Mahāsudassana.”

245. “Atha kho taṃ, ānanda, cakkaratanaṃ samuddapariyantaṃ pathaviṃ abhivijinitvā kusāvatiṃ rājadhāniṃ paccāgantvā rañño mahāsudassanassa antepuradvāre atthakaraṇapamukhe akkhāhataṃ maññe aṭṭhāsi rañño mahāsudassanassa antepuraṃ upasobhayamānaṃ. Rañño, ānanda, mahāsudassanassa evarūpaṃ cakkaratanaṃ pāturahosi.

245. “Then, Ānanda, that Wheel-Treasure, having conquered the earth to its ocean boundaries, returned to the royal capital, Kusāvatī, and stood at the gate of King Mahāsudassana’s inner palace, at the entrance to the hall of justice, as if fixed by its axle, beautifying the inner palace of King Mahāsudassana. For King Mahāsudassana, Ānanda, such a Wheel-Treasure appeared.”

Hatthiratanaṃ

The Elephant-Treasure

246. “Puna caparaṃ, ānanda, rañño mahāsudassanassa hatthiratanaṃ pāturahosi sabbaseto sattappatiṭṭho iddhimā vehāsaṅgamo uposatho nāma nāgarājā. Taṃ disvā rañño mahāsudassanassa cittaṃ pasīdi – ‘bhaddakaṃ vata bho hatthiyānaṃ, sace damathaṃ upeyyā’ti. Atha kho taṃ, ānanda, hatthiratanaṃ – seyyathāpi nāma gandhahatthājāniyo dīgharattaṃ suparidanto, evameva damathaṃ upagacchi. Bhūtapubbaṃ, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano tameva hatthiratanaṃ vīmaṃsamāno pubbaṇhasamayaṃ abhiruhitvā samuddapariyantaṃ pathaviṃ anuyāyitvā kusāvatiṃ rājadhāniṃ paccāgantvā pātarāsamakāsi. Rañño, ānanda, mahāsudassanassa evarūpaṃ hatthiratanaṃ pāturahosi.

246. “Furthermore, Ānanda, the Elephant-Treasure appeared to King Mahāsudassana—all white, with seven points of contact, endowed with psychic power, able to travel through the sky, the elephant king named Uposatha. Upon seeing it, King Mahāsudassana's mind was gladdened: ‘Truly excellent is this elephant vehicle, if only it would submit to training.’ Then, Ānanda, that Elephant-Treasure attained tameness, just as a noble elephant of the Gandha breed, well-tamed for a long time. Formerly, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana, testing that very Elephant-Treasure, mounted it in the morning, traveled around the earth to its ocean boundary, returned to the capital city of Kusāvatī, and took his morning meal. Such, Ānanda, was the Elephant-Treasure that appeared to King Mahāsudassana.”

Assaratanaṃ

The Horse-Treasure

247. “Puna [M 2.0143] caparaṃ, ānanda, rañño mahāsudassanassa assaratanaṃ pāturahosi sabbaseto kāḷasīso muñjakeso iddhimā vehāsaṅgamo valāhako nāma assarājā. Taṃ disvā rañño mahāsudassanassa cittaṃ pasīdi – ‘bhaddakaṃ vata bho assayānaṃ sace damathaṃ upeyyā’ti. Atha [T 2.0202] kho taṃ[P 2.0175], ānanda, assaratanaṃ seyyathāpi nāma bhaddo assājāniyo dīgharattaṃ suparidanto, evameva damathaṃ upagacchi. Bhūtapubbaṃ, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano tameva assaratanaṃ vīmaṃsamāno pubbaṇhasamayaṃ abhiruhitvā samuddapariyantaṃ pathaviṃ anuyāyitvā kusāvatiṃ rājadhāniṃ paccāgantvā pātarāsamakāsi. Rañño, ānanda, mahāsudassanassa evarūpaṃ assaratanaṃ pāturahosi.

247. “Furthermore, Ānanda, the Horse-Treasure appeared to King Mahāsudassana—all white, with a black head and a mane like muñja grass, endowed with psychic power, able to travel through the sky, the horse king named Valāhaka. Upon seeing it, King Mahāsudassana's mind was gladdened: ‘Truly excellent is this horse vehicle, if only it would submit to training.’ Then, Ānanda, that Horse-Treasure attained tameness, just as a fine thoroughbred horse, well-tamed for a long time. Formerly, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana, testing that very Horse-Treasure, mounted it in the morning, traveled around the earth to its ocean boundary, returned to the capital city of Kusāvatī, and took his morning meal. Such, Ānanda, was the Horse-Treasure that appeared to King Mahāsudassana.”

Maṇiratanaṃ

The Jewel-Treasure

248. “Puna [V 2.0131] caparaṃ, ānanda, rañño mahāsudassanassa maṇiratanaṃ pāturahosi. So ahosi maṇi veḷuriyo subho jātimā aṭṭhaṃso suparikammakato accho vippasanno anāvilo sabbākārasampanno. Tassa kho panānanda, maṇiratanassa ābhā samantā yojanaṃ phuṭā ahosi. Bhūtapubbaṃ, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano tameva maṇiratanaṃ vīmaṃsamāno caturaṅginiṃ senaṃ sannayhitvā maṇiṃ dhajaggaṃ āropetvā rattandhakāratimisāya pāyāsi. Ye kho panānanda, samantā gāmā ahesuṃ, te tenobhāsena kammante payojesuṃ divāti maññamānā. Rañño, ānanda, mahāsudassanassa evarūpaṃ maṇiratanaṃ pāturahosi.

248. “Furthermore, Ānanda, the Jewel-Treasure appeared to King Mahāsudassana. It was a beryl gem, beautiful, of fine quality, eight-faceted, excellently wrought, clear, bright, unclouded, and perfect in every way. The radiance of that Jewel-Treasure, Ānanda, shone out for a league in all directions. Formerly, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana, testing that very Jewel-Treasure, assembled his fourfold army, placed the jewel atop his banner, and set out in the thick darkness of night. The villages all around, Ānanda, by that light, applied themselves to their work, thinking it was day. Such, Ānanda, was the Jewel-Treasure that appeared to King Mahāsudassana.”

Itthiratanaṃ

The Woman-Treasure

249. “Puna caparaṃ, ānanda, rañño mahāsudassanassa itthiratanaṃ pāturahosi abhirūpā dassanīyā pāsādikā paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgatā nātidīghā nātirassā nātikisā nātithūlā nātikāḷikā nāccodātā atikkantā mānusivaṇṇaṃ mānussivaṇṇaṃ (syā.) appattā dibbavaṇṇaṃ. Tassa kho panānanda, itthiratanassa evarūpo kāyasamphasso [T 2.0203] hoti, seyyathāpi [M 2.0144] nāma tūlapicuno vā kappāsapicuno vā. Tassa kho panānanda, itthiratanassa sīte uṇhāni gattāni honti, uṇhe sītāni. Tassa kho panānanda, itthiratanassa kāyato candanagandho vāyati, mukhato uppalagandho. Taṃ kho panānanda, itthiratanaṃ rañño mahāsudassanassa pubbuṭṭhāyinī ahosi pacchānipātinī [P 2.0176] kiṅkārapaṭissāvinī manāpacārinī piyavādinī. Taṃ kho panānanda, itthiratanaṃ rājānaṃ mahāsudassanaṃ manasāpi no aticari aticarī (ka.), aticārī (sī. syā. pī.), kuto pana kāyena. Rañño, ānanda, mahāsudassanassa evarūpaṃ itthiratanaṃ pāturahosi.

249. “Furthermore, Ānanda, the woman treasure appeared to King Mahāsudassana—beautiful, lovely, and charming, possessing supreme beauty of complexion, neither too tall nor too short, neither too thin nor too fat, neither too dark nor too fair, surpassing human complexion but not reaching divine complexion. The touch of this woman treasure, Ānanda, was like a tuft of silk-cotton or a tuft of cotton wool. In the cold, her limbs were warm; in the heat, they were cool. From her body wafted the scent of sandalwood, and from her mouth, the scent of a blue lotus. This woman treasure, Ānanda, rose before King Mahāsudassana and retired after him, was responsive to his commands, pleasing in conduct, and amiable in speech. This woman treasure, Ānanda, never transgressed against King Mahāsudassana even in thought—how much less in deed? Ānanda, such was the woman treasure that appeared to King Mahāsudassana.”

Gahapatiratanaṃ

The Householder Treasure

250. “Puna caparaṃ, ānanda, rañño mahāsudassanassa gahapatiratanaṃ pāturahosi. Tassa kammavipākajaṃ dibbacakkhu pāturahosi yena nidhiṃ passati sassāmikampi assāmikampi. So rājānaṃ mahāsudassanaṃ upasaṅkamitvā evamāha – ‘appossukko tvaṃ, deva, hohi, ahaṃ te dhanena dhanakaraṇīyaṃ karissāmī’ti. Bhūtapubbaṃ, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano tameva gahapatiratanaṃ vīmaṃsamāno nāvaṃ abhiruhitvā majjhe gaṅgāya nadiyā sotaṃ ogāhitvā gahapatiratanaṃ [V 2.0132] etadavoca – ‘attho me, gahapati, hiraññasuvaṇṇenā’ti. ‘Tena hi, mahārāja, ekaṃ tīraṃ nāvā upetū’ti. ‘Idheva me, gahapati, attho hiraññasuvaṇṇenā’ti. Atha kho taṃ, ānanda, gahapatiratanaṃ ubhohi hatthehi udakaṃ omasitvā pūraṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇassa kumbhiṃ uddharitvā rājānaṃ mahāsudassanaṃ etadavoca [T 2.0204] – ‘alamettāvatā mahārāja, katamettāvatā mahārāja, pūjitamettāvatā mahārājā’ti? Rājā mahāsudassano evamāha – ‘alamettāvatā gahapati, katamettāvatā gahapati, pūjitamettāvatā gahapatī’ti. Rañño[P 2.0177], ānanda, mahāsudassanassa evarūpaṃ gahapatiratanaṃ pāturahosi.

250. “Furthermore, Ānanda, the householder treasure appeared to King Mahāsudassana. Through the ripening of his kamma, a divine eye arose in him, by which he could see treasure, whether with an owner or without an owner. He approached King Mahāsudassana and said, ‘Be without anxiety, Your Majesty, I will perform for you the duties to be done with wealth.’ Once, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana, wishing to test that householder treasure, boarded a boat and, having entered the current in the middle of the Ganges River, said to the householder treasure, ‘I need gold and silver, householder.’ ‘Then, great king, let the boat approach one of the banks.’ ‘Right here, householder, I need gold and silver.’ Then, Ānanda, that householder treasure, dipping both hands into the water, drew up a pot full of gold and silver and said to King Mahāsudassana, ‘Is this much sufficient, great king? Is this much a fulfillment, great king? Is this much an offering, great king?’ King Mahāsudassana replied, ‘This much is sufficient, householder. This much is a fulfillment, householder. This much is an offering, householder.’ Ānanda, such was the householder treasure that appeared to King Mahāsudassana.”

Pariṇāyakaratanaṃ

The Counselor Treasure

251. “Puna caparaṃ, ānanda, rañño mahāsudassanassa pariṇāyakaratanaṃ pāturahosi paṇḍito viyatto medhāvī paṭibalo rājānaṃ mahāsudassanaṃ [M 2.0145] upayāpetabbaṃ upayāpetuṃ, apayāpetabbaṃ apayāpetuṃ, ṭhapetabbaṃ ṭhapetuṃ. So rājānaṃ mahāsudassanaṃ upasaṅkamitvā evamāha – ‘appossukko tvaṃ, deva, hohi, ahamanusāsissāmī’ti. Rañño, ānanda, mahāsudassanassa evarūpaṃ pariṇāyakaratanaṃ pāturahosi.

251. “Furthermore, Ānanda, the counselor treasure appeared to King Mahāsudassana. He was wise, astute, and intelligent, capable of having King Mahāsudassana associate with those who should be associated with, avoid those who should be avoided, and appoint those who should be appointed. He approached King Mahāsudassana and said: ‘Be without anxiety, Your Majesty. I shall administer.’ Ānanda, such was the counselor treasure that appeared to King Mahāsudassana.”

“Rājā, ānanda, mahāsudassano imehi sattahi ratanehi samannāgato ahosi.

“King Mahāsudassana, Ānanda, was endowed with these seven treasures.”

Catuiddhisamannāgato

Endowed with Four Powers

252. “Rājā, ānanda, mahāsudassano catūhi iddhīhi samannāgato ahosi. Katamāhi catūhi iddhīhi? Idhānanda, rājā mahāsudassano abhirūpo ahosi dassanīyo pāsādiko paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgato ativiya aññehi manussehi. Rājā, ānanda, mahāsudassano imāya paṭhamāya iddhiyā samannāgato ahosi.

252. “King Mahāsudassana, Ānanda, was endowed with four powers. With which four? Here, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana was handsome, pleasant to behold, and gracious, endowed with supreme beauty of complexion, far surpassing other human beings. King Mahāsudassana, Ānanda, was endowed with this first power.”

“Puna caparaṃ, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano dīghāyuko ahosi ciraṭṭhitiko ativiya aññehi manussehi. Rājā, ānanda, mahāsudassano [T 2.0205] imāya dutiyāya iddhiyā samannāgato ahosi.

“Furthermore, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana was long-lived and long-enduring, far more so than other human beings. King Mahāsudassana, Ānanda, was endowed with this second power.”

“Puna [V 2.0133] caparaṃ, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano appābādho ahosi appātaṅko samavepākiniyā gahaṇiyā samannāgato nātisītāya nāccuṇhāya ativiya aññehi manussehi. Rājā, ānanda, mahāsudassano imāya tatiyāya iddhiyā samannāgato ahosi.

“Furthermore, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana was free from illness and affliction, endowed with a balanced digestion that was neither too cold nor too hot, far surpassing that of other human beings. King Mahāsudassana, Ānanda, was endowed with this third power.”

“Puna caparaṃ[P 2.0178], ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano brāhmaṇagahapatikānaṃ piyo ahosi manāpo. Seyyathāpi, ānanda, pitā puttānaṃ piyo hoti manāpo, evameva kho, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano brāhmaṇagahapatikānaṃ piyo ahosi manāpo. Raññopi, ānanda, mahāsudassanassa brāhmaṇagahapatikā piyā ahesuṃ manāpā. Seyyathāpi, ānanda, pitu puttā piyā honti manāpā, evameva kho, ānanda, raññopi mahāsudassanassa brāhmaṇagahapatikā piyā ahesuṃ manāpā.

“Furthermore, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana was dear and beloved to the brahmins and householders. Just as a father, Ānanda, is dear and beloved to his sons, even so, Ānanda, was King Mahāsudassana dear and beloved to the brahmins and householders. And to King Mahāsudassana, Ānanda, the brahmins and householders were dear and beloved. Just as sons, Ānanda, are dear and beloved to their father, even so, Ānanda, were the brahmins and householders dear and beloved to King Mahāsudassana.”

“Bhūtapubbaṃ, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano caturaṅginiyā senāya uyyānabhūmiṃ niyyāsi. Atha kho, ānanda, brāhmaṇagahapatikā rājānaṃ mahāsudassanaṃ upasaṅkamitvā evamāhaṃsu – ‘ataramāno, deva, yāhi, yathā [M 2.0146] taṃ mayaṃ cirataraṃ passeyyāmā’ti. Rājāpi, ānanda, mahāsudassano sārathiṃ āmantesi – ‘ataramāno, sārathi, rathaṃ pesehi, yathā ahaṃ brāhmaṇagahapatike cirataraṃ passeyya’nti. Rājā, ānanda, mahāsudassano imāya catutthiyā catutthāya (syā.) iddhiyā samannāgato ahosi. Rājā, ānanda, mahāsudassano imāhi [T 2.0206] catūhi iddhīhi samannāgato ahosi.

“Once, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana went out to the pleasure grounds with his fourfold army. Then, Ānanda, the brahmins and householders approached King Mahāsudassana and said: ‘Go slowly, Your Majesty, so that we may behold you for a longer time.’ King Mahāsudassana, Ānanda, also addressed his charioteer: ‘Drive the chariot slowly, charioteer, so that I may behold the brahmins and householders for a longer time.’ King Mahāsudassana, Ānanda, was endowed with this fourth power. King Mahāsudassana, Ānanda, was endowed with these four powers.”

Dhammapāsādapokkharaṇī

The Dhamma Palace and the Dhamma Lotus Pond

253. “Atha kho, ānanda, rañño mahāsudassanassa etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ imāsu tālantarikāsu dhanusate dhanusate pokkharaṇiyo māpeyya’nti.

253. Then, Ānanda, this thought occurred to King Mahāsudassana: 'It would be good if I were to have ponds created in the intervals between these rows of palm trees, at every hundred bow-lengths.'

“Māpesi kho, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano tāsu tālantarikāsu dhanusate dhanusate pokkharaṇiyo. Tā kho panānanda, pokkharaṇiyo catunnaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ iṭṭhakāhi citā ahesuṃ – ekā iṭṭhakā sovaṇṇamayā, ekā rūpiyamayā, ekā veḷuriyamayā, ekā phalikamayā.

Indeed, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana had ponds created in the intervals between those rows of palm trees, at every hundred bow-lengths. And those ponds, Ānanda, were lined with bricks of four colors: one kind of brick was of gold, one of silver, one of beryl, and one of crystal.

“Tāsu kho panānanda, pokkharaṇīsu cattāri cattāri sopānāni ahesuṃ catunnaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ, ekaṃ sopānaṃ sovaṇṇamayaṃ ekaṃ rūpiyamayaṃ ekaṃ veḷuriyamayaṃ ekaṃ phalikamayaṃ. Sovaṇṇamayassa [V 2.0134] sopānassa sovaṇṇamayā [P 2.0179] thambhā ahesuṃ, rūpiyamayā sūciyo ca uṇhīsañca. Rūpiyamayassa sopānassa rūpiyamayā thambhā ahesuṃ, sovaṇṇamayā sūciyo ca uṇhīsañca. Veḷuriyamayassa sopānassa veḷuriyamayā thambhā ahesuṃ, phalikamayā sūciyo ca uṇhīsañca. Phalikamayassa sopānassa phalikamayā thambhā ahesuṃ, veḷuriyamayā sūciyo ca uṇhīsañca. Tā kho panānanda, pokkharaṇiyo dvīhi vedikāhi parikkhittā ahesuṃ ekā vedikā sovaṇṇamayā, ekā rūpiyamayā. Sovaṇṇamayāya vedikāya sovaṇṇamayā thambhā ahesuṃ, rūpiyamayā sūciyo ca uṇhīsañca. Rūpiyamayāya vedikāya rūpiyamayā thambhā ahesuṃ, sovaṇṇamayā sūciyo ca uṇhīsañca. Atha kho, ānanda[T 2.0207], rañño mahāsudassanassa etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ imāsu pokkharaṇīsu evarūpaṃ mālaṃ ropāpeyyaṃ uppalaṃ padumaṃ kumudaṃ puṇḍarīkaṃ sabbotukaṃ sabbajanassa anāvaṭa’nti. Ropāpesi kho[M 2.0147], ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano tāsu pokkharaṇīsu evarūpaṃ mālaṃ uppalaṃ padumaṃ kumudaṃ puṇḍarīkaṃ sabbotukaṃ sabbajanassa anāvaṭaṃ.

In those ponds, Ānanda, there were four stairways of four colors: one stairway of gold, one of silver, one of beryl, and one of crystal. Of the golden stairway, the posts were of gold, and the crossbars and coping were of silver. Of the silver stairway, the posts were of silver, and the crossbars and coping were of gold. Of the beryl stairway, the posts were of beryl, and the crossbars and coping were of crystal. Of the crystal stairway, the posts were of crystal, and the crossbars and coping were of beryl. Furthermore, Ānanda, those ponds were enclosed by two railings: one railing was of gold, and one was of silver. Of the golden railing, the posts were of gold, and the crossbars and coping were of silver. Of the silver railing, the posts were of silver, and the crossbars and coping were of gold. Then, Ānanda, this thought occurred to King Mahāsudassana: 'It would be good if I were to have flowers of this kind planted in these ponds—blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water lilies, and white lotuses—blooming in all seasons and unrestricted for all people.' Indeed, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana had flowers of this kind planted in those ponds—blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water lilies, and white lotuses—blooming in all seasons and unrestricted for all people.

254. “Atha kho, ānanda, rañño mahāsudassanassa etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ imāsaṃ pokkharaṇīnaṃ tīre nhāpake purise ṭhapeyyaṃ, ye āgatāgataṃ janaṃ nhāpessantī’ti. Ṭhapesi kho, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano tāsaṃ pokkharaṇīnaṃ tīre nhāpake purise, ye āgatāgataṃ janaṃ nhāpesuṃ.

254. Then, Ānanda, this thought occurred to King Mahāsudassana: 'It would be good if I were to station bath attendants on the banks of these ponds, who would bathe the people who come and go.' Indeed, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana stationed bath attendants on the banks of those ponds, who bathed the people who came and went.

“Atha kho, ānanda, rañño mahāsudassanassa etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ imāsaṃ pokkharaṇīnaṃ tīre evarūpaṃ dānaṃ paṭṭhapeyyaṃ – annaṃ annaṭṭhikassa annatthitassa (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.), evaṃ sabbattha pakabhirūpeneva dissati, pānaṃ pānaṭṭhikassa, vatthaṃ vatthaṭṭhikassa, yānaṃ yānaṭṭhikassa, sayanaṃ sayanaṭṭhikassa, itthiṃ itthiṭṭhikassa, hiraññaṃ hiraññaṭṭhikassa, suvaṇṇaṃ suvaṇṇaṭṭhikassā’ti. Paṭṭhapesi [P 2.0180] kho, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano tāsaṃ pokkharaṇīnaṃ tīre evarūpaṃ dānaṃ – annaṃ annaṭṭhikassa, pānaṃ pānaṭṭhikassa, vatthaṃ vatthaṭṭhikassa, yānaṃ yānaṭṭhikassa, sayanaṃ sayanaṭṭhikassa, itthiṃ itthiṭṭhikassa, hiraññaṃ hiraññaṭṭhikassa, suvaṇṇaṃ suvaṇṇaṭṭhikassa.

Then, Ānanda, this thought occurred to King Mahāsudassana: 'It would be good if I were to establish a gift of this kind on the banks of these ponds: food for one who desires food, drink for one who desires drink, clothing for one who desires clothing, a vehicle for one who desires a vehicle, a bed for one who desires a bed, a woman for one who desires a woman, silver for one who desires silver, and gold for one who desires gold.' Indeed, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana established a gift of this kind on the banks of those ponds: food for one who desires food, drink for one who desires drink, clothing for one who desires clothing, a vehicle for one who desires a vehicle, a bed for one who desires a bed, a woman for one who desires a woman, silver for one who desires silver, and gold for one who desires gold.

255. “Atha kho, ānanda, brāhmaṇagahapatikā pahūtaṃ sāpateyyaṃ ādāya rājānaṃ mahāsudassanaṃ upasaṅkamitvā evamāhaṃsu – ‘idaṃ, deva, pahūtaṃ [T 2.0208] sāpateyyaṃ devaññeva uddissa ābhataṃ, taṃ devo paṭiggaṇhatū’ti. ‘Alaṃ bho, mamapidaṃ pahūtaṃ sāpateyyaṃ dhammikena balinā abhisaṅkhataṃ, tañca vo hotu, ito ca bhiyyo harathā’ti. Te raññā paṭikkhittā ekamantaṃ apakkamma [V 2.0135] evaṃ samacintesuṃ – ‘na kho etaṃ amhākaṃ patirūpaṃ, yaṃ mayaṃ imāni sāpateyyāni punadeva sakāni gharāni paṭihareyyāma. Yaṃnūna mayaṃ rañño mahāsudassanassa nivesanaṃ māpeyyāmā’ti. Te rājānaṃ mahāsudassanaṃ upasaṅkamitvā evamāhaṃsu – ‘nivesanaṃ te deva, māpessāmā’ti. Adhivāsesi kho, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano tuṇhībhāvena.

255. Then, Ānanda, brahmins and householders, taking abundant wealth, approached King Mahāsudassana and said thus: 'This abundant wealth, Your Majesty, has been brought intended just for you. May Your Majesty accept it.' 'It is enough, sirs. I have abundant wealth accumulated by righteous taxation. Let this be yours, and take even more from here.' Having been refused by the king, they withdrew to one side and considered together thus: 'It is not fitting for us that we should take this wealth back to our own homes. It would be good if we were to build a residence for King Mahāsudassana.' They approached King Mahāsudassana and said thus: 'Your Majesty, we shall build a residence for you.' Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana consented by means of silence.

256. “Atha kho, ānanda, sakko devānamindo rañño mahāsudassanassa cetasā cetoparivitakkamaññāya vissakammaṃ visukammaṃ (ka.) devaputtaṃ āmantesi – ‘ehi [M 2.0148] tvaṃ, samma vissakamma, rañño mahāsudassanassa nivesanaṃ māpehi dhammaṃ nāma pāsāda’nti. ‘Evaṃ bhaddantavā’ti kho, ānanda, vissakammo devaputto [P 2.0181] sakkassa devānamindassa paṭissutvā seyyathāpi nāma balavā puriso samiñjitaṃ vā bāhaṃ pasāreyya pasāritaṃ vā bāhaṃ samiñjeyya, evameva devesu tāvatiṃsesu antarahito rañño mahāsudassanassa purato pāturahosi. Atha kho, ānanda, vissakammo devaputto rājānaṃ mahāsudassanaṃ etadavoca – ‘nivesanaṃ te deva, māpessāmi dhammaṃ nāma [T 2.0209] pāsāda’nti. Adhivāsesi kho, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano tuṇhībhāvena.

256. Then, Ānanda, Sakka, the lord of the devas, knowing with his own mind the reflection in the mind of King Mahāsudassana, addressed the devaputta Vissakamma: 'Come, friend Vissakamma, create a residence for King Mahāsudassana, a palace named Dhamma.' 'Yes, venerable sir,' Ānanda, the devaputta Vissakamma replied, assenting to Sakka, the lord of the devas. Then, just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm or bend his outstretched arm, even so, he vanished from among the Tāvatiṃsa devas and appeared before King Mahāsudassana. Then, Ānanda, the devaputta Vissakamma said this to King Mahāsudassana: 'Your Majesty, I shall create a residence for you, a palace named Dhamma.' Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana consented by means of silence.

“Māpesi kho, ānanda, vissakammo devaputto rañño mahāsudassanassa nivesanaṃ dhammaṃ nāma pāsādaṃ. Dhammo, ānanda, pāsādo puratthimena pacchimena ca yojanaṃ āyāmena ahosi. Uttarena dakkhiṇena ca aḍḍhayojanaṃ vitthārena. Dhammassa, ānanda, pāsādassa tiporisaṃ uccatarena vatthu citaṃ ahosi catunnaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ iṭṭhakāhi – ekā iṭṭhakā sovaṇṇamayā, ekā rūpiyamayā, ekā veḷuriyamayā, ekā phalikamayā.

Indeed, Ānanda, the devaputta Vissakamma built the palace named Dhamma for King Mahāsudassana as his residence. The Dhamma palace, Ānanda, was a league in length from east to west and half a league in width from north to south. The foundation of the Dhamma palace, Ānanda, was three purisas high, built with bricks of four kinds—one brick of gold, one of silver, one of beryl, and one of crystal.

“Dhammassa, ānanda, pāsādassa caturāsīti thambhasahassāni ahesuṃ catunnaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ – eko thambho sovaṇṇamayo, eko rūpiyamayo, eko veḷuriyamayo, eko phalikamayo. Dhammo, ānanda, pāsādo catunnaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ phalakehi santhato ahosi – ekaṃ phalakaṃ sovaṇṇamayaṃ, ekaṃ rūpiyamayaṃ, ekaṃ veḷuriyamayaṃ, ekaṃ phalikamayaṃ.

The Dhamma palace, Ānanda, had eighty-four thousand pillars of four kinds—one pillar of gold, one of silver, one of beryl, and one of crystal. The Dhamma palace, Ānanda, was laid with planks of four kinds—one plank of gold, one of silver, one of beryl, and one of crystal.

“Dhammassa, ānanda, pāsādassa catuvīsati sopānāni ahesuṃ catunnaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ – ekaṃ sopānaṃ sovaṇṇamayaṃ, ekaṃ rūpiyamayaṃ, ekaṃ veḷuriyamayaṃ, ekaṃ phalikamayaṃ. Sovaṇṇamayassa sopānassa sovaṇṇamayā thambhā ahesuṃ rūpiyamayā sūciyo ca uṇhīsañca. Rūpiyamayassa sopānassa rūpiyamayā thambhā ahesuṃ sovaṇṇamayā sūciyo ca uṇhīsañca. Veḷuriyamayassa sopānassa [V 2.0136] veḷuriyamayā [P 2.0182] thambhā ahesuṃ phalikamayā sūciyo ca uṇhīsañca. Phalikamayassa sopānassa phalikamayā thambhā ahesuṃ veḷuriyamayā sūciyo [T 2.0210] ca uṇhīsañca.

The Dhamma palace, Ānanda, had twenty-four staircases of four kinds—one staircase of gold, one of silver, one of beryl, and one of crystal. The golden staircase had golden pillars with silver crossbars and coping. The silver staircase had silver pillars with golden crossbars and coping. The beryl staircase had beryl pillars with crystal crossbars and coping. The crystal staircase had crystal pillars with beryl crossbars and coping.

“Dhamme, ānanda, pāsāde caturāsīti kūṭāgārasahassāni ahesuṃ catunnaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ – ekaṃ kūṭāgāraṃ sovaṇṇamayaṃ, ekaṃ rūpiyamayaṃ, ekaṃ veḷuriyamayaṃ[M 2.0149], ekaṃ phalikamayaṃ. Sovaṇṇamaye kūṭāgāre rūpiyamayo pallaṅko paññatto ahosi, rūpiyamaye kūṭāgāre sovaṇṇamayo pallaṅko paññatto ahosi, veḷuriyamaye kūṭāgāre dantamayo pallaṅko paññatto ahosi, phalikamaye kūṭāgāre sāramayo pallaṅko paññatto ahosi. Sovaṇṇamayassa kūṭāgārassa dvāre rūpiyamayo tālo ṭhito ahosi, tassa rūpiyamayo khandho sovaṇṇamayāni pattāni ca phalāni ca. Rūpiyamayassa kūṭāgārassa dvāre sovaṇṇamayo tālo ṭhito ahosi, tassa sovaṇṇamayo khandho, rūpiyamayāni pattāni ca phalāni ca. Veḷuriyamayassa kūṭāgārassa dvāre phalikamayo tālo ṭhito ahosi, tassa phalikamayo khandho, veḷuriyamayāni pattāni ca phalāni ca. Phalikamayassa kūṭāgārassa dvāre veḷuriyamayo tālo ṭhito ahosi, tassa veḷuriyamayo khandho, phalikamayāni pattāni ca phalāni ca.

In the Dhamma palace, Ānanda, there were eighty-four thousand pinnacled chambers of four kinds—one chamber was of gold, one of silver, one of beryl, and one of crystal. In the golden chamber, a silver couch was prepared; in the silver chamber, a golden couch was prepared; in the beryl chamber, an ivory couch was prepared; and in the crystal chamber, a couch of heartwood was prepared. At the door of the golden chamber stood a silver palm tree; its trunk was of silver, and its leaves and fruits were of gold. At the door of the silver chamber stood a golden palm tree; its trunk was of gold, and its leaves and fruits were of silver. At the door of the beryl chamber stood a crystal palm tree; its trunk was of crystal, and its leaves and fruits were of beryl. At the door of the crystal chamber stood a beryl palm tree; its trunk was of beryl, and its leaves and fruits were of crystal.

257. “Atha kho, ānanda, rañño mahāsudassanassa etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ mahāviyūhassa kūṭāgārassa dvāre sabbasovaṇṇamayaṃ tālavanaṃ māpeyyaṃ, yattha divāvihāraṃ nisīdissāmī’ti. Māpesi kho, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano mahāviyūhassa kūṭāgārassa dvāre sabbasovaṇṇamayaṃ tālavanaṃ, yattha divāvihāraṃ nisīdi. Dhammo, ānanda[T 2.0211], pāsādo dvīhi vedikāhi parikkhitto [P 2.0183] ahosi, ekā vedikā sovaṇṇamayā, ekā rūpiyamayā. Sovaṇṇamayāya vedikāya sovaṇṇamayā thambhā ahesuṃ, rūpiyamayā sūciyo ca uṇhīsañca. Rūpiyamayāya vedikāya rūpiyamayā thambhā ahesuṃ, sovaṇṇamayā sūciyo ca uṇhīsañca.

257. Then, Ānanda, this thought occurred to King Mahāsudassana: ‘What if I were to have a palm grove made entirely of gold at the entrance of the Great Array Chamber, where I might sit for my day’s abiding?’ So, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana had a palm grove made entirely of gold at the entrance of the Great Array Chamber, where he sat for his day’s abiding. The Dhamma palace, Ānanda, was surrounded by two railings: one railing was of gold, the other of silver. The golden railing had golden pillars with silver crossbars and coping. The silver railing had silver pillars with golden crossbars and coping.

258. “Dhammo, ānanda, pāsādo dvīhi kiṅkiṇikajālehi kiṅkaṇikajālehi (syā. ka.) parikkhitto ahosi – ekaṃ jālaṃ sovaṇṇamayaṃ ekaṃ rūpiyamayaṃ. Sovaṇṇamayassa jālassa rūpiyamayā kiṅkiṇikā ahesuṃ, rūpiyamayassa jālassa sovaṇṇamayā kiṅkiṇikā ahesuṃ. Tesaṃ kho panānanda, kiṅkiṇikajālānaṃ vāteritānaṃ saddo ahosi vaggu ca rajanīyo ca khamanīyo ca madanīyo ca. Seyyathāpi, ānanda, pañcaṅgikassa tūriyassa suvinītassa suppaṭitāḷitassa [M 2.0150] sukusalehi kusalehi (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) samannāhatassa saddo hoti, vaggu ca rajanīyo ca khamanīyo ca madanīyo ca, evameva kho, ānanda, tesaṃ kiṅkiṇikajālānaṃ vāteritānaṃ saddo ahosi vaggu ca rajanīyo ca khamanīyo ca [V 2.0137] madanīyo ca. Ye kho panānanda, tena samayena kusāvatiyā rājadhāniyā dhuttā ahesuṃ soṇḍā pipāsā, te tesaṃ kiṅkiṇikajālānaṃ vāteritānaṃ saddena paricāresuṃ. Niṭṭhito kho panānanda, dhammo pāsādo duddikkho ahosi musati cakkhūni. Seyyathāpi, ānanda, vassānaṃ pacchime māse saradasamaye viddhe vigatavalāhake deve ādicco nabhaṃ abbhussakkamāno abbhuggamamāno (sī. pī. ka.) duddikkho [T 2.0212] dudikkho (pī.) hoti [P 2.0184] musati cakkhūni; evameva kho, ānanda, dhammo pāsādo duddikkho ahosi musati cakkhūni.

258. The Dhamma palace, Ānanda, was surrounded by two nets of tinkling bells—one net was of gold, and one of silver. The golden net had silver bells, and the silver net had golden bells. Indeed, Ānanda, when those nets of tinkling bells were stirred by the wind, the sound was pleasing, delightful, agreeable, and intoxicating. Just as, Ānanda, the sound of a five-piece orchestra, well-tuned, well-played, and performed by skilled musicians, is pleasing, delightful, agreeable, and intoxicating, so too, Ānanda, was the sound of those nets of tinkling bells when stirred by the wind—pleasing, delightful, agreeable, and intoxicating. And at that time, Ānanda, in the royal capital of Kusāvatī, the gamblers, sensualists, and drunkards delighted in the sound of those nets of tinkling bells stirred by the wind. The Dhamma palace, Ānanda, when it was completed, was difficult to look at; it dazzled the eyes. Just as, Ānanda, in the last month of the rains, in the autumn season, when the sky is clear and cloudless, the sun, rising into the heavens, is difficult to look at and dazzles the eyes; even so, Ānanda, the Dhamma palace was difficult to look at and dazzled the eyes.

259. “Atha kho, ānanda, rañño mahāsudassanassa etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ dhammassa pāsādassa purato dhammaṃ nāma pokkharaṇiṃ māpeyya’nti. Māpesi kho, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano dhammassa pāsādassa purato dhammaṃ nāma pokkharaṇiṃ. Dhammā, ānanda, pokkharaṇī puratthimena pacchimena ca yojanaṃ āyāmena ahosi, uttarena dakkhiṇena ca aḍḍhayojanaṃ vitthārena. Dhammā, ānanda, pokkharaṇī catunnaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ iṭṭhakāhi citā ahosi – ekā iṭṭhakā sovaṇṇamayā, ekā rūpiyamayā, ekā veḷuriyamayā, ekā phalikamayā.

259. Then, Ānanda, this thought occurred to King Mahāsudassana: ‘What if I were to have a pond named Dhamma created in front of the Dhamma Palace?’ And so, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana had a pond named Dhamma created in front of the Dhamma Palace. The Dhamma pond, Ānanda, was a yojana in length from east to west and half a yojana in width from north to south. The Dhamma pond, Ānanda, was constructed with bricks of four colors—one brick of gold, one of silver, one of beryl, and one of crystal.

“Dhammāya, ānanda, pokkharaṇiyā catuvīsati sopānāni ahesuṃ catunnaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ – ekaṃ sopānaṃ sovaṇṇamayaṃ, ekaṃ rūpiyamayaṃ, ekaṃ veḷuriyamayaṃ, ekaṃ phalikamayaṃ. Sovaṇṇamayassa sopānassa sovaṇṇamayā thambhā ahesuṃ rūpiyamayā sūciyo ca uṇhīsañca. Rūpiyamayassa sopānassa rūpiyamayā thambhā ahesuṃ sovaṇṇamayā sūciyo ca uṇhīsañca. Veḷuriyamayassa sopānassa veḷuriyamayā thambhā ahesuṃ phalikamayā sūciyo ca uṇhīsañca. Phalikamayassa sopānassa phalikamayā thambhā ahesuṃ veḷuriyamayā sūciyo ca uṇhīsañca.

Ānanda, the Dhamma pond had twenty-four staircases of four colors: one staircase of gold, one of silver, one of beryl, and one of crystal. The golden staircase had golden pillars, with silver crossbars and coping. The silver staircase had silver pillars, with golden crossbars and coping. The beryl staircase had beryl pillars, with crystal crossbars and coping. The crystal staircase had crystal pillars, with beryl crossbars and coping.

“Dhammā, ānanda, pokkharaṇī dvīhi vedikāhi parikkhittā ahosi – ekā vedikā sovaṇṇamayā, ekā rūpiyamayā. Sovaṇṇamayāya vedikāya sovaṇṇamayā [M 2.0151] thambhā ahesuṃ [T 2.0213] rūpiyamayā sūciyo ca uṇhīsañca. Rūpiyamayāya vedikāya rūpiyamayā thambhā ahesuṃ sovaṇṇamayā sūciyo ca uṇhīsañca.

Ānanda, the Dhamma pond was surrounded by two railings: one railing of gold, and one of silver. The golden railing had golden pillars, with silver crossbars and coping. The silver railing had silver pillars, with golden crossbars and coping.

“Dhammā, ānanda, pokkharaṇī sattahi tālapantīhi parikkhittā ahosi – ekā tālapanti sovaṇṇamayā, ekā rūpiyamayā, ekā veḷuriyamayā, ekā phalikamayā, ekā lohitaṅkamayā, ekā masāragallamayā, ekā sabbaratanamayā. Sovaṇṇamayassa tālassa sovaṇṇamayo khandho ahosi rūpiyamayāni [P 2.0185] pattāni ca phalāni ca. Rūpiyamayassa tālassa rūpiyamayo [V 2.0138] khandho ahosi sovaṇṇamayāni pattāni ca phalāni ca. Veḷuriyamayassa tālassa veḷuriyamayo khandho ahosi phalikamayāni pattāni ca phalāni ca. Phalikamayassa tālassa phalikamayo khandho ahosi veḷuriyamayāni pattāni ca phalāni ca. Lohitaṅkamayassa tālassa lohitaṅkamayo khandho ahosi masāragallamayāni pattāni ca phalāni ca. Masāragallamayassa tālassa masāragallamayo khandho ahosi lohitaṅkamayāni pattāni ca phalāni ca. Sabbaratanamayassa tālassa sabbaratanamayo khandho ahosi, sabbaratanamayāni pattāni ca phalāni ca. Tāsaṃ kho panānanda, tālapantīnaṃ vāteritānaṃ saddo ahosi, vaggu ca rajanīyo ca khamanīyo ca madanīyo ca. Seyyathāpi, ānanda, pañcaṅgikassa tūriyassa suvinītassa suppaṭitāḷitassa sukusalehi samannāhatassa saddo hoti vaggu ca rajanīyo ca khamanīyo ca madanīyo ca, evameva kho, ānanda, tāsaṃ tālapantīnaṃ vāteritānaṃ saddo [T 2.0214] ahosi vaggu ca rajanīyo ca khamanīyo ca madanīyo ca. Ye kho panānanda, tena samayena kusāvatiyā rājadhāniyā dhuttā ahesuṃ soṇḍā pipāsā, te tāsaṃ tālapantīnaṃ vāteritānaṃ saddena paricāresuṃ.

Ānanda, the Dhamma pond was surrounded by seven rows of palm trees: one row of gold, one of silver, one of beryl, one of crystal, one of ruby, one of agate, and one of all kinds of gems. For the golden palm tree, the trunk was of gold, and the leaves and fruits were of silver. For the silver palm tree, the trunk was of silver, and the leaves and fruits were of gold. For the beryl palm tree, the trunk was of beryl, and the leaves and fruits were of crystal. For the crystal palm tree, the trunk was of crystal, and the leaves and fruits were of beryl. For the ruby palm tree, the trunk was of ruby, and the leaves and fruits were of agate. For the agate palm tree, the trunk was of agate, and the leaves and fruits were of ruby. For the palm tree of all kinds of gems, the trunk was of all kinds of gems, and the leaves and fruits were of all kinds of gems. And, Ānanda, when those rows of palm trees were stirred by the wind, their sound was lovely, enchanting, pleasing, and intoxicating. Just as, Ānanda, the sound of a five-piece orchestra, well-composed, well-played, and performed by skilled musicians, is lovely, enchanting, pleasing, and intoxicating, even so, Ānanda, was the sound of those rows of palm trees when stirred by the wind lovely, enchanting, pleasing, and intoxicating. At that time, Ānanda, in the royal capital of Kusāvatī, those who were gamblers, debauched, and drunkards amused themselves with the sound of those rows of palm trees stirred by the wind.

“Niṭṭhite kho panānanda, dhamme pāsāde niṭṭhitāya dhammāya ca pokkharaṇiyā rājā mahāsudassano ‘ye ye ko panānanda (syā. ka.) tena samayena samaṇesu vā samaṇasammatā brāhmaṇesu vā brāhmaṇasammatā’, te sabbakāmehi santappetvā dhammaṃ pāsādaṃ abhiruhi.

Now, Ānanda, when the Dhamma Palace was completed and the Dhamma pond was completed, King Mahāsudassana satisfied with all sensual pleasures those who at that time were considered recluses among recluses or brahmins among brahmins, and then ascended the Dhamma Palace.

Paṭhamabhāṇavāro.

The First Recitation Section.

Jhānasampatti

Accomplishment in Jhāna

260. “Atha [M 2.0152] kho, ānanda, rañño mahāsudassanassa etadahosi – ‘kissa nu kho me idaṃ kammassa phalaṃ kissa kammassa vipāko, yenāhaṃ etarahi evaṃmahiddhiko evaṃmahānubhāvo’ti? Atha [P 2.0186] kho, ānanda, rañño mahāsudassanassa etadahosi – ‘tiṇṇaṃ kho me idaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ tiṇṇaṃ kammānaṃ vipāko, yenāhaṃ etarahi evaṃmahiddhiko evaṃmahānubhāvo, seyyathidaṃ dānassa damassa saṃyamassā’ti.

260. Then, Ānanda, this thought occurred to King Mahāsudassana: ‘Of what action of mine is this the fruit, of what action is this the result, that I am now so mighty and so majestic?’ Then, Ānanda, this thought occurred to King Mahāsudassana: ‘This is the fruit of three actions of mine, the result of three actions, that I am now so mighty and so majestic, namely: of giving, of self-control, and of restraint.’

“Atha [V 2.0139] kho, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano yena mahāviyūhaṃ kūṭāgāraṃ tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā mahāviyūhassa kūṭāgārassa dvāre ṭhito udānaṃ udānesi – ‘tiṭṭha, kāmavitakka, tiṭṭha, byāpādavitakka, tiṭṭha, vihiṃsāvitakka. Ettāvatā kāmavitakka, ettāvatā byāpādavitakka, ettāvatā vihiṃsāvitakkā’ti.

Then, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana went to the Mahāviyūha gabled hall. Having gone there, standing at the door of the Mahāviyūha gabled hall, he uttered an inspired utterance: ‘Stop, sensual thought! Stop, malevolent thought! Stop, harmful thought! Thus far, sensual thought. Thus far, malevolent thought. Thus far, harmful thoughts.’

261. “Atha kho, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano mahāviyūhaṃ [T 2.0215] kūṭāgāraṃ pavisitvā sovaṇṇamaye pallaṅke nisinno vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihāsi. Vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihāsi. Pītiyā ca virāgā upekkhako ca vihāsi, sato ca sampajāno sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedesi, yaṃ taṃ ariyā ācikkhanti – ‘upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī’ti tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihāsi. Sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihāsi.

261. Then, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana, having entered the Great Array Hall and seated himself on the golden couch, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, entered and dwelled in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, born of seclusion, and filled with rapture and happiness. With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, by gaining internal confidence and unification of mind, he entered and dwelled in the second jhāna, which is without applied and sustained thought, born of concentration, and filled with rapture and happiness. With the fading away of rapture, he dwelled equanimously, and mindful and clearly comprehending, he experienced happiness with the body; he entered and dwelled in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, he dwells happily.’ With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and displeasure, he entered and dwelled in the fourth jhāna, which is without pleasure and pain, and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness.

262. “Atha kho, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano mahāviyūhā kūṭāgārā nikkhamitvā sovaṇṇamayaṃ kūṭāgāraṃ pavisitvā rūpiyamaye pallaṅke nisinno mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā vihāsi. Tathā dutiyaṃ tathā tatiyaṃ tathā catutthaṃ. Iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ mettāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyāpajjena pharitvā vihāsi. Karuṇāsahagatena [M 2.0153] cetasā…pe… muditāsahagatena cetasā…pe… upekkhāsahagatena [P 2.0187] cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā vihāsi tathā dutiyaṃ tathā tatiyaṃ tathā catutthaṃ. Iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ upekkhāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena [T 2.0216] averena abyāpajjena pharitvā vihāsi.

262. Then, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana, having emerged from the Great Array Hall, entered the golden hall and seated himself on the silver couch. With a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, he dwelled pervading one direction. Likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, and across, everywhere, identifying with all, he dwelled pervading the entire world with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness—abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, and without ill will. With a mind accompanied by compassion… with a mind accompanied by appreciative joy… with a mind accompanied by equanimity, he dwelled pervading one direction. Likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, and across, everywhere, identifying with all, he dwelled pervading the entire world with a mind accompanied by equanimity—abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, and without ill will.

Caturāsīti nagarasahassādi

Eighty-four Thousand Cities, Etc.

263. “Rañño, ānanda, mahāsudassanassa caturāsīti nagarasahassāni ahesuṃ kusāvatīrājadhānippamukhāni; caturāsīti pāsādasahassāni ahesuṃ dhammapāsādappamukhāni; caturāsīti kūṭāgārasahassāni ahesuṃ mahāviyūhakūṭāgārappamukhāni; caturāsīti pallaṅkasahassāni [V 2.0140] ahesuṃ sovaṇṇamayāni rūpiyamayāni dantamayāni sāramayāni gonakatthatāni paṭikatthatāni paṭalikatthatāni kadalimigapavarapaccattharaṇāni sauttaracchadāni ubhatolohitakūpadhānāni; caturāsīti nāgasahassāni ahesuṃ sovaṇṇālaṅkārāni sovaṇṇadhajāni hemajālapaṭicchannāni uposathanāgarājappamukhāni; caturāsīti assasahassāni ahesuṃ sovaṇṇālaṅkārāni sovaṇṇadhajāni hemajālapaṭicchannāni valāhakaassarājappamukhāni; caturāsīti rathasahassāni ahesuṃ sīhacammaparivārāni byagghacammaparivārāni dīpicammaparivārāni paṇḍukambalaparivārāni sovaṇṇālaṅkārāni sovaṇṇadhajāni hemajālapaṭicchannāni vejayantarathappamukhāni; caturāsīti maṇisahassāni ahesuṃ maṇiratanappamukhāni; caturāsīti itthisahassāni ahesuṃ subhaddādevippamukhāni; caturāsīti [P 2.0188] gahapatisahassāni ahesuṃ gahapatiratanappamukhāni; caturāsīti khattiyasahassāni ahesuṃ anuyantāni pariṇāyakaratanappamukhāni; caturāsīti dhenusahassāni ahesuṃ duhasandanāni dukūlasandanāni(pī.) dukūlasandānāni dukūlasandanāni (pī.) dukūlasandānāni (saṃ. ni. 3.96) kaṃsūpadhāraṇāni; caturāsīti vatthakoṭisahassāni ahesuṃ khomasukhumānaṃ kappāsikasukhumānaṃ koseyyasukhumānaṃ kambalasukhumānaṃ[T 2.0217]; (rañño, ānanda, mahāsudassanassa) ( ) sī. ipotthakesu natthi caturāsīti thālipākasahassāni ahesuṃ sāyaṃ pātaṃ bhattābhihāro abhihariyittha.

263. Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana had eighty-four thousand cities, with the royal capital Kusāvatī as the foremost; eighty-four thousand palaces, with the Dhamma Palace as the foremost; eighty-four thousand pinnacled halls, with the Great Array Hall as the foremost; eighty-four thousand couches made of gold, silver, ivory, and precious heartwood, spread with long-fleeced woolen carpets, woolen coverlets, flower-patterned coverlets, and choice antelope-skin rugs, with canopies above and red cushions at both ends; eighty-four thousand elephants, adorned with gold ornaments and gold banners, covered with golden netting, with Uposatha the elephant king as the foremost; eighty-four thousand horses, adorned with gold ornaments and gold banners, covered with golden netting, with Valāhaka the horse king as the foremost; eighty-four thousand chariots, draped with lion skins, tiger skins, leopard skins, and pale woolen blankets, adorned with gold ornaments and gold banners, covered with golden netting, with the Vejayanta chariot as the foremost; eighty-four thousand jewels, with the jewel treasure as the foremost; eighty-four thousand women, with Queen Subhaddā as the foremost; eighty-four thousand householders, with the householder treasure as the foremost; eighty-four thousand nobles, who were his attendants, with the heir-apparent treasure as the foremost; eighty-four thousand cows, whose milk flowed readily, who were tethered with fine cloth ropes, and for whom bronze bowls were held underneath; eighty-four thousand crores of garments, of fine linen, fine cotton, fine silk, and fine wool. For King Mahāsudassana, Ānanda, eighty-four thousand portions of food cooked in pots were brought as his meal morning and evening.

264. “Tena [M 2.0154] kho panānanda, samayena rañño mahāsudassanassa caturāsīti nāgasahassāni sāyaṃ pātaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ āgacchanti. Atha kho, ānanda, rañño mahāsudassanassa etadahosi – ‘imāni kho me caturāsīti nāgasahassāni sāyaṃ pātaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ āgacchanti, yaṃnūna vassasatassa vassasatassa accayena dvecattālīsaṃ dvecattālīsaṃ nāgasahassāni sakiṃ sakiṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ āgaccheyyu’nti. Atha kho, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano pariṇāyakaratanaṃ āmantesi – ‘imāni kho me, samma pariṇāyakaratana, caturāsīti nāgasahassāni sāyaṃ pātaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ āgacchanti, tena hi, samma pariṇāyakaratana, vassasatassa vassasatassa accayena dvecattālīsaṃ dvecattālīsaṃ [P 2.0189] nāgasahassāni sakiṃ sakiṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ āgacchantū’ti. ‘Evaṃ, devā’ti kho, ānanda, pariṇāyakaratanaṃ rañño mahāsudassanassa paccassosi. Atha kho, ānanda, rañño mahāsudassanassa aparena samayena vassasatassa vassasatassa accayena dvecattālīsaṃ dvecattālīsaṃ nāgasahassāni sakiṃ sakiṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ āgamaṃsu.

264. At that time, Ānanda, eighty-four thousand elephants came to attend upon King Mahāsudassana morning and evening. Then, Ānanda, this thought occurred to King Mahāsudassana: ‘These eighty-four thousand elephants attend upon me morning and evening. What if, at the end of every hundred years, forty-two thousand elephants at a time were to attend upon me just once?’ Then, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana addressed the heir-apparent treasure: ‘My dear heir apparent, these eighty-four thousand elephants attend upon me morning and evening. Therefore, my dear heir apparent, let forty-two thousand elephants at a time attend upon me just once at the end of every hundred years.’ ‘Yes, Your Majesty,’ the heir-apparent treasure assented to King Mahāsudassana. And so, Ānanda, after that, at the end of every hundred years, forty-two thousand elephants at a time came to attend upon King Mahāsudassana just once.

Subhaddādeviupasaṅkamanaṃ

The Approach of Queen Subhaddā

265. “Atha kho, ānanda, subhaddāya deviyā bahunnaṃ vassānaṃ bahunnaṃ vassasatānaṃ bahunnaṃ [V 2.0141] vassasahassānaṃ accayena etadahosi – ‘ciraṃ diṭṭho kho me rājā mahāsudassano. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ rājānaṃ mahāsudassanaṃ dassanāya upasaṅkameyya’nti. Atha kho, ānanda, subhaddā devī [T 2.0218] itthāgāraṃ āmantesi – ‘etha tumhe sīsāni nhāyatha pītāni vatthāni pārupatha. Ciraṃ diṭṭho no rājā mahāsudassano, rājānaṃ mahāsudassanaṃ dassanāya upasaṅkamissāmā’ti. ‘Evaṃ, ayye’ti kho, ānanda, itthāgāraṃ subhaddāya deviyā paṭissutvā sīsāni nhāyitvā pītāni vatthāni pārupitvā yena subhaddā devī tenupasaṅkami. Atha kho, ānanda, subhaddā devī pariṇāyakaratanaṃ āmantesi – ‘kappehi, samma pariṇāyakaratana, caturaṅginiṃ senaṃ, ciraṃ diṭṭho no rājā mahāsudassano, rājānaṃ mahāsudassanaṃ dassanāya upasaṅkamissāmā’ti. ‘Evaṃ, devī’ti kho, ānanda, pariṇāyakaratanaṃ subhaddāya deviyā paṭissutvā caturaṅginiṃ senaṃ kappāpetvā subhaddāya deviyā paṭivedesi – ‘kappitā kho, devi, caturaṅginī senā, yassadāni kālaṃ maññasī’ti. Atha [P 2.0190] kho, ānanda, subhaddā [M 2.0155] devī caturaṅginiyā senāya saddhiṃ itthāgārena yena dhammo pāsādo tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ pāsādaṃ abhiruhitvā yena mahāviyūhaṃ kūṭāgāraṃ tenupasaṅkami. Upasaṅkamitvā mahāviyūhassa kūṭāgārassa dvārabāhaṃ ālambitvā aṭṭhāsi. Atha kho, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano saddaṃ sutvā – ‘kiṃ nu kho mahato viya janakāyassa saddo’ti mahāviyūhā kūṭāgārā nikkhamanto addasa subhaddaṃ deviṃ dvārabāhaṃ ālambitvā ṭhitaṃ, disvāna subhaddaṃ deviṃ etadavoca – ‘ettheva, devi, tiṭṭha mā pāvisī’ti. Atha kho, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano aññataraṃ [T 2.0219] purisaṃ āmantesi – ‘ehi tvaṃ, ambho purisa, mahāviyūhā kūṭāgārā sovaṇṇamayaṃ pallaṅkaṃ nīharitvā sabbasovaṇṇamaye tālavane paññapehī’ti. ‘Evaṃ, devā’ti kho, ānanda, so puriso rañño mahāsudassanassa paṭissutvā mahāviyūhā kūṭāgārā sovaṇṇamayaṃ pallaṅkaṃ nīharitvā sabbasovaṇṇamaye tālavane paññapesi. Atha kho, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano dakkhiṇena passena sīhaseyyaṃ kappesi pāde pādaṃ accādhāya sato sampajāno.

265. Then, Ānanda, after the passing of many years, many hundreds of years, and many thousands of years, this thought occurred to Queen Subhaddā: ‘It has been a long time since I have seen King Mahāsudassana. It would be well were I to approach King Mahāsudassana for an audience.’ Then, Ānanda, Queen Subhaddā addressed the women of the inner quarters: ‘Come, wash your heads and put on golden-colored garments. It has been a long time since we have seen King Mahāsudassana; we shall approach King Mahāsudassana for an audience.’ ‘Yes, my lady,’ the women of the inner quarters replied to Queen Subhaddā. Having washed their heads and put on golden-colored garments, they approached Queen Subhaddā. Then, Ānanda, Queen Subhaddā addressed the counselor-gem: ‘Prepare, dear counselor-gem, the four-division army. It has been a long time since we have seen King Mahāsudassana; we shall approach King Mahāsudassana for an audience.’ ‘Yes, Queen,’ the counselor-gem replied to Queen Subhaddā. Having had the four-division army prepared, he informed Queen Subhaddā: ‘The four-division army has been prepared, Queen. The time is now for whatever you deem fit.’ Then, Ānanda, Queen Subhaddā, together with the four-division army and the women of the inner quarters, approached the Dhamma Palace. Having approached and ascended the Dhamma Palace, she went to the Great Array Gabled Hall. Having approached, she stood holding on to the doorpost of the Great Array Gabled Hall. Then, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana, hearing the sound, thought: ‘What is this sound, as of a great crowd of people?’ Emerging from the Great Array Gabled Hall, he saw Queen Subhaddā standing, holding on to the doorpost. Seeing her, he said this to Queen Subhaddā: ‘Stay right there, Queen. Do not enter.’ Then, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana addressed a certain man: ‘Come, good man. Take the golden couch from the Great Array Gabled Hall and set it up in the all-golden palm grove.’ ‘Yes, sire,’ that man replied to King Mahāsudassana. Taking the golden couch from the Great Array Gabled Hall, he set it up in the all-golden palm grove. Then, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana lay down on his right side in the lion’s posture, placing one foot slightly over the other, mindful and clearly comprehending.

266. “Atha kho, ānanda, subhaddāya deviyā etadahosi – ‘vippasannāni kho rañño mahāsudassanassa indriyāni, parisuddho chavivaṇṇo pariyodāto, mā heva kho rājā mahāsudassano kālamakāsī’ti rājānaṃ mahāsudassanaṃ etadavoca –

266. Then, Ānanda, this thought occurred to Queen Subhaddā: ‘The faculties of King Mahāsudassana are exceedingly serene, the color of his skin is pure and radiant. May King Mahāsudassana not pass away!’ She then spoke this to King Mahāsudassana:

‘Imāni te, deva, caturāsīti nagarasahassāni kusāvatīrājadhānippamukhāni. Ettha, deva, chandaṃ janehi jīvite apekkhaṃ karohi. Imāni [P 2.0191] te, deva, caturāsīti pāsādasahassāni dhammapāsādappamukhāni. Ettha, deva, chandaṃ janehi jīvite apekkhaṃ karohi. Imāni te, deva, caturāsīti [V 2.0142] kūṭāgārasahassāni mahāviyūhakūṭāgārappamukhāni. Ettha, deva, chandaṃ janehi jīvite apekkhaṃ karohi. Imāni te, deva, caturāsīti pallaṅkasahassāni sovaṇṇamayāni rūpiyamayāni dantamayāni sāramayāni gonakatthatāni paṭikatthatāni paṭalikatthatāni kadalimigapavarapaccattharaṇāni sauttaracchadāni ubhatolohitakūpadhānāni. Ettha, deva, chandaṃ janehi, jīvite [T 2.0220] apekkhaṃ karohi. Imāni te, deva, caturāsīti nāgasahassāni sovaṇṇālaṅkārāni sovaṇṇadhajāni hemajālapaṭicchannāni uposathanāgarājappamukhāni. Ettha, deva[M 2.0156], chandaṃ janehi jīvite apekkhaṃ karohi. Imāni te, deva, caturāsīti assasahassāni sovaṇṇālaṅkārāni sovaṇṇadhajāni hemajālapaṭicchannāni valāhakaassarājappamukhāni. Ettha, deva, chandaṃ janehi jīvite apekkhaṃ karohi. Imāni te, deva caturāsīti rathasahassāni sīhacammaparivārāni byagghacammaparivārāni dīpicammaparivārāni paṇḍukambalaparivārāni sovaṇṇālaṅkārāni sovaṇṇadhajāni hemajālapaṭicchannāni vejayantarathappamukhāni. Ettha, deva, chandaṃ janehi jīvite apekkhaṃ karohi. Imāni te, deva, caturāsīti maṇisahassāni maṇiratanappamukhāni. Ettha, deva, chandaṃ janehi jīvite apekkhaṃ karohi. Imāni te, deva, caturāsīti itthisahassāni itthiratanappamukhāni. Ettha, deva, chandaṃ janehi jīvite apekkhaṃ karohi. Imāni te, deva, caturāsīti gahapatisahassāni gahapatiratanappamukhāni. Ettha, deva, chandaṃ janehi jīvite apekkhaṃ karohi. Imāni te, deva, caturāsīti khattiyasahassāni anuyantāni pariṇāyakaratanappamukhāni. Ettha, deva, chandaṃ janehi jīvite apekkhaṃ karohi. Imāni te, deva, caturāsīti dhenusahassāni duhasandanāni [P 2.0192] kaṃsūpadhāraṇāni. Ettha, deva, chandaṃ janehi jīvite apekkhaṃ karohi. Imāni te, deva, caturāsīti vatthakoṭisahassāni khomasukhumānaṃ kappāsikasukhumānaṃ koseyyasukhumānaṃ [T 2.0221] kambalasukhumānaṃ. Ettha, deva, chandaṃ janehi, jīvite apekkhaṃ karohi. Imāni te, deva, caturāsīti thālipākasahassāni sāyaṃ pātaṃ bhattābhihāro abhihariyati. Ettha, deva, chandaṃ janehi jīvite apekkhaṃ karohī’ti.

‘These, O king, are your eighty-four thousand cities, with the royal capital Kusāvatī as the foremost. In these, O king, arouse desire; have regard for your life. These, O king, are your eighty-four thousand palaces, with the Dhamma Palace as the foremost. In these, O king, arouse desire; have regard for your life. These, O king, are your eighty-four thousand gabled chambers, with the Mahāviyūha gabled chamber as the foremost. In these, O king, arouse desire; have regard for your life. These, O king, are your eighty-four thousand couches, made of gold, silver, ivory, and heartwood, spread with long-fleeced coverlets, white woolen blankets, woolen coverlets with floral designs, and excellent coverings of antelope hide, with red canopies above and red cushions at both ends. In these, O king, arouse desire; have regard for your life. These, O king, are your eighty-four thousand elephants, adorned with gold ornaments and gold banners, covered with golden nets, with Uposatha, the king of elephants, as the foremost. In these, O king, arouse desire; have regard for your life. These, O king, are your eighty-four thousand horses, adorned with gold ornaments and gold banners, covered with golden nets, with Valāhaka, the king of horses, as the foremost. In these, O king, arouse desire; have regard for your life. These, O king, are your eighty-four thousand chariots, draped with lion skins, tiger skins, leopard skins, and pale-yellow woolen blankets, adorned with gold ornaments and gold banners, covered with golden nets, with the Vejayanta chariot as the foremost. In these, O king, arouse desire; have regard for your life. These, O king, are your eighty-four thousand jewels, with the jewel-treasure as the foremost. In these, O king, arouse desire; have regard for your life. These, O king, are your eighty-four thousand women, with the woman-treasure as the foremost. In these, O king, arouse desire; have regard for your life. These, O king, are your eighty-four thousand householders, with the householder-treasure as the foremost. In these, O king, arouse desire; have regard for your life. These, O king, are your eighty-four thousand attendant warriors, with the counsellor-treasure as the foremost. In these, O king, arouse desire; have regard for your life. These, O king, are your eighty-four thousand milch cows, from which milk flows readily, for which bronze pails are held out. In these, O king, arouse desire; have regard for your life. These, O king, are your eighty-four thousand pairs of garments of fine linen, fine cotton, fine silk, and fine wool. In these, O king, arouse desire; have regard for your life. These, O king, are your eighty-four thousand dishes of food, from which a meal is brought morning and evening. In these, O king, arouse desire; have regard for your life.’

267. “Evaṃ vutte, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano subhaddaṃ deviṃ etadavoca –

267. When this was said, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana said this to Queen Subhaddā:

‘Dīgharattaṃ kho maṃ tvaṃ, devi, iṭṭhehi kantehi piyehi manāpehi samudācarittha; atha ca pana maṃ tvaṃ pacchime kāle aniṭṭhehi akantehi appiyehi amanāpehi samudācarasī’ti. ‘Kathaṃ carahi taṃ, deva, samudācarāmī’ti? ‘Evaṃ kho maṃ tvaṃ, devi, samudācara – “sabbeheva, deva, piyehi manāpehi nānābhāvo vinābhāvo aññathābhāvo, mā kho tvaṃ, deva, sāpekkho kālamakāsi, dukkhā sāpekkhassa kālaṅkiriyā, garahitā ca sāpekkhassa kālaṅkiriyā. Imāni [V 2.0143] te, deva, caturāsīti nagarasahassāni [M 2.0157] kusāvatīrājadhānippamukhāni. Ettha, deva, chandaṃ pajaha jīvite apekkhaṃ mākāsi. Imāni te, deva, caturāsīti pāsādasahassāni dhammapāsādappamukhāni. Ettha, deva, chandaṃ pajaha jīvite apekkhaṃ mākāsi. Imāni te[P 2.0193], deva, caturāsīti kūṭāgārasahassāni mahāviyūhakūṭāgārappamukhāni. Ettha, deva, chandaṃ pajaha jīvite apekkhaṃ mākāsi. Imāni te, deva, caturāsīti pallaṅkasahassāni sovaṇṇamayāni rūpiyamayāni dantamayāni sāramayāni gonakatthatāni paṭikatthatāni paṭalikatthatāni kadalimigapavarapaccattharaṇāni sauttaracchadāni ubhatolohitakūpadhānāni. Ettha, deva, chandaṃ pajaha jīvite apekkhaṃ mākāsi. Imāni te, deva, caturāsīti nāgasahassāni sovaṇṇālaṅkārāni sovaṇṇadhajāni hemajālapaṭicchannāni [T 2.0222] uposathanāgarājappamukhāni. Ettha, deva, chandaṃ pajaha jīvite apekkhaṃ mākāsi. Imāni te, deva, caturāsīti assasahassāni sovaṇṇālaṅkārāni sovaṇṇadhajāni hemajālapaṭicchannāni valāhakaassarājappamukhāni. Ettha, deva, chandaṃ pajaha jīvite apekkhaṃ mākāsi. Imāni te, deva, caturāsīti rathasahassāni sīhacammaparivārāni byagghacammaparivārāni dīpicammaparivārāni paṇḍukambalaparivārāni sovaṇṇālaṅkārāni sovaṇṇadhajāni hemajālapaṭicchannāni vejayantarathappamukhāni. Ettha, deva, chandaṃ pajaha jīvite apekkhaṃ mākāsi. Imāni te, deva, caturāsīti maṇisahassāni maṇiratanappamukhāni. Ettha, deva, chandaṃ pajaha jīvite apekkhaṃ mākāsi. Imāni te, deva, caturāsīti itthisahassāni subhaddādevippamukhāni. Ettha, deva, chandaṃ pajaha jīvite apekkhaṃ mākāsi. Imāni te, deva, caturāsīti gahapatisahassāni gahapatiratanappamukhāni. Ettha, deva, chandaṃ pajaha jīvite apekkhaṃ mākāsi. Imāni te, deva, caturāsīti khattiyasahassāni anuyantāni pariṇāyakaratanappamukhāni. Ettha, deva, chandaṃ pajaha jīvite apekkhaṃ mākāsi. Imāni te, deva, caturāsīti dhenusahassāni duhasandanāni kaṃsūpadhāraṇāni. Ettha deva, chandaṃ pajaha jīvite apekkhaṃ mākāsi. Imāni [P 2.0194] te, deva, caturāsīti vatthakoṭisahassāni khomasukhumānaṃ kappāsikasukhumānaṃ koseyyasukhumānaṃ kambalasukhumānaṃ. Ettha, deva, chandaṃ pajaha jīvite apekkhaṃ [T 2.0223] mākāsi. Imāni te deva caturāsīti thālipākasahassāni sāyaṃ pātaṃ bhattābhihāro abhihariyati. Ettha, deva, chandaṃ pajaha jīvite apekkhaṃ mākāsī’”ti.

“For a long time, O queen, you have addressed me with words that are desirable, lovely, dear, and pleasing; yet now, in my final moments, you address me with words that are undesirable, unlovely, not dear, and unpleasing.” “How then, O king, should I address you?” “Thus, O queen, you should address me: ‘With all that is dear and pleasing, O king, there is change, separation, and alteration. Do not, O king, pass away with attachment. Painful is the passing away of one with attachment, and blameworthy is the passing away of one with attachment. These, O king, are your eighty-four thousand cities, with Kusāvatī the royal capital as their chief. Here, O king, abandon desire; do not have longing for life. These, O king, are your eighty-four thousand palaces, with the Dhamma Palace as their chief. Here, O king, abandon desire; do not have longing for life. These, O king, are your eighty-four thousand gabled mansions, with the Great Viyūha gabled mansion as their chief. Here, O king, abandon desire; do not have longing for life.
