In this regard, should one know of a certain mental pleasure: ‘When I cultivate this mental pleasure, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase,’ such a mental pleasure should be cultivated. Now, of that mental pleasure that is to be cultivated, there is that which is accompanied by initial application and sustained application, and that which is not. Of these, that which is without initial application and sustained application is more sublime. ‘Ruler of the devas, I declare mental pleasure to be of two kinds: that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.’ Thus was it said, and it was said in reference to this.”

361. “Domanassaṃpāhaṃ, devānaminda, duvidhena vadāmi sevitabbampi[P 2.0279], asevitabbampīti. Iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Tattha yaṃ jaññā domanassaṃ ‘imaṃ kho me domanassaṃ sevato akusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, kusalā dhammā parihāyantī’ti, evarūpaṃ domanassaṃ na sevitabbaṃ. Tattha yaṃ jaññā domanassaṃ ‘imaṃ kho me domanassaṃ sevato akusalā dhammā parihāyanti, kusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhantī’ti, evarūpaṃ domanassaṃ sevitabbaṃ. Tattha yaṃ ce savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ, yaṃ ce avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ, ye avitakke avicāre, te paṇītatare. Domanassaṃpāhaṃ, devānaminda, duvidhena vadāmi sevitabbampi, asevitabbampī’ti iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ, idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.

361. “‘Ruler of the devas, I declare mental pain to be of two kinds: that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.’ Now, in reference to what was this said? In this regard, should one know of a certain mental pain: ‘When I cultivate this mental pain, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline,’ such a mental pain should not be cultivated. In this regard, should one know of a certain mental pain: ‘When I cultivate this mental pain, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase,’ such a mental pain should be cultivated. Now, of that mental pain that is to be cultivated, there is that which is accompanied by initial application and sustained application, and that which is not. Of these, that which is without initial application and sustained application is more sublime. ‘Ruler of the devas, I declare mental pain to be of two kinds: that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.’ Thus was it said, and it was said in reference to this.”

362. “Upekkhaṃpāhaṃ, devānaminda, duvidhena vadāmi sevitabbampi, asevitabbampīti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Tattha yaṃ jaññā upekkhaṃ ‘imaṃ kho me upekkhaṃ sevato [T 2.0314] akusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, kusalā dhammā parihāyantī’ti, evarūpā upekkhā [V 2.0206] na sevitabbā. Tattha yaṃ jaññā upekkhaṃ ‘imaṃ kho me upekkhaṃ sevato akusalā dhammā parihāyanti, kusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhantī’ti, evarūpā upekkhā sevitabbā. Tattha yaṃ ce savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ, yaṃ ce avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ, ye avitakke avicāre, te paṇītatare. Upekkhaṃpāhaṃ, devānaminda, duvidhena vadāmi sevitabbampi, asevitabbampīti iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ, idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.

362. “‘Lord of the devas, I declare equanimity to be of two kinds: that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.’ Now, in reference to what was this said? In this regard, should one know of a certain equanimity: ‘When I cultivate this equanimity, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline,’ such an equanimity should not be cultivated. In this regard, should one know of a certain equanimity: ‘When I cultivate this equanimity, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase,’ such an equanimity should be cultivated. Therein, there is equanimity with initial application and sustained application, and there is equanimity without initial application and without sustained application. Of these, that which is without initial application and without sustained application is more sublime. ‘Lord of the devas, I declare equanimity to be of two kinds: that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.’ Thus was it said, and it was said in reference to this.”

363. “Evaṃ paṭipanno kho, devānaminda, bhikkhu papañcasaññāsaṅkhānirodhasāruppagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ paṭipanno hotī”ti. Itthaṃ bhagavā sakkassa devānamindassa pañhaṃ puṭṭho byākāsi. Attamano sakko devānamindo bhagavato bhāsitaṃ [M 2.0223] abhinandi anumodi – “evametaṃ, bhagavā, evametaṃ, sugata, tiṇṇā mettha kaṅkhā vigatā kathaṃkathā bhagavato pañhaveyyākaraṇaṃ sutvā”ti.

363. “Lord of the devas, a bhikkhu who practices in this way has entered upon the path suitable for and leading to the cessation of the proliferation of perceptions and concepts.” In this manner, the Blessed One answered the question put to him by Sakka, lord of the devas. Pleased, Sakka, lord of the devas, rejoiced at the Blessed One's words and approved, saying: “So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Well-gone One! Having heard the Blessed One’s answer to the question, my doubt is crossed over, my perplexity is gone.”

Pātimokkhasaṃvaro

The Restraint of the Pātimokkha

364. Itiha sakko devānamindo bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā bhagavantaṃ uttariṃ pañhaṃ apucchi –

364. Thus Sakka, the lord of the devas, having acclaimed and rejoiced at the Blessed One's teaching, asked the Blessed One a further question:

“Kathaṃ paṭipanno pana, mārisa, bhikkhu pātimokkhasaṃvarāya paṭipanno hotī”ti? “Kāyasamācāraṃpāhaṃ, devānaminda, duvidhena vadāmi – sevitabbampi, asevitabbampi. Vacīsamācāraṃpāhaṃ, devānaminda, duvidhena vadāmi – sevitabbampi, asevitabbampi. Pariyesanaṃpāhaṃ, devānaminda, duvidhena vadāmi – sevitabbampi, asevitabba”mpi.

“Venerable Sir, how does a bhikkhu practice for the restraint of the Pātimokkha?” “Lord of the devas, I declare bodily conduct to be of two kinds: that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated. Lord of the devas, I declare verbal conduct to be of two kinds: that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated. Lord of the devas, I declare seeking to be of two kinds: that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.”

“Kāyasamācāraṃpāhaṃ[P 2.0280], devānaminda, duvidhena vadāmi sevitabbampi asevitabbampīti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Tattha yaṃ jaññā kāyasamācāraṃ ‘imaṃ kho me kāyasamācāraṃ sevato akusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, kusalā dhammā parihāyantī’ti, evarūpo kāyasamācāro na sevitabbo. Tattha yaṃ jaññā kāyasamācāraṃ ‘imaṃ kho me kāyasamācāraṃ [T 2.0315] sevato akusalā dhammā parihāyanti, kusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhantī’ti, evarūpo kāyasamācāro sevitabbo. Kāyasamācāraṃpāhaṃ, devānaminda, duvidhena vadāmi – sevitabbampi, asevitabbampīti iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ, idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.

“‘Lord of the devas, I declare bodily conduct to be of two kinds: that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.’ Now, in reference to what was this said? In this regard, should one know of a certain bodily conduct: ‘When I cultivate this bodily conduct, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline,’ such bodily conduct should not be cultivated. In this regard, should one know of a certain bodily conduct: ‘When I cultivate this bodily conduct, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase,’ such bodily conduct should be cultivated. ‘Lord of the devas, I declare bodily conduct to be of two kinds: that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.’ Thus was it said, and it was said in reference to this.”

“Vacīsamācāraṃpāhaṃ[V 2.0207], devānaminda, duvidhena vadāmi – sevitabbampi, asevitabbampī’ti. Iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Tattha yaṃ jaññā vacīsamācāraṃ ‘imaṃ kho me vacīsamācāraṃ sevato akusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, kusalā dhammā parihāyantī’ti, evarūpo vacīsamācāro na sevitabbo. Tattha yaṃ jaññā vacīsamācāraṃ ‘imaṃ kho me vacīsamācāraṃ sevato akusalā dhammā parihāyanti, kusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhantī’ti, evarūpo vacīsamācāro sevitabbo. Vacīsamācāraṃpāhaṃ, devānaminda, duvidhena vadāmi – sevitabbampi, asevitabbampīti iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ, idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.

“‘Lord of the devas, I declare verbal conduct to be of two kinds: that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.’ Now, in reference to what was this said? In this regard, should one know of a certain verbal conduct: ‘When I cultivate this verbal conduct, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline,’ such verbal conduct should not be cultivated. In this regard, should one know of a certain verbal conduct: ‘When I cultivate this verbal conduct, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase,’ such verbal conduct should be cultivated. ‘Lord of the devas, I declare verbal conduct to be of two kinds: that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.’ Thus was it said, and it was said in reference to this.”

“Pariyesanaṃpāhaṃ[M 2.0224], devānaminda, duvidhena vadāmi – sevitabbampi, asevitabbampīti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Tattha yaṃ jaññā pariyesanaṃ ‘imaṃ kho me pariyesanaṃ sevato akusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, kusalā dhammā parihāyantī’ti, evarūpā pariyesanā na sevitabbā. Tattha yaṃ jaññā pariyesanaṃ ‘imaṃ [T 2.0316] kho me pariyesanaṃ sevato akusalā dhammā parihāyanti, kusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhantī’ti, evarūpā pariyesanā sevitabbā. Pariyesanaṃpāhaṃ, devānaminda, duvidhena vadāmi – sevitabbampi, asevitabbampīti iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ, idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.

“‘Lord of the devas, I declare seeking to be of two kinds: that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.’ Now, in reference to what was this said? In this regard, should one know of a certain seeking: ‘When I cultivate this seeking, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline,’ such seeking should not be cultivated. In this regard, should one know of a certain seeking: ‘When I cultivate this seeking, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase,’ such seeking should be cultivated. ‘Lord of the devas, I declare seeking to be of two kinds: that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.’ Thus was it said, and it was said in reference to this.”

“Evaṃ [P 2.0281] paṭipanno kho, devānaminda, bhikkhu pātimokkhasaṃvarāya paṭipanno hotī”ti. Itthaṃ bhagavā sakkassa devānamindassa pañhaṃ puṭṭho byākāsi. Attamano sakko devānamindo bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandi anumodi – “evametaṃ, bhagavā, evametaṃ, sugata. Tiṇṇā mettha kaṅkhā vigatā kathaṃkathā bhagavato pañhaveyyākaraṇaṃ sutvā”ti.

“Lord of the devas, a bhikkhu who practices in this way is one who practices for the restraint of the Pātimokkha.” Thus the Blessed One, having been asked a question by Sakka, the lord of the devas, answered. Pleased in mind, Sakka, the lord of the devas, acclaimed and rejoiced at the Blessed One's teaching, saying: “So it is, Blessed One! So it is, Well-gone One! Having heard the Blessed One's answer to the question, my doubt is crossed, my perplexity is dispelled.”

Indriyasaṃvaro

Restraint of the Faculties

365. Itiha sakko devānamindo bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā bhagavantaṃ uttariṃ pañhaṃ apucchi –

365. Thus Sakka, the lord of the devas, having acclaimed and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s discourse, asked the Blessed One a further question:

“Kathaṃ paṭipanno pana, mārisa, bhikkhu indriyasaṃvarāya paṭipanno hotī”ti? “Cakkhuviññeyyaṃ rūpaṃpāhaṃ, devānaminda, duvidhena vadāmi – sevitabbampi, asevitabbampi. Sotaviññeyyaṃ saddaṃpāhaṃ, devānaminda, duvidhena vadāmi – sevitabbampi, asevitabbampi. Ghānaviññeyyaṃ gandhaṃpāhaṃ, devānaminda, duvidhena vadāmi – sevitabbampi, asevitabbampi. Jivhāviññeyyaṃ [V 2.0208] rasaṃpāhaṃ, devānaminda, duvidhena vadāmi – sevitabbampi, asevitabbampi. Kāyaviññeyyaṃ phoṭṭhabbaṃpāhaṃ, devānaminda, duvidhena vadāmi – sevitabbampi, asevitabbampi. Manoviññeyyaṃ dhammaṃpāhaṃ, devānaminda, duvidhena vadāmi – sevitabbampi, asevitabbampī”ti.

“But how, venerable sir, is a bhikkhu practicing for the restraint of the senses?” “Lord of the devas, I say that forms cognizable by the eye are of two kinds: those to be cultivated and those not to be cultivated. Lord of the devas, I say that sounds cognizable by the ear are of two kinds: those to be cultivated and those not to be cultivated. Lord of the devas, I say that odors cognizable by the nose are of two kinds: those to be cultivated and those not to be cultivated. Lord of the devas, I say that flavors cognizable by the tongue are of two kinds: those to be cultivated and those not to be cultivated. Lord of the devas, I say that tangibles cognizable by the body are of two kinds: those to be cultivated and those not to be cultivated. Lord of the devas, I say that mental phenomena cognizable by the mind are of two kinds: those to be cultivated and those not to be cultivated.”

Evaṃ vutte, sakko devānamindo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca –

When this was said, Sakka, the lord of the devas, said this to the Blessed One:

“Imassa kho ahaṃ, bhante, bhagavatā saṅkhittena bhāsitassa evaṃ vitthārena atthaṃ ājānāmi. Yathārūpaṃ, bhante, cakkhuviññeyyaṃ rūpaṃ sevato akusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, kusalā dhammā parihāyanti, evarūpaṃ cakkhuviññeyyaṃ rūpaṃ [M 2.0225] na sevitabbaṃ[P 2.0282]. Yathārūpañca kho, bhante, cakkhuviññeyyaṃ rūpaṃ sevato akusalā dhammā parihāyanti, kusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, evarūpaṃ cakkhuviññeyyaṃ rūpaṃ sevitabbaṃ. Yathārūpañca kho, bhante, sotaviññeyyaṃ [T 2.0317] saddaṃ sevato…pe… ghānaviññeyyaṃ gandhaṃ sevato… jivhāviññeyyaṃ rasaṃ sevato… kāyaviññeyyaṃ phoṭṭhabbaṃ sevato… manoviññeyyaṃ dhammaṃ sevato akusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, kusalā dhammā parihāyanti, evarūpo manoviññeyyo dhammo na sevitabbo. Yathārūpañca kho, bhante, manoviññeyyaṃ dhammaṃ sevato akusalā dhammā parihāyanti, kusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, evarūpo manoviññeyyo dhammo sevitabbo.

“Venerable sir, of this which was spoken in brief by the Blessed One, I understand the meaning in detail thus: Venerable sir, whatever kind of form cognizable by the eye one cultivates, by which unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline, that kind of form cognizable by the eye should not be cultivated. And whatever kind of form cognizable by the eye one cultivates, by which unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase, that kind of form cognizable by the eye should be cultivated. And whatever kind of sound cognizable by the ear one cultivates… and whatever kind of odor cognizable by the nose one cultivates… and whatever kind of flavor cognizable by the tongue one cultivates… and whatever kind of tangible cognizable by the body one cultivates… and whatever kind of mental phenomenon cognizable by the mind one cultivates, by which unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline, that kind of mental phenomenon cognizable by the mind should not be cultivated. And whatever kind of mental phenomenon cognizable by the mind one cultivates, by which unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase, that kind of mental phenomenon cognizable by the mind should be cultivated.

“Imassa kho me, bhante, bhagavatā saṅkhittena bhāsitassa evaṃ vitthārena atthaṃ ājānato tiṇṇā mettha kaṅkhā vigatā kathaṃkathā bhagavato pañhaveyyākaraṇaṃ sutvā”ti.

“Venerable sir, for me who understands in this way the meaning in detail of what was spoken in brief by the Blessed One, having heard the Blessed One's explanation of the question, my doubt herein is overcome, my uncertainty is gone.”

366. Itiha sakko devānamindo bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā bhagavantaṃ uttariṃ pañhaṃ apucchi –

366. Thus Sakka, the lord of the devas, having acclaimed and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s discourse, asked the Blessed One a further question:

“Sabbeva nu kho, mārisa, samaṇabrāhmaṇā ekantavādā ekantasīlā ekantachandā ekantaajjhosānā”ti? “Na kho, devānaminda, sabbe samaṇabrāhmaṇā ekantavādā ekantasīlā ekantachandā ekantaajjhosānā”ti.

“Venerable sir, are all ascetics and brahmins of a single doctrine, a single virtue, a single inclination, and a single consummation?” “No, lord of the devas, not all ascetics and brahmins are of a single doctrine, a single virtue, a single inclination, and a single consummation.”

“Kasmā pana, mārisa, na sabbe samaṇabrāhmaṇā ekantavādā ekantasīlā ekantachandā ekantaajjhosānā”ti? “Anekadhātu nānādhātu kho, devānaminda, loko. Tasmiṃ anekadhātunānādhātusmiṃ loke yaṃ yadeva sattā dhātuṃ abhinivisanti, taṃ tadeva thāmasā parāmāsā [V 2.0209] abhinivissa voharanti – ‘idameva saccaṃ moghamañña’nti. Tasmā [T 2.0318] na sabbe samaṇabrāhmaṇā ekantavādā ekantasīlā ekantachandā ekantaajjhosānā”ti.

“But why, venerable sir, are not all ascetics and brahmins of a single doctrine, a single virtue, a single inclination, and a single consummation?” “The world, lord of the devas, has many elements, various elements. In that world of many and various elements, whatever element beings adhere to, that very element they, with force and misapprehension, cling to and declare: ‘This alone is true; anything else is futile.’ Therefore, not all ascetics and brahmins are of a single doctrine, a single virtue, a single inclination, and a single consummation.”

“Sabbeva nu kho, mārisa, samaṇabrāhmaṇā accantaniṭṭhā [P 2.0283] accantayogakkhemī accantabrahmacārī accantapariyosānā”ti? “Na kho, devānaminda, sabbe samaṇabrāhmaṇā accantaniṭṭhā accantayogakkhemī accantabrahmacārī accantapariyosānā”ti.

“Venerable sir, are all ascetics and brahmins absolutely consummate, absolutely secure from bonds, absolute in the holy life, and absolute in their conclusion?” “No, lord of the devas, not all ascetics and brahmins are absolutely consummate, absolutely secure from bonds, absolute in the holy life, and absolute in their conclusion.”

“Kasmā [M 2.0226] pana, mārisa, na sabbe samaṇabrāhmaṇā accantaniṭṭhā accantayogakkhemī accantabrahmacārī accantapariyosānā”ti? “Ye kho, devānaminda, bhikkhū taṇhāsaṅkhayavimuttā te accantaniṭṭhā accantayogakkhemī accantabrahmacārī accantapariyosānā. Tasmā na sabbe samaṇabrāhmaṇā accantaniṭṭhā accantayogakkhemī accantabrahmacārī accantapariyosānā”ti.

“But why, venerable sir, are not all ascetics and brahmins absolutely consummate, absolutely secure from bonds, absolute in the holy life, and absolute in their conclusion?” “Those bhikkhus, lord of the devas, who are liberated through the destruction of craving, they are absolutely consummate, absolutely secure from bonds, absolute in the holy life, and absolute in their conclusion. Therefore, not all ascetics and brahmins are absolutely consummate, absolutely secure from bonds, absolute in the holy life, and absolute in their conclusion.”

Itthaṃ bhagavā sakkassa devānamindassa pañhaṃ puṭṭho byākāsi. Attamano sakko devānamindo bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandi anumodi – “evametaṃ, bhagavā, evametaṃ, sugata. Tiṇṇā mettha kaṅkhā vigatā kathaṃkathā bhagavato pañhaveyyākaraṇaṃ sutvā”ti.

In this manner, the Blessed One, being asked, answered the question of Sakka, the lord of the devas. With a pleased mind, Sakka, the lord of the devas, acclaimed and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s discourse, saying: “So it is, Blessed One! So it is, Sugata! Having heard the Blessed One's explanation of the question, my doubt herein is overcome, my uncertainty is gone.”

367. Itiha sakko devānamindo bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā bhagavantaṃ etadavoca –

367. Thus Sakka, lord of the devas, having acclaimed and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s discourse, said this to the Blessed One:

“Ejā, bhante, rogo, ejā gaṇḍo, ejā sallaṃ, ejā imaṃ purisaṃ parikaḍḍhati tassa tasseva bhavassa abhinibbattiyā. Tasmā ayaṃ puriso uccāvacamāpajjati[T 2.0319]. Yesāhaṃ, bhante, pañhānaṃ ito bahiddhā aññesu samaṇabrāhmaṇesu okāsakammampi nālatthaṃ, te me bhagavatā byākatā. Dīgharattānusayitañca pana dīgharattānupassatā, yañca pana (syā.), dīgharattānusayino, yañca pana (sī. pī.) me vicikicchākathaṃkathāsallaṃ, tañca bhagavatā abbuḷha”nti.

“Venerable sir, agitation is a disease, agitation is a tumor, agitation is a dart. It is agitation that drags this person on to renewed existence in this or that state of being. Therefore this person falls into high and low states. Venerable sir, those questions for which I could not find even an opportunity among other ascetics and brahmins outside of this teaching, have been answered for me by the Blessed One. And the dart of doubt and uncertainty that has long lain latent within me, that too has been extracted by the Blessed One.”

“Abhijānāsi [P 2.0284] no tvaṃ, devānaminda, ime pañhe aññe samaṇabrāhmaṇe pucchitā”ti? “Abhijānāmahaṃ, bhante, ime pañhe aññe samaṇabrāhmaṇe pucchitā”ti. “Yathā kathaṃ pana te, devānaminda, byākaṃsu? Sace te agaru bhāsassū”ti. “Na kho me, bhante, garu yatthassa bhagavā nisinno bhagavantarūpo vā”ti. “Tena hi, devānaminda, bhāsassū”ti. “Yesvāhaṃ yesāhaṃ (sī. syā. pī.), bhante[V 2.0210], maññāmi samaṇabrāhmaṇā āraññikā pantasenāsanāti, tyāhaṃ upasaṅkamitvā ime pañhe pucchāmi, te mayā puṭṭhā na sampāyanti, asampāyantā mamaṃyeva paṭipucchanti – ‘ko nāmo āyasmā’ti? Tesāhaṃ puṭṭho byākaromi – ‘ahaṃ kho, mārisa, sakko devānamindo’ti. Te mamaṃyeva uttari paṭipucchanti – ‘kiṃ panāyasmā, devānaminda devānamindo (sī. pī.), kammaṃ katvā imaṃ ṭhānaṃ patto’ti? Tesāhaṃ yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ desemi. Te tāvatakeneva attamanā [M 2.0227] honti – ‘sakko ca no devānamindo diṭṭho, yañca no apucchimhā, tañca no byākāsī’ti. Te aññadatthu mamaṃyeva sāvakā sampajjanti, na cāhaṃ tesaṃ. Ahaṃ kho pana, bhante, bhagavato sāvako sotāpanno avinipātadhammo niyato sambodhiparāyaṇo”ti[T 2.0320].

“Do you recall, Lord of the Devas, having asked these questions of other ascetics and brahmins?” “I do recall, venerable sir, having asked these questions of other ascetics and brahmins.” “But how did they answer, Lord of the Devas? If it is not burdensome for you, please speak.” “It is not burdensome for me, venerable sir, where the Blessed One is seated, or one like the Blessed One.” “Then, Lord of the Devas, please speak.” “Venerable sir, those ascetics and brahmins whom I considered to be forest-dwellers, living in remote lodgings—I approached them and asked these questions. When questioned by me, they could not answer satisfactorily. Being unable to answer, they questioned me in return: ‘What is your name, venerable one?’ When asked, I replied: ‘I, sirs, am Sakka, the Lord of the Devas.’ Then they questioned me further: ‘But what kamma did you perform, venerable Lord of the Devas, to attain this position?’ I then taught them the Dhamma as I had heard and learned it. They were pleased merely by that much, thinking: ‘We have seen Sakka, the Lord of the Devas, and he has answered the questions we asked.’ Indeed, they become my disciples, but I do not become theirs. But I, venerable sir, am a disciple of the Blessed One, a stream-enterer, not subject to the state of downfall, assured, and destined for enlightenment.”

Somanassapaṭilābhakathā

The Discourse on the Acquisition of Joy

368. “Abhijānāsi no tvaṃ, devānaminda, ito pubbe evarūpaṃ vedapaṭilābhaṃ somanassapaṭilābha”nti? “Abhijānāmahaṃ[P 2.0285], bhante, ito pubbe evarūpaṃ vedapaṭilābhaṃ somanassapaṭilābha”nti. “Yathā kathaṃ pana tvaṃ, devānaminda, abhijānāsi ito pubbe evarūpaṃ vedapaṭilābhaṃ somanassapaṭilābha”nti?

368. “Do you recall, Lord of the Devas, ever before having such an acquisition of delight and an acquisition of joy?” “Yes, venerable sir, I recall having had such an acquisition of delight and an acquisition of joy before.” “But how, Lord of the Devas, do you recall having had such an acquisition of delight and an acquisition of joy before?”

“Bhūtapubbaṃ, bhante, devāsurasaṅgāmo samupabyūḷho samūpabbuḷho (sī. pī.) ahosi. Tasmiṃ kho pana, bhante, saṅgāme devā jiniṃsu, asurā parājayiṃsu parājiṃsu (sī. pī.). Tassa mayhaṃ, bhante, taṃ saṅgāmaṃ abhivijinitvā vijitasaṅgāmassa etadahosi – ‘yā ceva dāni dibbā ojā yā ca asurā ojā, ubhayametaṃ ubhayamettha (syā.) devā paribhuñjissantī’ti. So kho pana me, bhante, vedapaṭilābho somanassapaṭilābho sadaṇḍāvacaro sasatthāvacaro na nibbidāya na virāgāya na nirodhāya na upasamāya na abhiññāya na sambodhāya na nibbānāya saṃvattati. Yo kho pana me ayaṃ, bhante, bhagavato dhammaṃ sutvā vedapaṭilābho somanassapaṭilābho, so adaṇḍāvacaro asatthāvacaro ekantanibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattatī”ti.

“Once, venerable sir, a battle between the devas and asuras was arrayed. In that battle, venerable sir, the devas were victorious, and the asuras were defeated. Then, venerable sir, after winning that battle, this thought occurred to me, the victor: ‘Now the devas will enjoy both the divine sustenance and the asura sustenance.’ But that acquisition of delight, venerable sir, that acquisition of joy, was accompanied by the rod, accompanied by weapons; it did not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna. But this acquisition of delight, venerable sir, this acquisition of joy that comes from hearing the Blessed One’s Dhamma is unaccompanied by the rod, unaccompanied by weapons; it leads exclusively to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna.”

369. “Kiṃ pana tvaṃ, devānaminda, atthavasaṃ sampassamāno evarūpaṃ vedapaṭilābhaṃ somanassapaṭilābhaṃ pavedesī”ti? “Cha kho ahaṃ, bhante, atthavase sampassamāno evarūpaṃ vedapaṭilābhaṃ somanassapaṭilābhaṃ pavedemi.

369. “But what benefit do you see, Lord of the Devas, that you declare such an acquisition of delight and an acquisition of joy?” “Venerable sir, seeing six benefits, I declare such an acquisition of delight and an acquisition of joy.

“Idheva [T 2.0321][V 2.0211] tiṭṭhamānassa, devabhūtassa me sato;

Punarāyu ca me laddho, evaṃ jānāhi mārisa.

‘While still remaining here, being a deva, my lifespan has been renewed. Thus, Mārisa, you should know.’

“Imaṃ [M 2.0228] kho ahaṃ, bhante, paṭhamaṃ atthavasaṃ sampassamāno [P 2.0286] evarūpaṃ vedapaṭilābhaṃ somanassapaṭilābhaṃ pavedemi.

“Seeing this first benefit, venerable sir, I declare such an acquisition of delight and an acquisition of joy.

“Cutāhaṃ diviyā kāyā, āyuṃ hitvā amānusaṃ;

Amūḷho gabbhamessāmi, yattha me ramatī mano.

‘Having passed from the divine body, abandoning the non-human lifespan, unconfused, I will enter a womb where my mind delights.’

“Imaṃ kho ahaṃ, bhante, dutiyaṃ atthavasaṃ sampassamāno evarūpaṃ vedapaṭilābhaṃ somanassapaṭilābhaṃ pavedemi.

“Seeing this second benefit, venerable sir, I declare such an acquisition of delight and an acquisition of joy.

“Svāhaṃ amūḷhapaññassa amūḷhapañhassa (?), viharaṃ sāsane rato;

Ñāyena viharissāmi, sampajāno paṭissato.

‘I, with unconfused wisdom, delighting in the Dispensation, will dwell rightly, clearly comprehending and mindful.’

“Imaṃ kho ahaṃ, bhante, tatiyaṃ atthavasaṃ sampassamāno evarūpaṃ vedapaṭilābhaṃ somanassapaṭilābhaṃ pavedemi.

“Seeing this third benefit, venerable sir, I declare such an acquisition of delight and an acquisition of joy.

“Ñāyena me carato ca, sambodhi ce bhavissati;

Aññātā viharissāmi, sveva anto bhavissati.

‘If, while I am practicing rightly, further enlightenment should come to be, I will dwell in order to fully understand, and that itself will be the end.’

“Imaṃ kho ahaṃ, bhante, catutthaṃ atthavasaṃ sampassamāno evarūpaṃ vedapaṭilābhaṃ somanassapaṭilābhaṃ pavedemi.

“Seeing this fourth benefit, venerable sir, I declare such an acquisition of delight and an acquisition of joy.

“Cutāhaṃ mānusā kāyā, āyuṃ hitvāna mānusaṃ;

Puna devo bhavissāmi, devalokamhi uttamo.

‘Having passed from the human body, abandoning the human lifespan, I will again become a deva, supreme in the deva world.’

“Imaṃ kho ahaṃ, bhante, pañcamaṃ atthavasaṃ sampassamāno evarūpaṃ vedapaṭilābhaṃ somanassapaṭilābhaṃ pavedemi.

“Seeing this fifth benefit, venerable sir, I declare such an acquisition of delight and an acquisition of joy.

“Te [T 2.0322][V 2.0212] ye (?) paṇītatarā devā, akaniṭṭhā yasassino;

Antime vattamānamhi, so nivāso bhavissati.

‘Those devas, more sublime, the glorious Akaniṭṭha devas; when my final existence occurs, that will be my abode.’

“Imaṃ [P 2.0287] kho ahaṃ, bhante, chaṭṭhaṃ atthavasaṃ sampassamāno evarūpaṃ vedapaṭilābhaṃ somanassapaṭilābhaṃ pavedemi.

“Seeing this sixth benefit, venerable sir, I declare such an acquisition of delight and an acquisition of joy.

“Ime kho ahaṃ, bhante, cha atthavase sampassamāno evarūpaṃ vedapaṭilābhaṃ somanassapaṭilābhaṃ pavedemi.

“Seeing these six benefits, venerable sir, I declare such an acquisition of delight and an acquisition of joy.”

370.“Apariyositasaṅkappo[M 2.0229], vicikiccho kathaṃkathī.

370. “With unfulfilled intention, doubtful, and perplexed,

Vicariṃ dīghamaddhānaṃ, anvesanto tathāgataṃ.

I wandered for a long time, seeking the Tathāgata.

“Yassu maññāmi samaṇe, pavivittavihārino;

Sambuddhā iti maññāno, gacchāmi te upāsituṃ.

“Those ascetics whom I considered to be dwelling in seclusion, thinking ‘They are fully enlightened ones,’ I went to attend upon them.

“‘Kathaṃ ārādhanā hoti, kathaṃ hoti virādhanā’;

Iti puṭṭhā na sampāyanti sambhonti (syā.), magge paṭipadāsu ca.

“‘How does accomplishment come about? How does failure come about?’ When asked thus, they could not answer regarding the path and the practices.

“Tyassu yadā maṃ jānanti, sakko devānamāgato;

Tyassu mameva pucchanti, ‘kiṃ katvā pāpuṇī idaṃ’.

“When they recognized me, thinking, ‘Sakka, lord of the devas, has come,’ they would then ask me, ‘Having done what, did you attain this?’”

“Tesaṃ yathāsutaṃ dhammaṃ, desayāmi jane sutaṃ janesuta (ka. sī.);

Tena attamanā honti, ‘diṭṭho no vāsavoti ca’.

“To them I teach the Dhamma as I have heard it among people. By that they become pleased, thinking, ‘We have seen Vāsava!’”

“Yadā ca buddhamaddakkhiṃ, vicikicchāvitāraṇaṃ;

Somhi vītabhayo ajja, sambuddhaṃ payirupāsiya payirupāsayiṃ (syā. ka.).

And when I saw the Buddha, the overcomer of doubt, I became free from fear. Today, having attended upon the Fully Enlightened One, I am free from fear.

“Taṇhāsallassa hantāraṃ, buddhaṃ appaṭipuggalaṃ;

Ahaṃ [T 2.0323] vande mahāvīraṃ, buddhamādiccabandhunaṃ.

I pay homage to the slayer of the dart of craving, the peerless Buddha, the one of great energy, the kinsman of the sun.

“Yaṃ [P 2.0288][V 2.0213] karomasi brahmuno, samaṃ devehi mārisa;

Tadajja tuyhaṃ kassāma dassāma (syā. ka.), handa sāmaṃ karoma te.

Venerable Sir, that homage which we formerly performed to Brahmā, together with the devas, that homage we shall give to you today. Come now, let us ourselves perform homage to you.

“Tvameva asi tuvamevasi (pī.) sambuddho, tuvaṃ satthā anuttaro;

Sadevakasmiṃ lokasmiṃ, natthi te paṭipuggalo”ti.

You alone are the Fully Enlightened One; you are the unsurpassed teacher. In the world with its devas, there is no one to compare with you.”

371. Atha kho sakko devānamindo pañcasikhaṃ gandhabbaputtaṃ āmantesi – “bahūpakāro kho mesi tvaṃ, tāta pañcasikha, yaṃ tvaṃ bhagavantaṃ paṭhamaṃ pasādesi. Tayā, tāta, paṭhamaṃ pasāditaṃ pacchā mayaṃ taṃ bhagavantaṃ dassanāya upasaṅkamimhā arahantaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ. Pettike vā ṭhāne ṭhapayissāmi[M 2.0230], gandhabbarājā bhavissasi, bhaddañca te sūriyavacchasaṃ dammi, sā hi te abhipatthitā”ti.

371. Then Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed the gandhabba deva-son Pañcasikha: ‘You have been of great help to me, dear Pañcasikha, in that you first inspired confidence in the Blessed One. After confidence was first inspired in him by you, dear one, we later approached that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, for the sake of seeing him. I will establish you in your father's position; you shall be king of the gandhabbas, and I give you the fair Sūriyavacchasā, for she is desired by you.’”

Atha kho sakko devānamindo pāṇinā pathaviṃ parāmasitvā tikkhattuṃ udānaṃ udānesi – “namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassā”ti.

Then Sakka, lord of the devas, having touched the earth with his hand, uttered an exclamation of joy three times: ‘Homage to that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One!’”

Imasmiñca pana veyyākaraṇasmiṃ bhaññamāne sakkassa devānamindassa virajaṃ vītamalaṃ dhammacakkhuṃ udapādi – “yaṃ kiñci samudayadhammaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ nirodhadhamma”nti. Aññesañca asītiyā devatāsahassānaṃ[P 2.0289], iti ye sakkena devānamindena ajjhiṭṭhapañhā puṭṭhā[T 2.0324], te bhagavatā byākatā. Tasmā imassa veyyākaraṇassa sakkapañhātveva adhivacananti.

And while this exposition was being spoken, the dust-free, stainless Dhamma-eye arose in Sakka, lord of the devas: ‘Whatever has the nature of arising, all that has the nature of ceasing.’ And for eighty thousand other devas, the Dhamma-eye also arose. Thus, those questions which were requested and asked by Sakka, lord of the devas, were answered by the Blessed One. Therefore, the designation of this exposition is ‘The Questions of Sakka.’”

Sakkapañhasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Sakkapañha Sutta, the eighth, is concluded.

9. Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasuttaṃ

9. The Great Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness

372. Evaṃ [T 2.0325][M 2.0231][V 2.0214] me [P 2.0290] sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā kurūsu viharati kammāsadhammaṃ nāma kurūnaṃ nigamo. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “bhikkhavo”ti. “Bhaddante”ti bhadanteti (sī. syā. pī.) te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca –

372. Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kurus, at a market town of the Kurus named Kammāsadhamma. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus." "Venerable sir," they replied. The Blessed One said this:

Uddeso

The Outline

373. “Ekāyano ayaṃ, bhikkhave, maggo sattānaṃ visuddhiyā, sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāya dukkhadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamāya ñāyassa adhigamāya nibbānassa sacchikiriyāya, yadidaṃ cattāro satipaṭṭhānā.

373. “Bhikkhus, this is the one and only path for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true way, for the realization of Nibbāna—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness.

“Katame cattāro? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ, vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ, citte cittānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ, dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ.

“What are the four? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and grief in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and grief in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and grief in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating dhammas in dhammas, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and grief in regard to the world.

Uddeso niṭṭhito.

The Outline is concluded.

Kāyānupassanā ānāpānapabbaṃ

Contemplation of the Body: The Section on Breathing

374. “Kathañca [V 2.0215][P 2.0291] pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu araññagato vā rukkhamūlagato vā suññāgāragato vā nisīdati pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā. So satova assasati, satova passasati. Dīghaṃ [T 2.0326] vā assasanto ‘dīghaṃ assasāmī’ti pajānāti, dīghaṃ vā passasanto ‘dīghaṃ passasāmī’ti pajānāti. Rassaṃ vā assasanto ‘rassaṃ assasāmī’ti pajānāti, rassaṃ vā passasanto ‘rassaṃ passasāmī’ti pajānāti. ‘Sabbakāyapaṭisaṃvedī assasissāmī’ti sikkhati[M 2.0232], ‘sabbakāyapaṭisaṃvedī passasissāmī’ti sikkhati. ‘Passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ passasissāmī’ti sikkhati.

374. “And how, bhikkhus, does a bhikkhu dwell contemplating the body in the body? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty place, sits down. Having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him, ever mindful he breathes in, and ever mindful he breathes out. Breathing in long, he knows: ‘I breathe in long’; or breathing out long, he knows: ‘I breathe out long’. Breathing in short, he knows: ‘I breathe in short’; or breathing out short, he knows: ‘I breathe out short’. He trains himself: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body’; he trains himself: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body’. He trains himself: ‘I shall breathe in calming the bodily formation’; he trains himself: ‘I shall breathe out calming the bodily formation’.

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, dakkho bhamakāro vā bhamakārantevāsī vā dīghaṃ vā añchanto ‘dīghaṃ añchāmī’ti pajānāti, rassaṃ vā añchanto ‘rassaṃ añchāmī’ti pajānāti evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dīghaṃ vā assasanto ‘dīghaṃ assasāmī’ti pajānāti, dīghaṃ vā passasanto ‘dīghaṃ passasāmī’ti pajānāti, rassaṃ vā assasanto ‘rassaṃ assasāmī’ti pajānāti, rassaṃ vā passasanto ‘rassaṃ passasāmī’ti pajānāti. ‘Sabbakāyapaṭisaṃvedī assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘sabbakāyapaṭisaṃvedī passasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ passasissāmī’ti sikkhati. Iti [P 2.0292] ajjhattaṃ vā kāye kāyānupassī viharati, bahiddhā vā kāye kāyānupassī viharati, ajjhattabahiddhā vā kāye kāyānupassī viharati. Samudayadhammānupassī vā kāyasmiṃ viharati, vayadhammānupassī vā kāyasmiṃ viharati, samudayavayadhammānupassī vā kāyasmiṃ viharati. ‘Atthi kāyo’ti vā [T 2.0327] panassa sati paccupaṭṭhitā hoti yāvadeva ñāṇamattāya paṭissatimattāya anissito ca viharati, na ca kiñci loke upādiyati. Evampi kho evampi (sī. syā. pī.), bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati.

“Just as, bhikkhus, a skilled turner or his apprentice, when making a long turn, knows: ‘I am making a long turn,’ or when making a short turn, knows: ‘I am making a short turn’; even so, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, breathing in long, knows: ‘I breathe in long’; or breathing out long, he knows: ‘I breathe out long’; breathing in short, he knows: ‘I breathe in short’; or breathing out short, he knows: ‘I breathe out short’. He trains himself: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body’; he trains himself: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body’. He trains himself: ‘I shall breathe in calming the bodily formation’; he trains himself: ‘I shall breathe out calming the bodily formation’. In this way he dwells contemplating the body in the body internally, or he dwells contemplating the body in the body externally, or he dwells contemplating the body in the body both internally and externally. He dwells contemplating the nature of arising in the body, or he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in the body, or he dwells contemplating the nature of both arising and passing away in the body. Or his mindfulness is established with the thought: ‘The body exists,’ just to the extent necessary for knowledge and mindfulness. And he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world. In this way too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body.

Ānāpānapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Section on Breathing is concluded.

Kāyānupassanā iriyāpathapabbaṃ

Contemplation of the Body: The Section on Postures

375. “Puna [V 2.0216] caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu gacchanto vā ‘gacchāmī’ti pajānāti, ṭhito vā ‘ṭhitomhī’ti pajānāti, nisinno vā ‘nisinnomhī’ti pajānāti, sayāno vā ‘sayānomhī’ti pajānāti, yathā yathā vā panassa kāyo paṇihito hoti, tathā tathā naṃ pajānāti. Iti ajjhattaṃ vā kāye kāyānupassī viharati, bahiddhā vā kāye kāyānupassī [M 2.0233] viharati, ajjhattabahiddhā vā kāye kāyānupassī viharati. Samudayadhammānupassī vā kāyasmiṃ viharati, vayadhammānupassī vā kāyasmiṃ viharati, samudayavayadhammānupassī vā kāyasmiṃ viharati. ‘Atthi kāyo’ti vā panassa sati paccupaṭṭhitā hoti yāvadeva ñāṇamattāya paṭissatimattāya anissito ca viharati, na ca kiñci loke upādiyati. Evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati.

375. Furthermore, O monks, a monk, when walking, knows, ‘I am walking.’ When standing, he knows, ‘I am standing.’ When sitting, he knows, ‘I am sitting.’ When lying down, he knows, ‘I am lying down.’ Or, in whatever way his body is disposed, he knows it in that very way. Thus he dwells contemplating the body in the body internally, or he dwells contemplating the body in the body externally, or he dwells contemplating the body in the body both internally and externally. He dwells contemplating the phenomena of arising in the body, or he dwells contemplating the phenomena of passing away in the body, or he dwells contemplating the phenomena of arising and passing away in the body. Or, his mindfulness is established with the thought, ‘The body exists,’ just to the extent necessary for knowledge and mindfulness. And he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world. In this way too, O monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body.

Iriyāpathapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Section on Postures is concluded.

Kāyānupassanā sampajānapabbaṃ

Contemplation of the Body: The Section on Clear Comprehension

376. “Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu abhikkante paṭikkante sampajānakārī hoti, ālokite vilokite sampajānakārī hoti, samiñjite pasārite sampajānakārī hoti, saṅghāṭipattacīvaradhāraṇe sampajānakārī [T 2.0328] hoti, asite pīte khāyite sāyite sampajānakārī hoti, uccārapassāvakamme sampajānakārī hoti, gate ṭhite nisinne sutte jāgarite bhāsite tuṇhībhāve sampajānakārī hoti. Iti [P 2.0293] ajjhattaṃ vā…pe… evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati.

376. Furthermore, O monks, a monk acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; he acts with clear comprehension when looking straight ahead and looking aside; he acts with clear comprehension when bending and stretching his limbs; he acts with clear comprehension in wearing the double-robe, bowl, and other robes; he acts with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, and savoring; he acts with clear comprehension in the act of defecating and urinating; he acts with clear comprehension when walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and keeping silent. Thus he dwells contemplating the body in the body internally... and so forth... In this way too, O monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body.

Sampajānapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Section on Clear Comprehension is concluded.

Kāyānupassanā paṭikūlamanasikārapabbaṃ

Contemplation of the Body: The Section on Attention to Repulsiveness

377. “Puna [V 2.0217] caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu imameva kāyaṃ uddhaṃ pādatalā adho kesamatthakā tacapariyantaṃ pūraṃ nānappakārassa asucino paccavekkhati – ‘atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesā lomā nakhā dantā taco, maṃsaṃ nhāru aṭṭhi aṭṭhimiñjaṃ vakkaṃ, hadayaṃ yakanaṃ kilomakaṃ pihakaṃ papphāsaṃ, antaṃ antaguṇaṃ [M 2.0234] udariyaṃ karīsaṃ karīsaṃ matthaluṅgaṃ (ka.), pittaṃ semhaṃ pubbo lohitaṃ sedo medo, assu vasā kheḷo siṅghāṇikā lasikā mutta’nti.

377. Furthermore, O monks, a monk reflects on this very body, upwards from the soles of the feet, downwards from the tips of the hair, bounded by skin, and full of many kinds of impurities: ‘In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, pleura, spleen, lungs, large intestine, small intestine, stomach contents, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, solid fat, tears, liquid fat, saliva, nasal mucus, synovial fluid, and urine.’

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, ubhatomukhā putoḷi mūtoḷī (syā.), mutoli (pī.) pūrā nānāvihitassa dhaññassa, seyyathidaṃ sālīnaṃ vīhīnaṃ muggānaṃ māsānaṃ tilānaṃ [T 2.0329] taṇḍulānaṃ. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso muñcitvā paccavekkheyya – ‘ime sālī, ime vīhī ime muggā ime māsā ime tilā ime taṇḍulā’ti. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu imameva kāyaṃ uddhaṃ pādatalā adho kesamatthakā tacapariyantaṃ pūraṃ nānappakārassa asucino paccavekkhati – ‘atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesā lomā…pe… [P 2.0294] mutta’nti.

Just as, O monks, there might be a bag with an opening at both ends, full of many kinds of grain—such as fine rice, paddy, mung beans, black gram, sesame seeds, and husked rice—and a man with good eyesight, having opened it, might reflect: ‘These are fine rice, these are paddy, these are mung beans, these are black gram, these are sesame seeds, these are husked rice.’ In the very same way, O monks, a monk reflects on this very body, upwards from the soles of the feet, downwards from the tips of the hair, bounded by skin, and full of many kinds of impurities: ‘In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs... and so forth... and urine.’

Iti ajjhattaṃ vā…pe… evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati.

Thus he dwells contemplating the body in the body internally... and so forth... In this way too, O monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body.

Paṭikūlamanasikārapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Section on Attention to Repulsiveness is concluded.

Kāyānupassanā dhātumanasikārapabbaṃ

Contemplation of the Body: The Section on Attending to the Elements

378. “Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu imameva kāyaṃ yathāṭhitaṃ yathāpaṇihitaṃ dhātuso paccavekkhati – ‘atthi imasmiṃ kāye pathavīdhātu āpodhātu tejodhātu vāyodhātū’ti.

378. Furthermore, O monks, a monk reflects on this very body, just as it is placed, just as it is disposed, by way of the elements: ‘In this body there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.’

“Seyyathāpi[V 2.0218], bhikkhave, dakkho goghātako vā goghātakantevāsī vā gāviṃ vadhitvā catumahāpathe bilaso [T 2.0330] vibhajitvā nisinno assa, evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu imameva kāyaṃ yathāṭhitaṃ yathāpaṇihitaṃ dhātuso paccavekkhati – ‘atthi imasmiṃ kāye pathavīdhātu āpodhātu tejodhātu vāyodhātū’ti.

Just as, O monks, a skilled butcher or a butcher’s apprentice, having killed a cow, might sit at a crossroads after dividing it into portions; in the same way, O monks, a monk reflects on this very body—just as it is placed, just as it is disposed—by way of the elements: ‘In this body there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.’

“Iti ajjhattaṃ vā kāye kāyānupassī viharati…pe… [P 2.0295] evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati.

Thus he dwells contemplating the body in the body internally... and so forth... In this way too, O monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body.

Dhātumanasikārapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Section on Attending to the Elements is concluded.

Kāyānupassanā navasivathikapabbaṃ

Contemplation of the Body: The Section on the Nine Charnel Ground Contemplations

379. “Puna [M 2.0235] caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu seyyathāpi passeyya sarīraṃ sivathikāya chaḍḍitaṃ ekāhamataṃ vā dvīhamataṃ vā tīhamataṃ vā uddhumātakaṃ vinīlakaṃ vipubbakajātaṃ. So imameva kāyaṃ upasaṃharati – ‘ayampi kho kāyo evaṃdhammo evaṃbhāvī evaṃanatīto’ti.

379. Furthermore, O monks, a monk might see a body discarded in a charnel ground—dead for one day, two days, or three days—bloated, discolored, and festering. He applies this to his own body, thinking: ‘This body, too, has such a nature, will become like that, and has not gone beyond that state.’

“Iti ajjhattaṃ vā [T 2.0331] …pe… evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati.

Thus he dwells contemplating the body in the body internally... and so forth... In this way too, O monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu seyyathāpi passeyya sarīraṃ sivathikāya chaḍḍitaṃ kākehi vā [V 2.0219] khajjamānaṃ kulalehi vā khajjamānaṃ gijjhehi vā khajjamānaṃ kaṅkehi vā khajjamānaṃ sunakhehi vā khajjamānaṃ byagghehi vā khajjamānaṃ dīpīhi vā khajjamānaṃ siṅgālehi vā gijjhehi vā khajjamānaṃ, suvānehi vā khajjamānaṃ, sigālehi vā khajjamānaṃ, (syā. pī.) khajjamānaṃ vividhehi vā pāṇakajātehi khajjamānaṃ. So imameva kāyaṃ upasaṃharati – ‘ayampi kho kāyo evaṃdhammo evaṃbhāvī evaṃanatīto’ti.

Furthermore, O monks, a monk might see a body discarded in a charnel ground, being devoured by crows, hawks, vultures, herons, dogs, tigers, leopards, jackals, or by various kinds of creatures. He applies this to his own body, thinking: ‘This body, too, has such a nature, will become like that, and has not gone beyond that state.’

“Iti [P 2.0296] ajjhattaṃ vā…pe… evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati.

Thus he dwells contemplating the body in the body internally... and so forth... In this way too, O monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu seyyathāpi passeyya sarīraṃ sivathikāya chaḍḍitaṃ aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikaṃ samaṃsalohitaṃ nhārusambandhaṃ…pe… aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikaṃ nimaṃsalohitamakkhitaṃ nhārusambandhaṃ…pe… aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikaṃ apagatamaṃsalohitaṃ nhārusambandhaṃ…pe… aṭṭhikāni apagatasambandhāni apagatanhārusambandhāni (syā.) disā vidisā vikkhittāni, aññena hatthaṭṭhikaṃ aññena pādaṭṭhikaṃ aññena gopphakaṭṭhikaṃ “aññena gopphakaṭṭhika”nti idaṃ sī. syā. pī. potthakesu natthi aññena jaṅghaṭṭhikaṃ aññena ūruṭṭhikaṃ aññena kaṭiṭṭhikaṃ aññena kaṭaṭṭhikaṃ aññena piṭṭhaṭṭhikaṃ aññena kaṇḍakaṭṭhikaṃ aññena phāsukaṭṭhikaṃ aññena uraṭṭhikaṃ aññena aṃsaṭṭhikaṃ aññena bāhuṭṭhikaṃ (syā.) aññena phāsukaṭṭhikaṃ aññena [P 2.0297] piṭṭhiṭṭhikaṃ aññena khandhaṭṭhikaṃ aññena kaṭaṭṭhikaṃ aññena piṭṭhaṭṭhikaṃ aññena kaṇḍakaṭṭhikaṃ aññena phāsukaṭṭhikaṃ aññena uraṭṭhikaṃ aññena aṃsaṭṭhikaṃ aññena bāhuṭṭhikaṃ (syā.) aññena gīvaṭṭhikaṃ aññena hanukaṭṭhikaṃ aññena dantaṭṭhikaṃ aññena sīsakaṭāhaṃ. So imameva kāyaṃ upasaṃharati – ‘ayampi kho kāyo evaṃdhammo evaṃbhāvī evaṃanatīto’ti.

Furthermore, monks, just as a monk might see a body discarded in a charnel ground: a skeleton with flesh and blood, held together by sinews... a skeleton without flesh but smeared with blood, held together by sinews... a skeleton without flesh and blood, held together by sinews... bones unconnected and scattered in various directions—a hand-bone in one place, a foot-bone in another, an ankle-bone in another, a shin-bone in another, a thigh-bone in another, a hip-bone in another, a rib-bone in another, a spine-bone in another, a shoulder-bone in another, a neck-bone in another, a jaw-bone in another, a tooth-bone in another, a skull in another. He applies this to his own body, reflecting: ‘This body, too, is of such a nature, it will become like that, it cannot transcend it.’

“Iti ajjhattaṃ vā [T 2.0332] …pe… viharati.

Thus he dwells contemplating the body in the body internally...

“Puna [M 2.0236] caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu seyyathāpi passeyya sarīraṃ sivathikāya chaḍḍitaṃ aṭṭhikāni setāni saṅkhavaṇṇapaṭibhāgāni…pe… aṭṭhikāni puñjakitāni terovassikāni [V 2.0220] …pe… aṭṭhikāni pūtīni cuṇṇakajātāni. So imameva kāyaṃ upasaṃharati – ‘ayampi kho kāyo evaṃdhammo evaṃbhāvī evaṃanatīto’ti. Iti ajjhattaṃ vā kāye kāyānupassī viharati, bahiddhā vā kāye kāyānupassī viharati, ajjhattabahiddhā vā kāye kāyānupassī [P 2.0298] viharati. Samudayadhammānupassī vā kāyasmiṃ viharati, vayadhammānupassī vā kāyasmiṃ viharati, samudayavayadhammānupassī vā kāyasmiṃ viharati. ‘Atthi kāyo’ti vā panassa sati paccupaṭṭhitā hoti yāvadeva ñāṇamattāya paṭissatimattāya anissito ca viharati, na ca kiñci loke upādiyati. Evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati.

Furthermore, monks, just as a monk might see a body discarded in a charnel ground: bones white, like the color of a conch shell... a heap of bones more than a year old... bones rotten and crumbled to dust. He applies this to his own body, reflecting: ‘This body, too, is of such a nature, it will become like that, it cannot transcend it.’ Thus he dwells contemplating the body in the body internally, or he dwells contemplating the body in the body externally, or he dwells contemplating the body in the body both internally and externally. He dwells contemplating the nature of arising in the body, or he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in the body, or he dwells contemplating the nature of arising and passing away in the body. Or his mindfulness that ‘there is a body’ is established, just to the extent necessary for knowledge and mindfulness. And he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world. In this way too, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body.

Navasivathikapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Section on the Nine Charnel Grounds is finished.

Cuddasa kāyānupassanā niṭṭhitā.

The fourteen contemplations of the body are completed.

Vedanānupassanā

Contemplation of Feelings

380. “Kathañca pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sukhaṃ vā vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti[T 2.0333]. Dukkhaṃ vā vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti. Adukkhamasukhaṃ vā vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti. Sāmisaṃ vā sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘sāmisaṃ sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti, nirāmisaṃ vā sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘nirāmisaṃ sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti. Sāmisaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘sāmisaṃ dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti, nirāmisaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘nirāmisaṃ dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti. Sāmisaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘sāmisaṃ adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti, nirāmisaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘nirāmisaṃ adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti. Iti ajjhattaṃ vā vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati, bahiddhā vā vedanāsu [M 2.0237] vedanānupassī viharati, ajjhattabahiddhā vā vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati. Samudayadhammānupassī vā vedanāsu viharati, vayadhammānupassī [P 2.0299] vā vedanāsu viharati, samudayavayadhammānupassī vā vedanāsu viharati. ‘Atthi vedanā’ti vā panassa sati paccupaṭṭhitā hoti [V 2.0221] yāvadeva ñāṇamattāya paṭissatimattāya anissito ca viharati, na ca kiñci loke upādiyati. Evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati.

380. And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating feelings in feelings? Here, monks, when experiencing a pleasant feeling, he discerns: ‘I am experiencing a pleasant feeling.’ When experiencing a painful feeling, he discerns: ‘I am experiencing a painful feeling.’ When experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he discerns: ‘I am experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.’ When experiencing a worldly pleasant feeling, he discerns: ‘I am experiencing a worldly pleasant feeling’; when experiencing an unworldly pleasant feeling, he discerns: ‘I am experiencing an unworldly pleasant feeling.’ When experiencing a worldly painful feeling, he discerns: ‘I am experiencing a worldly painful feeling’; when experiencing an unworldly painful feeling, he discerns: ‘I am experiencing an unworldly painful feeling.’ When experiencing a worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he discerns: ‘I am experiencing a worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling’; when experiencing an unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he discerns: ‘I am experiencing an unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.’ Thus he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings internally, or he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings externally, or he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings both internally and externally. He dwells contemplating the nature of arising in feelings, or he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in feelings, or he dwells contemplating the nature of arising and passing away in feelings. Or his mindfulness is established that ‘There is feeling,’ just to the extent necessary for knowledge and mindfulness. And he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world. In this way too, monks, a monk dwells contemplating feelings in feelings.

Vedanānupassanā niṭṭhitā.

The Contemplation of Feelings is concluded.

Cittānupassanā

Contemplation of the Mind

381. “Kathañca [T 2.0334] pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu citte cittānupassī viharati? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sarāgaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘sarāgaṃ citta’nti pajānāti, vītarāgaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘vītarāgaṃ citta’nti pajānāti. Sadosaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘sadosaṃ citta’nti pajānāti, vītadosaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘vītadosaṃ citta’nti pajānāti. Samohaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘samohaṃ citta’nti pajānāti, vītamohaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘vītamohaṃ citta’nti pajānāti. Saṅkhittaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘saṅkhittaṃ citta’nti pajānāti, vikkhittaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘vikkhittaṃ citta’nti pajānāti. Mahaggataṃ vā cittaṃ ‘mahaggataṃ citta’nti pajānāti, amahaggataṃ vā cittaṃ ‘amahaggataṃ citta’nti pajānāti. Sauttaraṃ vā cittaṃ ‘sauttaraṃ citta’nti pajānāti, anuttaraṃ vā cittaṃ ‘anuttaraṃ citta’nti pajānāti. Samāhitaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘samāhitaṃ citta’nti pajānāti, asamāhitaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘asamāhitaṃ citta’nti pajānāti. Vimuttaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘vimuttaṃ citta’nti pajānāti. Avimuttaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘avimuttaṃ citta’nti pajānāti. Iti ajjhattaṃ vā citte cittānupassī viharati, bahiddhā vā citte cittānupassī viharati, ajjhattabahiddhā vā citte cittānupassī viharati. Samudayadhammānupassī vā cittasmiṃ viharati, vayadhammānupassī vā cittasmiṃ viharati, samudayavayadhammānupassī vā cittasmiṃ viharati, ‘atthi citta’nti vā panassa sati paccupaṭṭhitā hoti [P 2.0300] yāvadeva ñāṇamattāya paṭissatimattāya anissito ca viharati, na ca kiñci loke upādiyati[T 2.0335]. Evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu citte cittānupassī viharati.

381. And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating the mind in the mind? Here, monks, he understands a mind with lust as 'a mind with lust,' and a mind without lust as 'a mind without lust.' He understands a mind with hatred as 'a mind with hatred,' and a mind without hatred as 'a mind without hatred.' He understands a mind with delusion as 'a mind with delusion,' and a mind without delusion as 'a mind without delusion.' He understands a constricted mind as 'a constricted mind,' and a scattered mind as 'a scattered mind.' He understands an exalted mind as 'an exalted mind,' and an unexalted mind as 'an unexalted mind.' He understands a surpassable mind as 'a surpassable mind,' and an unsurpassable mind as 'an unsurpassable mind.' He understands a concentrated mind as 'a concentrated mind,' and an unconcentrated mind as 'an unconcentrated mind.' He understands a liberated mind as 'a liberated mind,' and an unliberated mind as 'an unliberated mind.' Thus he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind internally, or he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind externally, or he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind both internally and externally. He dwells contemplating the nature of arising in the mind, or he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in the mind, or he dwells contemplating the nature of both arising and passing away in the mind. Or his mindfulness is established with the thought, 'Mind exists,' just for the sake of knowledge and mindfulness. He dwells independent and clings to nothing in the world. In this way too, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the mind in the mind.

Cittānupassanā niṭṭhitā.

The Contemplation of the Mind is concluded.

Dhammānupassanā nīvaraṇapabbaṃ

Contemplation of Phenomena: The Section on the Hindrances

382. “Kathañca [M 2.0238][V 2.0222] pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati pañcasu nīvaraṇesu. Kathañca pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati pañcasu nīvaraṇesu?

382. And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena with regard to the five hindrances. And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena with regard to the five hindrances?

“Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu santaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ kāmacchandaṃ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ kāmacchando’ti pajānāti, asantaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ kāmacchandaṃ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ kāmacchando’ti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa kāmacchandassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa kāmacchandassa pahānaṃ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa kāmacchandassa āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti.

Here, monks, when sensual desire is present internally, a monk understands: ‘Sensual desire is present in me internally’; when sensual desire is not present internally, he understands: ‘Sensual desire is not present in me internally.’ He understands how unarisen sensual desire comes to arise, how arisen sensual desire is abandoned, and how abandoned sensual desire does not arise again in the future.

“Santaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ byāpādaṃ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ byāpādo’ti pajānāti, asantaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ byāpādaṃ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ byāpādo’ti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa byāpādassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa byāpādassa pahānaṃ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa byāpādassa āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti.

When ill will is present internally, he understands: ‘Ill will is present in me internally’; when ill will is not present internally, he understands: ‘Ill will is not present in me internally.’ He understands how unarisen ill will comes to arise, how arisen ill will is abandoned, and how abandoned ill will does not arise again in the future.

“Santaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ thinamiddhaṃ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ thinamiddha’nti pajānāti, asantaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ thinamiddhaṃ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ thinamiddha’nti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa thinamiddhassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa thinamiddhassa [T 2.0336] pahānaṃ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa thinamiddhassa āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti.

When sloth and torpor are present internally, he understands: ‘Sloth and torpor are present in me internally’; when sloth and torpor are not present internally, he understands: ‘Sloth and torpor are not present in me internally.’ He understands how unarisen sloth and torpor come to arise, how arisen sloth and torpor are abandoned, and how abandoned sloth and torpor do not arise again in the future.

“Santaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ uddhaccakukkuccaṃ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ [P 2.0301] uddhaccakukkucca’nti pajānāti, asantaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ uddhaccakukkuccaṃ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ uddhaccakukkucca’nti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa uddhaccakukkuccassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa uddhaccakukkuccassa pahānaṃ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa uddhaccakukkuccassa āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti.

When restlessness and remorse are present internally, he understands: ‘Restlessness and remorse are present in me internally’; when restlessness and remorse are not present internally, he understands: ‘Restlessness and remorse are not present in me internally.’ He understands how unarisen restlessness and remorse come to arise, how arisen restlessness and remorse are abandoned, and how abandoned restlessness and remorse do not arise again in the future.

“Santaṃ [V 2.0223] vā ajjhattaṃ vicikicchaṃ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ vicikicchā’ti pajānāti, asantaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ vicikicchaṃ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ vicikicchā’ti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannāya vicikicchāya uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā [M 2.0239] ca uppannāya vicikicchāya pahānaṃ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnāya vicikicchāya āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti.

When doubt is present internally, he understands: ‘Doubt is present in me internally’; when doubt is not present internally, he understands: ‘Doubt is not present in me internally.’ He understands how unarisen doubt comes to arise, how arisen doubt is abandoned, and how abandoned doubt does not arise again in the future.

“Iti ajjhattaṃ vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati, bahiddhā vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati, ajjhattabahiddhā vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati samudayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati, vayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati, samudayavayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati ‘atthi dhammā’ti vā panassa sati paccupaṭṭhitā hoti yāvadeva ñāṇamattāya paṭissatimattāya anissito ca viharati, na ca kiñci [T 2.0337] loke upādiyati. Evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati pañcasu nīvaraṇesu.

Thus he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena internally, or externally, or both internally and externally. He dwells contemplating the nature of arising in phenomena, or the nature of passing away in phenomena, or the nature of both arising and passing away in phenomena. Or his mindfulness is established with the thought, 'Phenomena exist,' just for the sake of knowledge and mindfulness. And he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world. In this way too, monks, a monk dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena with regard to the five hindrances.

Nīvaraṇapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The section on the hindrances is finished.

Dhammānupassanā khandhapabbaṃ

Contemplation of Phenomena: The Section on the Aggregates

383. “Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu. Kathañca pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu – ‘iti rūpaṃ, iti rūpassa samudayo, iti rūpassa atthaṅgamo; iti vedanā, iti vedanāya samudayo, iti vedanāya atthaṅgamo; iti saññā, iti saññāya samudayo, iti saññāya atthaṅgamo; iti saṅkhārā, iti [P 2.0302] saṅkhārānaṃ samudayo, iti saṅkhārānaṃ atthaṅgamo, iti viññāṇaṃ, iti viññāṇassa samudayo, iti viññāṇassa atthaṅgamo’ti, iti ajjhattaṃ vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati, bahiddhā vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati, ajjhattabahiddhā vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati. Samudayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati, vayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati, samudayavayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati. ‘Atthi dhammā’ti vā panassa sati paccupaṭṭhitā hoti yāvadeva ñāṇamattāya paṭissatimattāya, anissito ca viharati, na ca kiñci loke upādiyati[V 2.0224]. Evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu.

383. “Furthermore, monks, a monk dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena with regard to the five aggregates of clinging. And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena with regard to the five aggregates of clinging? Here, monks, a monk understands: ‘Such is form, such is the arising of form, such is the cessation of form; such is feeling, such is the arising of feeling, such is the cessation of feeling; such is perception, such is the arising of perception, such is the cessation of perception; such are formations, such is the arising of formations, such is the cessation of formations; such is consciousness, such is the arising of consciousness, such is the cessation of consciousness.’ Thus he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena internally, or he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena externally, or he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena both internally and externally. He dwells contemplating the nature of arising in phenomena, or he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in phenomena, or he dwells contemplating the nature of both arising and passing away in phenomena. Or, his mindfulness that ‘phenomena exist’ is established just for the sake of knowledge and continued mindfulness. And he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world. In this way, monks, a monk dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena with regard to the five aggregates of clinging.”

Khandhapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Section on the Aggregates is concluded.

Dhammānupassanā āyatanapabbaṃ

Contemplation of Phenomena: The Section on the Sense Bases

384. “Puna [T 2.0338][M 2.0240] caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati chasu ajjhattikabāhiresu āyatanesu. Kathañca pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati chasu ajjhattikabāhiresu āyatanesu?

384. “Furthermore, monks, a monk dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena with regard to the six internal and external sense bases. And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena with regard to the six internal and external sense bases?

“Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cakkhuñca pajānāti, rūpe ca pajānāti, yañca tadubhayaṃ paṭicca uppajjati saṃyojanaṃ tañca pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa saṃyojanassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa saṃyojanassa pahānaṃ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa saṃyojanassa āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti.

“Here, monks, a monk knows distinctly the eye, and he knows distinctly forms, and he knows distinctly the fetter that arises dependent on both. He knows distinctly how the arising of an unarisen fetter comes to be; he knows distinctly how the abandonment of an arisen fetter comes to be; and he knows distinctly how the non-arising in the future of an abandoned fetter comes to be.

“Sotañca pajānāti, sadde ca pajānāti, yañca tadubhayaṃ paṭicca uppajjati saṃyojanaṃ tañca pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa saṃyojanassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa saṃyojanassa pahānaṃ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa saṃyojanassa āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti.

“He knows distinctly the ear, and he knows distinctly sounds, and he knows distinctly the fetter that arises dependent on both. He knows distinctly how the arising of an unarisen fetter comes to be; he knows distinctly how the abandonment of an arisen fetter comes to be; and he knows distinctly how the non-arising in the future of an abandoned fetter comes to be.

“Ghānañca pajānāti, gandhe ca pajānāti, yañca tadubhayaṃ paṭicca uppajjati saṃyojanaṃ tañca pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa saṃyojanassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa saṃyojanassa pahānaṃ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa saṃyojanassa āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti.

“He knows distinctly the nose, and he knows distinctly odors, and he knows distinctly the fetter that arises dependent on both. He knows distinctly how the arising of an unarisen fetter comes to be; he knows distinctly how the abandonment of an arisen fetter comes to be; and he knows distinctly how the non-arising in the future of an abandoned fetter comes to be.

“Jivhañca pajānāti, rase ca pajānāti, yañca tadubhayaṃ paṭicca uppajjati saṃyojanaṃ tañca pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa saṃyojanassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti[V 2.0225], yathā ca uppannassa saṃyojanassa pahānaṃ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa saṃyojanassa āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti.

“He knows distinctly the tongue, and he knows distinctly tastes, and he knows distinctly the fetter that arises dependent on both. He knows distinctly how the arising of an unarisen fetter comes to be; he knows distinctly how the abandonment of an arisen fetter comes to be; and he knows distinctly how the non-arising in the future of an abandoned fetter comes to be.

“Kāyañca pajānāti, phoṭṭhabbe ca pajānāti, yañca tadubhayaṃ paṭicca uppajjati saṃyojanaṃ tañca pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa saṃyojanassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa saṃyojanassa pahānaṃ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa saṃyojanassa āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti.

“He knows distinctly the body, and he knows distinctly tangible objects, and he knows distinctly the fetter that arises dependent on both. He knows distinctly how the arising of an unarisen fetter comes to be; he knows distinctly how the abandonment of an arisen fetter comes to be; and he knows distinctly how the non-arising in the future of an abandoned fetter comes to be.

“Manañca [M 2.0241] pajānāti, dhamme ca pajānāti, yañca tadubhayaṃ [P 2.0303] paṭicca uppajjati saṃyojanaṃ tañca pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa saṃyojanassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa saṃyojanassa pahānaṃ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa saṃyojanassa āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti.

“He knows distinctly the mind, and he knows distinctly mental objects, and he knows distinctly the fetter that arises dependent on both. He knows distinctly how the arising of an unarisen fetter comes to be; he knows distinctly how the abandonment of an arisen fetter comes to be; and he knows distinctly how the non-arising in the future of an abandoned fetter comes to be.

“Iti ajjhattaṃ vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati, bahiddhā vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati, ajjhattabahiddhā vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati. Samudayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati, vayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati, samudayavayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati. ‘Atthi [T 2.0339] dhammā’ti vā panassa sati paccupaṭṭhitā hoti yāvadeva ñāṇamattāya paṭissatimattāya, anissito ca viharati, na ca kiñci loke upādiyati. Evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati chasu ajjhattikabāhiresu āyatanesu.

“Thus he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena internally, or he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena externally, or he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena both internally and externally. He dwells contemplating the nature of arising in phenomena, or he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in phenomena, or he dwells contemplating the nature of both arising and passing away in phenomena. Or, his mindfulness that ‘phenomena exist’ is established just for the sake of knowledge and continued mindfulness. And he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world. In this way, monks, a monk dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena with regard to the six internal and external sense bases.”

Āyatanapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Section on the Sense Bases is concluded.

Dhammānupassanā bojjhaṅgapabbaṃ

Contemplation of Phenomena: The Section on the Enlightenment Factors

385. “Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati sattasu bojjhaṅgesu. Kathañca pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati sattasu bojjhaṅgesu? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu santaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ satisambojjhaṅgaṃ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ satisambojjhaṅgo’ti pajānāti, asantaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ satisambojjhaṅgaṃ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ satisambojjhaṅgo’ti [V 2.0226] pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa satisambojjhaṅgassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa satisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya pāripūrī hoti tañca pajānāti.

385. Furthermore, O monks, a monk dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena with regard to the seven factors of enlightenment. And how, O monks, does a monk dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena with regard to the seven factors of enlightenment? Here, O monks, when the mindfulness-enlightenment-factor is present internally, a monk knows distinctly, ‘The mindfulness-enlightenment-factor is present in me internally.’ When the mindfulness-enlightenment-factor is not present internally, he knows distinctly, ‘The mindfulness-enlightenment-factor is not present in me internally.’ He also knows distinctly the cause whereby the unarisen mindfulness-enlightenment-factor arises, and he knows distinctly the cause whereby the arisen mindfulness-enlightenment-factor comes to fulfillment through development.

“Santaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgaṃ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgo’ti pajānāti, asantaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgaṃ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgo’ti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa [M 2.0242] dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya pāripūrī hoti tañca pajānāti.

When the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor is present internally, he knows distinctly, ‘The investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor is present in me internally.’ When the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor is not present internally, he knows distinctly, ‘The investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor is not present in me internally.’ He also knows distinctly the cause whereby the unarisen investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor arises, and he knows distinctly the cause whereby the arisen investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor comes to fulfillment through development.

“Santaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ vīriyasambojjhaṅgaṃ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ vīriyasambojjhaṅgo’ti pajānāti, asantaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ vīriyasambojjhaṅgaṃ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ vīriyasambojjhaṅgo’ti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya pāripūrī hoti tañca pajānāti.

When the energy enlightenment factor is present internally, he knows distinctly, ‘The energy enlightenment factor is present in me internally.’ When the energy enlightenment factor is not present internally, he knows distinctly, ‘The energy enlightenment factor is not present in me internally.’ He also knows distinctly the cause whereby the unarisen energy enlightenment factor arises, and he knows distinctly the cause whereby the arisen energy enlightenment factor comes to fulfillment through development.

“Santaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ pītisambojjhaṅgaṃ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ pītisambojjhaṅgo’ti pajānāti, asantaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ pītisambojjhaṅgaṃ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ pītisambojjhaṅgo’ti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa pītisambojjhaṅgassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa pītisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya pāripūrī hoti tañca pajānāti.

When the rapture enlightenment factor is present internally, he knows distinctly, ‘The rapture enlightenment factor is present in me internally.’ When the rapture enlightenment factor is not present internally, he knows distinctly, ‘The rapture enlightenment factor is not present in me internally.’ He also knows distinctly the cause whereby the unarisen rapture enlightenment factor arises, and he knows distinctly the cause whereby the arisen rapture enlightenment factor comes to fulfillment through development.

“Santaṃ [P 2.0304] vā ajjhattaṃ passaddhisambojjhaṅgaṃ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ passaddhisambojjhaṅgo’ti pajānāti, asantaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ passaddhisambojjhaṅgaṃ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ passaddhisambojjhaṅgo’ti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya pāripūrī hoti tañca pajānāti.

When the tranquility enlightenment factor is present internally, he knows distinctly, ‘The tranquility enlightenment factor is present in me internally.’ When the tranquility enlightenment factor is not present internally, he knows distinctly, ‘The tranquility enlightenment factor is not present in me internally.’ He also knows distinctly the cause whereby the unarisen tranquility enlightenment factor arises, and he knows distinctly the cause whereby the arisen tranquility enlightenment factor comes to fulfillment through development.

“Santaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ samādhisambojjhaṅgaṃ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ samādhisambojjhaṅgo’ti pajānāti, asantaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ samādhisambojjhaṅgaṃ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ samādhisambojjhaṅgo’ti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa samādhisambojjhaṅgassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa samādhisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya pāripūrī hoti tañca pajānāti.

When the concentration enlightenment factor is present internally, he knows distinctly, ‘The concentration enlightenment factor is present in me internally.’ When the concentration enlightenment factor is not present internally, he knows distinctly, ‘The concentration enlightenment factor is not present in me internally.’ He also knows distinctly the cause whereby the unarisen concentration enlightenment factor arises, and he knows distinctly the cause whereby the arisen concentration enlightenment factor comes to fulfillment through development.

“Santaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṃ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ upekkhāsambojjhaṅgo’ti pajānāti[V 2.0227], asantaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṃ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ upekkhāsambojjhaṅgo’ti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa [T 2.0340] upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya pāripūrī hoti tañca pajānāti.
