When the equanimity enlightenment factor is present internally, he knows distinctly, ‘The equanimity enlightenment factor is present in me internally.’ When the equanimity enlightenment factor is not present internally, he knows distinctly, ‘The equanimity enlightenment factor is not present in me internally.’ He also knows distinctly the cause whereby the unarisen equanimity enlightenment factor arises, and he knows distinctly the cause whereby the arisen equanimity enlightenment factor comes to fulfillment through development.

“Iti ajjhattaṃ vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati, bahiddhā vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati, ajjhattabahiddhā vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati. Samudayadhammānupassī [M 2.0243] vā dhammesu viharati, vayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati, samudayavayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati ‘atthi dhammā’ti vā panassa sati paccupaṭṭhitā hoti yāvadeva ñāṇamattāya paṭissatimattāya anissito ca viharati, na ca kiñci loke upādiyati. Evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati sattasu bojjhaṅgesu.

Thus he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena internally, or he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena externally, or he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena both internally and externally. He dwells contemplating the nature of arising in phenomena, or he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in phenomena, or he dwells contemplating the nature of arising and passing away in phenomena. Or his mindfulness is established with the thought, ‘Phenomena exist,’ just for the sake of knowledge and mindfulness. And he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world. In this way, O monks, a monk dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena with regard to the seven factors of enlightenment.

Bojjhaṅgapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ. bojjhaṅgapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ, paṭhamabhāṇavāraṃ (syā.)

The section on the Factors of Enlightenment is finished.

Dhammānupassanā saccapabbaṃ

Contemplation of Phenomena: The Section on the Truths

386. “Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati catūsu ariyasaccesu. Kathañca pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati catūsu ariyasaccesu? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodho’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti.

386. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena with regard to the four Noble Truths. And how, bhikkhus, does a bhikkhu dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena with regard to the four Noble Truths? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands as it actually is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’

Paṭhamabhāṇavāro niṭṭhito.

The first recitation section is finished.

Dukkhasaccaniddeso

The Exposition of the Truth of Suffering

387. “Katamañca[T 2.0341][V 2.0228][P 2.0305], bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ? Jātipi dukkhā, jarāpi dukkhā, maraṇampi dukkhaṃ, sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsāpi dukkhā, appiyehi sampayogopi dukkho, piyehi vippayogopi dukkho appiyehi…pe… vippayogo dukkhotipāṭho ceva taṃniddeso ca katthaci na dissati, aṭṭhakathāyaṃpi taṃsaṃvaṇṇanā natthi, yampicchaṃ na labhati tampi dukkhaṃ, saṅkhittena pañcupādānakkhandhā pañcupādānakkhandhāpi (ka.) dukkhā.

387. And what, bhikkhus, is the Noble Truth of Suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair are suffering; association with the unloved is suffering; separation from the loved is suffering; not getting what one wants is suffering; in brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering.

388. “Katamā ca, bhikkhave, jāti? Yā tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ tamhi tamhi sattanikāye jāti sañjāti okkanti abhinibbatti khandhānaṃ pātubhāvo āyatanānaṃ paṭilābho, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, jāti.

388. And what, bhikkhus, is birth? Whatever, for various beings in the various orders of beings, is the birth, coming to be, descent, production, the manifestation of the aggregates, the acquisition of the sense bases—this, bhikkhus, is called birth.

389. “Katamā [M 2.0244] ca, bhikkhave, jarā? Yā tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ tamhi tamhi sattanikāye jarā jīraṇatā khaṇḍiccaṃ pāliccaṃ valittacatā āyuno saṃhāni indriyānaṃ paripāko, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, jarā.

389. And what, bhikkhus, is aging? Whatever, for various beings in the various orders of beings, is the aging, decrepitude, brokenness of teeth, graying of hair, wrinkling of skin, the decline of life, the ripening of the faculties—this, bhikkhus, is called aging.

390. “Katamañca, bhikkhave, maraṇaṃ? Yaṃ aṭṭhakathā oloketabbā tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ tamhā tamhā sattanikāyā cuti cavanatā bhedo antaradhānaṃ maccu maraṇaṃ kālakiriyā khandhānaṃ bhedo kaḷevarassa nikkhepo jīvitindriyassupacchedo, idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, maraṇaṃ.

390. And what, bhikkhus, is death? Whatever, for various beings from this or that order of beings, is the passing, the passing away, the breaking up, the disappearance, dying, death, the completion of time, the breaking up of the aggregates, the casting off of the body, the cutting off of the life faculty—this, bhikkhus, is called death.

391. “Katamo ca, bhikkhave, soko? Yo kho, bhikkhave, aññataraññatarena byasanena samannāgatassa aññataraññatarena [P 2.0306] dukkhadhammena phuṭṭhassa soko socanā socitattaṃ antosoko antoparisoko, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, soko.

391. And what, bhikkhus, is sorrow? Whatever, bhikkhus, for one who is beset by some misfortune or other, who is touched by some painful state or other, is the sorrow, the sorrowing, the state of sorrow, inner sorrow, inner deep sorrow—this, bhikkhus, is called sorrow.

392. “Katamo ca, bhikkhave, paridevo? Yo kho, bhikkhave, aññataraññatarena byasanena samannāgatassa aññataraññatarena dukkhadhammena phuṭṭhassa ādevo paridevo ādevanā paridevanā ādevitattaṃ paridevitattaṃ, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave paridevo.

392. And what, bhikkhus, is lamentation? Whatever, bhikkhus, for one who is beset by some misfortune or other, who is touched by some painful state or other, is the wailing, the lamenting, the act of wailing, the act of lamenting, the state of one who wails, the state of one who laments—this, bhikkhus, is called lamentation.

393. “Katamañca[T 2.0342], bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ? Yaṃ kho, bhikkhave, kāyikaṃ dukkhaṃ kāyikaṃ asātaṃ kāyasamphassajaṃ dukkhaṃ asātaṃ vedayitaṃ, idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ.

393. And what, bhikkhus, is pain? Whatever, bhikkhus, is bodily pain, bodily displeasure, the painful, unpleasant feeling born of bodily contact—this, bhikkhus, is called pain.

394. “Katamañca[V 2.0229], bhikkhave, domanassaṃ? Yaṃ kho, bhikkhave, cetasikaṃ dukkhaṃ cetasikaṃ asātaṃ manosamphassajaṃ dukkhaṃ asātaṃ vedayitaṃ, idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, domanassaṃ.

394. And what, bhikkhus, is distress? Whatever, bhikkhus, is mental pain, mental displeasure, the painful, unpleasant feeling born of mental contact—this, bhikkhus, is called distress.

395. “Katamo ca, bhikkhave, upāyāso? Yo kho, bhikkhave, aññataraññatarena byasanena samannāgatassa aññataraññatarena dukkhadhammena phuṭṭhassa āyāso upāyāso āyāsitattaṃ upāyāsitattaṃ, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, upāyāso.

395. And what, bhikkhus, is despair? Whatever, bhikkhus, for one who is beset by some misfortune or other, who is touched by some painful state or other, is the tribulation, the deep tribulation, the state of tribulation, the state of deep tribulation—this, bhikkhus, is called despair.

396. “Katamo [M 2.0245] ca, bhikkhave, appiyehi sampayogo dukkho? Idha yassa te honti aniṭṭhā akantā amanāpā rūpā saddā gandhā rasā phoṭṭhabbā dhammā, ye vā panassa te honti anatthakāmā ahitakāmā aphāsukakāmā ayogakkhemakāmā, yā tehi saddhiṃ saṅgati samāgamo samodhānaṃ missībhāvo, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, appiyehi sampayogo dukkho.

396. And what, bhikkhus, is the suffering of association with the unloved? Here, for a person, there are forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangible objects, or mental phenomena which are unwished for, unloved, and disagreeable; or there are those who wish one ill, who wish one harm, who wish one discomfort, who wish one insecurity; whatever association, meeting, coming together, or mixing with them there is—this, bhikkhus, is called the suffering of association with the unloved.

397. “Katamo ca, bhikkhave, piyehi vippayogo dukkho? Idha yassa te honti iṭṭhā kantā manāpā rūpā saddā gandhā rasā phoṭṭhabbā dhammā, ye vā panassa te honti atthakāmā hitakāmā phāsukakāmā yogakkhemakāmā mātā vā pitā vā bhātā vā bhaginī vā mittā vā amaccā vā ñātisālohitā vā, yā tehi saddhiṃ asaṅgati asamāgamo asamodhānaṃ amissībhāvo, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, piyehi vippayogo dukkho.

397. And what, bhikkhus, is the suffering of separation from the loved? Here, for a person, there are forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangible objects, or mental phenomena which are wished for, loved, and agreeable; or there are those who wish one well, who wish one good, who wish one comfort, who wish one security—mother or father, brother or sister, friends or companions, or blood relatives; whatever non-association, non-meeting, not coming together, or non-mixing with them there is—this, bhikkhus, is called the suffering of separation from the loved.

398. “Katamañca[T 2.0343][P 2.0307], bhikkhave, yampicchaṃ na labhati tampi dukkhaṃ? Jātidhammānaṃ, bhikkhave, sattānaṃ evaṃ icchā uppajjati – ‘aho vata mayaṃ na jātidhammā assāma, na ca vata no jāti āgaccheyyā’ti. Na kho panetaṃ icchāya pattabbaṃ, idampi yampicchaṃ na labhati tampi dukkhaṃ. Jarādhammānaṃ, bhikkhave, sattānaṃ evaṃ icchā uppajjati – ‘aho vata mayaṃ na jarādhammā assāma, na ca vata no jarā āgaccheyyā’ti. Na kho panetaṃ icchāya pattabbaṃ, idampi yampicchaṃ na labhati tampi dukkhaṃ. Byādhidhammānaṃ, bhikkhave, sattānaṃ evaṃ icchā uppajjati ‘aho vata mayaṃ na byādhidhammā assāma, na ca vata no byādhi āgaccheyyā’ti. Na kho panetaṃ icchāya pattabbaṃ, idampi yampicchaṃ na labhati tampi dukkhaṃ. Maraṇadhammānaṃ, bhikkhave, sattānaṃ evaṃ icchā uppajjati ‘aho vata mayaṃ na maraṇadhammā assāma, na ca vata no maraṇaṃ āgaccheyyā’ti. Na kho panetaṃ icchāya pattabbaṃ, idampi yampicchaṃ na labhati tampi dukkhaṃ. Sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsadhammānaṃ, bhikkhave, sattānaṃ evaṃ [V 2.0230] icchā uppajjati ‘aho vata mayaṃ na sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsadhammā assāma, na ca vata no sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsadhammā āgaccheyyu’nti. Na kho panetaṃ icchāya pattabbaṃ, idampi yampicchaṃ na labhati tampi dukkhaṃ.

398. And what, bhikkhus, is ‘not getting what one wishes is also suffering’? To beings subject to birth, bhikkhus, this wish arises: ‘Oh, that we were not subject to birth, and that birth would not come to us!’ But this is not to be attained by wishing. This, too, is not getting what one wishes, which is suffering. To beings subject to aging, bhikkhus, this wish arises: ‘Oh, that we were not subject to aging, and that aging would not come to us!’ But this is not to be attained by wishing. This, too, is not getting what one wishes, which is suffering. To beings subject to illness, bhikkhus, this wish arises: ‘Oh, that we were not subject to illness, and that illness would not come to us!’ But this is not to be attained by wishing. This, too, is not getting what one wishes, which is suffering. To beings subject to death, bhikkhus, this wish arises: ‘Oh, that we were not subject to death, and that death would not come to us!’ But this is not to be attained by wishing. This, too, is not getting what one wishes, which is suffering. To beings subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair, bhikkhus, this wish arises: ‘Oh, that we were not subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair, and that sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair would not come to us!’ But this is not to be attained by wishing. This, too, is not getting what one wishes, which is suffering.

399. “Katame [M 2.0246] ca, bhikkhave, saṅkhittena pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhā? Seyyathidaṃ – rūpupādānakkhandho, vedanupādānakkhandho, saññupādānakkhandho, saṅkhārupādānakkhandho, viññāṇupādānakkhandho. Ime vuccanti, bhikkhave, saṅkhittena pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhā. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ.

399. And what, bhikkhus, in brief, are the five aggregates of clinging that are suffering? They are as follows: the aggregate of clinging to form, the aggregate of clinging to feeling, the aggregate of clinging to perception, the aggregate of clinging to formations, and the aggregate of clinging to consciousness. These, bhikkhus, in brief, are called the five aggregates of clinging that are suffering. This, bhikkhus, is called the Noble Truth of Suffering.

Samudayasaccaniddeso

The Exposition of the Truth of the Origin

400. “Katamañca[P 2.0308], bhikkhave, dukkhasamudayaṃ dukkhasamudayo (syā.) ariyasaccaṃ? Yāyaṃ taṇhā ponobbhavikā ponobhavikā (sī. pī.) nandīrāgasahagatā nandirāgasahagatā (sī. syā. pī.) tatratatrābhinandinī, seyyathidaṃ – kāmataṇhā bhavataṇhā vibhavataṇhā.

400. And what, bhikkhus, is the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering? It is this craving, which brings about renewed existence, is accompanied by delight and lust, and delights in this and that. It is as follows: craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence.

“Sā kho panesā, bhikkhave, taṇhā kattha uppajjamānā uppajjati, kattha nivisamānā nivisati? Yaṃ loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā [T 2.0344] taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, ettha nivisamānā nivisati.

And where, bhikkhus, does this craving, when arising, arise? Where, when settling, does it settle? Whatever in the world is of a dear nature and a pleasant nature, it is there that this craving, when arising, arises; it is there that, when settling, it settles.

“Kiñca loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ? Cakkhu loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, ettha nivisamānā nivisati. Sotaṃ loke…pe… ghānaṃ loke… jivhā loke… kāyo loke… mano loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, ettha nivisamānā nivisati.

And what in the world is of a dear nature and a pleasant nature? The eye in the world is of a dear nature and a pleasant nature; it is there that this craving, when arising, arises; it is there that, when settling, it settles. The ear in the world… the nose in the world… the tongue in the world… the body in the world… the mind in the world is of a dear nature and a pleasant nature; it is there that this craving, when arising, arises; it is there that, when settling, it settles.

“Rūpā loke… saddā loke… gandhā loke… rasā loke… phoṭṭhabbā loke… dhammā loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, ettha nivisamānā nivisati.

Forms in the world… sounds in the world… odors in the world… tastes in the world… tangible objects in the world… mental phenomena in the world are of a dear nature and a pleasant nature; it is there that this craving, when arising, arises; it is there that, when settling, it settles.

“Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ loke… sotaviññāṇaṃ loke… ghānaviññāṇaṃ loke… jivhāviññāṇaṃ loke… kāyaviññāṇaṃ loke… manoviññāṇaṃ loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, ettha nivisamānā nivisati.

Eye-consciousness in the world… ear-consciousness in the world… nose-consciousness in the world… tongue-consciousness in the world… body-consciousness in the world… mind-consciousness in the world is of a dear nature and a pleasant nature; it is there that this craving, when arising, arises; it is there that, when settling, it settles.

“Cakkhusamphasso [V 2.0231] loke… sotasamphasso loke… ghānasamphasso loke… jivhāsamphasso [P 2.0309] loke… kāyasamphasso loke… manosamphasso loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, ettha nivisamānā nivisati.

Eye-contact in the world… ear-contact in the world… nose-contact in the world… tongue-contact in the world… body-contact in the world… mind-contact in the world is of a dear nature and a pleasant nature; it is there that this craving, when arising, arises; it is there that, when settling, it settles.

“Cakkhusamphassajā [M 2.0247] vedanā loke… sotasamphassajā vedanā loke… ghānasamphassajā vedanā loke… jivhāsamphassajā vedanā loke… kāyasamphassajā vedanā loke… manosamphassajā vedanā loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, ettha [T 2.0345] nivisamānā nivisati.

Feeling born of eye-contact in the world… feeling born of ear-contact in the world… feeling born of nose-contact in the world… feeling born of tongue-contact in the world… feeling born of body-contact in the world… feeling born of mind-contact in the world is of a dear nature and a pleasant nature; it is there that this craving, when arising, arises; it is there that, when settling, it settles.

“Rūpasaññā loke… saddasaññā loke… gandhasaññā loke… rasasaññā loke… phoṭṭhabbasaññā loke… dhammasaññā loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, ettha nivisamānā nivisati.

Perception of forms in the world… perception of sounds in the world… perception of odors in the world… perception of tastes in the world… perception of tangible objects in the world… perception of mental phenomena in the world is of a dear nature and a pleasant nature; it is there that this craving, when arising, arises; it is there that, when settling, it settles.

“Rūpasañcetanā loke… saddasañcetanā loke… gandhasañcetanā loke… rasasañcetanā loke… phoṭṭhabbasañcetanā loke… dhammasañcetanā loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, ettha nivisamānā nivisati.

Volition regarding forms in the world… volition regarding sounds in the world… volition regarding odors in the world… volition regarding tastes in the world… volition regarding tangible objects in the world… volition regarding mental phenomena in the world is of a dear nature and a pleasant nature; it is there that this craving, when arising, arises; it is there that, when settling, it settles.

“Rūpataṇhā loke… saddataṇhā loke… gandhataṇhā loke… rasataṇhā loke… phoṭṭhabbataṇhā loke… dhammataṇhā loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, ettha nivisamānā nivisati.

Craving for forms in the world… craving for sounds in the world… craving for odors in the world… craving for tastes in the world… craving for tangible objects in the world… craving for mental phenomena in the world is of a dear nature and a pleasant nature; it is there that this craving, when arising, arises; it is there that, when settling, it settles.

“Rūpavitakko loke… saddavitakko loke… gandhavitakko loke… rasavitakko loke… phoṭṭhabbavitakko loke… dhammavitakko loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, ettha nivisamānā nivisati.

Initial thought regarding forms in the world… initial thought regarding sounds in the world… initial thought regarding odors in the world… initial thought regarding tastes in the world… initial thought regarding tangible objects in the world… initial thought regarding mental phenomena in the world is of a dear nature and a pleasant nature; it is there that this craving, when arising, arises; it is there that, when settling, it settles.

“Rūpavicāro loke… saddavicāro loke… gandhavicāro loke… rasavicāro loke… phoṭṭhabbavicāro loke… dhammavicāro loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā [P 2.0310] uppajjamānā uppajjati, ettha nivisamānā nivisati. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, dukkhasamudayaṃ ariyasaccaṃ.

Sustained thought regarding forms in the world… sustained thought regarding sounds in the world… sustained thought regarding odors in the world… sustained thought regarding tastes in the world… sustained thought regarding tangible objects in the world… sustained thought regarding mental phenomena in the world is of a dear nature and a pleasant nature; it is there that this craving, when arising, arises; it is there that, when settling, it settles. This, bhikkhus, is called the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering.

Nirodhasaccaniddeso

Exposition of the Truth of Cessation

401. “Katamañca[V 2.0232], bhikkhave, dukkhanirodhaṃ dukkhanirodho (syā.) ariyasaccaṃ? Yo tassāyeva [T 2.0346] taṇhāya asesavirāganirodho cāgo paṭinissaggo mutti anālayo.

401. And what, bhikkhus, is the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering? It is the remainderless fading and cessation of that very craving, the relinquishing, the casting off, the liberation from, and the non-reliance on it.

“Sā [M 2.0248] kho panesā, bhikkhave, taṇhā kattha pahīyamānā pahīyati, kattha nirujjhamānā nirujjhati? Yaṃ loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā pahīyamānā pahīyati, ettha nirujjhamānā nirujjhati.

And where, bhikkhus, when this craving is being abandoned, is it abandoned? Where, when it is ceasing, does it cease? Whatever in the world is of a dear nature and a pleasant nature, it is there that this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; it is there that, when ceasing, it ceases.

“Kiñca loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ? Cakkhu loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā pahīyamānā pahīyati, ettha nirujjhamānā nirujjhati. Sotaṃ loke…pe… ghānaṃ loke… jivhā loke… kāyo loke… mano loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā pahīyamānā pahīyati, ettha nirujjhamānā nirujjhati.

And what in the world is of a dear nature and a pleasant nature? The eye in the world is of a dear nature and a pleasant nature; it is there that this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; it is there that, when ceasing, it ceases. The ear in the world… the nose in the world… the tongue in the world… the body in the world… the mind in the world is of a dear nature and a pleasant nature; it is there that this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; it is there that, when ceasing, it ceases.

“Rūpā loke… saddā loke… gandhā loke… rasā loke… phoṭṭhabbā loke… dhammā loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā pahīyamānā pahīyati, ettha nirujjhamānā nirujjhati.

Visible forms in the world… sounds in the world… odors in the world… tastes in the world… tangible objects in the world… mental phenomena in the world are of a dear nature and a pleasant nature; it is there that this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; it is there that, when ceasing, it ceases.

“Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ loke… sotaviññāṇaṃ loke… ghānaviññāṇaṃ loke… jivhāviññāṇaṃ loke… kāyaviññāṇaṃ loke… manoviññāṇaṃ loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā pahīyamānā pahīyati, ettha nirujjhamānā nirujjhati.

Eye-consciousness in the world… ear-consciousness in the world… nose-consciousness in the world… tongue-consciousness in the world… body-consciousness in the world… mind-consciousness in the world is of a dear nature and a pleasant nature; it is there that this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; it is there that, when ceasing, it ceases.

“Cakkhusamphasso loke… sotasamphasso loke… ghānasamphasso loke… jivhāsamphasso loke… kāyasamphasso loke… manosamphasso [P 2.0311] loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā pahīyamānā pahīyati, ettha nirujjhamānā nirujjhati.

Eye-contact in the world… ear-contact in the world… nose-contact in the world… tongue-contact in the world… body-contact in the world… mind-contact in the world is of a dear nature and a pleasant nature; it is there that this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; it is there that, when ceasing, it ceases.

“Cakkhusamphassajā vedanā loke… sotasamphassajā vedanā loke [T 2.0347]… ghānasamphassajā vedanā loke… jivhāsamphassajā vedanā loke… kāyasamphassajā vedanā loke… manosamphassajā vedanā loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā pahīyamānā pahīyati, ettha nirujjhamānā nirujjhati.

Feeling born of eye-contact in the world… feeling born of ear-contact in the world… feeling born of nose-contact in the world… feeling born of tongue-contact in the world… feeling born of body-contact in the world… feeling born of mind-contact in the world is of a dear nature and a pleasant nature; it is there that this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; it is there that, when ceasing, it ceases.

“Rūpasaññā [V 2.0233] loke… saddasaññā loke… gandhasaññā loke… rasasaññā loke… phoṭṭhabbasaññā loke… dhammasaññā loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā pahīyamānā pahīyati, ettha nirujjhamānā nirujjhati.

Perception of forms in the world… perception of sounds in the world… perception of odors in the world… perception of tastes in the world… perception of tangible objects in the world… perception of mental phenomena in the world is a dear form and a pleasant form; therein this craving, being abandoned, is abandoned; therein, ceasing, it ceases.

“Rūpasañcetanā [M 2.0249] loke… saddasañcetanā loke… gandhasañcetanā loke… rasasañcetanā loke… phoṭṭhabbasañcetanā loke… dhammasañcetanā loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā pahīyamānā pahīyati, ettha nirujjhamānā nirujjhati.

Volition regarding forms in the world… volition regarding sounds in the world… volition regarding odors in the world… volition regarding tastes in the world… volition regarding tangible objects in the world… volition regarding mental phenomena in the world is a dear form and a pleasant form; therein this craving, being abandoned, is abandoned; therein, ceasing, it ceases.

“Rūpataṇhā loke… saddataṇhā loke… gandhataṇhā loke… rasataṇhā loke… phoṭṭhabbataṇhā loke… dhammataṇhā loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā pahīyamānā pahīyati, ettha nirujjhamānā nirujjhati.

Craving for forms in the world… craving for sounds in the world… craving for odors in the world… craving for tastes in the world… craving for tangible objects in the world… craving for mental phenomena in the world is a dear form and a pleasant form; therein this craving, being abandoned, is abandoned; therein, ceasing, it ceases.

“Rūpavitakko loke… saddavitakko loke… gandhavitakko loke… rasavitakko loke… phoṭṭhabbavitakko loke… dhammavitakko loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā pahīyamānā pahīyati, ettha nirujjhamānā nirujjhati.

Initial thought on forms in the world… initial thought on sounds in the world… initial thought on odors in the world… initial thought on tastes in the world… initial thought on tangible objects in the world… initial thought on mental phenomena in the world is a dear form and a pleasant form; therein this craving, being abandoned, is abandoned; therein, ceasing, it ceases.

“Rūpavicāro loke… saddavicāro loke… gandhavicāro loke… rasavicāro loke… phoṭṭhabbavicāro loke… dhammavicāro loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ[T 2.0348], etthesā taṇhā pahīyamānā pahīyati, ettha nirujjhamānā nirujjhati. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, dukkhanirodhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ.

Sustained thought on forms in the world… sustained thought on sounds in the world… sustained thought on odors in the world… sustained thought on tastes in the world… sustained thought on tangible objects in the world… sustained thought on mental phenomena in the world is a dear form and a pleasant form; therein this craving, being abandoned, is abandoned; therein, ceasing, it ceases. This, bhikkhus, is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering.

Maggasaccaniddeso

Exposition of the Truth of the Path

402. “Katamañca, bhikkhave, dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā ariyasaccaṃ? Ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi sammāsaṅkappo sammāvācā sammākammanto sammāājīvo sammāvāyāmo sammāsati sammāsamādhi.

402. “And what, bhikkhus, is the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering? It is this very Noble Eightfold Path, namely: Right View, Right Intention, Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, and Right Concentration.”

“Katamā ca, bhikkhave, sammādiṭṭhi? Yaṃ [P 2.0312] kho, bhikkhave, dukkhe ñāṇaṃ, dukkhasamudaye ñāṇaṃ, dukkhanirodhe ñāṇaṃ, dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya ñāṇaṃ, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sammādiṭṭhi.

“And what, bhikkhus, is Right View? Knowledge of suffering, bhikkhus, knowledge of the origin of suffering, knowledge of the cessation of suffering, and knowledge of the path leading to the cessation of suffering—this, bhikkhus, is called Right View.”

“Katamo [V 2.0234] ca, bhikkhave, sammāsaṅkappo? Nekkhammasaṅkappo abyāpādasaṅkappo avihiṃsāsaṅkappo, ayaṃ vuccati bhikkhave, sammāsaṅkappo.

“And what, bhikkhus, is Right Intention? The intention of renunciation, the intention of non-ill will, and the intention of non-harming—this, bhikkhus, is called Right Intention.”

“Katamā [M 2.0250] ca, bhikkhave, sammāvācā? Musāvādā veramaṇī veramaṇi (ka.) pisuṇāya vācāya veramaṇī pharusāya vācāya veramaṇī samphappalāpā veramaṇī, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sammāvācā.

“And what, bhikkhus, is Right Speech? Abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, and abstaining from idle chatter—this, bhikkhus, is called Right Speech.”

“Katamo ca, bhikkhave, sammākammanto? Pāṇātipātā veramaṇī adinnādānā veramaṇī kāmesumicchācārā veramaṇī, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sammākammanto.

“And what, bhikkhus, is Right Action? Abstaining from the destruction of life, abstaining from taking what is not given, and abstaining from sexual misconduct—this, bhikkhus, is called Right Action.”

“Katamo ca, bhikkhave, sammāājīvo? Idha, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako micchāājīvaṃ pahāya sammāājīvena jīvitaṃ kappeti, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sammāājīvo.

“And what, bhikkhus, is Right Livelihood? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple, having abandoned wrong livelihood, earns his living by Right Livelihood—this, bhikkhus, is called Right Livelihood.”

“Katamo ca, bhikkhave, sammāvāyāmo? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ [T 2.0349] ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati; uppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati; anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati; uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ṭhitiyā asammosāya bhiyyobhāvāya [P 2.0313] vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sammāvāyāmo.

“And what, bhikkhus, is Right Effort? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states. He generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states. He generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the arising of unarisen wholesome states. He generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the maintenance, non-disappearance, growth, increase, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states. This, bhikkhus, is called Right Effort.”

“Katamā ca, bhikkhave, sammāsati? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; citte cittānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sammāsati.

“And what, bhikkhus, is Right Mindfulness? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. This, bhikkhus, is called Right Mindfulness.”

“Katamo ca, bhikkhave, sammāsamādhi? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ [M 2.0251] sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ avitakkaṃ [V 2.0235] avicāraṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Pītiyā ca virāgā upekkhako ca viharati, sato ca sampajāno, sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedeti, yaṃ taṃ ariyā ācikkhanti ‘upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī’ti tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave[T 2.0350], sammāsamādhi. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā ariyasaccaṃ.

“And what, bhikkhus, is Right Concentration? Here, bhikkhus, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial thought and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. With the stilling of initial and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without initial and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of concentration. With the fading of rapture, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending; he experiences happiness with the body and enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘Equanimous and mindful, one dwells happily.’ With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and includes the purification of mindfulness by equanimity. This, bhikkhus, is called Right Concentration. This, bhikkhus, is called the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.”

403. “Iti ajjhattaṃ vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati, bahiddhā [P 2.0314] vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati, ajjhattabahiddhā vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati. Samudayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati, vayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati, samudayavayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati. ‘Atthi dhammā’ti vā panassa sati paccupaṭṭhitā hoti yāvadeva ñāṇamattāya paṭissatimattāya anissito ca viharati, na ca kiñci loke upādiyati. Evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati catūsu ariyasaccesu.

403. “Thus he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena internally, or he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena externally, or he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena both internally and externally. He dwells contemplating the nature of origination in phenomena, or he dwells contemplating the nature of dissolution in phenomena, or he dwells contemplating the nature of origination and dissolution in phenomena. Or, his mindfulness is established with the thought, ‘Phenomena exist,’ just to the extent necessary for knowledge and mindfulness. And he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world. In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena with regard to the Four Noble Truths.”

Saccapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Section on the Truths is completed.

Dhammānupassanā niṭṭhitā.

The Contemplation of Phenomena is completed.

404. “Yo hi koci, bhikkhave, ime cattāro satipaṭṭhāne evaṃ bhāveyya sattavassāni, tassa dvinnaṃ phalānaṃ aññataraṃ phalaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme aññā; sati vā upādisese [T 2.0351] anāgāmitā.

404. “Bhikkhus, whoever develops these four foundations of mindfulness in this way for seven years, one of two fruits is to be expected for him: either final knowledge in this very life, or, if there is a residue of clinging, non-returning.”

“Tiṭṭhantu, bhikkhave, sattavassāni. Yo hi koci, bhikkhave, ime cattāro satipaṭṭhāne evaṃ bhāveyya cha vassāni…pe… pañca vassāni… cattāri vassāni… tīṇi vassāni… dve vassāni… ekaṃ vassaṃ… tiṭṭhatu, bhikkhave, ekaṃ vassaṃ. Yo hi koci, bhikkhave, ime cattāro satipaṭṭhāne evaṃ bhāveyya sattamāsāni, tassa dvinnaṃ phalānaṃ aññataraṃ phalaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme aññā; sati vā upādisese anāgāmitā.

“Let alone seven years, bhikkhus. Whoever, bhikkhus, should develop these four foundations of mindfulness in this way for six years… five years… four years… three years… two years… one year… Let alone one year, bhikkhus. Whoever, bhikkhus, should develop these four foundations of mindfulness in this way for seven months, one of two fruits is to be expected for him: either final knowledge in this very life or, if there is a residue of clinging, non-returning.”

“Tiṭṭhantu[M 2.0252], bhikkhave, satta māsāni. Yo hi koci, bhikkhave, ime cattāro satipaṭṭhāne evaṃ bhāveyya cha māsāni…pe… pañca māsāni… cattāri māsāni… tīṇi māsāni [V 2.0236] … dve māsāni… ekaṃ [P 2.0315] māsaṃ… aḍḍhamāsaṃ… tiṭṭhatu, bhikkhave, aḍḍhamāso. Yo hi koci, bhikkhave, ime cattāro satipaṭṭhāne evaṃ bhāveyya sattāhaṃ, tassa dvinnaṃ phalānaṃ aññataraṃ phalaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme aññā; sati vā upādisese anāgāmitāti.

“Let alone seven months, bhikkhus. Whoever, bhikkhus, should develop these four foundations of mindfulness in this way for six months… five months… four months… three months… two months… one month… half a month… Let alone half a month, bhikkhus. Whoever, bhikkhus, should develop these four foundations of mindfulness in this way for seven days, one of two fruits is to be expected for him: either final knowledge in this very life or, if there is a residue of clinging, non-returning.”

405. “Ekāyano ayaṃ, bhikkhave, maggo sattānaṃ visuddhiyā sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāya dukkhadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamāya ñāyassa adhigamāya nibbānassa sacchikiriyāya yadidaṃ cattāro satipaṭṭhānāti. Iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ, idametaṃ paṭicca vutta”nti. Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

405. “Bhikkhus, this is the direct path for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the cessation of pain and grief, for the attainment of the right method, and for the realization of Nibbāna—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness. Thus it was said, and it was in reference to this that it was said. This is what the Blessed One said. The bhikkhus were delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.”

Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ navamaṃ.

The Great Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness, the Ninth, is concluded.

10. Pāyāsisuttaṃ

10. The Discourse to Pāyāsi

406. Evaṃ [T 2.0352][M 2.0253][P 2.0316][V 2.0237] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ āyasmā kumārakassapo kosalesu cārikaṃ caramāno mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi yena setabyā nāma kosalānaṃ nagaraṃ tadavasari. Tatra sudaṃ āyasmā kumārakassapo setabyāyaṃ viharati uttarena setabyaṃ siṃsapāvane sīsapāvane (syā.). Tena kho pana samayena pāyāsi rājañño setabyaṃ ajjhāvasati sattussadaṃ satiṇakaṭṭhodakaṃ sadhaññaṃ rājabhoggaṃ raññā pasenadinā kosalena dinnaṃ rājadāyaṃ brahmadeyyaṃ.

406. Thus have I heard. At one time the Venerable Kumārakassapa was wandering in the Kosalan country with a great Saṅgha of bhikkhus, with about five hundred bhikkhus, and arrived at Setabyā, a Kosalan town. There the Venerable Kumārakassapa was dwelling to the north of Setabyā in the Siṃsapā Grove. Now at that time the chieftain Pāyāsi was dwelling in Setabyā, a place teeming with beings, well-supplied with grass, timber, and water, rich in grain, a royal possession given by King Pasenadi of Kosala, a royal gift, a noble grant.

Pāyāsirājaññavatthu

The Account of the Chieftain Pāyāsi

407. Tena kho pana samayena pāyāsissa rājaññassa evarūpaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ uppannaṃ hoti – “itipi natthi paro loko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ [P 2.0317] sukaṭakkaṭānaṃ (sī. pī.) kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko”ti. Assosuṃ kho setabyakā brāhmaṇagahapatikā – “samaṇo khalu bho kumārakassapo samaṇassa gotamassa sāvako kosalesu cārikaṃ caramāno mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi setabyaṃ anuppatto setabyāyaṃ viharati uttarena setabyaṃ siṃsapāvane. Taṃ kho pana bhavantaṃ kumārakassapaṃ evaṃ kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggato – ‘paṇḍito byatto medhāvī bahussuto cittakathī kalyāṇapaṭibhāno vuddho buddho (syā. ka.) ceva arahā ca. Sādhu kho pana tathārūpānaṃ arahataṃ dassanaṃ hotī’”ti. Atha kho setabyakā brāhmaṇagahapatikā setabyāya nikkhamitvā [T 2.0353] saṅghasaṅghī gaṇībhūtā uttarenamukhā gacchanti yena siṃsapāvanaṃ yena siṃsapāvanaṃ, tenupasaṅkamanti (sī. pī.).

407. Now at that time this evil wrong view had arisen in the chieftain Pāyāsi: “There is no other world; there are no spontaneously arisen beings; there is no fruit or result of good and bad actions.” The brahmins and householders of Setabyā heard: “The ascetic Kumārakassapa, a disciple of the ascetic Gotama, while wandering in the Kosalan country with a great Saṅgha of bhikkhus, with about five hundred bhikkhus, has arrived at Setabyā and is dwelling to the north of Setabyā in the Siṃsapā Grove. Now concerning the Venerable Kumārakassapa, this good report has spread: ‘He is wise, competent, intelligent, very learned, an eloquent speaker, of excellent delivery, mature, and an Arahant.’ Indeed, it is good to see such Arahants.” Then the brahmins and householders of Setabyā, having departed from Setabyā, went forth in groups and companies, heading north toward the Siṃsapā Grove.

408. Tena kho pana samayena pāyāsi rājañño uparipāsāde divāseyyaṃ upagato hoti. Addasā kho pāyāsi rājañño setabyake brāhmaṇagahapatike setabyāya nikkhamitvā saṅghasaṅghī gaṇībhūte uttarenamukhe gacchante yena siṃsapāvanaṃ yena siṃsapāvanaṃ, tenupasaṅkamante (sī. pī.), disvā khattaṃ āmantesi [M 2.0254] – “kiṃ nu [V 2.0238] kho, bho khatte, setabyakā brāhmaṇagahapatikā setabyāya nikkhamitvā saṅghasaṅghī gaṇībhūtā uttarenamukhā gacchanti yena siṃsapāvana”nti ettha pana sabbatthapi evameva dissati, natthi pāṭhantaraṃ?

408. Now at that time the chieftain Pāyāsi had gone to the upper story of his palace for his midday rest. The chieftain Pāyāsi saw the brahmins and householders of Setabyā leaving Setabyā in groups and companies, heading north toward the Siṃsapā Grove. Having seen them, he addressed his minister: “Why, good minister, are the brahmins and householders of Setabyā leaving Setabyā in groups and companies, heading north toward the Siṃsapā Grove?”

“Atthi [P 2.0318] kho, bho, samaṇo kumārakassapo, samaṇassa gotamassa sāvako kosalesu cārikaṃ caramāno mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi setabyaṃ anuppatto setabyāyaṃ viharati uttarena setabyaṃ siṃsapāvane. Taṃ kho pana bhavantaṃ kumārakassapaṃ evaṃ kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggato – ‘paṇḍito byatto medhāvī bahussuto cittakathī kalyāṇapaṭibhāno vuddho ceva arahā cā’ti arahā ca (syā. ka.). Tamete tamenaṃ te (sī. ka.), tamenaṃ (pī.) bhavantaṃ kumārakassapaṃ dassanāya upasaṅkamantī”ti. “Tena hi, bho khatte, yena setabyakā brāhmaṇagahapatikā tenupasaṅkama; upasaṅkamitvā setabyake brāhmaṇagahapatike evaṃ vadehi – ‘pāyāsi, bho, rājañño evamāha [T 2.0354] – āgamentu kira bhavanto, pāyāsipi rājañño samaṇaṃ kumārakassapaṃ dassanāya upasaṅkamissatī’ti. Purā samaṇo kumārakassapo setabyake brāhmaṇagahapatike bāle abyatte saññāpeti – ‘itipi atthi paro loko, atthi sattā opapātikā, atthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’ti. Natthi hi, bho khatte, paro loko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko”ti. “Evaṃ bho”ti kho so khattā pāyāsissa rājaññassa paṭissutvā yena setabyakā brāhmaṇagahapatikā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā setabyake brāhmaṇagahapatike etadavoca – “pāyāsi, bho, rājañño evamāha, āgamentu kira bhavanto, pāyāsipi rājañño samaṇaṃ kumārakassapaṃ dassanāya upasaṅkamissatī”ti.

“Indeed, sir, there is the ascetic Kumārakassapa, a disciple of the ascetic Gotama, who, while wandering in the Kosalan country with a great Saṅgha of bhikkhus, with about five hundred bhikkhus, has arrived at Setabyā and is dwelling to the north of Setabyā in the Siṃsapā Grove. And concerning the Venerable Kumārakassapa, this good report has spread: ‘He is wise, competent, intelligent, very learned, an eloquent speaker, of excellent delivery, both a senior and an Arahant.’ They are approaching to see the Venerable Kumārakassapa.” “Then, good minister, go to the brahmins and householders of Setabyā. Having gone, tell the brahmins and householders of Setabyā: ‘The chieftain Pāyāsi says this: “Let the venerable ones wait, for the chieftain Pāyāsi will also approach to see the ascetic Kumārakassapa.”’ This is before the ascetic Kumārakassapa convinces the foolish and unwise brahmins and householders of Setabyā that: ‘There is another world, there are spontaneously arisen beings, there is fruit and result of good and bad actions.’ For indeed, good minister, there is no other world, there are no spontaneously arisen beings, there is no fruit and result of good and bad actions.” “Yes, sir,” replied that minister to the chieftain Pāyāsi. He then went to the brahmins and householders of Setabyā and said this: “The chieftain Pāyāsi says this: ‘Let the venerable ones wait, for the chieftain Pāyāsi will also approach to see the ascetic Kumārakassapa.’”

409. Atha kho pāyāsi rājañño setabyakehi brāhmaṇagahapatikehi parivuto yena siṃsapāvanaṃ yenāyasmā kumārakassapo tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmatā kumārakassapena saddhiṃ [M 2.0255] sammodi, sammodanīyaṃ [P 2.0319] kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Setabyakāpi kho brāhmaṇagahapatikā appekacce āyasmantaṃ kumārakassapaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ [T 2.0355] nisīdiṃsu; appekacce āyasmatā kumārakassapena saddhiṃ sammodiṃsu; sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Appekacce yenāyasmā kumārakassapo tenañjaliṃ paṇāmetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Appekacce nāmagottaṃ sāvetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Appekacce tuṇhībhūtā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu.

409. Then the chieftain Pāyāsi, surrounded by the brahmins and householders of Setabyā, went to the Siṃsapā Grove, to where the Venerable Kumārakassapa was. Having approached, he exchanged joyful greetings with the Venerable Kumārakassapa. When the joyful and memorable talk was concluded, he sat down to one side. And some of the brahmins and householders of Setabyā paid homage to the Venerable Kumārakassapa and sat down to one side; some exchanged joyful greetings with the Venerable Kumārakassapa, and when the joyful and memorable talk was concluded, they sat down to one side; some, toward where the Venerable Kumārakassapa was, raised their joined palms in reverence and sat down to one side; some announced their name and clan and sat down to one side; and some remained silent and sat down to one side.

Natthikavādo

The Doctrine of Non-existence

410. Ekamantaṃ [V 2.0239] nisinno kho pāyāsi rājañño āyasmantaṃ kumārakassapaṃ etadavoca – “ahañhi, bho kassapa, evaṃvādī evaṃdiṭṭhī – ‘itipi natthi paro loko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’”ti. “Nāhaṃ, rājañña, evaṃvādiṃ evaṃdiṭṭhiṃ addasaṃ vā assosiṃ vā. Kathañhi nāma evaṃ vadeyya – ‘itipi natthi paro loko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’ti?

410. Seated to one side, the chieftain Pāyāsi said to the Venerable Kumārakassapa: "Venerable Kassapa, I am one who speaks thus and holds this view: ‘There is no other world, there are no spontaneously arisen beings, there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds.’"

"I have never, chieftain, seen or heard of one who speaks thus and holds this view. How, indeed, could one say: ‘There is no other world, there are no spontaneously arisen beings, there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds’?

Candimasūriyaupamā

The Simile of the Moon and Sun

411. “Tena hi, rājañña, taññevettha paṭipucchissāmi, yathā te khameyya, tathā naṃ byākareyyāsi. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, rājañña, ime candimasūriyā imasmiṃ vā loke parasmiṃ vā, devā vā te manussā vā”ti? “Ime, bho kassapa, candimasūriyā parasmiṃ loke, na imasmiṃ; devā te na manussā”ti. “Imināpi kho te, rājañña, pariyāyena evaṃ hotu – itipi atthi paro loko, atthi sattā opapātikā, atthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko”ti.

411. "Well then, chieftain, I will in turn question you about this very matter. Answer as it pleases you. What do you think, chieftain—are these moon and sun in this world or in another world? Are they devas or humans?"

"These moon and sun, Venerable Kassapa, are in another world, not in this one; they are devas, not humans."

"By this line of reasoning too, chieftain, let it be thus for you: 'There is another world, there are spontaneously arisen beings, and there is a fruit and result of good and bad deeds.'"

412. “Kiñcāpi bhavaṃ kassapo evamāha, atha kho evaṃ me ettha hoti – ‘itipi natthi paro loko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi [P 2.0320] sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’”ti. “Atthi pana, rājañña, pariyāyo, yena te pariyāyena evaṃ hoti – ‘itipi natthi paro loko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’”ti? “Atthi[M 2.0256], bho kassapa, pariyāyo, yena me pariyāyena evaṃ [T 2.0356] hoti – ‘itipi natthi paro loko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’”ti. “Yathā kathaṃ viya, rājaññā”ti? “Idha me, bho kassapa, mittāmaccā ñātisālohitā pāṇātipātī adinnādāyī kāmesumicchācārī musāvādī pisuṇavācā pharusavācā samphappalāpī abhijjhālū byāpannacittā micchādiṭṭhī. Te aparena samayena ābādhikā honti dukkhitā bāḷhagilānā. Yadāhaṃ jānāmi – ‘na dānime imamhā ābādhā vuṭṭhahissantī’ti tyāhaṃ upasaṅkamitvā evaṃ vadāmi – ‘santi kho, bho, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ye te pāṇātipātī adinnādāyī kāmesumicchācārī musāvādī pisuṇavācā pharusavācā samphappalāpī abhijjhālū byāpannacittā micchādiṭṭhī, te kāyassa bhedā [V 2.0240] paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjantī’ti. Bhavanto kho pāṇātipātī adinnādāyī kāmesumicchācārī musāvādī pisuṇavācā pharusavācā samphappalāpī abhijjhālū byāpannacittā micchādiṭṭhī. Sace tesaṃ bhavataṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ saccaṃ vacanaṃ, bhavanto kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjissanti. Sace, bho, kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjeyyātha, yena me āgantvā āroceyyātha – ‘itipi atthi paro loko, atthi sattā opapātikā, atthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’ti[T 2.0357]. Bhavanto kho pana me saddhāyikā paccayikā, yaṃ bhavantehi diṭṭhaṃ, yathā sāmaṃ diṭṭhaṃ evametaṃ bhavissatī’ti. Te me ‘sādhū’ti paṭissutvā [P 2.0321] neva āgantvā ārocenti, na pana dūtaṃ pahiṇanti. Ayampi kho, bho kassapa, pariyāyo, yena me pariyāyena evaṃ hoti – ‘itipi natthi paro loko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’”ti.

412. “Although the venerable Kassapa says this, nevertheless, this is my view on the matter: ‘There is no other world, there are no spontaneously arisen beings, there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds.’”

“But is there a reason, chieftain, by which you have this view: ‘There is no other world, there are no spontaneously arisen beings, there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds’?”

“There is a reason, Venerable Kassapa, by which I have this view: ‘There is no other world, there are no spontaneously arisen beings, there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds.’”

“And how is that, chieftain?”

“Here, Venerable Kassapa, my friends and companions, my kinsmen and relatives, are destroyers of life, takers of what is not given, they engage in sexual misconduct, speak falsehood, speak slanderously, speak harshly, engage in frivolous chatter, are covetous, have minds of ill will, and hold wrong view. In the course of time, they become afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill. When I know, ‘They will not now recover from this affliction,’ I approach them and say this: ‘Sirs, there are some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold this view: “Those who are destroyers of life... and hold wrong view, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in the plane of deprivation, a bad destination, a state of ruin, in hell.” You, sirs, are destroyers of life... and hold wrong view. If the words of those venerable ascetics and brahmins are true, then you, sirs, with the breakup of the body, after death, will be reborn in the plane of deprivation, a bad destination, a state of ruin, in hell. If, sirs, with the breakup of the body, after death, you are reborn in the plane of deprivation, a bad destination, a state of ruin, in hell, may you come and inform me thus: “There is another world, there are spontaneously arisen beings, there is a fruit and result of good and bad deeds.” You, sirs, are trustworthy and credible to me; what is seen by you will be for me as if seen by myself.’

“They, having agreed with ‘Very well,’ neither come back to inform me, nor do they send a messenger. This too, Venerable Kassapa, is the reason by which I have this view: ‘There is no other world, there are no spontaneously arisen beings, there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds.’”

Coraupamā

The Simile of the Thief

413. “Tena hi, rājañña, taññevettha paṭipucchissāmi. Yathā te khameyya tathā naṃ byākareyyāsi. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, rājañña, idha te purisā coraṃ āgucāriṃ gahetvā dasseyyuṃ – ‘ayaṃ te, bhante, coro āgucārī; imassa yaṃ icchasi, taṃ daṇḍaṃ paṇehī’ti. Te tvaṃ evaṃ vadeyyāsi – ‘tena hi, bho, imaṃ purisaṃ daḷhāya rajjuyā pacchābāhaṃ gāḷhabandhanaṃ bandhitvā [M 2.0257] khuramuṇḍaṃ karitvā kāretvā (syā. ka.) kharassarena paṇavena rathikāya rathikaṃ rathiyāya rathiyaṃ (bahūsū) siṅghāṭakena siṅghāṭakaṃ parinetvā dakkhiṇena dvārena nikkhamitvā dakkhiṇato nagarassa āghātane sīsaṃ chindathā’ti. Te ‘sādhū’ti paṭissutvā taṃ purisaṃ daḷhāya rajjuyā pacchābāhaṃ gāḷhabandhanaṃ bandhitvā khuramuṇḍaṃ karitvā kharassarena paṇavena rathikāya rathikaṃ siṅghāṭakena siṅghāṭakaṃ parinetvā dakkhiṇena dvārena nikkhamitvā dakkhiṇato nagarassa āghātane nisīdāpeyyuṃ. Labheyya nu kho so coro coraghātesu – ‘āgamentu tāva bhavanto coraghātā, amukasmiṃ [T 2.0358] me gāme vā nigame vā mittāmaccā ñātisālohitā, yāvāhaṃ tesaṃ uddisitvā āgacchāmī’ti[P 2.0322], udāhu vippalapantasseva coraghātā sīsaṃ chindeyyu”nti? “Na hi so, bho kassapa, coro labheyya coraghātesu – ‘āgamentu tāva bhavanto coraghātā amukasmiṃ me gāme vā nigame vā mittāmaccā ñātisālohitā, yāvāhaṃ tesaṃ uddisitvā āgacchāmī’ti. Atha kho naṃ vippalapantasseva coraghātā sīsaṃ chindeyyu”nti. “So hi nāma, rājañña, coro manusso manussabhūtesu coraghātesu na labhissati – ‘āgamentu tāva bhavanto coraghātā, amukasmiṃ me gāme [V 2.0241] vā nigame vā mittāmaccā ñātisālohitā, yāvāhaṃ tesaṃ uddisitvā āgacchāmī’ti. Kiṃ pana te mittāmaccā ñātisālohitā pāṇātipātī adinnādāyī kāmesumicchācārī musāvādī pisuṇavācā pharusavācā samphappalāpī abhijjhālū byāpannacittā micchādiṭṭhī, te kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapannā labhissanti nirayapālesu – ‘āgamentu tāva bhavanto nirayapālā, yāva mayaṃ pāyāsissa rājaññassa gantvā ārocema – “itipi atthi paro loko, atthi sattā opapātikā, atthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’”ti? Imināpi kho te, rājañña, pariyāyena evaṃ hotu – ‘itipi atthi paro loko, atthi sattā opapātikā, atthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’”ti.

413. “Well then, chieftain, I will question you in return on this very matter. Answer as you see fit. What do you think, chieftain? Suppose your men were to capture a thief, a criminal, and present him to you, saying, ‘Sire, this is your thief, a criminal; impose on him whatever punishment you wish.’ And you were to say, ‘Well then, sirs, having bound this man’s arms tightly behind his back with a strong rope, having shaved his head, and having led him from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads to the beating of a harsh-sounding drum, take him out through the southern gate and behead him at the execution ground to the south of the city.’ They would reply, ‘Very well,’ and having bound that man’s arms tightly behind his back with a strong rope, having shaved his head, and having led him from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads to the beating of a harsh-sounding drum, they would take him out through the southern gate and make him sit at the execution ground to the south of the city. Would that thief obtain a delay from the executioners by saying: ‘Please wait, sirs, executioners! In such-and-such village or town I have friends, companions, or kinsmen by blood. Let me inform them before I return’? Or would the executioners behead him even as he was wailing?” “He would not, venerable Kassapa. That thief would not obtain a delay from the executioners by saying: ‘Please wait, sirs, executioners! In such-and-such village or town I have friends, companions, or kinsmen by blood. Let me inform them before I return.’ Rather, the executioners would behead him even as he was wailing.” “Indeed, chieftain, that thief, a human being, will not obtain a delay from human executioners by saying: ‘Please wait, sirs, executioners! In such-and-such village or town I have friends, companions, or kinsmen by blood. Let me inform them before I return.’ What then? Will your friends, companions, or kinsmen by blood—who destroy life, take what is not given, engage in sexual misconduct, speak falsehood, speak divisive speech, speak harsh speech, engage in idle chatter, are covetous, have minds of ill will, and hold wrong view—will they, after the breakup of the body, after death, having been reborn in the plane of deprivation, the bad destination, the lower world, in hell, obtain a delay from the hell-wardens by saying: ‘Please wait, sirs, hell-wardens, while we go and inform Pāyāsi the chieftain that “There is another world, there are beings spontaneously born, there is the fruit and result of good and bad actions”’? By this line of reasoning too, chieftain, let it be thus for you: ‘There is another world, there are beings spontaneously born, there is the fruit and result of good and bad actions.’”

414. “Kiñcāpi [T 2.0359] bhavaṃ kassapo evamāha, atha kho evaṃ me ettha hoti – ‘itipi natthi paro loko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ [M 2.0258] kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko”ti. “Atthi pana, rājañña, pariyāyo yena te pariyāyena evaṃ hoti – ‘itipi natthi paro loko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’”ti? “Atthi, bho kassapa, pariyāyo, yena me pariyāyena evaṃ hoti – ‘itipi natthi paro loko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’”ti. “Yathā kathaṃ viya, rājaññā”ti? “Idha me, bho kassapa, mittāmaccā ñātisālohitā pāṇātipātā paṭiviratā adinnādānā paṭiviratā kāmesumicchācārā [P 2.0323] paṭiviratā musāvādā paṭiviratā pisuṇāya vācāya paṭiviratā pharusāya vācāya paṭiviratā samphappalāpā paṭiviratā anabhijjhālū abyāpannacittā sammādiṭṭhī. Te aparena samayena ābādhikā honti dukkhitā bāḷhagilānā. Yadāhaṃ jānāmi – ‘na dānime imamhā ābādhā vuṭṭhahissantī’ti tyāhaṃ upasaṅkamitvā evaṃ vadāmi – ‘santi kho, bho, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ye te pāṇātipātā paṭiviratā adinnādānā paṭiviratā kāmesumicchācārā paṭiviratā musāvādā paṭiviratā pisuṇāya vācāya paṭiviratā pharusāya vācāya paṭiviratā samphappalāpā paṭiviratā anabhijjhālū abyāpannacittā sammādiṭṭhī te kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjantīti[T 2.0360]. Bhavanto kho pāṇātipātā paṭiviratā adinnādānā paṭiviratā kāmesumicchācārā paṭiviratā musāvādā paṭiviratā pisuṇāya vācāya paṭiviratā pharusāya vācāya paṭiviratā samphappalāpā paṭiviratā anabhijjhālū abyāpannacittā sammādiṭṭhī. Sace tesaṃ bhavataṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ saccaṃ vacanaṃ, bhavanto kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjissanti. Sace, bho, kāyassa bhedā [V 2.0242] paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjeyyātha, yena me āgantvā āroceyyātha – ‘itipi atthi paro loko, atthi sattā opapātikā, atthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’ti. Bhavanto kho pana me saddhāyikā paccayikā, yaṃ bhavantehi diṭṭhaṃ, yathā sāmaṃ diṭṭhaṃ evametaṃ bhavissatī’ti. Te me ‘sādhū’ti paṭissutvā neva āgantvā ārocenti, na pana dūtaṃ pahiṇanti. Ayampi kho, bho kassapa, pariyāyo, yena me pariyāyena evaṃ hoti – ‘itipi [P 2.0324] natthi paro loko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’”ti.

414. “Although the venerable Kassapa speaks thus, still it occurs to me in this matter: ‘For this reason, there is no other world, there are no spontaneously arisen beings, there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds.’” “But is there, Rājañña, a reason by which it occurs to you thus: ‘For this reason, there is no other world, there are no spontaneously arisen beings, there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds’?” “There is, venerable Kassapa, a reason by which it occurs to me thus: ‘For this reason, there is no other world, there are no spontaneously arisen beings, there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds.’” “In what way, Rājañña?” “Here, venerable Kassapa, my friends and companions, kinsmen and relatives, abstain from the destruction of life, abstain from taking what is not given, abstain from sexual misconduct, abstain from false speech, abstain from divisive speech, abstain from harsh speech, abstain from idle chatter; they are uncovetous, have minds without ill will, and possess right view. At a later time, they become ill, afflicted, and gravely sick. When I know, ‘They will not now recover from this illness,’ I approach them and say this: ‘Sirs, there are some ascetics and brahmins with such a doctrine, with such a view, who say: “Those who abstain from the destruction of life, abstain from taking what is not given, abstain from sexual misconduct, abstain from false speech, abstain from divisive speech, abstain from harsh speech, abstain from idle chatter, are uncovetous, have minds without ill will, and possess right view—they, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.” You, sirs, abstain from the destruction of life... and possess right view. If the words of those venerable ascetics and brahmins are true, you, with the breakup of the body, after death, will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. If, sirs, with the breakup of the body, after death, you are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world, then you should come and inform me: “For this reason, there is another world, there are spontaneously arisen beings, there is fruit and result of good and bad deeds.” You, sirs, are trustworthy and reliable to me; what is seen by you will be for me as if seen by myself.’ They, having agreed to my words, saying ‘Very well,’ neither come and inform me, nor do they send a messenger. This too, venerable Kassapa, is the reason by which it occurs to me thus: ‘For this reason, there is no other world, there are no spontaneously arisen beings, there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds.’”

Gūthakūpapurisaupamā

The Simile of the Man in the Cesspool

415. “Tena [M 2.0259] hi, rājañña, upamaṃ te karissāmi. Upamāya midhekacce upamāyapidhekacce (sī. syā.), upamāyapiidhekacce (pī.) viññū purisā bhāsitassa atthaṃ ājānanti. Seyyathāpi, rājañña, puriso gūthakūpe sasīsakaṃ sasīsako (syā.) nimuggo assa. Atha tvaṃ purise āṇāpeyyāsi – ‘tena hi, bho, taṃ purisaṃ tamhā gūthakūpā uddharathā’ti. Te ‘sādhū’ti paṭissutvā taṃ purisaṃ tamhā gūthakūpā uddhareyyuṃ. Te tvaṃ evaṃ vadeyyāsi – ‘tena hi, bho, tassa purisassa kāyā [T 2.0361] veḷupesikāhi gūthaṃ sunimmajjitaṃ nimmajjathā’ti. Te ‘sādhū’ti paṭissutvā tassa purisassa kāyā veḷupesikāhi gūthaṃ sunimmajjitaṃ nimmajjeyyuṃ. Te tvaṃ evaṃ vadeyyāsi – ‘tena hi, bho, tassa purisassa kāyaṃ paṇḍumattikāya tikkhattuṃ subbaṭṭitaṃ ubbaṭṭethā’ti suppaṭṭitaṃ uppaṭṭethāti (ka.). Te tassa purisassa kāyaṃ paṇḍumattikāya tikkhattuṃ subbaṭṭitaṃ ubbaṭṭeyyuṃ. Te tvaṃ evaṃ vadeyyāsi – ‘tena hi, bho, taṃ purisaṃ telena abbhañjitvā sukhumena cuṇṇena tikkhattuṃ suppadhotaṃ karothā’ti. Te taṃ purisaṃ telena abbhañjitvā sukhumena cuṇṇena tikkhattuṃ suppadhotaṃ kareyyuṃ. Te tvaṃ evaṃ vadeyyāsi – ‘tena hi, bho, tassa purisassa kesamassuṃ kappethā’ti. Te tassa purisassa kesamassuṃ kappeyyuṃ. Te tvaṃ evaṃ vadeyyāsi – ‘tena hi, bho, tassa purisassa mahagghañca mālaṃ mahagghañca vilepanaṃ mahagghāni ca vatthāni upaharathā’ti. Te tassa purisassa mahagghañca mālaṃ mahagghañca vilepanaṃ [P 2.0325] mahagghāni ca vatthāni upahareyyuṃ. Te tvaṃ evaṃ vadeyyāsi – ‘tena hi, bho, taṃ purisaṃ pāsādaṃ āropetvā pañcakāmaguṇāni upaṭṭhāpethā’ti. Te taṃ purisaṃ pāsādaṃ āropetvā pañcakāmaguṇāni upaṭṭhāpeyyuṃ.

415. “In that case, Rājañña, I will make a simile for you. For by means of a simile, some wise men in this world understand the meaning of what is said. Suppose, Rājañña, a man were to be sunk, including his head, in a cesspool. Then you would command your men: ‘Come now, sirs, lift that man out of that cesspool.’ They, having agreed, saying ‘Very well,’ would lift that man out of that cesspool. You would say to them thus: ‘Come now, sirs, thoroughly scrape the filth from that man’s body with bamboo scrapers.’ They, having agreed, saying ‘Very well,’ would thoroughly scrape the filth from that man’s body with bamboo scrapers. You would say to them thus: ‘Come now, sirs, rub that man’s body three times with pale clay, thoroughly applied.’ They would rub that man’s body three times with pale clay, thoroughly applied. You would say to them thus: ‘Come now, sirs, having anointed that man with oil, cleanse him three times with fine powder.’ They would, having anointed that man with oil, cleanse him three times with fine powder. You would say to them thus: ‘Come now, sirs, dress that man’s hair and beard.’ They would dress that man’s hair and beard. You would say to them thus: ‘Come now, sirs, bring to that man an expensive garland, expensive ointment, and expensive clothes.’ They would bring to that man an expensive garland, expensive ointment, and expensive clothes. You would say to them thus: ‘Come now, sirs, having taken that man up to a palace, provide him with the five strands of sensual pleasure.’ They would, having taken that man up to a palace, provide him with the five strands of sensual pleasure.

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, rājañña, api nu tassa purisassa sunhātassa suvilittassa sukappitakesamassussa āmukkamālābharaṇassa odātavatthavasanassa uparipāsādavaragatassa pañcahi [V 2.0243] kāmaguṇehi samappitassa samaṅgībhūtassa [T 2.0362] paricārayamānassa punadeva tasmiṃ gūthakūpe nimujjitukāmatā nimujjitukāmyatā (syā. ka.) assā”ti? “No hidaṃ, bho kassapa”. “Taṃ kissa hetu”? “Asuci, bho kassapa, gūthakūpo asuci ceva asucisaṅkhāto ca duggandho ca duggandhasaṅkhāto ca jeguccho ca jegucchasaṅkhāto [M 2.0260] ca paṭikūlo ca paṭikūlasaṅkhāto cā”ti. “Evameva kho, rājañña, manussā devānaṃ asucī ceva asucisaṅkhātā ca, duggandhā ca duggandhasaṅkhātā ca, jegucchā ca jegucchasaṅkhātā ca, paṭikūlā ca paṭikūlasaṅkhātā ca. Yojanasataṃ kho, rājañña, manussagandho deve ubbādhati. Kiṃ pana te mittāmaccā ñātisālohitā pāṇātipātā paṭiviratā adinnādānā paṭiviratā kāmesumicchācārā paṭiviratā musāvādā paṭiviratā pisuṇāya vācāya paṭiviratā pharusāya vācāya paṭiviratā samphappalāpā paṭiviratā anabhijjhālū abyāpannacittā sammādiṭṭhī, kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapannā te āgantvā ārocessanti – ‘itipi atthi paro loko, atthi sattā opapātikā, atthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ [P 2.0326] kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’ti? Imināpi kho te, rājañña, pariyāyena evaṃ hotu – ‘itipi atthi paro loko, atthi sattā opapātikā, atthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’”ti.

“What do you think, chieftain? Suppose that a man—well-bathed, well-anointed, with hair and beard finely trimmed, adorned with garlands and ornaments, wearing white clothes, staying on the upper story of a fine palace—is supplied and endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure. Would he then wish to plunge back into that cesspool?” “No, Master Kassapa.” “Why is that?” “Because, Master Kassapa, the cesspool is impure, considered impure; foul-smelling, considered foul-smelling; disgusting, considered disgusting; and repulsive, considered repulsive.” “Just so, chieftain, humans are impure to the devas, considered impure; foul-smelling, considered foul-smelling; disgusting, considered disgusting; and repulsive, considered repulsive. The smell of humans, chieftain, afflicts the devas even from a hundred leagues away. Why then would your friends, companions, relatives, and kin—who abstain from killing living beings, abstain from taking what is not given, abstain from sexual misconduct, abstain from false speech, abstain from divisive speech, abstain from harsh speech, abstain from idle chatter, are without covetousness, with minds free from ill will, and possess right view; and who, after the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a good destination, the heavenly world—come and inform you: ‘Truly, there is another world, there are beings reborn spontaneously, there is the fruit and result of good and bad deeds’? By this line of reasoning too, chieftain, let it be thus for you: ‘Truly, there is another world, there are beings reborn spontaneously, there is the fruit and result of good and bad deeds.’”

416. “Kiñcāpi bhavaṃ kassapo evamāha, atha kho evaṃ me ettha hoti – ‘itipi natthi paro loko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’”ti. “Atthi pana, rājañña, pariyāyo [T 2.0363] …pe… “atthi, bho kassapa, pariyāyo…pe… ``yathā kathaṃ viya, rājaññāti? “Idha me, bho kassapa, mittāmaccā ñātisālohitā pāṇātipātā paṭiviratā adinnādānā paṭiviratā kāmesumicchācārā paṭiviratā musāvādā paṭiviratā surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānā paṭiviratā, te aparena samayena ābādhikā honti dukkhitā bāḷhagilānā. Yadāhaṃ jānāmi – ‘na dānime imamhā ābādhā vuṭṭhahissantī’ti tyāhaṃ upasaṅkamitvā evaṃ vadāmi – ‘santi kho, bho, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ye te pāṇātipātā paṭiviratā adinnādānā paṭiviratā kāmesumicchācārā paṭiviratā musāvādā paṭiviratā surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānā paṭiviratā, te kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjanti devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ sahabyatanti. Bhavanto kho pāṇātipātā paṭiviratā adinnādānā paṭiviratā kāmesumicchācārā paṭiviratā musāvādā paṭiviratā surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānā paṭiviratā. Sace tesaṃ bhavataṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ saccaṃ vacanaṃ, bhavanto kāyassa bhedā paraṃ [M 2.0261] maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjissanti, devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ sahabyataṃ. Sace, bho, kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjeyyātha [V 2.0244] devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ sahabyataṃ, yena me āgantvā āroceyyātha – `itipi atthi paro loko, atthi sattā opapātikā, atthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipākoti. Bhavanto kho [T 2.0364] pana me saddhāyikā paccayikā, yaṃ bhavantehi diṭṭhaṃ, yathā sāmaṃ [P 2.0327] diṭṭhaṃ evametaṃ bhavissatīti. Te me ‘sādhū’ti paṭissutvā neva āgantvā ārocenti, na pana dūtaṃ pahiṇanti. Ayampi kho, bho kassapa, pariyāyo, yena me pariyāyena evaṃ hoti – ‘itipi natthi paro loko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’”ti.

416. “Although you, Venerable Kassapa, say this, still this is what occurs to me: ‘Indeed, there is no other world, there are no beings born spontaneously, there is no fruit or result of good or bad deeds.’” “Is there, chieftain, a reason for this?” … “There is, Venerable Kassapa, a reason.” … “And what is that reason, chieftain?” “Here, Venerable Kassapa, I have friends, ministers, relatives, and kin who abstain from killing living beings, abstain from taking what is not given, abstain from sexual misconduct, abstain from false speech, and abstain from intoxicants that are a basis for heedlessness. At a later time, they become sick, suffering, and gravely ill. When I know, ‘They will not now recover from this illness,’ I approach them and say: ‘There are, sirs, some ascetics and brahmins who hold this view and doctrine: “Those who abstain from killing living beings, abstain from taking what is not given, abstain from sexual misconduct, abstain from false speech, and abstain from intoxicants that are a basis for heedlessness—after the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world, in the company of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.” You, sirs, have abstained from killing living beings, abstain from taking what is not given, abstain from sexual misconduct, abstain from false speech, and abstain from intoxicants that are a basis for heedlessness. If the words of those venerable ascetics and brahmins are true, then after the breakup of the body, after death, you will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world, in the company of the Tāvatiṃsa devas. If, sirs, after the breakup of the body, after death, you are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world, in the company of the Tāvatiṃsa devas, then please come and inform me: “Indeed, there is another world, there are beings born spontaneously, there is the fruit and result of good and bad deeds.” You, sirs, are trustworthy and reliable to me; what is seen by you will be as if seen by myself.’ Having agreed, saying, ‘Very well,’ they neither come and inform me, nor do they send a messenger. This, Venerable Kassapa, is the reason why it occurs to me: ‘Indeed, there is no other world, there are no beings born spontaneously, there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds.’”

Tāvatiṃsadevaupamā

The Simile of the Tāvatiṃsa Devas

417. “Tena hi, rājañña, taññevettha paṭipucchissāmi; yathā te khameyya, tathā naṃ byākareyyāsi. Yaṃ kho pana, rājañña, mānussakaṃ vassasataṃ, devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ eso eko rattindivo rattidivo (ka.), tāya rattiyā tiṃsarattiyo māso, tena māsena dvādasamāsiyo saṃvaccharo, tena saṃvaccharena dibbaṃ vassasahassaṃ devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ āyuppamāṇaṃ. Ye te mittāmaccā ñātisālohitā pāṇātipātā paṭiviratā adinnādānā paṭiviratā kāmesumicchācārā paṭiviratā musāvādā paṭiviratā surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānā paṭiviratā, te kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapannā devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ sahabyataṃ. Sace pana tesaṃ evaṃ bhavissati – ‘yāva mayaṃ dve vā tīṇi vā rattindivā dibbehi pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappitā samaṅgībhūtā paricārema, atha mayaṃ pāyāsissa rājaññassa gantvā āroceyyāma – “itipi atthi paro loko, atthi sattā opapātikā, atthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko”ti. Api nu te āgantvā āroceyyuṃ [T 2.0365] – ‘itipi atthi paro loko, atthi sattā opapātikā, atthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’”ti? “No hidaṃ, bho kassapa. Api hi mayaṃ, bho kassapa, ciraṃ kālaṅkatāpi bhaveyyāma. Ko panetaṃ bhoto kassapassa āroceti [M 2.0262] – ‘atthi devā tāvatiṃsā’ti vā ‘evaṃdīghāyukā devā tāvatiṃsā’ti vā. Na mayaṃ bhoto [P 2.0328] kassapassa saddahāma – ‘atthi devā tāvatiṃsā’ti vā ‘evaṃdīghāyukā devā tāvatiṃsā’ti vā”ti.

417. “Then, chieftain, I will question you in return. Answer as you see fit. Chieftain, that which is one hundred human years is a single day and night for the Tāvatiṃsa devas. Thirty such nights make a month, twelve such months make a year, and a thousand such divine years is the lifespan of the Tāvatiṃsa devas. Those friends, advisors, relatives, and kinsmen of yours who abstain from killing living beings, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from liquor, wine, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence—at the breaking up of the body, after death, they are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world, in the company of the Tāvatiṃsa devas. Now, if it were to occur to them: ‘Let us enjoy ourselves for two or three days and nights, endowed and furnished with the five divine strands of sensual pleasure, and then go to the chieftain Pāyāsi and inform him: “Indeed there is another world; there are spontaneously arisen beings; there is the fruit and result of good and bad deeds,”’ would they come and inform you: ‘Indeed there is another world; there are spontaneously arisen beings; there is the fruit and result of good and bad deeds’?” “No, venerable Kassapa. For by then, venerable Kassapa, we might have been dead for a long time. And who informs the venerable Kassapa: ‘There are Tāvatiṃsa devas,’ or ‘The Tāvatiṃsa devas are so long-lived’? We do not believe the venerable Kassapa when he says: ‘There are Tāvatiṃsa devas,’ or ‘The Tāvatiṃsa devas are so long-lived.’”

Jaccandhaupamā

The Simile of the Man Born Blind

418. “Seyyathāpi, rājañña, jaccandho puriso na passeyya kaṇha – sukkāni rūpāni[V 2.0245], na passeyya nīlakāni rūpāni, na passeyya pītakāni mañjeṭṭhakāni (syā.) rūpāni, na passeyya lohitakāni rūpāni, na passeyya mañjiṭṭhakāni rūpāni, na passeyya samavisamaṃ, na passeyya tārakāni rūpāni, na passeyya candimasūriye. So evaṃ vadeyya – ‘natthi kaṇhasukkāni rūpāni, natthi kaṇhasukkānaṃ rūpānaṃ dassāvī. Natthi nīlakāni rūpāni, natthi nīlakānaṃ rūpānaṃ dassāvī. Natthi pītakāni rūpāni, natthi pītakānaṃ rūpānaṃ dassāvī. Natthi lohitakāni rūpāni, natthi lohitakānaṃ rūpānaṃ dassāvī. Natthi mañjiṭṭhakāni rūpāni, natthi mañjiṭṭhakānaṃ rūpānaṃ dassāvī. Natthi samavisamaṃ, natthi samavisamassa dassāvī. Natthi tārakāni rūpāni, natthi tārakānaṃ rūpānaṃ dassāvī. Natthi candimasūriyā, natthi candimasūriyānaṃ dassāvī. Ahametaṃ na jānāmi, ahametaṃ na passāmi, tasmā taṃ natthī’ti. Sammā nu kho so, rājañña, vadamāno vadeyyā”ti? “No hidaṃ, bho [T 2.0366] kassapa. Atthi kaṇhasukkāni rūpāni, atthi kaṇhasukkānaṃ rūpānaṃ dassāvī. Atthi nīlakāni rūpāni, atthi nīlakānaṃ rūpānaṃ dassāvī…pe… [P 2.0329] atthi samavisamaṃ, atthi samavisamassa dassāvī. Atthi tārakāni rūpāni, atthi tārakānaṃ rūpānaṃ dassāvī. Atthi candimasūriyā, atthi candimasūriyānaṃ dassāvī. ‘Ahametaṃ na jānāmi, ahametaṃ na passāmi, tasmā taṃ natthī’ti. Na hi so, bho kassapa, sammā vadamāno vadeyyā”ti. “Evameva kho tvaṃ, rājañña, jaccandhūpamo maññe paṭibhāsi yaṃ maṃ tvaṃ evaṃ vadesi”.

418. “Suppose, chieftain, a man blind from birth would not see black and white forms, would not see blue forms, would not see yellow forms, would not see red forms, would not see madder-red forms, would not see the even and the uneven, would not see the forms of stars, and would not see the moon and sun. He might say: ‘There are no black and white forms, and no one who sees black and white forms. There are no blue forms, and no one who sees blue forms. There are no yellow forms, and no one who sees yellow forms. There are no red forms, and no one who sees red forms. There are no madder-red forms, and no one who sees madder-red forms. There is no even and uneven, and no one who sees the even and uneven. There are no forms of stars, and no one who sees the forms of stars. There are no moon and sun, and no one who sees the moon and sun. I do not know this, I do not see this, therefore it does not exist.’ In saying this, chieftain, would he be speaking rightly?” “No, venerable Kassapa. There are black and white forms, and there are those who see black and white forms. There are blue forms, and there are those who see blue forms… and so on… there is the even and the uneven, and there are those who see the even and the uneven. There are the forms of stars, and there are those who see the forms of stars. There are the moon and sun, and there are those who see the moon and sun. For him to say, ‘I do not know this, I do not see this, therefore it does not exist’—in saying this, venerable Kassapa, he would not be speaking rightly.” “In just the same way, chieftain, I think you appear to me like one who is blind from birth, when you speak to me in this way.”

“Ko panetaṃ bhoto kassapassa āroceti – ‘atthi devā tāvatiṃsā”ti vā, ‘evaṃdīghāyukā devā tāvatiṃsā’ti vā? Na mayaṃ bhoto kassapassa saddahāma – ‘atthi devā tāvatiṃsā’ti vā ‘evaṃdīghāyukā devā tāvatiṃsā’ti vā”ti. “Na kho, rājañña, evaṃ paro loko daṭṭhabbo, yathā tvaṃ maññasi iminā maṃsacakkhunā. Ye kho te rājañña samaṇabrāhmaṇā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti[M 2.0263], te tattha appamattā ātāpino pahitattā viharantā dibbacakkhuṃ visodhenti.
