Te dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena imaṃ ceva lokaṃ passanti parañca satte ca opapātike. Evañca kho, rājañña, paro loko daṭṭhabbo; natveva yathā tvaṃ maññasi iminā maṃsacakkhunā. Imināpi kho te, rājañña, pariyāyena evaṃ hotu – ‘itipi [T 2.0367] atthi paro loko, atthi sattā opapātikā, atthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’”ti.

“But who informs the venerable Kassapa: ‘There are Tāvatiṃsa devas,’ or ‘The Tāvatiṃsa devas are so long-lived’? We do not believe the venerable Kassapa when he says: ‘There are Tāvatiṃsa devas,’ or ‘The Tāvatiṃsa devas are so long-lived.’” “Chieftain, the other world is not to be seen in the way that you suppose with this eye of flesh. There are, chieftain, ascetics and brahmins who resort to remote forest and wilderness dwellings, secluded lodgings. Dwelling there, diligent, ardent, and resolute, they purify the divine eye. With the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, they see this world and the next, and spontaneously arisen beings. It is in this way, chieftain, that the other world is to be seen, and not as you suppose with this eye of flesh. By this line of reasoning, too, chieftain, let it be thus for you: ‘Indeed, there is another world, there are spontaneously arisen beings, and there is the fruit and result of good and bad deeds.’”

419. “Kiñcāpi bhavaṃ kassapo evamāha, atha kho evaṃ [P 2.0330] me ettha hoti – ‘itipi natthi paro loko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko”ti[V 2.0246]. “Atthi pana, rājañña, pariyāyo…pe… atthi, bho kassapa, pariyāyo…pe… yathā kathaṃ viya, rājaññā”ti? “Idhāhaṃ, bho kassapa, passāmi samaṇabrāhmaṇe sīlavante kalyāṇadhamme jīvitukāme amaritukāme sukhakāme dukkhapaṭikūle. Tassa mayhaṃ, bho kassapa, evaṃ hoti – sace kho ime bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā sīlavanto kalyāṇadhammā evaṃ jāneyyuṃ – ‘ito no matānaṃ seyyo bhavissatī’ti. Idānime bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā sīlavanto kalyāṇadhammā visaṃ vā khādeyyuṃ, satthaṃ vā āhareyyuṃ, ubbandhitvā vā kālaṅkareyyuṃ, papāte vā papateyyuṃ. Yasmā ca kho ime bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā sīlavanto kalyāṇadhammā na evaṃ jānanti – ‘ito no matānaṃ seyyo bhavissatī’ti, tasmā ime bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā sīlavanto kalyāṇadhammā jīvitukāmā amaritukāmā sukhakāmā dukkhapaṭikūlā attānaṃ na mārenti ( ) natthi (syā. pī.). Ayampi kho, bho kassapa, pariyāyo, yena me pariyāyena evaṃ hoti – ‘itipi natthi paro loko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’”ti.

419. “Although the venerable Kassapa speaks thus, nevertheless, it is thus for me in this matter: ‘There is no other world, there are no spontaneously arisen beings, there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds.’” “Is there then, chieftain, a reason for this?” … “There is, venerable Kassapa, a reason.” … “How so, chieftain?” “Here, venerable Kassapa, I see ascetics and brahmins who are virtuous, of good character, desiring to live, not desiring to die, desiring happiness, and averse to suffering. It occurs to me, venerable Kassapa: ‘If these venerable ascetics and brahmins, who are virtuous and of good character, were to know thus: “It will be better for us after death than this life,” then these venerable ascetics and brahmins, who are virtuous and of good character, would now eat poison, or take up a weapon, or hang themselves and die, or throw themselves from a precipice. And because these venerable ascetics and brahmins, who are virtuous and of good character, do not know thus: “It will be better for us after death than this life,” therefore these venerable ascetics and brahmins, who are virtuous and of good character, desiring to live, not desiring to die, desiring happiness, and averse to suffering, do not kill themselves.’ This, too, venerable Kassapa, is the line of reasoning by which it is thus for me: ‘There is no other world, there are no spontaneously arisen beings, there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds.’”

Gabbhinīupamā

The Simile of the Pregnant Woman

420. “Tena [T 2.0368] hi, rājañña, upamaṃ te karissāmi. Upamāya midhekacce viññū purisā bhāsitassa atthaṃ ājānanti. Bhūtapubbaṃ, rājañña, aññatarassa brāhmaṇassa [M 2.0264] dve pajāpatiyo ahesuṃ. Ekissā putto ahosi dasavassuddesiko vā dvādasavassuddesiko vā, ekā gabbhinī upavijaññā. Atha kho so brāhmaṇo kālamakāsi. Atha kho so māṇavako mātusapattiṃ mātusapatiṃ (syā.) etadavoca – ‘yamidaṃ, bhoti, dhanaṃ vā dhaññaṃ vā rajataṃ vā jātarūpaṃ vā, sabbaṃ taṃ mayhaṃ[P 2.0331]; natthi tuyhettha kiñci. Pitu me pitu me santako (syā.) bhoti, dāyajjaṃ niyyādehī’ti nīyyātehīti (sī. pī.). Evaṃ vutte sā brāhmaṇī taṃ māṇavakaṃ etadavoca – ‘āgamehi tāva, tāta, yāva vijāyāmi. Sace kumārako bhavissati, tassapi ekadeso bhavissati; sace kumārikā bhavissati, sāpi te opabhoggā upabhoggā (syā.) bhavissatī’ti. Dutiyampi kho so māṇavako mātusapattiṃ etadavoca – ‘yamidaṃ, bhoti, dhanaṃ vā dhaññaṃ vā rajataṃ vā jātarūpaṃ vā, sabbaṃ taṃ mayhaṃ; natthi tuyhettha kiñci. Pitu me, bhoti, dāyajjaṃ niyyādehī’ti. Dutiyampi kho sā brāhmaṇī taṃ māṇavakaṃ etadavoca – ‘āgamehi tāva, tāta, yāva vijāyāmi. Sace kumārako bhavissati, tassapi ekadeso bhavissati; sace kumārikā bhavissati sāpi te opabhoggā upabhoggā (syā.) bhavissatī’ti. Tatiyampi kho so māṇavako mātusapattiṃ etadavoca – ‘yamidaṃ, bhoti, dhanaṃ vā dhaññaṃ vā rajataṃ vā jātarūpaṃ [V 2.0247] vā[T 2.0369], sabbaṃ taṃ mayhaṃ; natthi tuyhettha kiñci. Pitu me, bhoti, dāyajjaṃ niyyādehī’ti.

420. “In that case, chieftain, I shall make a simile for you. For by means of a simile, some wise persons in this world understand the meaning of what is said. Once upon a time, chieftain, a certain brahmin had two wives. One had a son who was about ten or twelve years of age, while the other was pregnant and near to giving birth. Then that brahmin passed away. Thereupon, that young man said to his stepmother, ‘Whatever wealth, grain, silver, or gold there is, all of it is mine; you have nothing here. Madam, hand over my father’s inheritance.’ When this was said, that brahmin woman said to the young man, ‘Wait for now, dear, until I give birth. If it is a boy, he too will have a share. If it is a girl, she too will be your attendant.’ A second time, that young man said to his stepmother, ‘Whatever wealth, grain, silver, or gold there is, all of it is mine; you have nothing here. Madam, hand over my father’s inheritance.’ A second time, that brahmin woman said to the young man, ‘Wait for now, dear, until I give birth. If it is a boy, he too will have a share. If it is a girl, she too will be your attendant.’ A third time, that young man said to his stepmother, ‘Whatever wealth, grain, silver, or gold there is, all of it is mine; you have nothing here. Madam, hand over my father’s inheritance.’”

“Atha kho sā brāhmaṇī satthaṃ gahetvā ovarakaṃ pavisitvā udaraṃ opādesi uppātesi (syā.) – ‘yāva vijāyāmi yadi vā kumārako yadi vā kumārikā’ti. Sā attānaṃ ceva jīvitañca gabbhañca sāpateyyañca vināsesi. Yathā taṃ bālā abyattā anayabyasanaṃ āpannā ayoniso dāyajjaṃ gavesantī, evameva kho tvaṃ, rājañña, bālo abyatto anayabyasanaṃ āpajjissasi ayoniso paralokaṃ gavesanto[P 2.0332]; seyyathāpi sā brāhmaṇī bālā abyattā anayabyasanaṃ āpannā ayoniso dāyajjaṃ gavesantī. Na kho, rājañña, samaṇabrāhmaṇā sīlavanto kalyāṇadhammā apakkaṃ paripācenti; api ca paripākaṃ āgamenti. Paṇḍitānaṃ attho hi, rājañña, samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ sīlavantānaṃ kalyāṇadhammānaṃ jīvitena. Yathā yathā kho, rājañña, samaṇabrāhmaṇā sīlavanto kalyāṇadhammā ciraṃ dīghamaddhānaṃ tiṭṭhanti, tathā [M 2.0265] tathā bahuṃ puññaṃ pasavanti, bahujanahitāya ca paṭipajjanti bahujanasukhāya lokānukampāya atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ. Imināpi kho te, rājañña, pariyāyena evaṃ hotu – ‘itipi atthi paro loko, atthi sattā opapātikā, atthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’”ti.

“Then that brahmin woman took a knife, entered an inner chamber, and cut open her belly, thinking: ‘I will give birth now, whether it is a boy or a girl.’ She destroyed herself, her life, the fetus, and her property. Just as that foolish, unwise woman, seeking the inheritance improperly, met with calamity and disaster, so too, chieftain, you—foolish and unwise—will meet with calamity and disaster by seeking the other world improperly; just like that foolish, unwise brahmin woman who, seeking the inheritance improperly, met with calamity and disaster. Chieftain, virtuous ascetics and brahmins of good character do not force what is unripe to ripen; rather, they await its ripening. For, chieftain, the life of virtuous ascetics and brahmins of good character is a benefit to the wise. For the longer that virtuous ascetics and brahmins of good character remain for a long, long time, the more merit they generate, and they practice for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans. By this line of reasoning also, chieftain, let it be thus for you: ‘There is another world, there are spontaneously arisen beings, and there is the fruit and result of good and bad deeds.’”

421. “Kiñcāpi bhavaṃ kassapo evamāha, atha kho evaṃ me ettha hoti – ‘itipi natthi paro loko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’”ti. “Atthi pana, rājañña, pariyāyo…pe… atthi, bho kassapa, pariyāyo…pe… yathā kathaṃ viya, rājaññā”ti? “Idha me, bho kassapa, purisā coraṃ [T 2.0370] āgucāriṃ gahetvā dassenti – ‘ayaṃ te, bhante, coro āgucārī; imassa yaṃ icchasi, taṃ daṇḍaṃ paṇehī’ti. Tyāhaṃ evaṃ vadāmi – ‘tena hi, bho, imaṃ purisaṃ jīvantaṃyeva kumbhiyā pakkhipitvā mukhaṃ pidahitvā allena cammena onandhitvā allāya mattikāya bahalāvalepanaṃ bahalavilepanaṃ (syā. ka.) karitvā [P 2.0333] uddhanaṃ āropetvā aggiṃ dethā’ti. Te me ‘sādhū’ti paṭissutvā taṃ purisaṃ jīvantaṃyeva kumbhiyā pakkhipitvā mukhaṃ pidahitvā allena cammena onandhitvā allāya mattikāya bahalāvalepanaṃ karitvā uddhanaṃ āropetvā aggiṃ denti. Yadā mayaṃ jānāma ‘kālaṅkato so puriso’ti, atha naṃ kumbhiṃ oropetvā ubbhinditvā mukhaṃ vivaritvā saṇikaṃ nillokema vilokema (syā.) – ‘appeva nāmassa jīvaṃ nikkhamantaṃ passeyyāmā’ti. Nevassa mayaṃ jīvaṃ nikkhamantaṃ passāma. Ayampi kho, bho kassapa, pariyāyo, yena me pariyāyena evaṃ hoti – ‘itipi natthi paro loko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’”ti.

421. “Although the Venerable Kassapa says this, still it occurs to me thus: ‘For this reason, too, there is no other world, there are no spontaneously arisen beings, there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds.’ Is there, O chieftain, a reason...? There is, Venerable Kassapa, a reason... In what way, O chieftain? Here, Venerable Kassapa, my men seize a thief, a wrongdoer, and present him to me, saying: ‘Venerable sir, this is a thief, a wrongdoer; impose on him whatever punishment you wish.’ I then say to them: ‘In that case, sirs, put this man, while still alive, into a jar, close the mouth, bind it with a wet hide, smear it with a thick layer of wet clay, place it on a furnace, and light a fire.’ They, having replied, ‘Very well,’ put that man, while still alive, into a jar, close the mouth, bind it with a wet hide, smear it with a thick layer of wet clay, place it on a furnace, and light a fire. When we know that the man is dead, we take down the jar, break it open, uncover the mouth, and look carefully, thinking, ‘Perhaps we might see his life escaping.’ But we do not see his life escaping. This, Venerable Kassapa, is the reason by which it occurs to me thus: ‘For this reason, too, there is no other world, there are no spontaneously arisen beings, there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds.’”

Supinakaupamā

The Simile of the Dream

422. “Tena [V 2.0248] hi, rājañña, taññevettha paṭipucchissāmi, yathā te khameyya, tathā naṃ byākareyyāsi. Abhijānāsi no tvaṃ, rājañña, divā seyyaṃ upagato supinakaṃ passitā ārāmarāmaṇeyyakaṃ vanarāmaṇeyyakaṃ bhūmirāmaṇeyyakaṃ pokkharaṇīrāmaṇeyyaka”nti? “Abhijānāmahaṃ, bho kassapa, divāseyyaṃ upagato supinakaṃ passitā ārāmarāmaṇeyyakaṃ vanarāmaṇeyyakaṃ bhūmirāmaṇeyyakaṃ pokkharaṇīrāmaṇeyyaka”nti. “Rakkhanti taṃ [T 2.0371] tamhi samaye khujjāpi [M 2.0266] vāmanakāpi velāsikāpi celāvikāpi (syā.), keḷāyikāpi (sī.) komārikāpī”ti? “Evaṃ, bho kassapa, rakkhanti maṃ tamhi samaye khujjāpi vāmanakāpi velāsikāpi celāvikāpi (syā.), keḷāyikāpi (sī.) komārikāpī”ti. “Api nu tā tuyhaṃ jīvaṃ passanti pavisantaṃ vā nikkhamantaṃ vā”ti? “No [P 2.0334] hidaṃ, bho kassapa”. “Tā hi nāma, rājañña, tuyhaṃ jīvantassa jīvantiyo jīvaṃ na passissanti pavisantaṃ vā nikkhamantaṃ vā. Kiṃ pana tvaṃ kālaṅkatassa jīvaṃ passissasi pavisantaṃ vā nikkhamantaṃ vā. Imināpi kho te, rājañña, pariyāyena evaṃ hotu – “itipi atthi paro loko, atthi sattā opapātikā, atthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’”ti.

422. “In that case, O chieftain, I will question you in return on this very matter. As it pleases you, so you should answer. Do you recall, O chieftain, having gone to sleep during the day and seen in a dream a delightful park, a delightful forest, a delightful landscape, and a delightful lotus pond?” “I do recall, Venerable Kassapa, having gone to sleep during the day and seen in a dream a delightful park, a delightful forest, a delightful landscape, and a delightful lotus pond.” “At that time, were you being guarded by hunchbacked women, dwarfish women, sportive women, and young maidens?” “Yes, Venerable Kassapa, at that time I was being guarded by hunchbacked women, dwarfish women, sportive women, and young maidens.” “And did they see your life-principle entering or departing?” “Certainly not, Venerable Kassapa.” “Indeed, O chieftain, those living women do not see the life-principle of you, a living person, entering or departing. How then will you see the life-principle of a dead person entering or departing? By this reason also, O chieftain, let it be thus for you: ‘For this reason, too, there is another world, there are spontaneously arisen beings, there is the fruit and result of good and bad deeds.’”

423. “Kiñcāpi bhavaṃ kassapo evamāha, atha kho evaṃ me ettha hoti – ‘itipi natthi paro loko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’”ti. “Atthi pana, rājañña, pariyāyo…pe… “atthi, bho kassapa, pariyāyo…pe… yathā kathaṃ viya rājaññā”ti? “Idha me, bho kassapa, purisā coraṃ āgucāriṃ gahetvā dassenti – ‘ayaṃ te, bhante, coro āgucārī; imassa yaṃ icchasi, taṃ daṇḍaṃ paṇehī’ti. Tyāhaṃ evaṃ vadāmi – ‘tena hi, bho, imaṃ purisaṃ jīvantaṃyeva tulāya tuletvā jiyāya anassāsakaṃ māretvā punadeva tulāya tulethā’ti. Te me ‘sādhū’ti paṭissutvā taṃ purisaṃ jīvantaṃyeva tulāya tuletvā jiyāya anassāsakaṃ māretvā punadeva tulāya tulenti. Yadā so jīvati, tadā lahutaro ca hoti mudutaro [T 2.0372] ca kammaññataro ca. Yadā pana so kālaṅkato hoti tadā garutaro ca hoti patthinnataro ca akammaññataro ca. Ayampi kho, bho kassapa, pariyāyo, yena me pariyāyena evaṃ hoti – ‘itipi natthi paro loko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’”ti.

423. “Although the Venerable Kassapa says this, still it occurs to me thus: ‘For this reason, too, there is no other world, there are no spontaneously arisen beings, there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds.’ Is there, O chieftain, a reason...? There is, Venerable Kassapa, a reason... In what way, O chieftain? Here, Venerable Kassapa, my men seize a thief, a wrongdoer, and present him to me, saying: ‘Venerable sir, this is a thief, a wrongdoer; impose on him whatever punishment you wish.’ I say to them: ‘In that case, sirs, weigh this man on a scale while he is alive, kill him with a bowstring, making him breathless, and then weigh him again on the scale.’ They, having replied, ‘Very well,’ weigh the man on a scale while he is alive, kill him with a bowstring, making him breathless, and then weigh him again on the scale. When he is alive, he is lighter, softer, and more pliable. But when he is dead, he is heavier, stiffer, and less pliable. This too, Venerable Kassapa, is the reason by which it occurs to me: ‘For this reason, too, there is no other world, there are no spontaneously arisen beings, there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds.’”

Santattaayoguḷaupamā

The Simile of the Heated Iron Ball

424. “Tena [V 2.0249] hi, rājañña, upamaṃ te karissāmi. Upamāya midhekacce [P 2.0335] viññū purisā bhāsitassa atthaṃ ājānanti. Seyyathāpi, rājañña, puriso divasaṃ santattaṃ [M 2.0267] ayoguḷaṃ ādittaṃ sampajjalitaṃ sajotibhūtaṃ tulāya tuleyya. Tamenaṃ aparena samayena sītaṃ nibbutaṃ tulāya tuleyya. Kadā nu kho so ayoguḷo lahutaro vā hoti mudutaro vā kammaññataro vā, yadā vā āditto sampajjalito sajotibhūto, yadā vā sīto nibbuto”ti? “Yadā so, bho kassapa, ayoguḷo tejosahagato ca hoti vāyosahagato ca āditto sampajjalito sajotibhūto, tadā lahutaro ca hoti mudutaro ca kammaññataro ca. Yadā pana so ayoguḷo neva tejosahagato hoti na vāyosahagato sīto nibbuto, tadā garutaro ca hoti patthinnataro ca akammaññataro cā”ti. “Evameva kho, rājañña, yadāyaṃ kāyo āyusahagato ca hoti usmāsahagato ca viññāṇasahagato ca, tadā lahutaro ca hoti mudutaro ca kammaññataro ca. Yadā panāyaṃ kāyo neva āyusahagato hoti na usmāsahagato na viññāṇasahagato tadā [T 2.0373] garutaro ca hoti patthinnataro ca akammaññataro ca. Imināpi kho te, rājañña, pariyāyena evaṃ hotu – ‘itipi atthi paro loko, atthi sattā opapātikā, atthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’”ti.

424. “Well then, prince, I will give you a simile. For by means of a simile, some wise people here understand the meaning of what is said. Suppose, prince, a man were to weigh an iron ball, heated for a whole day, burning, blazing, and glowing, in a balance. Then at another time he were to weigh that same iron ball when it is cold and extinguished in the balance. Now, when is that iron ball lighter, softer, and more workable—when it is burning, blazing, and glowing, or when it is cold and extinguished?” “Master Kassapa, when that iron ball is accompanied by heat and air, burning, blazing, and glowing, then it is lighter, softer, and more workable. But when that iron ball is no longer accompanied by heat or air, when it is cold and extinguished, then it is heavier, stiffer, and less workable.” “Just so, prince, when this body is accompanied by life, heat, and consciousness, then it is lighter, softer, and more workable. But when this body is no longer accompanied by life, heat, or consciousness, then it is heavier, stiffer, and less workable. By this line of reasoning too, prince, let it be thus for you: ‘Indeed, there is another world, there are beings of spontaneous birth, there is fruit and result of good and bad deeds.’”

425. “Kiñcāpi bhavaṃ kassapo evamāha, atha kho evaṃ me ettha hoti – ‘itipi natthi paro loko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’”ti. “Atthi pana, rājañña, pariyāyo…pe… atthi, bho kassapa, pariyāyo…pe… yathā kathaṃ viya rājaññā”ti? “Idha me, bho kassapa, purisā coraṃ āgucāriṃ gahetvā dassenti – ‘ayaṃ te, bhante, coro āgucārī; imassa yaṃ icchasi[P 2.0336], taṃ daṇḍaṃ paṇehī’ti. Tyāhaṃ evaṃ vadāmi – ‘tena hi, bho, imaṃ purisaṃ anupahacca chaviñca cammañca maṃsañca nhāruñca aṭṭhiñca aṭṭhimiñjañca jīvitā voropetha, appeva nāmassa jīvaṃ nikkhamantaṃ passeyyāmā’ti. Te me ‘sādhū’ti paṭissutvā taṃ purisaṃ anupahacca chaviñca…pe… jīvitā voropenti. Yadā so āmato hoti, tyāhaṃ evaṃ vadāmi – ‘tena hi, bho, imaṃ purisaṃ uttānaṃ nipātetha, appeva nāmassa jīvaṃ nikkhamantaṃ passeyyāmā’ti. Te taṃ purisaṃ uttānaṃ nipātenti. Nevassa mayaṃ jīvaṃ nikkhamantaṃ passāma. Tyāhaṃ evaṃ vadāmi – ‘tena hi, bho, imaṃ purisaṃ avakujjaṃ nipātetha… passena nipātetha… dutiyena passena [T 2.0374][M 2.0268] nipātetha… uddhaṃ ṭhapetha… omuddhakaṃ ṭhapetha… pāṇinā ākoṭetha… leḍḍunā ākoṭetha… daṇḍena ākoṭetha… satthena ākoṭetha… odhunātha sandhunātha [V 2.0250] niddhunātha, appeva nāmassa jīvaṃ nikkhamantaṃ passeyyāmā’ti. Te taṃ purisaṃ odhunanti sandhunanti niddhunanti. Nevassa mayaṃ jīvaṃ nikkhamantaṃ passāma. Tassa tadeva cakkhu hoti te rūpā, tañcāyatanaṃ nappaṭisaṃvedeti. Tadeva sotaṃ hoti te saddā, tañcāyatanaṃ nappaṭisaṃvedeti. Tadeva ghānaṃ hoti te gandhā, tañcāyatanaṃ nappaṭisaṃvedeti[P 2.0337]. Sāva jivhā hoti te rasā, tañcāyatanaṃ nappaṭisaṃvedeti. Sveva kāyo hoti te phoṭṭhabbā, tañcāyatanaṃ nappaṭisaṃvedeti. Ayampi kho, bho kassapa, pariyāyo, yena me pariyāyena evaṃ hoti – ‘itipi natthi paro loko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’”ti.

425. “Even though Master Kassapa says this, still it occurs to me thus: ‘Indeed, there is no other world, there are no beings of spontaneous birth, there is no fruit and result of good and bad deeds.’” “But is there, prince, a line of reasoning by which it occurs to you thus?” “There is, Master Kassapa.” “In what way, prince?” “Here, Master Kassapa, my men bring me a thief, a wrongdoer, and present him to me, saying: ‘Sir, this is a thief, a wrongdoer. Impose on him whatever punishment you wish.’ I say to them: ‘Well then, sirs, without harming his skin, hide, flesh, sinews, bones, or marrow, deprive him of life; perhaps we might see his life departing.’ They agree, and without harming his skin, hide, flesh, sinews, bones, or marrow, they deprive the man of life. When he is half-dead, I say: ‘Now, sirs, lay this man on his back; perhaps we might see his life departing.’ They lay the man on his back. We do not see his life departing. I say: ‘Now, sirs, lay this man face down… on his side… on the other side… stand him upright… stand him upside down… strike him with your hand… strike him with a clod… strike him with a stick… strike him with a sword… shake him, shake him about, shake him thoroughly; perhaps we might see his life departing.’ They shake him, shake him about, and shake him thoroughly. We do not see his life departing. His eye is the same and those forms are the same, but he does not experience that sense-base. His ear is the same and those sounds are the same, but he does not experience that sense-base. His nose is the same and those smells are the same, but he does not experience that sense-base. His tongue is the same and those tastes are the same, but he does not experience that sense-base. His body is the same and those tangible objects are the same, but he does not experience that sense-base. This too, Master Kassapa, is the line of reasoning by which it occurs to me: ‘Indeed, there is no other world, there are no beings of spontaneous birth, there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds.’”

Saṅkhadhamaupamā

The Simile of the Conch-Blower

426. “Tena hi, rājañña, upamaṃ te karissāmi. Upamāya midhekacce viññū purisā bhāsitassa atthaṃ ājānanti. Bhūtapubbaṃ, rājañña, aññataro saṅkhadhamo saṅkhaṃ ādāya paccantimaṃ janapadaṃ agamāsi. So yena aññataro gāmo tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā majjhe gāmassa ṭhito tikkhattuṃ saṅkhaṃ upalāpetvā saṅkhaṃ bhūmiyaṃ nikkhipitvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Atha kho, rājañña, tesaṃ paccantajanapadānaṃ paccantajānaṃ (sī.) manussānaṃ etadahosi [T 2.0375] – ‘ambho kassa nu kho etadahosi “kissa dukho (pī.) eso saddo evaṃrajanīyo evaṃkamanīyo evaṃmadanīyo evaṃbandhanīyo evaṃmucchanīyo’ti. Sannipatitvā taṃ saṅkhadhamaṃ etadavocuṃ – ‘ambho, kassa nu kho eso saddo evaṃrajanīyo evaṃkamanīyo evaṃmadanīyo evaṃbandhanīyo evaṃmucchanīyo’ti. ‘Eso kho, bho, saṅkho nāma yasseso saddo evaṃrajanīyo evaṃkamanīyo evaṃmadanīyo evaṃbandhanīyo evaṃmucchanīyo’ti. Te taṃ saṅkhaṃ uttānaṃ nipātesuṃ – ‘vadehi, bho saṅkha, vadehi, bho saṅkhā’ti. Neva so saṅkho saddamakāsi. Te taṃ saṅkhaṃ avakujjaṃ nipātesuṃ, passena nipātesuṃ, dutiyena passena nipātesuṃ, uddhaṃ ṭhapesuṃ, omuddhakaṃ ṭhapesuṃ, pāṇinā [P 2.0338] ākoṭesuṃ, leḍḍunā ākoṭesuṃ, daṇḍena ākoṭesuṃ, satthena ākoṭesuṃ, odhuniṃsu [M 2.0269] sandhuniṃsu niddhuniṃsu – ‘vadehi, bho saṅkha, vadehi, bho saṅkhā’ti. Neva so saṅkho saddamakāsi.

426. “Well then, chieftain, I will make a simile for you. For by means of a simile, some wise people here understand the meaning of what is said. Once upon a time, chieftain, a certain conch-blower took a conch and went to a border region. He approached a certain village; and having approached, standing in the middle of the village, he blew the conch three times, then placed the conch on the ground and sat to one side. Then, chieftain, this thought occurred to those people of the border region: ‘Sirs, whose sound is this, so alluring, so pleasing, so intoxicating, so binding, so infatuating?’ Having gathered together, they said this to the conch-blower: ‘Sir, whose sound is this, so alluring, so pleasing, so intoxicating, so binding, so infatuating?’ ‘Sirs, this is what is called a conch, whose sound is so alluring, so pleasing, so intoxicating, so binding, so infatuating.’ They laid that conch on its back, saying: ‘Speak, good conch, speak, good conch!’ But that conch made no sound. They laid the conch face down, laid it on its side, laid it on its other side, stood it upright, stood it upside down, struck it with their hands, struck it with a clod of earth, struck it with a stick, struck it with a weapon; they shook it towards themselves, shook it away, and shook it back and forth, saying: ‘Speak, good conch, speak, good conch!’ But that conch made no sound.”

“Atha kho, rājañña, tassa saṅkhadhamassa etadahosi – ‘yāva bālā ime paccantajanapadāmanussā, kathañhi nāma ayoniso saṅkhasaddaṃ gavesissantī’ti. Tesaṃ pekkhamānānaṃ saṅkhaṃ gahetvā tikkhattuṃ saṅkhaṃ upalāpetvā saṅkhaṃ ādāya pakkāmi. Atha kho, rājañña, tesaṃ paccantajanapadānaṃ manussānaṃ etadahosi – ‘yadā kira, bho, ayaṃ saṅkho nāma purisasahagato [V 2.0251] ca hoti vāyāmasahagato vāyosahagato (syā.) ca vāyusahagato ca, tadāyaṃ saṅkho saddaṃ karoti, yadā panāyaṃ saṅkho neva purisasahagato hoti na vāyāmasahagato na vāyusahagato, nāyaṃ saṅkho saddaṃ karotī’ti[T 2.0376]. Evameva kho, rājañña, yadāyaṃ kāyo āyusahagato ca hoti usmāsahagato ca viññāṇasahagato ca, tadā abhikkamatipi paṭikkamatipi tiṭṭhatipi nisīdatipi seyyampi kappeti, cakkhunāpi rūpaṃ passati, sotenapi saddaṃ suṇāti, ghānenapi gandhaṃ ghāyati, jivhāyapi rasaṃ sāyati, kāyenapi phoṭṭhabbaṃ phusati, manasāpi dhammaṃ vijānāti. Yadā panāyaṃ kāyo neva āyusahagato hoti, na usmāsahagato, na viññāṇasahagato, tadā neva abhikkamati na paṭikkamati na tiṭṭhati na nisīdati na seyyaṃ kappeti, cakkhunāpi rūpaṃ na passati, sotenapi saddaṃ na suṇāti, ghānenapi gandhaṃ na ghāyati, jivhāyapi rasaṃ na sāyati, kāyenapi phoṭṭhabbaṃ na phusati, manasāpi dhammaṃ na vijānāti. Imināpi kho te, rājañña, pariyāyena evaṃ hotu – ‘itipi atthi paro loko, atthi sattā opapātikā, atthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’ti vipākoti, paṭhamabhāṇavāraṃ (syā.).

“Then, chieftain, this thought occurred to that conch-blower: ‘How very foolish are these people of the borderlands, that they should search for the sound of the conch so improperly!’ While they were watching, he took the conch, blew it three times, and then, taking the conch, he departed. Then, chieftain, this thought occurred to those people of the borderlands: ‘Sirs, it seems that when this thing called a conch is accompanied by a person, accompanied by effort, and accompanied by wind, then this conch makes a sound. But when this conch is not accompanied by a person, not accompanied by effort, and not accompanied by wind, then this conch does not make a sound.’ In the same way, chieftain, when this body is accompanied by life, accompanied by heat, and accompanied by consciousness, then it goes forward, goes back, stands, sits, and lies down; it sees forms with the eye, hears sounds with the ear, smells odors with the nose, tastes flavors with the tongue, feels tangibles with the body, and cognizes mental phenomena with the mind. But when this body is not accompanied by life, not accompanied by heat, and not accompanied by consciousness, then it does not go forward, does not go back, does not stand, does not sit, and does not lie down; it does not see forms with the eye, does not hear sounds with the ear, does not smell odors with the nose, does not taste flavors with the tongue, does not feel tangibles with the body, and does not cognize mental phenomena with the mind. By this line of reasoning too, chieftain, let it be so for you: ‘Thus, there is another world, there are beings who are spontaneously reborn, there is the fruit and result of good and bad actions.’”

427. “Kiñcāpi bhavaṃ kassapo evamāha, atha kho evaṃ [P 2.0339] me ettha hoti – ‘itipi natthi paro loko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’”ti. “Atthi pana, rājañña, pariyāyo…pe… atthi, bho kassapa, pariyāyo…pe… yathā kathaṃ viya rājaññā”ti? “Idha me, bho kassapa, purisā coraṃ āgucāriṃ gahetvā dassenti – ‘ayaṃ te, bhante, coro āgucārī, imassa yaṃ icchasi, taṃ [T 2.0377] daṇḍaṃ paṇehī’ti. Tyāhaṃ evaṃ vadāmi – ‘tena hi, bho, imassa purisassa chaviṃ chindatha[M 2.0270], appeva nāmassa jīvaṃ passeyyāmā’ti. Te tassa purisassa chaviṃ chindanti. Nevassa mayaṃ jīvaṃ passāma. Tyāhaṃ evaṃ vadāmi – ‘tena hi, bho, imassa purisassa cammaṃ chindatha, maṃsaṃ chindatha, nhāruṃ chindatha, aṭṭhiṃ chindatha, aṭṭhimiñjaṃ chindatha, appeva nāmassa jīvaṃ passeyyāmā’ti. Te tassa purisassa aṭṭhimiñjaṃ chindanti, nevassa mayaṃ jīvaṃ passeyyāma. Ayampi kho, bho kassapa, pariyāyo, yena me pariyāyena evaṃ hoti – ‘itipi natthi paro loko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’”ti.

427. “Although the venerable Kassapa speaks thus, still, this is my view on the matter: ‘Thus, there is no other world, there are no beings who are spontaneously reborn, there is no fruit or result of good and bad actions.’” “But is there, chieftain, a line of reasoning…?” … “There is, venerable Kassapa, a line of reasoning…” … “And what might that line of reasoning be, chieftain?” “Here, venerable Kassapa, my men seize a thief, a wrongdoer, and present him to me, saying: ‘Lord, this is a thief, a wrongdoer. Inflict upon him whatever punishment you wish.’ I say to them: ‘Well then, sirs, cut this man’s outer skin; perhaps we might see his life.’ They cut that man’s outer skin, but we do not see his life. I say to them: ‘Well then, sirs, cut this man’s hide, cut his flesh, cut his sinews, cut his bones, cut his bone marrow; perhaps we might see his life.’ They cut his bone marrow, but we do not see his life. This too, venerable Kassapa, is the line of reasoning, the reason by which my view is thus: ‘Thus, there is no other world, there are no beings who are spontaneously reborn, there is no fruit or result of good and bad actions.’”

Aggikajaṭilaupamā

The Simile of the Fire-Worshipping Matted-Hair Ascetic

428. “Tena hi, rājañña, upamaṃ te karissāmi. Upamāya midhekacce viññū purisā bhāsitassa atthaṃ ājānanti. Bhūtapubbaṃ, rājañña, aññataro aggiko jaṭilo araññāyatane [V 2.0252] paṇṇakuṭiyā sammati vasati (sī. pī.). Atha kho, rājañña, aññataro janapade sattho sattho janapadapadesā (sī.), janapado satthavāso (syā.), janapadapadeso (pī.) vuṭṭhāsi. Atha kho so sattho satthavāso (syā.) tassa aggikassa jaṭilassa assamassa sāmantā ekarattiṃ vasitvā pakkāmi. Atha kho, rājañña, tassa aggikassa jaṭilassa etadahosi [P 2.0340] – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ yena so satthavāso tenupasaṅkameyyaṃ, appeva nāmettha kiñci upakaraṇaṃ adhigaccheyya’nti. Atha kho so aggiko jaṭilo kālasseva vuṭṭhāya yena so satthavāso tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā addasa tasmiṃ satthavāse daharaṃ kumāraṃ mandaṃ [T 2.0378] uttānaseyyakaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ. Disvānassa etadahosi – ‘na kho me taṃ patirūpaṃ yaṃ me pekkhamānassa manussabhūto kālaṅkareyya; yaṃnūnāhaṃ imaṃ dārakaṃ assamaṃ netvā āpādeyyaṃ poseyyaṃ vaḍḍheyya’nti. Atha kho so aggiko jaṭilo taṃ dārakaṃ assamaṃ netvā āpādesi posesi vaḍḍhesi. Yadā so dārako dasavassuddesiko vā hoti ahosi (?) dvādasavassuddesiko vā, atha kho tassa aggikassa jaṭilassa janapade kañcideva karaṇīyaṃ uppajji. Atha kho so aggiko jaṭilo taṃ dārakaṃ etadavoca – ‘icchāmahaṃ, tāta, janapadaṃ nagaraṃ (ka.) gantuṃ; aggiṃ, tāta, paricareyyāsi. Mā ca te aggi nibbāyi. Sace ca te aggi nibbāyeyya, ayaṃ vāsī imāni kaṭṭhāni idaṃ araṇisahitaṃ, aggiṃ nibbattetvā aggiṃ [M 2.0271] paricareyyāsī’ti. Atha kho so aggiko jaṭilo taṃ dārakaṃ evaṃ anusāsitvā janapadaṃ agamāsi. Tassa khiḍḍāpasutassa aggi nibbāyi.

428. “Well then, Rājañña, I shall give you a simile. For by means of a simile some wise people here understand the meaning of what is said. Once upon a time, Rājañña, a certain fire-tending ascetic lived in a leaf hut in a forest dwelling. Then, Rājañña, a caravan encamped in a certain district. That caravan stayed near the hermitage of that fire-tending ascetic for one night and then departed. Then, Rājañña, that fire-tending ascetic thought: ‘What if I were to go to where that caravan encamped? Perhaps I might find something useful there.’ So that fire-tending ascetic rose early and went to where the caravan had encamped. Upon arriving, he saw in that caravan site a young boy, weak, lying on his back, abandoned. Seeing him, he thought: ‘It would not be proper for a human being to die while I am looking on. What if I were to take this child to my hermitage and raise him, nourish him, and bring him up?’ So that fire-tending ascetic took the child to his hermitage and raised him, nourished him, and brought him up. When the boy was about ten or twelve years old, some business arose for the fire-tending ascetic in the district. So he said to the boy: ‘I wish, dear, to go to the district. You, dear, should tend the fire. Do not let your fire go out. If your fire does go out, here is an adze, here is the firewood, and here is the fire-drill set. You should produce fire and tend it.’ Having thus instructed the boy, the fire-tending ascetic went to the district. While the boy was absorbed in play, the fire went out.”

“Atha kho tassa dārakassa etadahosi – ‘pitā kho maṃ evaṃ avaca – “aggiṃ, tāta, paricareyyāsi. Mā ca te aggi nibbāyi. Sace ca te aggi nibbāyeyya, ayaṃ vāsī imāni kaṭṭhāni idaṃ araṇisahitaṃ, aggiṃ nibbattetvā aggiṃ paricareyyāsī”ti. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ aggiṃ nibbattetvā aggiṃ paricareyya’nti. Atha [P 2.0341] kho so dārako araṇisahitaṃ vāsiyā tacchi – ‘appeva nāma aggiṃ adhigaccheyya’nti. Neva so aggiṃ adhigacchi. Araṇisahitaṃ dvidhā phālesi, tidhā phālesi, catudhā phālesi, pañcadhā phālesi, dasadhā phālesi, satadhā vīsatidhā (syā.) phālesi, sakalikaṃ sakalikaṃ akāsi, sakalikaṃ sakalikaṃ karitvā udukkhale koṭṭesi, udukkhale koṭṭetvā mahāvāte opuni ophuni (syā. ka.) – ‘appeva nāma aggiṃ adhigaccheyya’nti. Neva so aggiṃ adhigacchi.

“Then the boy thought: ‘My father told me: “You, dear, should tend the fire. Do not let your fire go out. If your fire does go out, here is an adze, here is the firewood, and here is the fire-drill set. You should produce fire and tend it.” What if I were to produce fire and tend it?’ So the boy chipped at the fire-drill set with the adze, thinking: ‘Perhaps I might get fire.’ But he did not get fire. He split the fire-drill set into two pieces, three pieces, four pieces, five pieces, ten pieces, a hundred pieces; he reduced it to fragments; having reduced it to fragments, he pounded it in a mortar; and having pounded it, he winnowed it in a strong wind, thinking: ‘Perhaps I might get fire.’ But he did not get fire.”

“Atha kho so aggiko jaṭilo janapade taṃ karaṇīyaṃ tīretvā yena sako assamo tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā taṃ dārakaṃ etadavoca – ‘kacci te, tāta, aggi na nibbuto’ti? ‘Idha me, tāta, khiḍḍāpasutassa aggi nibbāyi. Tassa me etadahosi – “pitā kho maṃ evaṃ avaca aggiṃ, tāta, paricareyyāsi. Mā ca te, tāta, aggi nibbāyi. Sace [V 2.0253] ca te aggi nibbāyeyya, ayaṃ vāsī imāni kaṭṭhāni idaṃ araṇisahitaṃ, aggiṃ nibbattetvā aggiṃ paricareyyāsīti. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ aggiṃ nibbattetvā aggiṃ paricareyya”nti. Atha khvāhaṃ, tāta, araṇisahitaṃ vāsiyā tacchiṃ – “appeva nāma aggiṃ adhigaccheyya”nti. Nevāhaṃ aggiṃ adhigacchiṃ. Araṇisahitaṃ dvidhā phālesiṃ, tidhā phālesiṃ, catudhā phālesiṃ, pañcadhā phālesiṃ, dasadhā phālesiṃ[T 2.0379], satadhā phālesiṃ, sakalikaṃ sakalikaṃ akāsiṃ, sakalikaṃ sakalikaṃ karitvā udukkhale koṭṭesiṃ, udukkhale koṭṭetvā mahāvāte opuniṃ – “appeva nāma aggiṃ adhigaccheyya”nti. Nevāhaṃ aggiṃ adhigacchi’”nti. Atha kho tassa aggikassa jaṭilassa etadahosi – ‘yāva bālo ayaṃ dārako abyatto, kathañhi nāma ayoniso aggiṃ gavesissatī’ti. Tassa pekkhamānassa araṇisahitaṃ gahetvā [T 2.0380] aggiṃ nibbattetvā taṃ dārakaṃ etadavoca [M 2.0272] – ‘evaṃ kho, tāta, aggi [P 2.0342] nibbattetabbo. Na tveva yathā tvaṃ bālo abyatto ayoniso aggiṃ gavesī’ti. Evameva kho tvaṃ, rājañña, bālo abyatto ayoniso paralokaṃ gavesissasi. Paṭinissajjetaṃ, rājañña, pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ, paṭinissajjetaṃ, rājañña, pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ, mā te ahosi dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāyā”ti.

“Then that fire-tending ascetic, having completed that business in the district, approached his own hermitage. Upon arriving, he said to the boy: ‘I hope, dear, your fire has not gone out?’ ‘Here, father, while I was absorbed in play, the fire went out. Then I thought: “My father told me: ‘Dear, tend the fire. Do not let your fire go out. If your fire goes out, here is an adze, here is the firewood, and here is the fire-drill set. You should produce fire and tend it.’ What if I were to produce fire and tend it?” So, father, I chipped at the fire-drill set with the adze, thinking, “Perhaps I’ll get fire.” But I did not get fire. I split the fire-drill set into two, three, four, five, ten, a hundred pieces; I reduced it to fragments; having reduced it to fragments, I pounded it in a mortar; and having pounded it, I winnowed it in a strong wind, thinking, “Perhaps I’ll get fire.” But I did not get fire.’ Then the fire-tending ascetic thought: ‘How foolish and unskilled this boy is! How could he possibly seek fire improperly?’ As the boy watched, he took the fire-drill set, produced a fire, and said to the boy: ‘This, dear, is how fire is to be produced. Not as you, being foolish and unskilled, improperly sought fire.’ In the same way, Rājañña, you are foolish and unskilled, improperly seeking the next world. Relinquish this evil view, Rājañña. Relinquish this evil view, lest it be for your harm and suffering for a long time.”

429. “Kiñcāpi bhavaṃ kassapo evamāha, atha kho nevāhaṃ sakkomi idaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ paṭinissajjituṃ. Rājāpi maṃ pasenadi kosalo jānāti tirorājānopi – ‘pāyāsi rājañño evaṃvādī evaṃdiṭṭhī – “itipi natthi paro loko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko”ti. Sacāhaṃ, bho kassapa, idaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ paṭinissajjissāmi, bhavissanti me vattāro – ‘yāva bālo pāyāsi rājañño abyatto duggahitagāhī’ti. Kopenapi naṃ harissāmi, makkhenapi naṃ harissāmi, palāsenapi naṃ harissāmī”ti.

429. “Although the Venerable Kassapa speaks thus, I am nevertheless unable to relinquish this evil view. King Pasenadi of Kosala knows me, and so do kings in other countries, thinking: ‘Prince Pāyāsi is one who speaks thus and holds such a view: “There is no other world, there are no spontaneously reborn beings, there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds.”’ If I, Venerable Kassapa, were to relinquish this evil view, there would be those who would say of me: ‘How foolish is Prince Pāyāsi, how unskilled, a holder of a wrongly grasped view.’ I will persist in it out of anger, I will persist in it out of disparagement, and I will persist in it out of rivalry.”

Dve satthavāhaupamā

The Simile of the Two Caravan Leaders

430. “Tena hi, rājañña, upamaṃ te karissāmi. Upamāya midhekacce viññū purisā bhāsitassa atthaṃ ājānanti. Bhūtapubbaṃ, rājañña, mahāsakaṭasattho sakaṭasahassaṃ puratthimā janapadā pacchimaṃ janapadaṃ agamāsi. So yena yena gacchi, khippaṃyeva pariyādiyati tiṇakaṭṭhodakaṃ haritakapaṇṇaṃ. Tasmiṃ kho pana satthe dve satthavāhā ahesuṃ eko [T 2.0381] pañcannaṃ [P 2.0343] sakaṭasatānaṃ, eko pañcannaṃ sakaṭasatānaṃ. Atha kho tesaṃ satthavāhānaṃ etadahosi – ‘ayaṃ kho mahāsakaṭasattho sakaṭasahassaṃ; te mayaṃ yena yena gacchāma, khippameva pariyādiyati tiṇakaṭṭhodakaṃ [V 2.0254] haritakapaṇṇaṃ. Yaṃnūna mayaṃ imaṃ satthaṃ dvidhā vibhajeyyāma – ekato pañca sakaṭasatāni ekato pañca sakaṭasatānī’ti. Te taṃ satthaṃ dvidhā vibhajiṃsu vibhajesuṃ (ka.) ekato pañca sakaṭasatāni, ekato pañca sakaṭasatāni. Eko satthavāho bahuṃ tiṇañca kaṭṭhañca udakañca āropetvā satthaṃ payāpesi pāyāpesi (sī. pī.). Dvīhatīhapayāto kho pana so sattho addasa purisaṃ kāḷaṃ lohitakkhaṃ lohitakkhiṃ (syā.) sannaddhakalāpaṃ āsannaddhakalāpaṃ (syā.) kumudamāliṃ allavatthaṃ allakesaṃ kaddamamakkhitehi cakkehi [M 2.0273] bhadrena rathena paṭipathaṃ āgacchantaṃ’, disvā etadavoca – ‘kuto, bho, āgacchasī’ti? ‘Amukamhā janapadā’ti. ‘Kuhiṃ gamissasī’ti? ‘Amukaṃ nāma janapada’nti. ‘Kacci, bho, purato kantāre mahāmegho abhippavuṭṭho’ti? ‘Evaṃ, bho, purato kantāre mahāmegho abhippavuṭṭho, āsittodakāni vaṭumāni, bahu tiṇañca kaṭṭhañca [P 2.0344] udakañca. Chaḍḍetha, bho, purāṇāni tiṇāni kaṭṭhāni udakāni, lahubhārehi sakaṭehi sīghaṃ sīghaṃ gacchatha, mā yoggāni kilamitthā’ti.

430. “Well then, Prince, I will make a simile for you. For by means of a simile, some wise men here understand the meaning of what is said. Once, Prince, a great caravan of a thousand carts went from an eastern country to a western country. Wherever it went, it quickly exhausted the grass, firewood, water, and green foliage. In that caravan, there were two caravan leaders: one for five hundred carts, and one for five hundred carts. Then it occurred to those caravan leaders: ‘This great caravan has a thousand carts; wherever we go, the grass, firewood, water, and green foliage are quickly exhausted. What if we were to divide this caravan in two: five hundred carts in one group and five hundred carts in another?’ So they divided that caravan in two: five hundred carts in one group, and five hundred carts in another. One caravan leader, having loaded up much grass, firewood, and water, set the caravan in motion. After traveling for two or three days, that caravan saw a man—dark, with red eyes, with an unslung quiver, wearing a water-lily garland, with wet clothes and wet hair—approaching on the opposite path in a fine chariot with mud-smeared wheels. Seeing him, he said this: ‘Sir, from where do you come?’ ‘From such-and-such a country.’ ‘Where will you go?’ ‘To such-and-such a country.’ ‘Sir, has a great cloud rained heavily in the wilderness ahead?’ ‘Yes, sir, a great cloud has rained heavily in the wilderness ahead. The paths are sprinkled with water, and there is much grass, firewood, and water. Discard, sirs, your old grass, firewood, and water. Travel swiftly with lightly-loaded carts. Do not tire out your draft animals.’”

“Atha kho so satthavāho satthike āmantesi – ‘ayaṃ, bho, puriso evamāha – “purato kantāre mahāmegho abhippavuṭṭho, āsittodakāni vaṭumāni, bahu tiṇañca kaṭṭhañca udakañca. Chaḍḍetha, bho, purāṇāni tiṇāni kaṭṭhāni udakāni, lahubhārehi sakaṭehi sīghaṃ sīghaṃ gacchatha, mā [T 2.0382] yoggāni kilamitthā”ti. Chaḍḍetha, bho, purāṇāni tiṇāni kaṭṭhāni udakāni, lahubhārehi sakaṭehi satthaṃ payāpethā’ti. ‘Evaṃ, bho’ti kho te satthikā tassa satthavāhassa paṭissutvā chaḍḍetvā purāṇāni tiṇāni kaṭṭhāni udakāni lahubhārehi sakaṭehi satthaṃ payāpesuṃ. Te paṭhamepi satthavāse na addasaṃsu tiṇaṃ vā kaṭṭhaṃ vā udakaṃ vā. Dutiyepi satthavāse… tatiyepi satthavāse… catutthepi satthavāse… pañcamepi satthavāse… chaṭṭhepi satthavāse… sattamepi satthavāse na addasaṃsu tiṇaṃ vā kaṭṭhaṃ vā udakaṃ vā. Sabbeva anayabyasanaṃ āpajjiṃsu. Ye ca tasmiṃ satthe ahesuṃ manussā vā pasū vā, sabbe so yakkho amanusso bhakkhesi. Aṭṭhikāneva sesāni.

“Then that caravan leader addressed the caravan-men: ‘Sirs, this man says this: “A great cloud has rained heavily in the wilderness ahead. The paths are sprinkled with water, and there is much grass, firewood, and water. Discard, sirs, your old grass, firewood, and water. Travel swiftly with lightly-loaded carts. Do not tire out your draft animals.” Discard, sirs, your old grass, firewood, and water, and set the caravan in motion with lightly-loaded carts.’ ‘Yes, sir,’ those caravan-men replied to the caravan leader, and having discarded the old grass, firewood, and water, they set the caravan in motion with lightly-loaded carts. At the first encampment, they did not see any grass, firewood, or water. At the second encampment… at the third encampment… at the fourth encampment… at the fifth encampment… at the sixth encampment… at the seventh encampment, they did not see any grass, firewood, or water. They all met with ruin and disaster. Whatever humans or beasts were in that caravan, that non-human yakkha devoured them all. Only bones remained.”

“Yadā aññāsi dutiyo satthavāho – ‘bahunikkhanto kho, bho, dāni so sattho’ti bahuṃ tiṇañca kaṭṭhañca udakañca āropetvā satthaṃ payāpesi. Dvīhatīhapayāto kho pana so sattho addasa purisaṃ kāḷaṃ lohitakkhaṃ sannaddhakalāpaṃ [P 2.0345] kumudamāliṃ allavatthaṃ allakesaṃ kaddamamakkhitehi cakkehi bhadrena rathena paṭipathaṃ āgacchantaṃ, disvā etadavoca – ‘kuto, bho, āgacchasī’ti? ‘Amukamhā janapadā’ti. ‘Kuhiṃ gamissasī’ti? ‘Amukaṃ nāma janapada’nti. ‘Kacci, bho, purato kantāre mahāmegho abhippavuṭṭho’ti? ‘Evaṃ, bho, purato kantāre mahāmegho abhippavuṭṭho. Āsittodakāni vaṭumāni, bahu [T 2.0383] tiṇañca kaṭṭhañca udakañca. Chaḍḍetha[M 2.0274][V 2.0255], bho, purāṇāni tiṇāni kaṭṭhāni udakāni, lahubhārehi sakaṭehi sīghaṃ sīghaṃ gacchatha, mā yoggāni kilamitthā’ti.

“When the second caravan leader knew, ‘That caravan has now been gone for a long time,’ he, having loaded up much grass, firewood, and water, set the caravan in motion. After traveling for two or three days, that caravan saw a man—dark, with red eyes, with an unslung quiver, wearing a water-lily garland, with wet clothes and wet hair—approaching on the opposite path in a fine chariot with mud-smeared wheels. Seeing him, he said this: ‘Sir, from where do you come?’ ‘From such-and-such a country.’ ‘Where will you go?’ ‘To such-and-such a country.’ ‘Sir, has a great cloud rained heavily in the wilderness ahead?’ ‘Yes, sir, a great cloud has rained heavily in the wilderness ahead. The paths are sprinkled with water, and there is much grass, firewood, and water. Discard, sirs, your old grass, firewood, and water. Travel swiftly with lightly-loaded carts. Do not tire out your draft animals.’”

“Atha kho so satthavāho satthike āmantesi – ‘ayaṃ, bho, “puriso evamāha – purato kantāre mahāmegho abhippavuṭṭho, āsittodakāni vaṭumāni, bahu tiṇañca kaṭṭhañca udakañca. Chaḍḍetha, bho, purāṇāni tiṇāni kaṭṭhāni udakāni, lahubhārehi sakaṭehi sīghaṃ sīghaṃ gacchatha; mā yoggāni kilamitthā”ti. Ayaṃ bho puriso neva amhākaṃ mitto, na ñātisālohito, kathaṃ mayaṃ imassa saddhāya gamissāma. Na vo chaḍḍetabbāni purāṇāni tiṇāni kaṭṭhāni udakāni, yathābhatena bhaṇḍena satthaṃ payāpetha. Na no purāṇaṃ chaḍḍessāmā’ti. ‘Evaṃ, bho’ti kho te satthikā tassa satthavāhassa paṭissutvā yathābhatena bhaṇḍena satthaṃ payāpesuṃ. Te paṭhamepi satthavāse na addasaṃsu tiṇaṃ vā kaṭṭhaṃ [P 2.0346] vā udakaṃ vā. Dutiyepi satthavāse… tatiyepi satthavāse… catutthepi satthavāse… pañcamepi satthavāse… chaṭṭhepi satthavāse… sattamepi satthavāse na addasaṃsu tiṇaṃ vā kaṭṭhaṃ vā udakaṃ vā. Tañca satthaṃ addasaṃsu anayabyasanaṃ āpannaṃ. Ye ca tasmiṃ satthepi ahesuṃ manussā vā pasū vā, tesañca aṭṭhikāneva addasaṃsu tena yakkhena amanussena bhakkhitānaṃ.

Then that caravan leader addressed the caravaneers: ‘Sirs, this man says: “Ahead in the wilderness, a great cloud has rained heavily. The roads and tracks are filled with water, and there is abundant grass, firewood, and water. Discard, sirs, the old grass, firewood, and water. Travel very quickly with lightly loaded carts; do not let your draft oxen become weary.” But this man, sirs, is neither our friend nor a blood relative. How can we proceed by trusting his word? You must not discard the old grass, firewood, and water. Let the caravan proceed with the goods as they were loaded. We will not discard our old supplies.’ ‘Yes, sir,’ replied those caravaneers to that caravan leader, and they had the caravan proceed with the goods as they were loaded. At the first encampment, they saw no grass, firewood, or water. At the second encampment… at the third encampment… at the fourth encampment… at the fifth encampment… at the sixth encampment… at the seventh encampment, they saw no grass, firewood, or water. And they saw that that caravan had met with ruin and disaster. And of the humans and animals that were in that caravan, they saw only their bones, having been devoured by that non-human yakkha.

“Atha kho so satthavāho satthike āmantesi – ‘ayaṃ kho, bho, sattho anayabyasanaṃ āpanno, yathā taṃ tena bālena [T 2.0384] satthavāhena pariṇāyakena. Tena hi, bho, yānamhākaṃ satthe appasārāni paṇiyāni, tāni chaḍḍetvā, yāni imasmiṃ satthe mahāsārāni paṇiyāni, tāni ādiyathā’ti. ‘Evaṃ, bho’ti kho te satthikā tassa satthavāhassa paṭissutvā yāni sakasmiṃ satthe appasārāni paṇiyāni, tāni chaḍḍetvā yāni tasmiṃ satthe mahāsārāni paṇiyāni, tāni ādiyitvā sotthinā taṃ kantāraṃ nitthariṃsu, yathā taṃ paṇḍitena satthavāhena pariṇāyakena. Evameva kho tvaṃ, rājañña, bālo abyatto anayabyasanaṃ āpajjissasi ayoniso paralokaṃ gavesanto seyyathāpi so purimo satthavāho. Yepi tava te (ka.) sotabbaṃ saddhātabbaṃ saddahātabbaṃ (pī. ka.) maññissanti, tepi anayabyasanaṃ āpajjissanti, seyyathāpi te satthikā. Paṭinissajjetaṃ, rājañña[M 2.0275], pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ; paṭinissajjetaṃ, rājañña, pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ. Mā te ahosi dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāyā”ti.

Then that caravan leader addressed the caravaneers: ‘Sirs, this caravan has met with ruin and disaster, and that is because of that foolish caravan leader, the guide. Therefore, sirs, whatever goods of little value are in our caravan, discard them, and whatever goods of great value are in this caravan, take them.’ ‘Yes, sir,’ replied those caravaneers to that caravan leader. Having discarded the goods of little value in their own caravan and taken up those of great value in that other caravan, they safely crossed that wilderness, and that was because of the wise caravan leader, the guide. In this very way, chieftain, you, being foolish and unskilled, will meet with ruin and disaster by improperly investigating the next world, just like that former caravan leader. And those who consider you should be listened to and trusted will also meet with ruin and disaster, just like those caravaneers. Relinquish this evil view, chieftain; relinquish this evil view. May it not be for your long-term harm and suffering.”

431. “Kiñcāpi bhavaṃ kassapo evamāha, atha kho nevāhaṃ sakkomi idaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ paṭinissajjituṃ. Rājāpi maṃ pasenadi kosalo jānāti tirorājānopi – ‘pāyāsi rājañño [V 2.0256] evaṃvādī evaṃdiṭṭhī – “itipi [P 2.0347] natthi paro loko…pe… vipāko’”ti. Sacāhaṃ, bho kassapa, idaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ paṭinissajjissāmi, bhavissanti me vattāro – ‘yāva bālo pāyāsi rājañño, abyatto duggahitagāhī’ti. Kopenapi [T 2.0385] naṃ harissāmi, makkhenapi naṃ harissāmi, palāsenapi naṃ harissāmī”ti.

431. “Although the Venerable Kassapa speaks thus, still I am unable to relinquish this evil view. King Pasenadi of Kosala knows me, and the kings of other regions also know me as: ‘Chieftain Pāyāsi is one who speaks thus, who holds this view: “There is no other world… no fruit or result.”’ If I, Venerable Kassapa, were to relinquish this evil view, there would be those who would say of me: ‘How foolish is Chieftain Pāyāsi, how unskilled, one who grasps a wrong view!’ I will maintain it out of anger; I will maintain it out of disparagement; I will maintain it out of rivalry.”

Gūthabhārikaupamā

The Simile of the Dung-Carrier

432. “Tena hi, rājañña, upamaṃ te karissāmi. Upamāya midhekacce viññū purisā bhāsitassa atthaṃ ājānanti. Bhūtapubbaṃ, rājañña, aññataro sūkaraposako puriso sakamhā gāmā aññaṃ gāmaṃ agamāsi. Tattha addasa pahūtaṃ sukkhagūthaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ. Disvānassa etadahosi – ‘ayaṃ kho pahuto sukkhagūtho chaḍḍito, mama ca sūkarabhattaṃ sūkarānaṃ bhakkho (syā.); yaṃnūnāhaṃ ito sukkhagūthaṃ hareyya’nti. So uttarāsaṅgaṃ pattharitvā pahūtaṃ sukkhagūthaṃ ākiritvā bhaṇḍikaṃ bandhitvā sīse ubbāhetvā uccāropetvā (ka. sī. ka.) agamāsi. Tassa antarāmagge mahāakālamegho pāvassi. So uggharantaṃ paggharantaṃ yāva agganakhā gūthena makkhito gūthabhāraṃ ādāya agamāsi. Tamenaṃ manussā disvā evamāhaṃsu – ‘kacci no tvaṃ, bhaṇe, ummatto, kacci viceto, kathañhi nāma uggharantaṃ paggharantaṃ yāva agganakhā gūthena makkhito gūthabhāraṃ harissasī’ti. ‘Tumhe khvettha, bhaṇe, ummattā, tumhe vicetā, tathā [P 2.0348] hi pana me sūkarabhatta’nti. Evameva kho tvaṃ, rājañña, gūthabhārikūpamo gūthahārikūpamo (sī. pī.) maññe paṭibhāsi. Paṭinissajjetaṃ, rājañña, pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ. Paṭinissajjetaṃ, rājañña, pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ. Mā te ahosi dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāyā”ti.

432. “In that case, chieftain, I will make a simile for you. For by a simile, some intelligent persons understand the meaning of what is said. Once upon a time, chieftain, a certain pig-rearer went from his own village to another village. There he saw a great deal of dry dung that had been discarded. Seeing it, this thought occurred to him: ‘Here is a great deal of dry dung that has been discarded, and it is food for my pigs. I should carry this dry dung from here.’ So he spread out his upper garment, gathered a great deal of dry dung, tied it into a bundle, placed it on his head, and went on his way. On the way, a great, unseasonal cloud rained down. Smeared with dung up to the tips of his fingernails and toenails, he went on, carrying the load of dung as it oozed and dripped. People who saw him said this: ‘Friend, are you not mad? Are you not out of your mind? How is it that you carry a load of dung, smeared with it up to the tips of your fingernails and toenails as it oozes and drips?’ ‘It is you, friends, who are mad! You are out of your minds! For this is food for my pigs.’ In this very way, chieftain, you appear to me to be like the man carrying the load of dung in the simile. Relinquish this evil view, chieftain. Relinquish this evil view. May it not be for your long-term harm and suffering.”

433. “Kiñcāpi [T 2.0386] bhavaṃ kassapo evamāha, atha kho nevāhaṃ sakkomi idaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ paṭinissajjituṃ. Rājāpi maṃ pasenadi kosalo jānāti tirorājānopi – ‘pāyāsi rājañño evaṃvādī evaṃdiṭṭhī – “itipi natthi [M 2.0276] paro loko…pe… vipāko”ti. Sacāhaṃ, bho kassapa, idaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ paṭinissajjissāmi, bhavissanti me vattāro – ‘yāva bālo pāyāsi rājañño abyatto duggahitagāhī’ti. Kopenapi naṃ harissāmi, makkhenapi naṃ harissāmi, palāsenapi naṃ harissāmī”ti.

433. “Although the Venerable Kassapa speaks thus, still I am unable to relinquish this evil view. King Pasenadi of Kosala knows me, and the kings of other regions also know me as: ‘Chieftain Pāyāsi is one who speaks thus, who holds this view: “There is no other world… there is no fruit or result of good and bad actions.”’ If I, Venerable Kassapa, were to relinquish this evil view, there would be those who would say of me: ‘How foolish is Chieftain Pāyāsi, how unskilled, one who grasps a wrong view!’ I will maintain it out of anger; I will maintain it out of disparagement; I will maintain it out of rivalry.”

Akkhadhuttakaupamā

The Simile of the Dice-Gambler

434. “Tena [V 2.0257] hi, rājañña, upamaṃ te karissāmi, upamāya midhekacce viññū purisā bhāsitassa atthaṃ ājānanti. Bhūtapubbaṃ, rājañña, dve akkhadhuttā akkhehi dibbiṃsu. Eko akkhadhutto āgatāgataṃ kaliṃ gilati. Addasā kho dutiyo akkhadhutto taṃ akkhadhuttaṃ āgatāgataṃ kaliṃ gilantaṃ, disvā taṃ akkhadhuttaṃ etadavoca – ‘tvaṃ kho, samma, ekantikena jināsi, dehi me, samma, akkhe pajohissāmī’ti. ‘Evaṃ sammā’ti kho so akkhadhutto tassa akkhadhuttassa akkhe pādāsi. Atha kho so akkhadhutto akkhe visena paribhāvetvā taṃ akkhadhuttaṃ etadavoca – ‘ehi kho, samma, akkhehi dibbissāmā’ti. ‘Evaṃ sammā’ti kho so akkhadhutto tassa akkhadhuttassa paccassosi. Dutiyampi kho te akkhadhuttā akkhehi dibbiṃsu. Dutiyampi kho so [T 2.0387] akkhadhutto āgatāgataṃ [P 2.0349] kaliṃ gilati. Addasā kho dutiyo akkhadhutto taṃ akkhadhuttaṃ dutiyampi āgatāgataṃ kaliṃ gilantaṃ, disvā taṃ akkhadhuttaṃ etadavoca –

434. “Well then, prince, I shall make a simile for you, for it is by means of a simile that some discerning people in this world understand the meaning of what is said. Once, prince, two gamblers were playing with dice. One gambler would swallow the losing die each time it came up. The second gambler saw that gambler swallowing the losing die each time it came up, and having seen him, he said to that gambler: ‘Friend, you are winning decisively. Give me the dice, friend; I shall make an offering with them.’ ‘Very well, friend,’ that gambler said, and gave the dice to the other gambler. Then that gambler, having treated the dice with poison, said to the other gambler: ‘Come, friend, let us play with the dice.’ ‘Very well, friend,’ that gambler agreed. For a second time, those gamblers played with dice. For a second time, that gambler swallowed the losing die each time it came up. The second gambler saw that gambler for a second time swallowing the losing die each time it came up, and having seen him, he said to that gambler:”

“Littaṃ paramena tejasā, gilamakkhaṃ puriso na bujjhati;

Gila re gila pāpadhuttaka gili re pāpadhuttaka (ka.), pacchā te kaṭukaṃ bhavissatīti.

“‘Coated with a most potent venom, the man swallowing the die does not realize it. Swallow, you wicked gambler, swallow! In the end, it will be bitter for you.’”

“Evameva kho tvaṃ, rājañña, akkhadhuttakūpamo maññe paṭibhāsi. Paṭinissajjetaṃ, rājañña, pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ; paṭinissajjetaṃ, rājañña, pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ. Mā te ahosi dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāyā”ti.

“Just so, prince, you seem to me like the gambler in the simile. Relinquish this evil view, prince; relinquish this evil view. May it not lead to your long-term harm and suffering.”

435. “Kiñcāpi bhavaṃ kassapo evamāha, atha kho nevāhaṃ sakkomi idaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ paṭinissajjituṃ. Rājāpi maṃ pasenadi kosalo jānāti tirorājānopi – ‘pāyāsi rājañño evaṃvādī evaṃdiṭṭhī – “itipi natthi paro loko…pe… vipāko”ti. Sacāhaṃ, bho kassapa, idaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ [M 2.0277] paṭinissajjissāmi, bhavissanti me vattāro – ‘yāva bālo pāyāsi rājañño abyatto duggahitagāhī’ti. Kopenapi naṃ harissāmi, makkhenapi naṃ harissāmi, palāsenapi naṃ harissāmī”ti.

435. “Although the Venerable Kassapa speaks thus, I am still unable to relinquish this evil view. King Pasenadi of Kosala knows me, and so do kings of other lands, that: ‘Prince Pāyāsi speaks thus and holds this view: “There is no other world… no fruit or result.”’ If I, Venerable Kassapa, were to relinquish this evil view, there would be those who would say of me: ‘How foolish is Prince Pāyāsi, how inept, how tenacious in his wrong grasp!’ I shall continue to hold it out of anger, I shall continue to hold it out of disparagement, and I shall continue to hold it out of rivalry.”

Sāṇabhārikaupamā

The Simile of the Hemp-Load Carrier

436. “Tena [V 2.0258] hi, rājañña, upamaṃ te karissāmi, upamāya midhekacce viññū [T 2.0388] purisā bhāsitassa atthaṃ ājānanti. Bhūtapubbaṃ, rājañña, aññataro janapado vuṭṭhāsi. Atha kho sahāyako sahāyakaṃ āmantesi – ‘āyāma, samma, yena so janapado tenupasaṅkamissāma, appeva nāmettha kiñci dhanaṃ adhigaccheyyāmā’ti. ‘Evaṃ sammā’ti kho sahāyako sahāyakassa paccassosi. Te yena so janapado, yena aññataraṃ gāmapaṭṭaṃ gāmapajjaṃ (syā.), gāmapattaṃ (sī.) tenupasaṅkamiṃsu[P 2.0350], tattha addasaṃsu pahūtaṃ sāṇaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ, disvā sahāyako sahāyakaṃ āmantesi – ‘idaṃ kho, samma, pahūtaṃ sāṇaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ, tena hi, samma, tvañca sāṇabhāraṃ bandha, ahañca sāṇabhāraṃ bandhissāmi, ubho sāṇabhāraṃ ādāya gamissāmā’ti. ‘Evaṃ sammā’ti kho sahāyako sahāyakassa paṭissutvā sāṇabhāraṃ bandhitvā te ubho sāṇabhāraṃ ādāya yena aññataraṃ gāmapaṭṭaṃ tenupasaṅkamiṃsu. Tattha addasaṃsu pahūtaṃ sāṇasuttaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ, disvā sahāyako sahāyakaṃ āmantesi – ‘yassa kho, samma, atthāya iccheyyāma sāṇaṃ, idaṃ pahūtaṃ sāṇasuttaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ. Tena hi, samma, tvañca sāṇabhāraṃ chaḍḍehi, ahañca sāṇabhāraṃ chaḍḍessāmi, ubho sāṇasuttabhāraṃ ādāya gamissāmā’ti. ‘Ayaṃ kho me, samma, sāṇabhāro dūrābhato ca susannaddho ca, alaṃ me tvaṃ pajānāhī’ti. Atha kho so sahāyako sāṇabhāraṃ chaḍḍetvā sāṇasuttabhāraṃ ādiyi.

436. “Well then, prince, I shall make a simile for you, for it is by means of a simile that some discerning people in this world understand the meaning of what is said. Once, prince, a certain region was abandoned. Then one friend said to another, ‘Come, friend, let us go to that region. Perhaps we may find some wealth there.’ ‘Very well, friend,’ the other replied. They went to that region and approached a certain abandoned village. There they saw a large amount of discarded hemp. Seeing it, one friend said to the other, ‘Friend, here is a large amount of discarded hemp. Therefore, friend, you tie up a load of hemp, and I shall tie up a load of hemp. We shall both take our loads of hemp and go.’ ‘Very well, friend,’ the other replied to his friend. They both tied up loads of hemp, and taking their loads, they went on to another abandoned village. There they saw a large amount of discarded hemp thread. Seeing it, one friend said to the other, ‘Friend, for the very purpose for which we would want hemp, here is a large amount of discarded hemp thread. Therefore, friend, you discard your load of hemp, and I shall discard my load of hemp. We shall both take loads of hemp thread and go.’ But the other said: ‘Friend, this load of hemp of mine was brought from afar and is well-bound. This is enough for me; you may do as you see fit.’ Then the first friend discarded his load of hemp and took up a load of hemp thread.

“Te yena aññataraṃ gāmapaṭṭaṃ tenupasaṅkamiṃsu. Tattha addasaṃsu pahūtā sāṇiyo chaḍḍitā, disvā sahāyako sahāyakaṃ āmantesi – ‘yassa kho[T 2.0389], samma, atthāya iccheyyāma sāṇaṃ vā sāṇasuttaṃ vā, imā pahūtā sāṇiyo chaḍḍitā. Tena hi, samma, tvañca sāṇabhāraṃ chaḍḍehi, ahañca sāṇasuttabhāraṃ chaḍḍessāmi, ubho sāṇibhāraṃ ādāya gamissāmā’ti[M 2.0278]. ‘Ayaṃ kho me, samma, sāṇabhāro dūrābhato ca susannaddho ca, alaṃ me, tvaṃ pajānāhī’ti. Atha kho so sahāyako sāṇasuttabhāraṃ chaḍḍetvā sāṇibhāraṃ ādiyi.

“They went on to another abandoned village. There they saw a large amount of discarded hemp cloth. Seeing it, the first friend said to the other, ‘Friend, for the very purpose for which we would want hemp or hemp thread, here is a large amount of discarded hemp cloth. Therefore, friend, you discard your load of hemp, and I shall discard my load of hemp thread. We shall both take loads of hemp cloth and go.’ But the other said: ‘Friend, this load of hemp of mine was brought from afar and is well-bound. This is enough for me; you may do as you see fit.’ Then the first friend discarded his load of hemp thread and took up a load of hemp cloth.”

“Te [P 2.0351] yena aññataraṃ gāmapaṭṭaṃ tenupasaṅkamiṃsu. Tattha addasaṃsu pahūtaṃ khomaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ, disvā…pe… pahūtaṃ khomasuttaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ, disvā… pahūtaṃ khomadussaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ, disvā… pahūtaṃ kappāsaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ, disvā… pahūtaṃ kappāsikasuttaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ, disvā… pahūtaṃ kappāsikadussaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ, disvā… pahūtaṃ ayaṃ ayasaṃ (syā.) chaḍḍitaṃ, disvā… pahūtaṃ lohaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ, disvā… pahūtaṃ tipuṃ chaḍḍitaṃ, disvā… pahūtaṃ sīsaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ, disvā… pahūtaṃ sajjhaṃ sajjhuṃ (sī. syā. pī.) chaḍḍitaṃ, disvā… pahūtaṃ suvaṇṇaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ, disvā sahāyako sahāyakaṃ āmantesi – ‘yassa kho, samma, atthāya iccheyyāma [V 2.0259] sāṇaṃ vā sāṇasuttaṃ vā sāṇiyo vā khomaṃ vā khomasuttaṃ vā khomadussaṃ vā kappāsaṃ vā kappāsikasuttaṃ vā kappāsikadussaṃ vā ayaṃ vā lohaṃ vā tipuṃ vā sīsaṃ vā sajjhaṃ vā, idaṃ pahūtaṃ suvaṇṇaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ. Tena hi, samma, tvañca sāṇabhāraṃ chaḍḍehi, ahañca sajjhabhāraṃ sajjhubhāraṃ (sī. syā. pī.) chaḍḍessāmi, ubho suvaṇṇabhāraṃ ādāya gamissāmā’ti. ‘Ayaṃ kho me, samma, sāṇabhāro dūrābhato ca susannaddho [T 2.0390] ca, alaṃ me tvaṃ pajānāhī’ti. Atha kho so sahāyako sajjhabhāraṃ chaḍḍetvā suvaṇṇabhāraṃ ādiyi.

They approached another deserted village. There they saw a large amount of discarded flax, and upon seeing it… a large amount of discarded flax thread, and upon seeing it… a large amount of discarded flax cloth, and upon seeing it… a large amount of discarded cotton, and upon seeing it… a large amount of discarded cotton thread, and upon seeing it… a large amount of discarded cotton cloth, and upon seeing it… a large amount of discarded iron, and upon seeing it… a large amount of discarded copper, and upon seeing it… a large amount of discarded tin, and upon seeing it… a large amount of discarded lead, and upon seeing it… a large amount of discarded silver, and upon seeing it… a large amount of discarded gold. Upon seeing this, one friend said to the other: ‘Friend, for whatever purpose we might want hemp, hemp thread, or hemp cloth; flax, flax thread, or flax cloth; cotton, cotton thread, or cotton cloth; iron, copper, tin, lead, or silver—here is a large amount of discarded gold. Come, friend, you discard your load of hemp, and I will discard my load of silver. Let us both take loads of gold and go.’ ‘But friend, this load of hemp of mine was brought from afar and is well-bound. It is enough for me—you may do as you see fit.’ Then that friend discarded his load of silver and took up a load of gold.

“Te yena sako gāmo tenupasaṅkamiṃsu. Tattha yo so sahāyako sāṇabhāraṃ ādāya agamāsi, tassa neva mātāpitaro abhinandiṃsu, na puttadārā abhinandiṃsu, na mittāmaccā abhinandiṃsu, na ca tatonidānaṃ sukhaṃ somanassaṃ [P 2.0352] adhigacchi. Yo pana so sahāyako suvaṇṇabhāraṃ ādāya agamāsi, tassa mātāpitaropi abhinandiṃsu, puttadārāpi abhinandiṃsu, mittāmaccāpi abhinandiṃsu, tatonidānañca sukhaṃ somanassaṃ adhigacchi. “Evameva kho tvaṃ, rājañña, sāṇabhārikūpamo maññe paṭibhāsi. Paṭinissajjetaṃ, rājañña, pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ; paṭinissajjetaṃ, rājañña, pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ. Mā te ahosi dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāyā”ti.

They approached their own village. There, the friend who had taken the load of hemp arrived, but his parents did not delight in him, his wife and children did not delight in him, and his friends and companions did not delight in him. And because of that, he did not gain any happiness or joy. But the friend who had taken the load of gold arrived, and his parents delighted in him, his wife and children delighted in him, and his friends and companions delighted in him. And because of that, he gained happiness and joy. Just so, chieftain, you appear to me like the man in the simile of the hemp-carrier. Renounce this evil view, chieftain; renounce this evil view. May it not lead to your long-term harm and suffering.

Saraṇagamanaṃ

The Going for Refuge

437. “Purimeneva [M 2.0279] ahaṃ opammena bhoto kassapassa attamano abhiraddho. Api cāhaṃ imāni vicitrāni pañhāpaṭibhānāni sotukāmo evāhaṃ bhavantaṃ kassapaṃ paccanīkaṃ kātabbaṃ amaññissaṃ. Abhikkantaṃ, bho kassapa, abhikkantaṃ, bho kassapa. Seyyathāpi, bho kassapa, nikkujjitaṃ vā ukkujjeyya, paṭicchannaṃ vā vivareyya, mūḷhassa vā maggaṃ ācikkheyya, andhakāre vā telapajjotaṃ dhāreyya ‘cakkhumanto rūpāni dakkhantī’ti evamevaṃ bhotā kassapena anekapariyāyena dhammo pakāsito. Esāhaṃ, bho kassapa, taṃ bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, dhammañca, bhikkhusaṅghañca. Upāsakaṃ maṃ bhavaṃ kassapo dhāretu [T 2.0391] ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gataṃ.

437. “Venerable Kassapa, even with the first simile, I was pleased and delighted with you. And yet, being desirous of hearing these various questions and answers, I thought to act in opposition to the venerable Kassapa. Excellent, venerable Kassapa, excellent! Just as, venerable Kassapa, one might set upright what was overturned, reveal what was hidden, show the way to one who was lost, or hold up an oil lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the venerable Kassapa through many methods. I, venerable Kassapa, go for refuge to that venerable Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha of bhikkhus. May the venerable Kassapa remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward, for as long as life lasts.”

“Icchāmi cāhaṃ, bho kassapa, mahāyaññaṃ yajituṃ, anusāsatu maṃ bhavaṃ kassapo, yaṃ mamassa dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyā”ti.

“I wish, venerable Kassapa, to perform a great sacrifice. May the venerable Kassapa instruct me in that which would be for my welfare and happiness for a long time.”

Yaññakathā

Discourse on Sacrifice

438. “Yathārūpe [V 2.0260] kho, rājañña, yaññe gāvo vā haññanti ajeḷakā vā haññanti, kukkuṭasūkarā vā haññanti, vividhā vā pāṇā saṃghātaṃ āpajjanti, paṭiggāhakā ca honti micchādiṭṭhī [P 2.0353] micchāsaṅkappā micchāvācā micchākammantā micchāājīvā micchāvāyāmā micchāsatī micchāsamādhī, evarūpo kho, rājañña, yañño na mahapphalo hoti na mahānisaṃso na mahājutiko na mahāvipphāro. Seyyathāpi, rājañña, kassako bījanaṅgalaṃ ādāya vanaṃ paviseyya. So tattha dukkhette dubbhūme avihatakhāṇukaṇṭake bījāni patiṭṭhāpeyya khaṇḍāni pūtīni vātātapahatāni asāradāni asukhasayitāni. Devo ca na kālena kālaṃ sammādhāraṃ anuppaveccheyya. Api nu tāni bījāni vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ viruḷhiṃ (moggalāne) vepullaṃ āpajjeyyuṃ, kassako vā vipulaṃ phalaṃ adhigaccheyyā”ti? “No hidaṃ na evaṃ (syā. ka.) bho kassapa”. “Evameva kho, rājañña, yathārūpe yaññe gāvo vā haññanti, ajeḷakā vā haññanti, kukkuṭasūkarā vā haññanti, vividhā vā pāṇā saṃghātaṃ āpajjanti, paṭiggāhakā ca honti micchādiṭṭhī micchāsaṅkappā micchāvācā micchākammantā micchāājīvā micchāvāyāmā micchāsatī [M 2.0280] micchāsamādhī, evarūpo kho[T 2.0392], rājañña, yañño na mahapphalo hoti na mahānisaṃso na mahājutiko na mahāvipphāro.

438. “In a sacrifice of such a nature, chieftain, where cattle are slain, goats and sheep are slain, fowl and pigs are slain, and various living beings meet their destruction; and the recipients are of wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration—such a sacrifice, chieftain, is not of great fruit, not of great benefit, not of great splendor, not of great pervasiveness. Just as, chieftain, a farmer might take seed and plow and enter a forest. There, in a poor field, on bad ground, where stumps and thorns have not been cleared, he might plant seeds that are broken, rotten, damaged by wind and sun, without substance, and not well-dried. And the rain-god would not send down a proper stream of rain from time to time. Would those seeds attain growth, sprouting, and abundance, or would the farmer obtain an abundant fruit?” “Not so, venerable Kassapa.” “Even so, chieftain, in a sacrifice where cattle are slain, goats and sheep are slain, fowl and pigs are slain, and various living beings meet their destruction; and the recipients are of wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration—such a sacrifice, chieftain, is not of great fruit, not of great benefit, not of great splendor, not of great pervasiveness.”

“Yathārūpe ca kho, rājañña, yaññe neva gāvo haññanti, na ajeḷakā haññanti, na kukkuṭasūkarā haññanti, na vividhā vā pāṇā saṃghātaṃ āpajjanti, paṭiggāhakā ca honti sammādiṭṭhī sammāsaṅkappā sammāvācā sammākammantā sammāājīvā sammāvāyāmā sammāsatī sammāsamādhī, evarūpo kho, rājañña, yañño mahapphalo hoti mahānisaṃso mahājutiko mahāvipphāro. Seyyathāpi, rājañña, kassako bījanaṅgalaṃ ādāya vanaṃ paviseyya. So tattha sukhette subhūme suvihatakhāṇukaṇṭake bījāni patiṭṭhapeyya [P 2.0354] akhaṇḍāni apūtīni avātātapahatāni sāradāni sukhasayitāni. Devo ca kālena kālaṃ sammādhāraṃ anuppaveccheyya. Api nu tāni bījāni vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ āpajjeyyuṃ, kassako vā vipulaṃ phalaṃ adhigaccheyyā”ti? “Evaṃ, bho kassapa”. “Evameva kho, rājañña, yathārūpe yaññe neva gāvo haññanti, na ajeḷakā haññanti, na kukkuṭasūkarā haññanti, na vividhā vā pāṇā saṃghātaṃ āpajjanti, paṭiggāhakā ca honti sammādiṭṭhī sammāsaṅkappā sammāvācā sammākammantā sammāājīvā sammāvāyāmā sammāsatī sammāsamādhī, evarūpo kho, rājañña, yañño mahapphalo hoti mahānisaṃso mahājutiko mahāvipphāro”ti.

“And in a sacrifice of such a nature, chieftain, where neither cattle are slain, nor goats and sheep are slain, nor fowl and pigs are slain, nor various living beings meet their destruction; and the recipients are of right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—such a sacrifice, chieftain, is of great fruit, of great benefit, of great splendor, and of great pervasiveness. Just as, chieftain, a farmer might take seed and plow and enter a forest. There, in a good field, on good ground, where stumps and thorns have been well-cleared, he might plant seeds that are unbroken, unspoiled, unharmed by wind and sun, with substance, and well-dried. And the rain-god would send down a proper stream of rain from time to time. Would those seeds attain growth, sprouting, and abundance, and would the farmer obtain an abundant fruit?” “So it is, venerable Kassapa.” “Even so, chieftain, in a sacrifice where neither cattle are slain, nor goats and sheep are slain, nor fowl and pigs are slain, nor various living beings meet their destruction; and the recipients are of right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—such a sacrifice, chieftain, is of great fruit, of great benefit, of great splendor, and of great pervasiveness.”

Uttaramāṇavavatthu

The Story of Uttara the Youth

439. Atha [V 2.0261] kho pāyāsi rājañño dānaṃ paṭṭhapesi samaṇabrāhmaṇakapaṇaddhikavaṇibbakayācakānaṃ[T 2.0393]. Tasmiṃ kho pana dāne evarūpaṃ bhojanaṃ dīyati kaṇājakaṃ bilaṅgadutiyaṃ, dhorakāni thorakāni (sī. pī.), corakāni (syā.) ca vatthāni guḷavālakāni guḷagāḷakāni (ka.). Tasmiṃ kho pana dāne uttaro nāma māṇavo vāvaṭo byāvaṭo (sī. pī.) ahosi. So dānaṃ datvā evaṃ anuddisati – “imināhaṃ dānena pāyāsiṃ rājaññameva imasmiṃ loke samāgacchiṃ, mā parasmi”nti. Assosi kho pāyāsi rājañño – “uttaro [P 2.0355] kira māṇavo dānaṃ datvā evaṃ anuddisati – ‘imināhaṃ dānena pāyāsiṃ rājaññameva imasmiṃ loke samāgacchiṃ, mā parasmi’”nti. Atha [M 2.0281] kho pāyāsi rājañño uttaraṃ māṇavaṃ āmantāpetvā etadavoca – “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ, tāta uttara, dānaṃ datvā evaṃ anuddisasi – ‘imināhaṃ dānena pāyāsiṃ rājaññameva imasmiṃ loke samāgacchiṃ, mā parasmi’”nti? “Evaṃ, bho”. “Kissa pana tvaṃ, tāta uttara, dānaṃ datvā evaṃ anuddisasi – ‘imināhaṃ dānena pāyāsiṃ rājaññameva imasmiṃ loke samāgacchiṃ, mā parasmi’nti? Nanu mayaṃ, tāta uttara, puññatthikā dānasseva phalaṃ pāṭikaṅkhino”ti? “Bhoto kho dāne evarūpaṃ bhojanaṃ dīyati kaṇājakaṃ bilaṅgadutiyaṃ, yaṃ bhavaṃ pādāpi pādāsi (ka.) na iccheyya samphusituṃ chupituṃ (pī. ka.), kuto bhuñjituṃ, dhorakāni ca vatthāni guḷavālakāni, yāni bhavaṃ pādāpi acittikataṃ (ka.) na iccheyya samphusituṃ, kuto paridahituṃ. Bhavaṃ kho panamhākaṃ piyo manāpo, kathaṃ mayaṃ manāpaṃ amanāpena saṃyojemā”ti? “Tena hi tvaṃ, tāta uttara, yādisāhaṃ bhojanaṃ bhuñjāmi, tādisaṃ bhojanaṃ [T 2.0394] paṭṭhapehi. Yādisāni cāhaṃ vatthāni paridahāmi, tādisāni ca vatthāni paṭṭhapehī”ti. “Evaṃ, bho”ti kho uttaro māṇavo pāyāsissa rājaññassa paṭissutvā yādisaṃ bhojanaṃ pāyāsi rājañño bhuñjati, tādisaṃ bhojanaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Yādisāni ca vatthāni pāyāsi rājañño paridahati, tādisāni ca vatthāni paṭṭhapesi.

439. Then the chieftain Pāyāsi established a donation for ascetics, brahmins, the poor, travelers, beggars, and the destitute. At that donation, such food was given: broken rice with sour gruel, and coarse cloths with tangled fringes. At that donation, a young man named Uttara was in charge. Having given the gift, he made this dedication: “By this gift, may I be associated with the chieftain Pāyāsi only in this world, not in the next.” The chieftain Pāyāsi heard: “It seems the young man Uttara, having given a gift, makes this dedication: ‘By this gift, may I be associated with the chieftain Pāyāsi only in this world, not in the next.’” Then the chieftain Pāyāsi had the young man Uttara summoned and said this: “Is it true, dear Uttara, that having given a gift, you make this dedication: ‘By this gift, may I be associated with the chieftain Pāyāsi only in this world, not in the next’?” “Yes, sir.” “But why, dear Uttara, having given a gift, do you make such a dedication? Do we not, dear Uttara, desire merit and expect the fruit of giving?” “Sir, at your donation, such food is given: broken rice with sour gruel—which you yourself would not even wish to touch with your foot, let alone eat—and coarse cloths with tangled fringes, which you yourself would not even wish to touch with your foot, let alone wear. You, sir, are dear and beloved to us. How could we associate one who is beloved with what is not beloved?” “In that case, dear Uttara, arrange food like that which I eat, and arrange clothes like those which I wear.” “Yes, sir,” the young man Uttara replied to the chieftain Pāyāsi. Having agreed, he arranged food like that which the chieftain Pāyāsi ate, and he arranged clothes like those which the chieftain Pāyāsi wore.

440. Atha [P 2.0356] kho pāyāsi rājañño asakkaccaṃ dānaṃ datvā asahatthā dānaṃ datvā acittīkataṃ dānaṃ datvā apaviddhaṃ dānaṃ datvā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā cātumahārājikānaṃ devānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajji suññaṃ serīsakaṃ vimānaṃ. Yo pana tassa dāne vāvaṭo ahosi uttaro nāma māṇavo. So sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ datvā sahatthā dānaṃ datvā cittīkataṃ dānaṃ datvā anapaviddhaṃ dānaṃ datvā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajji devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ sahabyataṃ.

440. Then the chieftain Pāyāsi, having given gifts disrespectfully, not with his own hand, without reverence, and as if discarded, upon the breakup of the body, after death, was reborn in the company of the gods of the Four Great Kings—in the empty Serīsaka mansion. But the young man named Uttara, who was in charge of that donation, having given gifts respectfully, with his own hand, with reverence, and not as if discarded, upon the breakup of the body, after death, was reborn in a good destination, the heavenly world, in the company of the Tāvatiṃsa gods.

Pāyāsidevaputto

Pāyāsi the Deva

441. Tena [V 2.0262] kho pana samayena āyasmā gavampati abhikkhaṇaṃ suññaṃ serīsakaṃ vimānaṃ divāvihāraṃ gacchati. Atha kho pāyāsi devaputto yenāyasmā gavampati tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ gavampatiṃ abhivādetvā [M 2.0282] ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Ekamantaṃ ṭhitaṃ kho pāyāsiṃ devaputtaṃ āyasmā gavampati etadavoca – “kosi tvaṃ, āvuso”ti? “Ahaṃ, bhante, pāyāsi rājañño”ti. “Nanu tvaṃ, āvuso, evaṃdiṭṭhiko ahosi – ‘itipi natthi paro loko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi [T 2.0395] sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’”ti? “Saccāhaṃ, bhante, evaṃdiṭṭhiko ahosiṃ – ‘itipi natthi paro loko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’ti. Api cāhaṃ ayyena [P 2.0357] kumārakassapena etasmā pāpakā diṭṭhigatā vivecito”ti. “Yo pana te, āvuso, dāne vāvaṭo ahosi uttaro nāma māṇavo, so kuhiṃ upapanno”ti? “Yo me, bhante, dāne vāvaṭo ahosi uttaro nāma māṇavo, so sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ datvā sahatthā dānaṃ datvā cittīkataṃ dānaṃ datvā anapaviddhaṃ dānaṃ datvā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapanno devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ sahabyataṃ. Ahaṃ pana, bhante, asakkaccaṃ dānaṃ datvā asahatthā dānaṃ datvā acittīkataṃ dānaṃ datvā apaviddhaṃ dānaṃ datvā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā cātumahārājikānaṃ devānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapanno suññaṃ serīsakaṃ vimānaṃ. Tena hi, bhante gavampati, manussalokaṃ gantvā evamārocehi – ‘sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ detha, sahatthā dānaṃ detha, cittīkataṃ dānaṃ detha, anapaviddhaṃ dānaṃ detha. Pāyāsi rājañño asakkaccaṃ dānaṃ datvā asahatthā dānaṃ datvā acittīkataṃ dānaṃ datvā apaviddhaṃ dānaṃ datvā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā cātumahārājikānaṃ devānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapanno suññaṃ serīsakaṃ vimānaṃ. Yo pana tassa dāne vāvaṭo ahosi uttaro nāma māṇavo, so sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ datvā sahatthā dānaṃ datvā cittīkataṃ dānaṃ datvā anapaviddhaṃ dānaṃ datvā [T 2.0396] kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapanno devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ sahabyata’”nti.

441. At that time, the Venerable Gavampati frequently went to the empty Serīsaka mansion for his daytime abiding.
